Recognition signals
A requirement directly mentions one of: TCP, UDP, socket, partial read.
Timing, memory, or power constraints make a naive blocking implementation unsafe.
The same data crosses foreground/ISR, DMA/CPU, or task boundaries and therefore needs an ownership/synchronization rule.

When a simpler peripheral/library primitive already provides the required guarantee.

Embedded C - Por Bod Training Blueprint
RAG curriculum for microcontrollers and bare-metal / RTOS firmware
track
domain
level
hardware_verified
embedded_c
Power & System Management
Intermediate
false
Platforms: STM32_HAL, RP2040_SDK, ESP_IDF, AVR_Bare_Metal, Arduino_C
Power-on reset and brown-out detection behavior, thresholds, startup sequencing, flash safety, and logging reset causes.
Learning outcomes
Explain Por Bod from the hardware and C-language perspective.
Implement bounded, testable patterns without assuming a desktop runtime.
Choose between polling, interrupt, DMA, state-machine, and RTOS designs where relevant.
Diagnose platform-specific failure modes and defend complexity, latency, memory, and power tradeoffs.
Prerequisites
C expressions, functions, arrays, pointers, fixed-width integers
binary/hex notation and bitwise operators
basic MCU execution model: reset -> initialization -> foreground loop / tasks
reading a datasheet/reference-manual register description

1. Mental model and hardware contract
Power-on reset and brown-out detection behavior, thresholds, startup sequencing, flash safety, and logging reset causes.
Key vocabulary
POR: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
BOD: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
brown-out: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
reset threshold: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
startup: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
Core invariant
The firmware must preserve the documented hardware/software contract for Por Bod: every state transition, buffer ownership change, register update, or timing assumption must be explicit and bounded.
Recognition signals
A requirement directly mentions one of: POR, BOD, brown-out, reset threshold.
Timing, memory, or power constraints make a naive blocking implementation unsafe.
The same data crosses foreground/ISR, DMA/CPU, or task boundaries and therefore needs an ownership/synchronization rule.
When not to reach for it
When a simpler peripheral/library primitive already provides the required guarantee.
When the hardware does not implement the assumed feature; select a valid peripheral or external component instead.
When correctness requires stronger synchronization or protocol guarantees than the technique provides.

2. Register, timing, and state model
Teach the learner to move from the datasheet block diagram to a small explicit state model. Avoid memorizing register names across MCU families; instead identify the repeated roles: clock/reset gate, configuration, status, data, interrupt enable, interrupt flags, and DMA request plumbing.
Hardware concern
Question to ask
Typical evidence
Failure if ignored
Clock/reset
Is the peripheral clocked and released from reset?
clock tree + enable bit
register writes appear ineffective
Configuration
Are mode/width/polarity/timing fields correct?
reference manual + datasheet
silent misbehavior or bus errors
Status/flags
Which flags are level, edge, sticky, read-to-clear, or write-one-to-clear?
status-register semantics
lost or repeated events
Data path
Who owns the buffer/register now: CPU, ISR, DMA, task, peripheral?
state diagram / ownership table
races, corruption, stale data
Timing
What is the maximum service latency and jitter?
datasheet timing + measured budget
overrun, protocol violation
Timing arithmetic
Use integer-safe formulas with explicit units. Derive timer, baud, sampling, PWM, and protocol timing from the actual peripheral clock rather than from the CPU headline frequency. Always document rounding error and acceptable tolerance.

3. Canonical C implementation pattern
// Canonical embedded-C pattern// 1) validate preconditions// 2) update only owned state/register fields// 3) keep bounded execution time// 4) return explicit status rather than hiding failureint operation(context_t *ctx) {    if (ctx == NULL) return ERR_ARG;    /* hardware/platform-specific work */    return OK;}
Implementation rules
Use <stdint.h> widths for registers, wire formats, counters, and masks.
Validate pointers, lengths, enum-like parameters, and range assumptions before touching hardware.
Prefer explicit status codes and caller-owned buffers over hidden allocation.
Keep ISR paths bounded; capture/acknowledge, signal, and defer.
Separate mechanism (register/HAL transport) from policy (retries, parsing, scheduling, application behavior).
Make buffer ownership transitions visible in names, state, or API contracts.
Test seam
Wrap hardware access behind the thinnest interface needed for host-side unit tests. Pure functions such as parsers, CRCs, unit conversion, state transitions, schedule decisions, and register-value construction should be testable without hardware.

4. Platform implementation matrix
platform
training emphasis
STM32_HAL
STM32 Cortex-M using STM32Cube HAL/LL and CMSIS concepts. Teach HAL APIs first, then show LL/register mapping and CMSIS/NVIC concepts where useful.
RP2040_SDK
RP2040 Cortex-M0+ using Pico SDK, PIO, DMA, and multicore-aware patterns. Emphasize Pico SDK APIs, dual-core implications, DMA, and PIO when timing-sensitive I/O applies.
ESP_IDF
ESP32-class targets using ESP-IDF; classic ESP32 is Xtensa, family variants may differ. Use driver/event/task-oriented ESP-IDF concepts; networking topics should account for FreeRTOS/lwIP integration.
AVR_Bare_Metal
ATmega/AVR register-level C with avr-libc style headers. Favor datasheet/register-driven examples, interrupt vectors, small RAM budgets, and 8-bit atomicity concerns.
Arduino_C
Arduino-style embedded development; sketches are compiled as C++ but this track emphasizes C-like embedded patterns. Use Arduino APIs as an approachable layer, while explaining the underlying timer/register/interrupt cost. Note that Arduino sketches are compiled as C++.
hardware_verified: false. These records teach portable reasoning and representative API/register patterns. Board-specific register addresses, alternate-function mappings, pin capabilities, DMA routing, peripheral instances, clock constraints, and electrical limits must be verified against the exact MCU/board reference manual before deployment.

5. Concurrency, latency, and ownership
Questions the learner must answer
Can this code run from foreground, ISR, DMA completion, RTOS task, or multiple contexts?
Which state is shared? Which access can be interrupted? Which width is naturally atomic on the target?
What is the worst-case execution time, service latency, and buffer fill rate?
If an interrupt arrives twice before foreground work completes, is the second event counted, coalesced, queued, or lost?
If DMA is active, when may the CPU safely modify or reuse the buffer?
Safe design pattern
Use a single-owner or explicit handoff model wherever possible. ISRs should write bounded event records or indices; foreground/tasks consume them. When multiple writers are unavoidable, use the smallest correct critical section or a documented atomic primitive rather than relying on volatile.
Latency budget exercise
Given an input event rate, buffer capacity, longest critical section, and foreground service period, compute whether overflow is possible. Require the learner to identify the actual bottleneck rather than merely increasing the buffer.

6. Reliability, failure modes, and common gotchas
writing flash during unstable power: create a minimal failing example, explain the hardware/software mechanism, and show a corrected design.
ignoring reset reason: create a minimal failing example, explain the hardware/software mechanism, and show a corrected design.
Forgetting volatile on a register or ISR-shared flag can let the optimizer reuse a stale value; adding volatile alone does not make compound operations atomic.
Pointer arithmetic scales by pointed-to type, not bytes; use uint8_t* when byte stepping is intended and preserve alignment requirements.
Never trust external lengths, counts, or frame fields without bounds checking before buffer access.
Avoid malloc/free in timing-critical or ISR paths unless the allocation strategy is explicitly designed and bounded.
Do not clear peripheral status flags using a guessed read-modify-write sequence; follow the documented clear semantics.
Test wraparound of tick counters, ring indices, sequence numbers, and timer capture values.
Debugging ladder
Confirm power/clock/reset and pin mux first.
Observe raw status/flags before blaming application logic.
Instrument timing with GPIO/SWO/trace or a logic analyzer when protocol/timing matters.
Reduce to a minimal register/HAL transaction.
Add deterministic fault counters and reset-cause logging.

7. Exercises and graded labs
format
prompt
grading focus
Predict
Given a configuration/register snippet, predict the resulting mode and identify unrelated bits that change.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Trace
Trace state, flags, indices, ownership, and timestamps across six events.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Spot the bug
Find at least three defects in a deliberately flawed Por Bod implementation.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Implement
Write a bounded implementation with explicit error returns and no hidden allocation.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Constraint flip
Rework a blocking version into interrupt-, DMA-, or state-machine-driven form while preserving behavior.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Platform transfer
Explain how the same design maps differently to STM32_HAL, RP2040_SDK, ESP_IDF, AVR_Bare_Metal, and Arduino_C.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Interview
Defend why this mechanism is appropriate and name the first three failure modes you would measure on hardware.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Host-side test expectations
boundary lengths: 0, 1, maximum, maximum+1
wraparound and repeated-event tests
known-answer vectors where applicable (CRC/checksum/protocol)
fault injection: timeout, NACK/error flag, queue full, malformed frame, stale DMA completion
property checks against a simpler oracle for parsers/encoders/math

8. Reference guide and interview checklist
One-minute reference
Mental model: Power-on reset and brown-out detection behavior, thresholds, startup sequencing, flash safety, and logging reset causes.
Key terms: POR, BOD, brown-out, reset threshold, startup
Primary hazards: writing flash during unstable power, ignoring reset reason
Default embedded rule: bounded work, explicit ownership, explicit timeout, explicit failure status.
Before hardware: verify exact MCU peripheral instance, pin mux, clock source, interrupt/DMA routing, electrical levels, and errata.
Interview prompts
Explain Por Bod without naming a vendor API.
What assumptions would make your implementation fail on an 8-bit AVR but appear fine on a 32-bit Cortex-M?
Which variables need volatile, which need atomicity, and which need neither?
How would you convert the design from polling to interrupt or DMA?
How would you prove that the implementation cannot overrun its buffer under the stated event rate?
What would you inspect first with a logic analyzer or debugger?
Suggested prerequisite links
bitwise register operations
fixed-width integers
MMIO register model
non-blocking state machines
volatile/shared state
pointers and buffer bounds

Curriculum levels
Beginner: mental model, terminology, safe C syntax, polling baseline.
Intermediate: interrupts, timeouts, state machines, reusable drivers, buffer design.
Advanced: DMA/RTOS/concurrency, timing proof, fault handling, power/performance optimization, portability.
RAG retrieval guidance
Filter by track + platform + level + record_type before semantic retrieval. Retrieve gotcha and reference records alongside concepts when the learner is debugging. Retrieve curriculum-outline records to choose prerequisites and the next concept rather than answering with a disconnected code snippet.
Dataset safety note: hardware_verified=false for all generated records. Do not treat register addresses, pin mappings, electrical limits, or peripheral availability as verified for a specific board without consulting that exact device documentation.

Which state is shared? Which access can be interrupted? Which width is naturally atomic on the target?
What is the worst-case execution time, service latency, and buffer fill rate?
If an interrupt arrives twice before foreground work completes, is the second event counted, coalesced, queued, or lost?
If DMA is active, when may the CPU safely modify or reuse the buffer?

Use a single-owner or explicit handoff model wherever possible. ISRs should write bounded event records or indices; foreground/tasks consume them. When multiple writers are unavoidable, use the smallest correct critical section or a documented atomic primitive rather than relying on volatile.
Latency budget exercise
Given an input event rate, buffer capacity, longest critical section, and foreground service period, compute whether overflow is possible. Require the learner to identify the actual bottleneck rather than merely increasing the buffer.

6. Reliability, failure modes, and common gotchas
silent capacity overflow: create a minimal failing example, explain the hardware/software mechanism, and show a corrected design.
global initialization order assumptions: create a minimal failing example, explain the hardware/software mechanism, and show a corrected design.
Forgetting volatile on a register or ISR-shared flag can let the optimizer reuse a stale value; adding volatile alone does not make compound operations atomic.
Pointer arithmetic scales by pointed-to type, not bytes; use uint8_t* when byte stepping is intended and preserve alignment requirements.
Never trust external lengths, counts, or frame fields without bounds checking before buffer access.
Avoid malloc/free in timing-critical or ISR paths unless the allocation strategy is explicitly designed and bounded.
Do not clear peripheral status flags using a guessed read-modify-write sequence; follow the documented clear semantics.
Test wraparound of tick counters, ring indices, sequence numbers, and timer capture values.

Observe raw status/flags before blaming application logic.

1. Mental model and hardware contract
Hard fault concepts, reset causes, fault capture, stack-frame inspection concepts, and reboot-safe diagnostic breadcrumbs.
Key vocabulary

fault status: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.

postmortem: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
Core invariant
The firmware must preserve the documented hardware/software contract for Fault Handlers Reset Reason: every state transition, buffer ownership change, register update, or timing assumption must be explicit and bounded.
Recognition signals
A requirement directly mentions one of: HardFault, reset cause, fault status, stack frame.
Timing, memory, or power constraints make a naive blocking implementation unsafe.
The same data crosses foreground/ISR, DMA/CPU, or task boundaries and therefore needs an ownership/synchronization rule.

When a simpler peripheral/library primitive already provides the required guarantee.

Implementation rules

Validate pointers, lengths, enum-like parameters, and range assumptions before touching hardware.
Prefer explicit status codes and caller-owned buffers over hidden allocation.
Keep ISR paths bounded; capture/acknowledge, signal, and defer.

Test seam
Wrap hardware access behind the thinnest interface needed for host-side unit tests. Pure functions such as parsers, CRCs, unit conversion, state transitions, schedule decisions, and register-value construction should be testable without hardware.

platform
training emphasis

STM32 Cortex-M using STM32Cube HAL/LL and CMSIS concepts. Teach HAL APIs first, then show LL/register mapping and CMSIS/NVIC concepts where useful.

RP2040 Cortex-M0+ using Pico SDK, PIO, DMA, and multicore-aware patterns. Emphasize Pico SDK APIs, dual-core implications, DMA, and PIO when timing-sensitive I/O applies.
ESP_IDF
ESP32-class targets using ESP-IDF; classic ESP32 is Xtensa, family variants may differ. Use driver/event/task-oriented ESP-IDF concepts; networking topics should account for FreeRTOS/lwIP integration.
AVR_Bare_Metal
ATmega/AVR register-level C with avr-libc style headers. Favor datasheet/register-driven examples, interrupt vectors, small RAM budgets, and 8-bit atomicity concerns.
Arduino_C
Arduino-style embedded development; sketches are compiled as C++ but this track emphasizes C-like embedded patterns. Use Arduino APIs as an approachable layer, while explaining the underlying timer/register/interrupt cost. Note that Arduino sketches are compiled as C++.

Embedded C - Dac Training Blueprint
RAG curriculum for microcontrollers and bare-metal / RTOS firmware
track
domain
level
hardware_verified
embedded_c
Peripherals & Hardware I/O
Intermediate
false
Platforms: STM32_HAL, RP2040_SDK, ESP_IDF, AVR_Bare_Metal, Arduino_C
DAC output generation where supported, settling time, output buffering, waveform playback via timer/DMA, and PWM fallback where hardware DAC is absent.
Learning outcomes
Explain Dac from the hardware and C-language perspective.
Implement bounded, testable patterns without assuming a desktop runtime.
Choose between polling, interrupt, DMA, state-machine, and RTOS designs where relevant.
Diagnose platform-specific failure modes and defend complexity, latency, memory, and power tradeoffs.
Prerequisites
C expressions, functions, arrays, pointers, fixed-width integers
binary/hex notation and bitwise operators
basic MCU execution model: reset -> initialization -> foreground loop / tasks
reading a datasheet/reference-manual register description

1. Mental model and hardware contract
DAC output generation where supported, settling time, output buffering, waveform playback via timer/DMA, and PWM fallback where hardware DAC is absent.
Key vocabulary
DAC: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
settling: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
buffer: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
waveform: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
DMA: learner must define it precisely and connect it to an observable hardware/software effect.
Core invariant
The firmware must preserve the documented hardware/software contract for Dac: every state transition, buffer ownership change, register update, or timing assumption must be explicit and bounded.
Recognition signals
A requirement directly mentions one of: DAC, settling, buffer, waveform.
Timing, memory, or power constraints make a naive blocking implementation unsafe.
The same data crosses foreground/ISR, DMA/CPU, or task boundaries and therefore needs an ownership/synchronization rule.
When not to reach for it
When a simpler peripheral/library primitive already provides the required guarantee.
When the hardware does not implement the assumed feature; select a valid peripheral or external component instead.
When correctness requires stronger synchronization or protocol guarantees than the technique provides.

2. Register, timing, and state model
Teach the learner to move from the datasheet block diagram to a small explicit state model. Avoid memorizing register names across MCU families; instead identify the repeated roles: clock/reset gate, configuration, status, data, interrupt enable, interrupt flags, and DMA request plumbing.
Hardware concern
Question to ask
Typical evidence
Failure if ignored
Clock/reset
Is the peripheral clocked and released from reset?
clock tree + enable bit
register writes appear ineffective
Configuration
Are mode/width/polarity/timing fields correct?
reference manual + datasheet
silent misbehavior or bus errors
Status/flags
Which flags are level, edge, sticky, read-to-clear, or write-one-to-clear?
status-register semantics
lost or repeated events
Data path
Who owns the buffer/register now: CPU, ISR, DMA, task, peripheral?
state diagram / ownership table
races, corruption, stale data
Timing
What is the maximum service latency and jitter?
datasheet timing + measured budget
overrun, protocol violation
Timing arithmetic
Use integer-safe formulas with explicit units. Derive timer, baud, sampling, PWM, and protocol timing from the actual peripheral clock rather than from the CPU headline frequency. Always document rounding error and acceptable tolerance.

3. Canonical C implementation pattern
// Canonical embedded-C pattern// 1) validate preconditions// 2) update only owned state/register fields// 3) keep bounded execution time// 4) return explicit status rather than hiding failureint operation(context_t *ctx) {    if (ctx == NULL) return ERR_ARG;    /* hardware/platform-specific work */    return OK;}
Implementation rules
Use <stdint.h> widths for registers, wire formats, counters, and masks.
Validate pointers, lengths, enum-like parameters, and range assumptions before touching hardware.
Prefer explicit status codes and caller-owned buffers over hidden allocation.
Keep ISR paths bounded; capture/acknowledge, signal, and defer.
Separate mechanism (register/HAL transport) from policy (retries, parsing, scheduling, application behavior).
Make buffer ownership transitions visible in names, state, or API contracts.
Test seam
Wrap hardware access behind the thinnest interface needed for host-side unit tests. Pure functions such as parsers, CRCs, unit conversion, state transitions, schedule decisions, and register-value construction should be testable without hardware.

4. Platform implementation matrix
platform
training emphasis
STM32_HAL
STM32 Cortex-M using STM32Cube HAL/LL and CMSIS concepts. Teach HAL APIs first, then show LL/register mapping and CMSIS/NVIC concepts where useful.
RP2040_SDK
RP2040 Cortex-M0+ using Pico SDK, PIO, DMA, and multicore-aware patterns. Emphasize Pico SDK APIs, dual-core implications, DMA, and PIO when timing-sensitive I/O applies. Many common targets in this category do not provide a true on-chip DAC; teach PWM/external-DAC alternatives explicitly.
ESP_IDF
ESP32-class targets using ESP-IDF; classic ESP32 is Xtensa, family variants may differ. Use driver/event/task-oriented ESP-IDF concepts; networking topics should account for FreeRTOS/lwIP integration.
AVR_Bare_Metal
ATmega/AVR register-level C with avr-libc style headers. Favor datasheet/register-driven examples, interrupt vectors, small RAM budgets, and 8-bit atomicity concerns. Many common targets in this category do not provide a true on-chip DAC; teach PWM/external-DAC alternatives explicitly.
Arduino_C
Arduino-style embedded development; sketches are compiled as C++ but this track emphasizes C-like embedded patterns. Use Arduino APIs as an approachable layer, while explaining the underlying timer/register/interrupt cost. Note that Arduino sketches are compiled as C++. Many common targets in this category do not provide a true on-chip DAC; teach PWM/external-DAC alternatives explicitly.
hardware_verified: false. These records teach portable reasoning and representative API/register patterns. Board-specific register addresses, alternate-function mappings, pin capabilities, DMA routing, peripheral instances, clock constraints, and electrical limits must be verified against the exact MCU/board reference manual before deployment.

5. Concurrency, latency, and ownership
Questions the learner must answer
Can this code run from foreground, ISR, DMA completion, RTOS task, or multiple contexts?
Which state is shared? Which access can be interrupted? Which width is naturally atomic on the target?
What is the worst-case execution time, service latency, and buffer fill rate?
If an interrupt arrives twice before foreground work completes, is the second event counted, coalesced, queued, or lost?
If DMA is active, when may the CPU safely modify or reuse the buffer?
Safe design pattern
Use a single-owner or explicit handoff model wherever possible. ISRs should write bounded event records or indices; foreground/tasks consume them. When multiple writers are unavoidable, use the smallest correct critical section or a documented atomic primitive rather than relying on volatile.
Latency budget exercise
Given an input event rate, buffer capacity, longest critical section, and foreground service period, compute whether overflow is possible. Require the learner to identify the actual bottleneck rather than merely increasing the buffer.

6. Reliability, failure modes, and common gotchas
assuming DAC exists: create a minimal failing example, explain the hardware/software mechanism, and show a corrected design.
load impedance: create a minimal failing example, explain the hardware/software mechanism, and show a corrected design.
update jitter: create a minimal failing example, explain the hardware/software mechanism, and show a corrected design.
Forgetting volatile on a register or ISR-shared flag can let the optimizer reuse a stale value; adding volatile alone does not make compound operations atomic.
Pointer arithmetic scales by pointed-to type, not bytes; use uint8_t* when byte stepping is intended and preserve alignment requirements.
Never trust external lengths, counts, or frame fields without bounds checking before buffer access.
Avoid malloc/free in timing-critical or ISR paths unless the allocation strategy is explicitly designed and bounded.
Do not clear peripheral status flags using a guessed read-modify-write sequence; follow the documented clear semantics.
Test wraparound of tick counters, ring indices, sequence numbers, and timer capture values.
Debugging ladder
Confirm power/clock/reset and pin mux first.
Observe raw status/flags before blaming application logic.
Instrument timing with GPIO/SWO/trace or a logic analyzer when protocol/timing matters.
Reduce to a minimal register/HAL transaction.
Add deterministic fault counters and reset-cause logging.

7. Exercises and graded labs
format
prompt
grading focus
Predict
Given a configuration/register snippet, predict the resulting mode and identify unrelated bits that change.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Trace
Trace state, flags, indices, ownership, and timestamps across six events.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Spot the bug
Find at least three defects in a deliberately flawed Dac implementation.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Implement
Write a bounded implementation with explicit error returns and no hidden allocation.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Constraint flip
Rework a blocking version into interrupt-, DMA-, or state-machine-driven form while preserving behavior.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Platform transfer
Explain how the same design maps differently to STM32_HAL, RP2040_SDK, ESP_IDF, AVR_Bare_Metal, and Arduino_C.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Interview
Defend why this mechanism is appropriate and name the first three failure modes you would measure on hardware.
correctness + boundedness + explanation of hardware effect
Host-side test expectations
boundary lengths: 0, 1, maximum, maximum+1
wraparound and repeated-event tests
known-answer vectors where applicable (CRC/checksum/protocol)
fault injection: timeout, NACK/error flag, queue full, malformed frame, stale DMA completion
property checks against a simpler oracle for parsers/encoders/math

8. Reference guide and interview checklist
One-minute reference
Mental model: DAC output generation where supported, settling time, output buffering, waveform playback via timer/DMA, and PWM fallback where hardware DAC is absent.
Key terms: DAC, settling, buffer, waveform, DMA
Primary hazards: assuming DAC exists, load impedance, update jitter
Default embedded rule: bounded work, explicit ownership, explicit timeout, explicit failure status.
Before hardware: verify exact MCU peripheral instance, pin mux, clock source, interrupt/DMA routing, electrical levels, and errata.
Interview prompts
Explain Dac without naming a vendor API.
What assumptions would make your implementation fail on an 8-bit AVR but appear fine on a 32-bit Cortex-M?
Which variables need volatile, which need atomicity, and which need neither?
How would you convert the design from polling to interrupt or DMA?
How would you prove that the implementation cannot overrun its buffer under the stated event rate?
What would you inspect first with a logic analyzer or debugger?
Suggested prerequisite links
bitwise register operations
fixed-width integers
MMIO register model
non-blocking state machines
volatile/shared state
pointers and buffer bounds

9. RAG record schema and curriculum placement

Curriculum levels
Beginner: mental model, terminology, safe C syntax, polling baseline.
Intermediate: interrupts, timeouts, state machines, reusable drivers, buffer design.
Advanced: DMA/RTOS/concurrency, timing proof, fault handling, power/performance optimization, portability.
RAG retrieval guidance
Filter by track + platform + level + record_type before semantic retrieval. Retrieve gotcha and reference records alongside concepts when the learner is debugging. Retrieve curriculum-outline records to choose prerequisites and the next concept rather than answering with a disconnected code snippet.
Dataset safety note: hardware_verified=false for all generated records. Do not treat register addresses, pin mappings, electrical limits, or peripheral availability as verified for a specific board without consulting that exact device documentation.

2. Overview and mental model: gpiozero on the Raspberry Pi
gpiozero is the beginner-friendly GPIO library for the Raspberry Pi. It offers devices such as LED, Button and
PWMLED and uses BCM pin numbers.
Typical mistakes are reading the raw pin instead of the device state, calling a callback while assigning it, passing
percentages to PWM and creating two devices on one pin.
Examples use the real gpiozero library with its mock pin factory and are driven with mock pins; they have not run on a
physical Raspberry Pi.
Toolbox
 from gpiozero import LED, Button
led = LED(17)
button = Button(6)
button.when_pressed = led.toggle
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

Python on hardware, gpiozero on the Raspberry Pi: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
Use LED(pin, active_high=False) for a device that lights when the pin is low
py-emb-gz-led   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-gz-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-gz-button. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. LED(17).on() always sets the pin high, whatever the wiring.
gpiozero numbers pins with the BCM (GPIO) numbering and not the board header position. LED.on() makes the
device active: with active_high=True that is a high level, with active_high=False it is a low level. Use it for LEDs wired
to 3.3 V, and read is_lit rather than the raw pin state.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from gpiozero import LED
led_bad = LED(17)
led_bad.on()
raw_bad = led_bad.pin.state
Correct:
 from gpiozero import LED
led = LED(18, active_high=False)
led.on()
lit = led.is_lit
raw = led.pin.state
Button has an internal pull-up: is_pressed is True when the pin is pulled low
py-emb-gz-button   lens: access   level: L2   family: py-emb-gz-access
Prerequisites: py-emb-gz-led. Follow-up: py-emb-gz-events. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A button reads True when the pin is high.
By default Button(pin) enables the pull-up resistor and expects the other contact to go to ground. gpiozero translates
that: is_pressed is True when the pin is low, and value is 1 when pressed. Pass pull_up=False for a button that
connects the pin to 3.3 V. Do not use GPIO2 or GPIO3 for this, since they have a fixed external pull-up.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from gpiozero import Button
btn_bad = Button(5)
def pressed_bad():
    return btn_bad.pin.state
Correct:
 from gpiozero import Button
btn = Button(6)
def pressed():
    return btn.is_pressed

Python on hardware, gpiozero on the Raspberry Pi: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Assign when_pressed and when_released callbacks instead of polling the pin
py-emb-gz-events   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: py-emb-gz-patterns
Prerequisites: py-emb-gz-button. Follow-up: py-emb-gz-pwm. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Call the function when you assign it: btn.when_pressed = f().
when_pressed takes a function object. Writing f() calls it once and assigns its return value (None), so nothing
happens on later presses. Assign the name without parentheses. The callbacks run on a background thread, so keep
them short and be careful with shared data.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from gpiozero import Button
log_bad = []
def on_press_bad():
    log_bad.append("p")
b_bad = Button(7)
b_bad.when_pressed = on_press_bad()
Correct:
 from gpiozero import Button
log = []
def on_press():
    log.append("p")
def on_release():
    log.append("r")
b_ok = Button(8)
b_ok.when_pressed = on_press
b_ok.when_released = on_release

4.4 Algorithm chunks
PWMLED.value is a fraction from 0.0 to 1.0, not a percentage or a byte
py-emb-gz-pwm   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-gz-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-gz-events. Follow-up: py-emb-gz-close. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. PWMLED.value = 50 sets the brightness to fifty percent.
The value of a PWMLED must be between 0 and 1, otherwise gpiozero raises OutputDeviceBadValue. Convert a
percentage with pct / 100 and a byte with level / 255. Keeping the fraction in one place avoids scaling mistakes in the
rest of the program.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from gpiozero import PWMLED
def set_bad(led, pct):
    led.value = pct
Correct:
 from gpiozero import PWMLED
def set_pct(led, pct):
    led.value = max(0, min(100, pct)) / 100

Python on hardware, gpiozero on the Raspberry Pi: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
Close a device before creating another object on the same pin
py-emb-gz-close   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-gz-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-gz-pwm. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Two objects can share one GPIO pin.
Each pin belongs to one device at a time. Creating a second LED(17) while the first still exists raises GPIOPinInUse.
Call close() on the first (or use it in a with block) to release the pin, then create the new device.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from gpiozero import LED, GPIOPinInUse
def reuse_bad(pin):
    a = LED(pin)
    b = LED(pin)
    return b
Correct:
 from gpiozero import LED, GPIOPinInUse
def reuse(pin):
    a = LED(pin)
    a.close()
    return LED(pin)

py-emb-gz-button-ex2   format: explain-why   level: L2   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Why does gpiozero report a Button as pressed when its pin is low?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Button enables the internal pull-up resistor by default, which holds the
pin high while the button is open. A pressed button connects the pin to ground and pulls it low. gpiozero hides this
active-low wiring: is_pressed is True and value is 1 while the pin is low. For a button wired to 3.3 V use pull_up=False.

2. Overview and mental model: Ring buffers and queues
A ring buffer is a fixed array used as a circle. It moves data between an interrupt handler and the main loop, or keeps
the last N readings, without ever allocating memory.
The classic faults are an index that does not wrap, full and empty looking the same, silent loss on overflow, wrong
reads across the wrap point and consuming data just to look at it.
The code is plain Python and behaves the same on a board; true interrupt safety depends on how the port schedules
handlers and is not shown here.
Toolbox
 class Ring:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.buf = bytearray(n)
        self.size = n
        self.head = 0
        self.tail = 0
        self.count = 0

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the

A ring buffer advances its write index with modulo so it wraps to the start
py-emb-rb-wrap   lens: access   level: L1   family: py-emb-rb-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-rb-state. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Increment the write index and the buffer keeps working.
A ring buffer uses a fixed array as a circle. After the last slot the next write goes to slot 0, so the index must wrap: i =
(i + 1) % size. Without the modulo the index passes the end and raises IndexError. The buffer never allocates after
creation, which suits interrupt handlers.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class RingBad:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.buf = bytearray(n)
        self.head = 0
    def push(self, b):
        self.buf[self.head] = b
        self.head += 1
Correct:
 class Ring:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.buf = bytearray(n)
        self.size = n
        self.head = 0
        self.tail = 0
        self.count = 0
    def push(self, b):
        self.buf[self.head] = b
        self.head = (self.head + 1) % self.size
        self.count = min(self.count + 1, self.size)
Keep a count, because head equal to tail means both full and empty
py-emb-rb-state   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: py-emb-rb-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-rb-wrap. Follow-up: py-emb-rb-policy. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. head == tail tells you the buffer is empty.
When the write index catches up with the read index, the buffer can be completely empty or completely full, and the
two indexes look the same. Keep a separate count (or leave one slot unused) to tell them apart, and test the count in
push and pop.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def empty_bad(head, tail):
    return head == tail

Page 4
Correct:
 class Fifo:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.buf = bytearray(n)
        self.size = n
        self.head = self.tail = self.count = 0
    def empty(self):
        return self.count == 0
    def full(self):
        return self.count == self.size
Read several bytes across the wrap point in order
py-emb-rb-bulk   lens: iteration   level: L3   family: py-emb-rb-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-rb-policy. Follow-up: py-emb-rb-peek. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Slicing the buffer from tail to head gives the stored bytes.
When the data wraps, it is stored in two pieces: from the tail to the end of the array and from the start of the array to
the head. buf[tail:head] is then empty or wrong. Read byte by byte with the modulo index, or join the two slices in the
right order.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def read_bad(buf, tail, head):
    return bytes(buf[tail:head])
Correct:
 def read_all(buf, tail, count):
    n = len(buf)
    return bytes(buf[(tail + i) % n] for i in range(count))

Decide what happens when the buffer is full: reject the new byte or overwrite the oldest
py-emb-rb-policy   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: py-emb-rb-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: py-emb-rb-state. Follow-up: py-emb-rb-bulk. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A full buffer silently keeps the newest data.
A buffer has to lose something when it is full. A receive buffer for a command protocol usually rejects the new byte, so
earlier bytes stay in order. A sensor history usually overwrites the oldest value, so it holds the latest readings. Make
the policy explicit and count the lost items.

 class FifoBad:
    def __init__(self, n):

        self.n = n
    def push(self, x):
        self.items.append(x)

Correct:
 class Queue:
    def __init__(self, n, overwrite=False):
        self.items = []
        self.n = n
        self.overwrite = overwrite
        self.dropped = 0
    def push(self, x):
        if len(self.items) >= self.n:
            self.dropped += 1
            if not self.overwrite:
                return False
            self.items.pop(0)
        self.items.append(x)
        return True
Peek at the next byte without consuming it to parse a frame header
py-emb-rb-peek   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L3   family: py-emb-rb-fit-and-alternatives
Prerequisites: py-emb-rb-bulk. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. The only way to look at the next byte is to remove it.
A parser often needs to see the start byte or a length before deciding to take the frame. peek returns the byte at the
tail without moving it. If the frame is incomplete, leave the bytes in place and try again when more data arrives.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def take_bad(items):
    return items.pop(0)
Correct:
 def peek(items, offset=0):
    return items[offset] if offset < len(items) else None
def take(items, n):
    out = items[:n]
    del items[:n]
    return out

Overview and mental model: Ring buffers and queues A ring buffer is a fixed array used as a circle. It moves data between an interrupt handler and the main loop, or keeps the last N readings, without ever allocating memory. The classic faults are an index that does not wrap, full and empty looking the same, silent loss on overflow, wrong reads across the wrap point and consuming data just to look at it. The code is plain Python and behaves the same on a board; true interrupt safety depends on how the port schedules handlers and is not shown here. Complexity: O(1). Common misconception. Increment the write index and the buffer keeps working. A ring buffer uses a fixed array as a circle. After the last slot the next write goes to slot 0, so the index must wrap: i = (i + 1) % size. Without the modulo the index passes the end and raises IndexError. The buffer never allocates after creation, which suits interrupt handlers. Incorrect (runs, but fails as described): class RingBad: def __init__(self, n): self.buf = bytearray(n) self.head = 0 def push(self, b): self.buf[self.head] = b self.head += 1 Correct: class Ring: def __init__(self, n): self.buf = bytearray(n) self.size = n self.head = 0 self.tail = 0 self.count = 0 def push(self, b): self.buf[self.head] = b self.head = (self.head + 1) % self.size self.count = min(self.count + 1, self.size) Keep a count, because head equal to tail means both full and empty py-emb-rb-state lens: edge-cases level: L2 family: py-emb-rb-edge-cases Prerequisites: py-emb-rb-wrap. Follow-up: py-emb-rb-policy. Complexity: O(1). Common misconception. head == tail tells you the buffer is empty. When the write index catches up with the read index, the buffer can be completely empty or completely full, and the two indexes look the same. Keep a separate count (or leave one slot unused) to tell them apart, and test the count in push and pop. 2. Overview and mental model: Memory and garbage collection
A microcontroller may have only tens or hundreds of kilobytes of RAM. MicroPython allocates objects on a small
heap and reclaims them with a garbage collector, so how you allocate matters.
Safe habits are preallocated buffers, memoryview slices, const for fixed numbers, collecting garbage at a chosen
time, and never letting a list grow without limit.
Examples run on the MicroPython unix port, whose heap is much larger than on a board; the free-memory numbers
are not representative, so only relative effects are checked.
Toolbox
 import gc
from micropython import const
_REG = const(0x20)
buf = bytearray(16)
mv = memoryview(buf)[4:8]
gc.collect()

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
Allocate a buffer once and fill it with readfrom_into instead of allocating on every read
py-emb-mem-prealloc   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-mem-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-mem-view. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. readfrom(addr, n) in a loop costs nothing extra.
Every readfrom call creates a new bytes object. In a sampling loop that makes many small allocations, fragments the
heap and gives the garbage collector work. Create one bytearray at start up and use readfrom_into(addr, buf) so the
same memory is reused for every sample.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def sample_bad(i2c, addr):
    return i2c.readfrom(addr, 2)
Correct:
 buf = bytearray(2)
def sample(i2c, addr):
    i2c.readfrom_into(addr, buf)
    return buf
Declare register addresses with micropython.const so they cost no run-time lookups
py-emb-mem-const   lens: creation   level: L2   family: py-emb-mem-creation
Prerequisites: py-emb-mem-view. Follow-up: py-emb-mem-gc. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A module-level name for a register address is as cheap as a constant.
A normal global is looked up in a dictionary every time it is used. A name assigned with micropython.const() and
starting with an underscore, or used within the same file, is replaced by the number when the file is compiled. Use it
for register addresses, bit masks and pin numbers that never change.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 REG_CTRL_BAD = 0x20
def ctrl_bad(value):
    return (REG_CTRL_BAD, value)
Correct:
 from micropython import const
_REG_CTRL = const(0x20)
_ENABLE = const(1 << 3)
def ctrl(value):
    return (_REG_CTRL, value | _ENABLE)

Python on hardware, Memory and garbage collection: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Collect garbage at a moment you choose, before a large allocation or a timing-critical section
py-emb-mem-gc   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-mem-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-mem-const. Follow-up: py-emb-mem-bound. Complexity: O(heap).
 Common misconception. The garbage collector runs only when you call it.
MicroPython runs the collector automatically when an allocation fails, which can happen at a bad moment and takes
a few milliseconds. Call gc.collect() at a quiet point, such as after start up or before a time-critical loop, and watch
gc.mem_free() to see the effect. Memory that is still referenced is not freed.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import gc
def free_after_drop_bad():
    data = [bytearray(100) for _ in range(20)]
    return gc.mem_free()
Correct:
 import gc
def free_after_collect():
    data = [bytearray(100) for _ in range(20)]
    before = gc.mem_free()
    del data
    gc.collect()
    return gc.mem_free() > before

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Slice a big buffer with memoryview, because slicing a bytearray copies the data
py-emb-mem-view   lens: access   level: L2   family: py-emb-mem-access
Prerequisites: py-emb-mem-prealloc. Follow-up: py-emb-mem-const. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. buf[2:6] gives a view of the same memory.
Slicing bytes or a bytearray creates a new object with a copy of the data, so changes to the slice do not reach the
original. A memoryview slice shares the memory and costs no copy. Use it for large frames and display buffers, and
for passing sub-ranges to readinto and write.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def poke_bad(ba):
    part = ba[1:3]
    part[0] = 99
    return ba[1]
Correct:

    part = memoryview(ba)[1:3]
    part[0] = 99
    return ba[1]

Keep logs and sample histories bounded so the heap cannot fill up
py-emb-mem-bound   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: py-emb-mem-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: py-emb-mem-gc. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Appending every reading to a list is a harmless way to keep a history.
A device may run for weeks, so any list that grows with time will exhaust the heap and raise MemoryError. Keep a
fixed-size history: drop the oldest item when the length reaches the limit. A fixed bytearray ring buffer avoids
allocation altogether.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def push_bad(hist, v):
    hist.append(v)
    return hist
Correct:
 def push(hist, v, limit=4):
    hist.append(v)
    if len(hist) > limit:
        hist.pop(0)
    return hist

Prompt. Why is memoryview preferred over slicing when you pass part of a large buffer to a read or write call on a
microcontroller?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Slicing a bytes or bytearray object copies the selected bytes into a new
object, which uses scarce heap memory and time and also means the original is not updated. A memoryview slice refers
to the same memory without copying, so a driver can fill or send a part of a big buffer with no allocation.

Overview and mental model: Memory and garbage collection A microcontroller may have only tens or hundreds of kilobytes of RAM. MicroPython allocates objects on a small heap and reclaims them with a garbage collector, so how you allocate matters. Safe habits are preallocated buffers, memoryview slices, const for fixed numbers, collecting garbage at a chosen time, and never letting a list grow without limit. Examples run on the MicroPython unix port, whose heap is much larger than on a board; the free-memory numbers are not representative, so only relative effects are checked. 2. Overview and mental model: Servos, steppers and motors
Actuators turn numbers into motion: servos hold an angle, steppers move in counted steps, DC motors spin through
an H-bridge. Each has mechanical limits that the code must respect.
Mistakes include the wrong steps per revolution, a sequence index that runs off the table, no acceleration, instant
jumps in the setpoint and an H-bridge with both inputs on.
The examples compute positions and pin patterns only; torque, resonance, current and driver timing are not
simulated, so check the motor and driver datasheets.

3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the

Convert an angle to steps with the steps per revolution of your motor
py-emb-act-steps   lens: transformation   level: L1   family: py-emb-act-transformation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-act-sequence. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A stepper always has 200 steps per revolution.
The common 28BYJ-48 geared stepper needs 2048 full steps (4096 half steps) for one turn of the output shaft, while
a plain NEMA 17 motor has 200. Compute steps = angle * steps_per_rev // 360 and keep the motor value as a
parameter. Integer division drops the remainder, so track the exact position to avoid drift.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def steps_bad(angle):
    return angle * 200 // 360
Correct:
 def steps_for(angle, steps_per_rev=2048):
    return angle * steps_per_rev // 360
Limit how far a servo or motor setpoint can move per update (slew rate)
py-emb-act-slew   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-act-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-act-ramp. Follow-up: py-emb-act-hbridge. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Jumping straight to the target angle is fine.
A big instant change draws a surge of current and can jerk the mechanism or reset the board. Move toward the target
by at most max_step per update. The move is a clamp on the difference, so it works in both directions and stops
exactly at the target.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def move_bad(cur, target, max_step):
    return target
Correct:
 def move(cur, target, max_step):
    diff = target - cur
    diff = max(-max_step, min(max_step, diff))
    return cur + diff

Python on hardware, Servos, steppers and motors: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Step through the coil patterns with modulo so the index wraps in both directions
py-emb-act-sequence   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-act-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-act-steps. Follow-up: py-emb-act-ramp. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Adding the direction to the index is enough to keep stepping.
A full-step sequence of four coil patterns repeats forever. index + 1 runs off the end of the table at the fourth step.
(index + direction) % 4 wraps both forward and backward, because Python gives a non-negative remainder for a
positive divisor. Write the pattern to the four coil pins as one value.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 SEQ = (0b1000, 0b0100, 0b0010, 0b0001)
def advance_bad(i, d):
    return SEQ[i + d]
Correct:
 SEQ2 = (0b1000, 0b0100, 0b0010, 0b0001)
def advance(i, d):
    return (i + d) % len(SEQ2)

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Accelerate a stepper with shrinking step delays instead of starting at full speed
py-emb-act-ramp   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: py-emb-act-complexity
Prerequisites: py-emb-act-sequence. Follow-up: py-emb-act-slew. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. The motor can start at its top speed.
A stepper that starts at its maximum rate cannot pick up its load and loses steps or stalls. Start with a long delay
between steps and shorten it a little each step until the cruise delay is reached. The list of delays can be computed
once and reused.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def delays_bad(n, cruise):
    return [cruise] * n
Correct:
 def delays(n, start, cruise):
    out = []
    d = start
    for _ in range(n):
        out.append(d)
        d = max(cruise, d - (start - cruise) // 4)
    return out
Switch both inputs of an H-bridge off before changing direction
py-emb-act-hbridge   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-act-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-act-slew. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Setting the new direction pin high and the old one low in any order is safe.
If both inputs of one half of an H-bridge are high for even an instant, the supply is shorted through the transistors
(shoot-through). Always turn the old input off first, wait the dead time that the driver needs, and only then turn the new
one on.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def reverse_bad(a, b):
    b.value(1)
    a.value(0)

 import time
def reverse(a, b, dead_ms=1):
    a.value(0)
    b.value(0)
    time.sleep_ms(dead_ms)
    b.value(1)

Prompt. Why must both H-bridge inputs be turned off before reversing a motor?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Each half of the bridge has a high-side and a low-side transistor. If both
inputs are on at once, both transistors conduct and the supply is shorted to ground through them, which can destroy the
driver. Switching everything off, waiting the dead time and then enabling the new input prevents the overlap.

Convert an angle to steps with the steps per revolution of your motor py-emb-act-steps lens: transformation level: L1 family: py-emb-act-transformation Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-act-sequence. Complexity: O(1). Common misconception. A stepper always has 200 steps per revolution. The common 28BYJ-48 geared stepper needs 2048 full steps (4096 half steps) for one turn of the output shaft, while a plain NEMA 17 motor has 200. The move is a clamp on the difference, so it works in both directions and stops exactly at the target. 2. Overview and mental model: Button debouncing
Mechanical switches bounce: one press makes the pin chatter for a few milliseconds. Without debouncing a program
counts several presses, or toggles twice.
The common fixes are a lockout time, requiring several identical samples, a bit-history pattern and a hardware filter.
The code needs wrap-safe time comparison and a test that actually bounces.
Examples run with simulated pins and a virtual clock; real contact bounce lasts 1 to 20 ms or more depending on the
switch.
Toolbox
 import time
last = 0
def on_press(now):
    global last
    if time.ticks_diff(now, last) >= 50:
        last = now

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
Ignore edges that arrive within a lockout time after the last accepted one
py-emb-deb-time   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: py-emb-deb-edge-cases
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-deb-samples. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Every edge a mechanical button produces is a separate press.
A mechanical contact bounces: one press produces a burst of edges over a few milliseconds. Accept the first edge,
remember its time and ignore edges closer than a lockout of about 20 to 50 ms. Compare times with ticks_diff so the
check survives counter wrap-around.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import time
class RawCounter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.n = 0
    def edge(self, now):
        self.n += 1
Correct:
 import time
class Lockout:
    def __init__(self, ms):
        self.ms = ms
        self.last = None
        self.n = 0
    def edge(self, now):
        if self.last is None or time.ticks_diff(now, self.last) >= self.ms:
            self.last = now
            self.n += 1
Require several identical samples in a row before the state changes
py-emb-deb-samples   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-deb-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-deb-time. Follow-up: py-emb-deb-history. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. One reading tells whether the button is pressed.
A sampling debouncer reads the pin at a fixed rate and changes its output only after the input has been the same for
N consecutive samples. A single glitch resets the count. This works in a timer callback or a polling loop and needs no
timestamps.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def stable_bad(samples):
    return samples[-1]

Python on hardware, Button debouncing: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Correct:
 def stable(samples, need, start=0):
    out = start
    run = 0
    last = start
    for s in samples:
        run = run + 1 if s == last else 1
        last = s
        if run >= need:
            out = s
    return out
Tell a short press from a long press by the time between press and release
py-emb-deb-long   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L2   family: py-emb-deb-fit-and-alternatives
Prerequisites: py-emb-deb-history. Follow-up: py-emb-deb-isr. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The press duration is known when the button goes down.
The duration is only known on release, or when a hold timeout expires. Record the press time and on release
compute the difference with ticks_diff. Classify against a threshold such as 800 ms. For a hold action while the button
is still down, check the elapsed time in the main loop.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def kind_bad(press_ms, release_ms):
    return 'long' if release_ms > 800 else 'short'
Correct:
 import time
def kind(press_ms, release_ms):
    held = time.ticks_diff(release_ms, press_ms)
    return 'long' if held >= 800 else 'short'

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Keep the last eight samples in one byte and detect a clean press as a bit pattern
py-emb-deb-history   lens: transformation   level: L3   family: py-emb-deb-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-deb-samples. Follow-up: py-emb-deb-long. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A press is detected when the latest sample is 0.
Shift each new sample into an integer: h = ((h << 1) | bit) & 0xFF. With a pull-up, the pattern 0b11110000 means four
released samples followed by four pressed ones. The test fires once on the transition, because the pattern cannot
match again until the pins go high and low again. It needs no timers and no per-button objects.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def pressed_bad(h, bit):
    return bit == 0
Correct:
 def push(h, bit):
    return ((h << 1) | bit) & 0xFF
def pressed(h):
    return h == 0xF0

Test a debouncer by driving a bouncing pin in simulated time
py-emb-deb-isr   lens: testing   level: L3   family: py-emb-deb-testing
Prerequisites: py-emb-deb-long. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A debouncer is correct if it works with one clean edge.
The failure only appears with bursts. Drive the pin high and low several times a millisecond apart, then once more
after the lockout, and assert that exactly two presses were counted. In a handler use the tick time at the moment of
the interrupt, not the time the main loop looks at it.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import time
from machine import Pin
raw_hits = []
bounce_pin_bad = Pin(60, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
bounce_pin_bad.irq(lambda p: raw_hits.append(1), Pin.IRQ_FALLING)
Correct:
 import time
from machine import Pin
good_hits = []
last_t = [None]
def on_fall(pin):
    now = time.ticks_ms()
    if last_t[0] is None or time.ticks_diff(now, last_t[0]) >= 50:
        last_t[0] = now
        good_hits.append(now)
bounce_pin = Pin(61, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
bounce_pin.irq(on_fall, Pin.IRQ_FALLING)

2. Overview and mental model: Sleep modes and power
Battery devices spend nearly all their time asleep. machine.lightsleep pauses the CPU and keeps RAM,
machine.deepsleep powers down and restarts the program on wake-up.
Mistakes include treating deep sleep like light sleep, keeping state in RAM, estimating battery life from the active
current and sleeping the full period after variable work.
The simulator advances a virtual clock for light sleep and raises SystemExit for deep sleep; real current, wake-up
sources and RTC memory depend on the port and must be measured.
Toolbox
 import machine
machine.lightsleep(1000)
machine.deepsleep(60000)

lightsleep(ms) pauses the CPU for a time and then continues with your variables intact
py-emb-slp-light   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-slp-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-slp-deep. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. time.sleep_ms saves as much power as lightsleep.
time.sleep_ms keeps the CPU running in a wait loop, while machine.lightsleep(ms) stops the CPU clock until the time
is up or a wake-up source fires. RAM is kept, so the program resumes on the next line. How much power it saves
depends on the port, so measure it.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import time
def pause_bad(ms):
    time.sleep_ms(ms)
Correct:
 import machine
def pause(ms):
    machine.lightsleep(ms)
Save the state to a file before deep sleep and load it again on the next start
py-emb-slp-persist   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-slp-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-slp-deep. Follow-up: py-emb-slp-budget. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A module-level counter keeps counting across wake-ups.
Each wake-up runs the program from the start, so a counter in RAM always starts again at zero. Read a small state
file at start-up, update it, write it back and then sleep. A temporary file and rename keeps it valid if the battery dies
during the write.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def boots_bad():
    boots = 0
    boots += 1
    return boots
Correct:
 import json, os
def boots(path="state.json"):
    n = 0
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            n = json.load(f)["n"]
    except (OSError, ValueError, KeyError):
        pass
    n += 1
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        json.dump({"n": n}, f)
    return n

Deep sleep ends in a reset, so no code after deepsleep() runs and variables are lost
py-emb-slp-deep   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: py-emb-slp-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-slp-light. Follow-up: py-emb-slp-persist. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The program continues after deepsleep() like after lightsleep.
machine.deepsleep(ms) powers down almost everything. When it wakes, the board restarts from the beginning of
boot.py and main.py, and RAM contents are gone. Put the work before the call, keep what must survive in a file or in
RTC memory, and treat the line after deepsleep() as unreachable.

def cycle_bad():

    counter_bad += 1
Correct:

def cycle(state):
    state["boots"] = state.get("boots", 0) + 1
    machine.deepsleep(1000)

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Estimate battery life from the duty cycle: average the active and sleep currents by time
py-emb-slp-budget   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: py-emb-slp-complexity
Prerequisites: py-emb-slp-persist. Follow-up: py-emb-slp-period. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Battery life is capacity divided by the active current.
A device that wakes for 1 s every 60 s spends most of its time asleep. The average current is (active * t_active +
sleep * t_sleep) / (t_active + t_sleep). Divide the battery capacity by that average for the life in hours. Use microamps
and integer arithmetic.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def hours_bad(capacity_mah, active_ua):
    return capacity_mah * 1000 // active_ua
Correct:
 def avg_ua(active_ua, t_active, sleep_ua, t_sleep):
    return (active_ua * t_active + sleep_ua * t_sleep) // (t_active + t_sleep)
def hours(capacity_mah, avg):
    return capacity_mah * 1000 // avg
Sleep for the rest of the period, not for the full period, to keep a steady sampling rate
py-emb-slp-period   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: py-emb-slp-patterns
Prerequisites: py-emb-slp-budget. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Sleeping the full period after the work keeps the period constant.
If the work takes 300 ms and you then sleep 1000 ms, the cycle is 1300 ms and the rate drifts with the work time.
Measure the elapsed time and sleep period - elapsed. If the work took longer than the period, do not sleep.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def rest_bad(period_ms, elapsed_ms):
    return period_ms
Correct:
 def rest(period_ms, elapsed_ms):
    return max(0, period_ms - elapsed_ms)

Overview and mental model: Sleep modes and power Battery devices spend nearly all their time asleep. machine.lightsleep pauses the CPU and keeps RAM, machine.deepsleep powers down and restarts the program on wake-up. Mistakes include treating deep sleep like light sleep, keeping state in RAM, estimating battery life from the active current and sleeping the full period after variable work. The simulator advances a virtual clock for light sleep and raises SystemExit for deep sleep; real current, wake-up sources and RTC memory depend on the port and must be measured. Follow-up: py-emb-slp-deep. Complexity: O(1). Common misconception. time.sleep_ms saves as much power as lightsleep. time.sleep_ms keeps the CPU running in a wait loop, while machine.lightsleep(ms) stops the CPU clock until the time is up or a wake-up source fires. RAM is kept, so the program resumes on the next line. How much power it saves depends on the port, so measure it. Incorrect (runs, but fails as described): import time def pause_bad(ms): time.sleep_ms(ms) Correct: import machine def pause(ms): machine.lightsleep(ms) Save the state to a file before deep sleep and load it again on the next start py-emb-slp-persist lens: mutation level: L2 family: py-emb-slp-mutation Prerequisites: py-emb-slp-deep. Follow-up: py-emb-slp-budget. Complexity: O(1). Common misconception. A module-level counter keeps counting across wake-ups. Each wake-up runs the program from the start, so a counter in RAM always starts again at zero. Read a small state file at start-up, update it, write it back and then sleep. A temporary file and rename keeps it valid if the battery dies during the write. Incorrect (runs, but fails as described): def boots_bad(): boots = 0 boots += 1 return boots Correct: import json, os def boots(path="state.json"): n = 0 try: with open(path) as f: n = json.load(f)["n"] except (OSError, ValueError, KeyError): pass n += 1 with open(path, "w") as f: json.dump({"n": n}, f) return n Python on hardware, Sleep modes and power: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot Page 4 Deep sleep ends in a reset, so no code after deepsleep()

2. Overview and mental model: smbus2 and spidev on the
Raspberry Pi
On a Raspberry Pi running Linux the buses are device files. The smbus2 library talks to I2C devices through
/dev/i2c-N and spidev talks to SPI devices through /dev/spidevN.M, both from ordinary CPython.
Typical errors are reading without selecting a register, byte-swapped words, block reads over 32 bytes, treating a
full-duplex transfer as half duplex and leaving the device open.
The examples run against simulated smbus2 and spidev modules that follow the library interfaces; they have not
touched a real Pi bus. Enable the interfaces with raspi-config before using the real ones.
Toolbox
 from smbus2 import SMBus
with SMBus(1) as bus:
    chip_id = bus.read_byte_data(0x68, 0x75)

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
Use read_byte_data(addr, reg) to read a register; read_byte ignores the register
py-emb-rpb-register   lens: access   level: L1   family: py-emb-rpb-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-rpb-word. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. bus.read_byte(addr) reads the register you want.
read_byte reads one byte from the device's current register pointer, which is wherever the last access left it.
read_byte_data(addr, register) first selects the register and then reads it, in one SMBus transaction. Use it for sensor
registers, and use write_byte_data to write one.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from smbus2 import SMBus
def who_bad(bus, addr):
    return bus.read_byte(addr)
Correct:
 from smbus2 import SMBus
def who(bus, addr, reg=0x0F):
    return bus.read_byte_data(addr, reg)
An SMBus block read is limited to 32 bytes, so read larger areas in pieces
py-emb-rpb-block   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-rpb-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-rpb-word. Follow-up: py-emb-rpb-xfer. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. read_i2c_block_data can read any length.
The SMBus block functions accept at most 32 bytes per call, and smbus2 raises ValueError for more. To read a
bigger register area, loop in chunks of 32, advancing the register number each time.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def dump_bad(bus, addr, reg, n):
    return bus.read_i2c_block_data(addr, reg, n)
Correct:
 def dump(bus, addr, reg, n):
    out = []
    while n > 0:
        k = min(32, n)
        out.extend(bus.read_i2c_block_data(addr, reg, k))
        reg += k
        n -= k
    return out

Python on hardware, smbus2 and spidev on the Raspberry Pi: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
read_word_data returns the low byte first, so swap the bytes for a big-endian sensor
py-emb-rpb-word   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-rpb-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-rpb-register. Follow-up: py-emb-rpb-block. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The word has the high byte of the register in its top half.
The SMBus protocol defines a word as low byte first. Many sensors store the high byte first. read_word_data
therefore returns 0x3412 for the bytes 12 34 at the register. Swap the two bytes when the datasheet says the register
pair is big-endian.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def word_bad(bus, addr, reg):
    return bus.read_word_data(addr, reg)
Correct:
 def word_be(bus, addr, reg):
    w = bus.read_word_data(addr, reg)
    return ((w & 0xFF) << 8) | (w >> 8)

4.4 Algorithm chunks
spidev xfer2 returns as many bytes as you send; the answer follows the command byte
py-emb-rpb-xfer   lens: access   level: L3   family: py-emb-rpb-access
Prerequisites: py-emb-rpb-block. Follow-up: py-emb-rpb-close. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. xfer2 returns only the reply bytes.
SPI is full duplex, so xfer2([cmd, 0]) returns two bytes: the first was clocked in while the command went out and is not
valid, the second is the reply. Send one dummy byte per reply byte and index the result from 1. The list has the same
length as the input.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def read_bad(spi, reg):
    return spi.xfer2([reg | 0x80])[0]
Correct:
 def read_reg(spi, reg):
    return spi.xfer2([reg | 0x80, 0])[1]
Open the SPI device, set mode and speed, and always close it in a finally block
py-emb-rpb-close   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-rpb-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-rpb-xfer. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The SPI device stays configured after the program ends.
An open /dev/spidev handle is a resource: another program cannot use the device until it is closed, and a crash
leaves it open until the process ends. Set max_speed_hz and mode after open, do the transfers inside try, and close
in finally.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import spidev
def probe_bad():
    spi = spidev.SpiDev()
    spi.open(0, 0)
    return spi

Correct:
 import spidev
def probe(hz=500000, mode=0):
    spi = spidev.SpiDev()
    spi.open(0, 0)
    try:
        spi.max_speed_hz = hz
        spi.mode = mode
        return spi.xfer2([0x01, 0])
    finally:
        spi.close()

Prompt. Why can read_word_data return bytes in the opposite order from what the sensor datasheet shows?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). The SMBus specification defines a word transfer with the low byte first.
Many sensors place the high byte of a 16-bit value in the first register, so the library delivers the two bytes swapped
relative to the datasheet value. The program has to swap them back, or read two single bytes and combine them.

Overview and mental model: smbus2 and spidev on the Raspberry Pi On a Raspberry Pi running Linux the buses are device files. 2. Overview and mental model: I2C bus
I2C connects many chips on two wires; each has a 7-bit address and a set of registers. MicroPython machine.I2C
offers scan, readfrom_mem and writeto_mem for register devices.
Typical errors are 8-bit addresses, reading without selecting a register, wrong byte order or sign, overwriting a whole
configuration register, and giving up on the first OSError.
Examples run against a simulated bus with register devices; real buses also need pull-up resistors and may stretch
the clock.
Toolbox
 from machine import I2C, Pin
i2c = I2C(0, scl=Pin(5), sda=Pin(4))
print(i2c.scan())
i2c.readfrom_mem(0x48, 0, 2)

I2C addresses are 7 bits; a datasheet 8-bit write address must be shifted right
py-emb-i2c-address   lens: access   level: L1   family: py-emb-i2c-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-i2c-register. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The address in the datasheet can be used as it is.
MicroPython expects the 7-bit address, which i2c.scan() returns. Some datasheets list the 8-bit write address (the
7-bit address shifted left by one) such as 0x90 for a sensor at 0x48. Using 0x90 addresses nothing and raises
OSError. Check the address with scan() and shift the datasheet value right by one if needed.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import I2C, Pin
i2c = I2C(0, scl=Pin(5), sda=Pin(4))
def read_temp_bad():
    return i2c.readfrom_mem(0x90, 0, 2)
Correct:
 from machine import I2C, Pin
i2c = I2C(0, scl=Pin(5), sda=Pin(4))
def read_temp():
    return i2c.readfrom_mem(0x90 >> 1, 0, 2)
Use readfrom_mem to select a register and read it in one call
py-emb-i2c-register   lens: access   level: L2   family: py-emb-i2c-access
Prerequisites: py-emb-i2c-address. Follow-up: py-emb-i2c-signed. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. readfrom(addr, n) reads the register you want.
Most I2C chips keep a register pointer. readfrom reads from wherever the pointer is, normally register 0 after power
up. To read register r, write r first and then read, which readfrom_mem(addr, r, n) does as one transaction with a
repeated start. Writing registers is writeto_mem(addr, r, data).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def read_id_bad(i2c, addr):
    return i2c.readfrom(addr, 1)[0]
Correct:
 def read_id(i2c, addr, reg=0x0F):
    return i2c.readfrom_mem(addr, reg, 1)[0]

Python on hardware, I2C bus: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Retry an I2C transaction a few times before giving up, because OSError can be transient
py-emb-i2c-retry   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-i2c-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-i2c-modify. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(tries).
 Common misconception. An OSError from I2C always means the device is missing.
A busy or noisy bus can raise OSError (ENODEV or ETIMEDOUT) for one transaction and work on the next. Retry a
small fixed number of times, wait briefly between tries and re-raise the last error so a real fault is not hidden. Never
loop forever.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def read_bad(dev):
    return dev.read()
Correct:
 import time
def read_retry(dev, tries=3):
    for i in range(tries):
        try:
            return dev.read()
        except OSError:
            if i == tries - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep_ms(5)

Combine bytes in the datasheet byte order and sign-extend 16-bit two's complement values
py-emb-i2c-signed   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-i2c-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-i2c-register. Follow-up: py-emb-i2c-modify. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Two bytes from a sensor form an unsigned number in either order.
Check the byte order: many sensors send the high byte first (big-endian), and some send the low byte first.
Temperatures and accelerations are signed, so a raw value of 0xFFFE is -2 and not 65534. Subtract 65536 when bit
15 is set, or use int.from_bytes(data, "big") and then adjust.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def raw16_bad(b):
    return (b[1] << 8) | b[0]
Correct:
 def raw16(b):
    v = (b[0] << 8) | b[1]
    return v - 65536 if v & 0x8000 else v

Change one bit of a configuration register with read, modify, write
py-emb-i2c-modify   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: py-emb-i2c-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-i2c-signed. Follow-up: py-emb-i2c-retry. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Writing the new value is enough to switch on one feature.
A configuration register packs several settings. Writing a constant overwrites every other bit. Read the register, clear
the bits you change with a mask, set the new bits, and write it back. A helper that takes the mask and value keeps
every call correct.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def enable_bad(i2c, addr, reg, bit):
    i2c.writeto_mem(addr, reg, bytes([1 << bit]))
Correct:
 def set_bits(i2c, addr, reg, mask, value):
    cur = i2c.readfrom_mem(addr, reg, 1)[0]
    new = (cur & ~mask) | (value & mask)
    i2c.writeto_mem(addr, reg, bytes([new]))

2. Overview and mental model: UART serial
A UART sends bytes one after another at an agreed baud rate. MicroPython machine.UART gives read, readline,
write and any, and they are non-blocking by default.
Common problems are treating an empty read as bytes, assuming a read contains one whole message, converting
bytes to text wrongly, and miscounting the time a message takes.
Examples run against a simulated UART whose receive buffer is filled by the test; a real line also needs matching
baud, parity, voltage levels and a common ground.
Toolbox
 from machine import UART, Pin
uart = UART(1, 115200, tx=Pin(4), rx=Pin(5))
if uart.any():
    line = uart.readline()
