uart.read() returns None when nothing has arrived, so check before using the result
py-emb-uart-none   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: py-emb-uart-edge-cases
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-uart-lines. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. read() returns an empty bytes object when the buffer is empty.
On MicroPython a non-blocking read() returns None when no data is waiting, and bytes otherwise. Calling len() or
indexing the result then raises TypeError. Test uart.any() first or compare the result with None.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import UART
def size_bad(uart):
    return len(uart.read())
Correct:
 from machine import UART
def size(uart):
    data = uart.read() if uart.any() else None
    return 0 if data is None else len(data)
Decode received bytes to text with decode(), and tolerate line noise
py-emb-uart-decode   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-uart-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-uart-lines. Follow-up: py-emb-uart-timing. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. str(data) turns received bytes into text.
str(b"hi") gives the text "b'hi'" with the prefix and quotes. Use data.decode() to get "hi". A noisy line can produce
invalid UTF-8, which raises UnicodeError, so decode with a fallback or discard the broken line instead of crashing the
loop.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def text_bad(data):
    return str(data)
Correct:
 def text(data):
    try:
        return data.decode()
    except UnicodeError:
        return None

A serial character takes 10 bit times in 8N1, so the byte rate is baud divided by 10
py-emb-uart-timing   lens: complexity   level: L2   family: py-emb-uart-complexity
Prerequisites: py-emb-uart-decode. Follow-up: py-emb-uart-drain. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. At 9600 baud you receive 1200 bytes per second of 8N1 data.
Each 8N1 character has a start bit, eight data bits and a stop bit: ten bits. At 9600 baud that is 960 characters per
second, and sending 100 bytes takes about 104 ms. With a parity bit or two stop bits the frame gets longer. Compute
the time from the frame size to choose timeouts and buffer sizes.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def tx_ms_bad(n, baud):
    return n * 8 * 1000 // baud
Correct:
 def tx_ms(n, baud, data_bits=8, parity=0, stop=1):
    bits = 1 + data_bits + parity + stop
    return n * bits * 1000 // baud

Accumulate received bytes in a buffer and split complete lines, since a read can end mid-line
py-emb-uart-lines   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-uart-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-uart-none. Follow-up: py-emb-uart-decode. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Each read() returns one complete line.
Bytes arrive in arbitrary chunks, so one read may end in the middle of a line or contain two lines. Append every chunk
to a bytearray, split off complete lines at the newline byte, and keep the remainder for the next call. Handle both
b"\r\n" and b"\n" endings by stripping the line.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def lines_bad(chunk):
    return chunk.split(b"\n")
Correct:
 class LineBuffer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.buf = bytearray()
    def feed(self, chunk):
        self.buf.extend(chunk)
        out = []
        while True:
            i = self.buf.find(b"\n")
            if i < 0:
                return out
            out.append(bytes(self.buf[:i]).strip())
            self.buf = self.buf[i + 1:]

Drain the receive buffer in a bounded loop so a chatty device cannot starve the program
py-emb-uart-drain   lens: creation   level: L3   family: py-emb-uart-creation
Prerequisites: py-emb-uart-timing. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. One read(4) empties the buffer.
The buffer may hold more than you asked for, and the data keeps arriving. Loop while any() is positive, collect the
bytes and stop at a limit so the loop ends even if the sender never stops. Anything left over stays in the driver buffer
for the next pass.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def drain_bad(uart):
    return uart.read(4)
Correct:
 def drain(uart, limit=64):
    out = bytearray()
    while uart.any() and len(out) < limit:
        out.extend(uart.read(min(uart.any(), limit - len(out))))
    return bytes(out)

2. Overview and mental model: GPIO digital I/O
Digital GPIO pins read or drive a logic level. In MicroPython the machine.Pin class configures the direction (IN or
OUT), the pull resistor (PULL_UP or PULL_DOWN) and reads or writes the level with value(), on(), off() and toggle().
Most bugs come from wiring assumptions: a floating input without a pull resistor, an active-low LED or button treated
as active-high, and bit order when several pins or a serial line form a number.
Examples here run on the MicroPython unix port against a simulated machine module; pin numbers are logical ids, so
check the pinout of your board (Pico, ESP32, STM32) before wiring.
Toolbox
 from machine import Pin, Signal
led = Pin(25, Pin.OUT)
button = Pin(14, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
led.value(button.value() == 0)

Set the pin direction before using it: only an OUT pin drives a level
py-emb-gpio-direction   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-gpio-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-gpio-pullup. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Calling value(1) on a pin is enough to switch an LED on, whatever its mode.
A GPIO pin is either an input that reads the voltage from the outside or an output that drives it. On an IN pin, value(x)
cannot change the level; the reading comes from the circuit. Create the pin with Pin.OUT for LEDs, relays and
transistors, and Pin.IN for buttons and sensors. value() with no argument reads, value(0 or 1) writes, and on(), off()
and toggle() are shortcuts for outputs.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin
led = Pin(2, Pin.IN)
led.value(1)
led_level = led.value()
Correct:
 from machine import Pin
led = Pin(3, Pin.OUT)
led.on()
led.toggle()
led_level = led.value()
A button with a pull-up reads 1 when released and 0 when pressed
py-emb-gpio-pullup   lens: access   level: L2   family: py-emb-gpio-access
Prerequisites: py-emb-gpio-direction. Follow-up: py-emb-gpio-signal. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A pressed button reads 1.
An input pin that is connected to nothing floats and reads random values. Wire the button between the pin and
ground and enable the internal pull-up (Pin.PULL_UP): the pin reads 1 while the button is open and 0 when it
connects the pin to ground. The logic is active-low, so pressed means value() == 0. With a pull-down and the button
wired to 3.3 V the logic is reversed.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin
button = Pin(14, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
def is_pressed_bad():
    return button.value() == 1
Correct:
 from machine import Pin
button2 = Pin(15, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
def is_pressed():
    return button2.value() == 0

Python on hardware, GPIO digital I/O: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Use machine.Signal for active-low outputs so that on() always means the device is on
py-emb-gpio-signal   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-gpio-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-gpio-pullup. Follow-up: py-emb-gpio-bus. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. pin.on() always turns the connected LED on.
An LED wired from 3.3 V through a resistor to the pin lights when the pin is low, so pin.on() turns it off. Wrapping the
pin in Signal(pin, invert=True) makes on() drive the pin low and value() report 1 for lit, keeping the logic in the
program independent of the wiring. Use it for active-low relays, LEDs and chip-select lines.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin
led_pin_bad = Pin(5, Pin.OUT)
led_pin_bad.on()
lit_bad = led_pin_bad.value() == 0
Correct:
 from machine import Pin, Signal
led_pin = Pin(6, Pin.OUT)
led = Signal(led_pin, invert=True)
led.on()

Combine several pins into one integer with shifts, choosing which pin is the least significant
bit
py-emb-gpio-bus   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-gpio-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-gpio-signal. Follow-up: py-emb-gpio-bitbang. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Shifting the accumulator left on every pin reads the pins as a number with the first pin as the
least significant bit.
The pin order decides the bit weights. Shifting the accumulator left before OR-ing the next pin makes the first pin the
most significant bit, so a list of pins wired least significant first gives the bits reversed. To make pins[0] bit 0, OR each
pin value shifted by its index. The same applies when writing an integer to several output pins.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def read_bus_bad(pins):
    value = 0
    for p in pins:
        value = (value << 1) | p.value()
    return value
Correct:
 def read_bus(pins):
    value = 0
    for i, p in enumerate(pins):
        value |= p.value() << i
    return value

Bit-banged serial output sends bits in the order the receiver expects, usually most significant
first
py-emb-gpio-bitbang   lens: iteration   level: L3   family: py-emb-gpio-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-gpio-bus. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(bits).
 Common misconception. Looping over range(8) sends a byte correctly.
range(8) visits bit 0 first, so the byte goes out least significant bit first. Shift registers such as the 74HC595 and most
SPI devices expect the most significant bit first: loop from 7 down to 0, put the bit on the data pin, then raise and
lower the clock. The receiver samples on the clock edge, so the data must be stable before the rising edge.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def shift_out_bad(data, clk, byte):
    for i in range(8):
        data.value((byte >> i) & 1)
        clk.value(1)
        clk.value(0)
Correct:
 def shift_out(data, clk, byte):
    for i in range(7, -1, -1):
        data.value((byte >> i) & 1)
        clk.value(1)
        clk.value(0)

A GPIO pin is either an input that reads the voltage from the outside or an output that drives it. On an IN pin, value(x) cannot change the level; the reading comes from the circuit. Create the pin with Pin.OUT for LEDs, relays and transistors, and Pin.IN for buttons and sensors. value() with no argument reads, value(0 or 1) writes, and on(), off() and toggle() are shortcuts for outputs. 2. Overview and mental model: CircuitPython digitalio, busio and
analogio
CircuitPython is Adafruit's fork of MicroPython. Pins come from the board module, and hardware is used through
digitalio, analogio, pwmio and busio, which differ from machine in names and in rules such as bus locking.
Typical mistakes are writing to an input, reading a pull-up button as active high, using a bus without the lock, scaling
analog values by the wrong number and writing to SPI before configure.
The examples run on CPython against simulated CircuitPython modules that mirror those interfaces; they have not
run on a CircuitPython board, and board pin names differ per board.
Toolbox
 import board, digitalio
led = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.LED)
led.direction = digitalio.Direction.OUTPUT
led.value = True

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
Set the direction of a DigitalInOut before writing its value
py-emb-cp-direction   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-cp-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-cp-pull. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A new DigitalInOut can be written straight away.
A DigitalInOut starts as an input, and writing value to an input raises AttributeError. Set direction = Direction.OUTPUT
first, or call switch_to_output(value=...). The value is a bool: True is high and False is low.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import board, digitalio
led_bad = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.GP14)
def on_bad():
    led_bad.value = True
Correct:
 import board, digitalio
led = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.LED)
led.direction = digitalio.Direction.OUTPUT
led.value = True
With Pull.UP a button reads True when released and False when pressed
py-emb-cp-pull   lens: access   level: L2   family: py-emb-cp-access
Prerequisites: py-emb-cp-direction. Follow-up: py-emb-cp-lock. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A pressed button reads True.
For an input wired between the pin and ground, enable the pull-up with pull = Pull.UP. The pin is then True while the
button is open and False when it is pressed, so the pressed test is "not button.value". Setting pull on an output raises
AttributeError, so set direction to INPUT first.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import board, digitalio
btn_bad = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.GP15)
btn_bad.direction = digitalio.Direction.INPUT
btn_bad.pull = digitalio.Pull.UP
def pressed_bad():
    return btn_bad.value
Correct:
 import board, digitalio
btn = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.GP16)
btn.switch_to_input(pull=digitalio.Pull.UP)
def pressed():
    return not btn.value

Python on hardware, CircuitPython digitalio, busio and analogio: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Lock the I2C bus with try_lock before using it and unlock it in finally
py-emb-cp-lock   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-cp-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-cp-pull. Follow-up: py-emb-cp-analog. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. busio.I2C can be used directly after it is created.
On CircuitPython an I2C bus can be shared by several libraries, so scan, readfrom_into and writeto raise
RuntimeError unless you hold the lock. Loop on try_lock() until it returns True, do the transfer in try, and call unlock()
in finally. Libraries that take the bus object do this for you.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import board, busio
i2c_bad = busio.I2C(board.SCL, board.SDA)
def scan_bad():
    return i2c_bad.scan()
Correct:
 import board, busio
i2c = busio.I2C(board.SCL, board.SDA)
def scan():
    while not i2c.try_lock():
        pass
    try:
        return i2c.scan()
    finally:
        i2c.unlock()

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Convert AnalogIn.value to volts with the reference voltage and 65536
py-emb-cp-analog   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-cp-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-cp-lock. Follow-up: py-emb-cp-spi. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The value is the voltage in millivolts.
AnalogIn.value is a 16-bit number from 0 to 65535 whatever the real converter resolution. The voltage is value *
reference_voltage / 65536. A value of 32768 is half of the reference, 1.65 V at 3.3 V. Use the reference_voltage
attribute and not a number that is hard-coded for one board.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import board, analogio
adc_bad = analogio.AnalogIn(board.A0)
def volts_bad():
    return adc_bad.value / 1000
Correct:

adc = analogio.AnalogIn(board.A1)
def volts():
    return adc.value * adc.reference_voltage / 65536

Configure the SPI bus while holding the lock, and write only after configure
py-emb-cp-spi   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: py-emb-cp-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-cp-analog. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. busio.SPI works with its default settings.
Like I2C, an SPI bus needs a lock, and its speed and mode are set with configure() while the lock is held. Libraries do
this for each transaction because several devices can share the bus with different settings. Release the lock when
the transfer is complete.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import board, busio
spi_bad = busio.SPI(board.SCK, board.MOSI, board.MISO)
def send_bad(data):
    spi_bad.write(data)
Correct:
 import board, busio
spi = busio.SPI(board.SCK, board.MOSI, board.MISO)
def send(data, baud=1000000):
    while not spi.try_lock():
        pass
    try:
        spi.configure(baudrate=baud, polarity=0, phase=0)
        spi.write(data)
    finally:
        spi.unlock()

2. Overview and mental model: SPI bus
SPI is a fast four-wire bus: clock, two data lines and a chip select per device. MicroPython machine.SPI offers write,
readinto and write_readinto, and the program controls chip select with a Pin.
The usual faults are the wrong clock mode, chip select not toggled properly, treating a duplex bus as half duplex, and
mishandled bit fields that span bytes.
Examples run against a simulated SPI that logs writes; real devices also care about clock speed and setup times.
Toolbox
 from machine import SPI, Pin
spi = SPI(1, baudrate=1000000, polarity=0, phase=0)
cs = Pin(9, Pin.OUT, value=1)
cs.value(0)
spi.write(b"\x01")
cs.value(1)

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
Match the SPI mode to the device: polarity is the idle clock level and phase is the sampling
edge
py-emb-spi-mode   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-spi-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-spi-cs. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Mode 1 means polarity 1 and phase 0.
SPI modes 0 to 3 combine two bits: polarity (CPOL), the idle level of the clock, and phase (CPHA), which edge
samples the data. The mode number is 2 * polarity + phase, so mode 1 is polarity 0 and phase 1. Swapping them
silently gives wrong or shifted data. Read the mode from the datasheet and create the bus with both values.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def mode_bits_bad(mode):
    return (mode & 1, mode >> 1)
Correct:
 from machine import SPI, Pin
def mode_bits(mode):
    return (mode >> 1, mode & 1)
def make_spi(mode, baud=1000000):
    pol, pha = mode_bits(mode)
    return SPI(1, baudrate=baud, polarity=pol, phase=pha,
               sck=Pin(10), mosi=Pin(11), miso=Pin(12))
Pull chip select low for the whole transaction and release it even if an error occurs
py-emb-spi-cs   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-spi-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-spi-mode. Follow-up: py-emb-spi-duplex. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Chip select can be left low between transfers.
The device frames each transaction with chip select (CS), active low. Lower it before the first byte, keep it low for the
whole command, and raise it afterwards so the device latches the result. Use try and finally so an exception cannot
leave the device selected, which would make the next transfer misaligned.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def write_bad(spi, cs, data):
    cs.value(0)
    spi.write(data)
Correct:
 def write_ok(spi, cs, data):
    cs.value(0)
    try:
        spi.write(data)
    finally:
        cs.value(1)

Python on hardware, SPI bus: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Extract a 10-bit sample that spans bytes by masking the high byte first
py-emb-spi-bits   lens: transformation   level: L3   family: py-emb-spi-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-spi-duplex. Follow-up: py-emb-spi-burst. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The last two reply bytes give the ten-bit result as they are.
An ADC such as the MCP3008 returns 10 bits spread over two bytes: the low two bits of the second byte are the top
bits of the result, and the third byte holds the low eight bits. Mask the second byte with 0x03, shift it left by 8 and add
the third byte. Forgetting the mask lets the leading junk bits into the result.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def sample_bad(rx):
    return (rx[1] << 8) | rx[2]
Correct:
 def sample(rx):
    return ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]

4.4 Algorithm chunks
SPI is full duplex: the reply arrives while you clock out the command, so use write_readinto
py-emb-spi-duplex   lens: access   level: L2   family: py-emb-spi-access
Prerequisites: py-emb-spi-cs. Follow-up: py-emb-spi-bits. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Write the register address, then read the answer with read().
Every clocked byte also receives a byte. For a register read, send the address with its read flag set and a dummy
byte for the clocking: the answer arrives while the dummy goes out. write_readinto(tx, rx) does both in one
transaction. Calling write() and then read() clocks the command and the answer in two different frames when CS is
toggled between them.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def read_reg_bad(spi, reg):
    return spi.read(1)[0]
Correct:
 def read_reg(spi, reg):
    tx = bytes([reg | 0x80, 0])
    rx = bytearray(2)
    spi.write_readinto(tx, rx)
    return rx[1]
Send a block with one write call rather than one call per byte
py-emb-spi-burst   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: py-emb-spi-complexity
Prerequisites: py-emb-spi-bits. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Writing bytes one at a time is the same as one block.
Every Python call has overhead, and with CS toggled per call the device may treat each byte as a new command.
Pass the whole bytes or memoryview slice to a single write(). For large buffers such as a display frame, slice with a
memoryview so no copy is made.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def send_bad(spi, data):
    for b in data:
        spi.write(bytes([b]))
Correct:
 def send(spi, data):
    spi.write(data)

Prompt. Why use try and finally around an SPI transaction, and why must chip select be raised at the end?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Chip select frames the transaction. Many devices only latch a command
or output when it goes high again, and a device that stays selected will interpret the next bytes as a continuation. try and
finally release it even when an exception is raised, so one failed transfer cannot leave the bus in a state that corrupts the
following transfers.

Overview and mental model: SPI bus SPI is a fast four-wire bus: clock, two data lines and a chip select per device. MicroPython machine.SPI offers write, readinto and write_readinto, and the program controls chip select with a Pin. The usual faults are the wrong clock mode, chip select not toggled properly, treating a duplex bus as half duplex, and mishandled bit fields that span bytes. Examples run against a simulated SPI that logs writes; real devices also care about clock speed and setup times. Match the SPI mode to the device: polarity is the idle clock level and phase is the sampling edge py-emb-spi-mode lens: creation level: L1 family: py-emb-spi-creation Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-spi-cs. Complexity: O(1). Common misconception. Mode 1 means polarity 1 and phase 0. SPI modes 0 to 3 combine two bits: polarity (CPOL), the idle level of the clock, and phase (CPHA), which edge samples the data. The mode number is 2 * polarity + phase, so mode 1 is polarity 0 and phase 1. Swapping them silently gives wrong or shifted data. Read the mode from the datasheet and create the bus with both values. Incorrect (runs, but fails as described): def mode_bits_bad(mode): return (mode & 1, mode >> 1) Correct: from machine import SPI, Pin def mode_bits(mode): return (mode >> 1, mode & 1) def make_spi(mode, baud=1000000): pol, pha = mode_bits(mode) return SPI(1, baudrate=baud, polarity=pol, phase=pha, sck=Pin(10), mosi=Pin(11), miso=Pin(12)) Pull chip select low for the whole transaction and release it even if an error occurs py-emb-spi-cs lens: mutation level: L2 family: py-emb-spi-mutation Prerequisites: py-emb-spi-mode. Follow-up: py-emb-spi-duplex. Complexity: O(n). Common misconception. Chip select can be left low between transfers. The device frames each transaction with chip select (CS), active low. Lower it before the first byte, keep it low for the whole command, and raise it afterwards so the device latches the result. Use try and finally so an exception cannot leave the device selected, which would make the next transfer misaligned. Incorrect (runs, but fails as described): def write_bad(spi, cs, data): cs.value(0) spi.write(data) Correct: def write_ok(spi, cs, data): cs.value(0) try: spi.write(data) finally: cs.value(1) Python on hardware,

Follow-up: py-emb-spi-burst. Complexity: O(1). Common misconception. The last two reply bytes give the ten-bit result as they are. An ADC such as the MCP3008 returns 10 bits spread over two bytes: the low two bits of the second byte are the top bits of the result, and the third byte holds the low eight bits. Mask the second byte with 0x03, shift it left by 8 and add the third byte. Forgetting the mask lets the leading junk bits into the result. 2. Overview and mental model: PWM output
PWM switches a pin on and off quickly; the duty cycle is the fraction of time it is high. It dims LEDs, drives servos and
makes tones. In MicroPython machine.PWM takes a frequency and a duty_u16 value between 0 and 65535.
Bugs come from forgetting the 16-bit scale, from values outside the range, from rounding in fades, and from treating a
servo like a dimmer.
Examples run on the MicroPython unix port against a simulated machine.PWM; duty ranges on real ports can differ
(some use duty() 0 to 1023), so check your port.
Toolbox
 from machine import Pin, PWM
pwm = PWM(Pin(15), freq=1000)
pwm.duty_u16(32768)
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

Page 3
Duty cycle is a fraction of 65535 in duty_u16, so convert a percentage before setting it
py-emb-pwm-duty   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-pwm-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-pwm-range. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. duty_u16(50) sets the brightness to 50 percent.
On MicroPython boards duty_u16 takes 0 to 65535, where 65535 means always on. Passing 50 gives about 0.08
percent and the LED looks off. Convert a percentage with pct * 65535 // 100. The frequency is set with freq() and
decides how fast the pin switches, not how bright the LED looks.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin, PWM
led_bad = PWM(Pin(2), freq=1000)
led_bad.duty_u16(50)
bad_duty = led_bad.duty_u16()
Correct:
 from machine import Pin, PWM
def pct_to_u16(pct):
    return pct * 65535 // 100
led = PWM(Pin(3), freq=1000)
led.duty_u16(pct_to_u16(50))
Clamp the duty value to the valid range so a calculation cannot raise or wrap
py-emb-pwm-range   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: py-emb-pwm-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-pwm-duty. Follow-up: py-emb-pwm-fade. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Any computed duty value can be passed to duty_u16.
A fade or a sensor-driven brightness can compute a value above 65535 or below 0. The driver rejects it with
ValueError on some ports and wraps it on others, so the LED flashes unexpectedly. Clamp with min and max before
the call, which behaves the same on every board.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin, PWM
fan_bad = PWM(Pin(4), freq=1000)
def set_duty_bad(d):
    fan_bad.duty_u16(d)
Correct:
 from machine import Pin, PWM
fan = PWM(Pin(5), freq=1000)
def set_duty(d):
    fan.duty_u16(max(0, min(65535, d)))

Python on hardware, PWM output: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Pick the PWM frequency for the load: audio tones need the pitch, LEDs need a flicker-free
rate
py-emb-pwm-freq   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L3   family: py-emb-pwm-fit-and-alternatives
Prerequisites: py-emb-pwm-servo. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. One frequency fits every PWM load.
For a buzzer the PWM frequency is the pitch, and a 50 percent duty gives the loudest square wave. For an LED,
anything above about 200 Hz looks steady; a slow frequency visibly flickers. A servo needs exactly 50 Hz. Set the
frequency first and the duty afterwards, because some ports reset the duty when the frequency changes.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin, PWM
buzzer_bad = PWM(Pin(6))
buzzer_bad.duty_u16(32768)
buzzer_bad.freq(440)
Correct:
 from machine import Pin, PWM
def tone(pwm, hz):
    if hz:
        pwm.freq(hz)
        pwm.duty_u16(32768)
    else:
        pwm.duty_u16(0)
buzzer = PWM(Pin(7))
tone(buzzer, 440)

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Fade with a loop over integer steps and compute each duty from the step, not by repeated
addition
py-emb-pwm-fade   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-pwm-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-pwm-range. Follow-up: py-emb-pwm-servo. Complexity: O(steps).
 Common misconception. Adding a rounded increment each step reaches the target exactly.
Adding int(65535 / steps) repeatedly loses the remainder, so the last duty falls short of the target. Compute the duty
from the step index as target * i // steps, which reaches the target exactly on the last step and needs no accumulated
error.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def fade_bad(target, steps):
    inc = int(target / steps)
    d = 0
    out = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        d += inc
        out.append(d)
    return out
Correct:
 def fade(target, steps):
    out = []
    for i in range(1, steps + 1):
        out.append(target * i // steps)
    return out

A hobby servo is driven by pulse width at 50 Hz, so map the angle to microseconds and then
to duty
py-emb-pwm-servo   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-pwm-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-pwm-fade. Follow-up: py-emb-pwm-freq. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A servo angle is set by the duty percentage, so 90 degrees is 50 percent.
A servo expects a pulse every 20 ms (50 Hz) whose width is about 1000 us for 0 degrees and 2000 us for 180
degrees. The duty is pulse / period, so 90 degrees (1500 us) is 7.5 percent, not 50. Map the angle linearly to
microseconds, then multiply by 65535 and divide by the 20000 us period. Check the pulse range in the servo
datasheet.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def angle_to_duty_bad(angle):
    return 65535 * angle // 180
Correct:
 def angle_to_duty(angle):
    us = 1000 + 1000 * angle // 180
    return 65535 * us // 20000

Prompt. Why is a servo at 90 degrees driven with a duty of about 7.5 percent and not 50 percent?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). A hobby servo reads the width of a pulse that repeats every 20 ms, not
the fraction of time the pin is high as a brightness. A 1500 us pulse is the centre position, and 1500 us out of 20000 us is
7.5 percent. The range 1000 us to 2000 us covers the full travel, so only a small part of the duty range is used.

Overview and mental model: PWM output PWM switches a pin on and off quickly; the duty cycle is the fraction of time it is high. It dims LEDs, drives servos and makes tones. In MicroPython machine.PWM takes a frequency and a duty_u16 value between 0 and 65535. Bugs come from forgetting the 16-bit scale, from values outside the range, from rounding in fades, and from treating a servo like a dimmer. Examples run on the MicroPython unix port against a simulated machine.PWM; duty ranges on real ports can differ (some use duty() 0 to 1023), so check your port. cycle is a fraction of 65535 in duty_u16, so convert a percentage before setting it py-emb-pwm-duty lens: creation level: L1 family: py-emb-pwm-creation Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-pwm-range. Complexity: O(1). Common misconception. duty_u16(50) sets the brightness to 50 percent. On MicroPython boards duty_u16 takes 0 to 65535, where 65535 means always on. Passing 50 gives about 0.08 percent and the LED looks off. Convert a percentage with pct * 65535 // 100. The frequency is set with freq() and decides how fast the pin switches, not how bright the LED looks. Incorrect (runs, but fails as described): from machine import Pin, PWM led_bad = PWM(Pin(2), freq=1000) led_bad.duty_u16(50) bad_duty = led_bad.duty_u16() Correct: from machine import Pin, PWM def pct_to_u16(pct): return pct * 65535 // 100 led = PWM(Pin(3), freq=1000) led.duty_u16(pct_to_u16(50)) Clamp the duty value to the valid range so a calculation cannot raise or wrap py-emb-pwm-range lens: edge-cases level: L2 family: py-emb-pwm-edge-cases Prerequisites: py-emb-pwm-duty. Follow-up: py-emb-pwm-fade. Complexity: O(1). Common misconception. Any computed duty value can be passed to duty_u16. A fade or a sensor-driven brightness can compute a value above 65535 or below 0. The driver rejects it with ValueError on some ports and wraps it on others, so the LED flashes unexpectedly. Clamp with min and max before the call, which behaves the same on every board. Incorrect (runs, but fails as described): from machine import Pin, PWM fan_bad = PWM(Pin(4), freq=1000) def set_duty_bad(d): fan_bad.duty_u16(d) Correct: from machine import Pin, PWM fan = PWM(Pin(5), freq=1000) def set_duty(d): fan.duty_u16(max(0, min(65535, d))) Python on hardware, PWM output: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot Page 4 Pick

Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1). Common misconception. One frequency fits every PWM load. For a buzzer the PWM frequency is the pitch, and a 50 percent duty gives the loudest square wave. Set the frequency first and the duty afterwards, because some ports reset the duty when the frequency changes. 2. Overview and mental model: Arduino from Python with
pyFirmata
Firmata is a protocol that lets a computer control an Arduino over USB serial. The Arduino runs the StandardFirmata
sketch and a Python program on the host calls pyfirmata to set pins and read inputs.
The Python code runs on the computer, not on the Arduino, so this is a different model from MicroPython: every pin
change is a serial message.
Typical mistakes are wrong pin specs, PWM values in the byte range, arithmetic on a missing reading, a wrong
reference voltage and servo angles beyond the stops.
Examples run against a simulated pyfirmata board; no Arduino or serial port was used.
Toolbox
 import pyfirmata
board = pyfirmata.Arduino("/dev/ttyACM0")
led = board.get_pin("d:13:o")
led.write(1)

3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
Name Arduino pins by kind, number and mode: analog A0 is a:0:i and not digital 14
py-emb-pfm-pins   lens: access   level: L1   family: py-emb-pfm-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-pfm-pwm. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Analog pin A0 can be opened as digital pin 14.
pyfirmata numbers digital and analog pins separately. get_pin takes a string "kind:number:mode": "d:13:o" is digital
13 as output, "d:9:p" is a PWM output, "a:0:i" is analog input 0. A0 on the Uno is analog index 0, so asking for d:14
gives a different object. Write a small helper that turns Arduino labels into these strings.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def spec_bad(label):
    return "d:" + str(int(label[1:])) + ":i"
Correct:
 def spec(label):
    kind, n = label[0], int(label[1:])
    if kind == "A":
        return "a:%d:i" % n
    return "d:%d:o" % n
Write PWM as a fraction from 0.0 to 1.0, not as a byte from 0 to 255
py-emb-pfm-pwm   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-pfm-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-pfm-pins. Follow-up: py-emb-pfm-none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. PWM pins take a duty value from 0 to 255 like analogWrite in Arduino C.
In pyfirmata the value you write to a PWM pin is a fraction between 0.0 and 1.0, which the library scales for the board.
analogWrite(pin, 128) in C becomes pin.write(128 / 255) in Python. Passing 128 directly is outside the range.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def level_bad(byte):
    return byte
Correct:
 def level(byte):
    return max(0, min(255, byte)) / 255

Python on hardware, Arduino from Python with pyFirmata: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
An analog read returns None until the first report arrives, so handle None
py-emb-pfm-none   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: py-emb-pfm-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-pfm-pwm. Follow-up: py-emb-pfm-lm35. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. read() always returns a number.
Input values arrive over the serial line as reports. The pin must have reporting enabled and an util.Iterator thread
must be running to receive them. Until the first report arrives, read() returns None, and arithmetic on it raises
TypeError. Check for None and decide what to do, for example skip the cycle.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def volts_bad(pin, vref=5.0):
    return pin.read() * vref
Correct:
 def volts(pin, vref=5.0):
    v = pin.read()
    if v is None:
        return None
    return v * vref

Clamp a servo angle to 0 to 180 before writing it
py-emb-pfm-servo   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-pfm-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-pfm-lm35. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Any angle can be written to a servo pin.
A servo in pyfirmata takes an angle in degrees, normally between 0 and 180. A computed angle such as 200 asks the
mechanism to move beyond its stop, which can strain it. Clamp the angle to the allowed range before every write.

py-emb-pfm-lm35   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L3   family: py-emb-pfm-fit-and-alternatives
Prerequisites: py-emb-pfm-none. Follow-up: py-emb-pfm-servo. Complexity: O(1).

An LM35 gives 10 mV per degree Celsius. The fraction from read() is a share of the reference voltage, so the
temperature is fraction * vref * 100. An Uno uses 5.0 V and a 3.3 V board uses 3.3. A hard-coded 5 V is wrong on the

2. Overview and mental model: Errors, retries and watchdog
Unattended devices must recover from faults: a hung loop, an absent sensor, a network that is down. A hardware
watchdog restarts the board when the program stops feeding it, and careful error handling keeps small faults small.
The mistakes are feeding the watchdog from a timer, a timeout that fits no real operation, immediate retries, trusting
raw sensor values and treating every OSError alike.
The simulated WDT only reports whether it would have expired; on hardware it resets the board, and some ports
cannot be stopped once started.
Toolbox
 from machine import WDT
wdt = WDT(timeout=5000)
while True:
    do_work()
    wdt.feed()

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
Back off exponentially between retries and cap the delay
py-emb-wdt-backoff   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-wdt-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-wdt-timeout. Follow-up: py-emb-wdt-validate. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Retrying immediately and often reconnects fastest.
Retrying at full speed hammers a server that is down and drains the battery. Double the delay after each failure:
base, 2 * base, 4 * base. Cap it at a maximum so the wait does not grow without bound, and reset it after a success.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def delay_bad(n, base):
    return base * n
Correct:
 def delay_ms(n, base=100, cap=5000):
    return min(cap, base << n)
Choose a timeout longer than the slowest legitimate loop iteration
py-emb-wdt-timeout   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: py-emb-wdt-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-wdt-feed. Follow-up: py-emb-wdt-backoff. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A short watchdog timeout detects hangs faster, so shorter is always better.
A timeout shorter than the longest normal operation, such as a Wi-Fi connect or a flash write, resets a healthy device.
Measure the slowest iteration and set the timeout to a multiple of it, for example twice. Break long operations into
steps that feed the watchdog.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def timeout_bad(longest_ms):
    return longest_ms // 2
Correct:
 def timeout_ms(longest_ms, margin=2):
    return longest_ms * margin

Python on hardware, Errors, retries and watchdog: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Reject sensor values outside the physical range instead of passing them on
py-emb-wdt-validate   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: py-emb-wdt-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-wdt-backoff. Follow-up: py-emb-wdt-errno. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Whatever the sensor returns is a valid measurement.
A disconnected or broken sensor reports 0, 0xFFFF or a constant error code, and a control loop that trusts it can heat
or run a motor. Check against the physical range and return None for readings outside it, so the caller can use the
last good value or raise a fault.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def temp_ok_bad(c):
    return c
Correct:
 def temp_ok(c, lo=-40, hi=125):
    if lo <= c <= hi:
        return c
    return None

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Feed the watchdog from the main loop after real work, not from a timer
py-emb-wdt-feed   lens: patterns   level: L1   family: py-emb-wdt-patterns
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-wdt-timeout. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A timer that feeds the watchdog keeps the program safe.
The watchdog resets the board when it is not fed within its timeout. If a timer callback feeds it, the callback keeps
running even when the main loop is stuck, so the hang is never detected. Feed it in the main loop, after the useful
work of the iteration has completed.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Timer, WDT
wdt_bad = WDT(timeout=1000)
def feed_cb(t):
    wdt_bad.feed()
feeder = Timer(mode=Timer.PERIODIC, period=200, callback=feed_cb)
Correct:
 from machine import WDT
wdt = WDT(timeout=1000)
def loop_once(work):
    work()
    wdt.feed()

Decide what to do from OSError.errno using the errno constants
py-emb-wdt-errno   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L3   family: py-emb-wdt-fit-and-alternatives
Prerequisites: py-emb-wdt-validate. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Every OSError should be retried the same way.
OSError carries an errno. ETIMEDOUT and EAGAIN are worth a retry, ENODEV means the device is absent and a
retry will not help, and ENOENT means a missing file. Compare e.errno with the constants from the errno module,
because the numeric values are port specific.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def action_bad(e):
    return "retry"
Correct:
 import errno
def action(e):
    if e.errno in (errno.ETIMEDOUT, errno.EAGAIN):
        return "retry"
    if e.errno == errno.ENODEV:
        return "absent"
    return "fail"

py-emb-wdt-feed-ex2   format: explain-why   level: L1   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Why is feeding the watchdog from a timer interrupt a bad idea?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). The purpose of the watchdog is to reset the device when the main
program stops making progress. A timer callback keeps running while the main loop is hung, so the watchdog is always
fed and never triggers. Feeding it from the main loop, after the work is done, ties the feed to real progress.

Overview and mental model: Errors, retries and watchdog Unattended devices must recover from faults: a hung loop, an absent sensor, a network that is down. A hardware watchdog restarts the board when the program stops feeding it, and careful error handling keeps small faults small. The mistakes are feeding the watchdog from a timer, a timeout that fits no real operation, immediate retries, trusting raw sensor values and treating every OSError alike. The simulated WDT only reports whether it would have expired; on hardware it resets the board, and some ports cannot be stopped once started. 2. Overview and mental model: Sensor drivers
A sensor driver turns register reads into useful numbers. Good drivers are small classes that check the chip, wait for
conversions, decode signed fields and apply calibration in the right order.
The common failures are shared globals, assuming the right chip, reading before the conversion finishes, forgetting
two's complement, and applying offset and gain in the wrong order.
The registers and values here are modelled on common chips (a 0x33 ID, a 13-bit temperature); check your own
datasheet. Examples ran on a simulated I2C bus.
Toolbox
 class Sensor:
    def __init__(self, i2c, addr=0x48):
        self.i2c = i2c
        self.addr = addr
    def read(self):
        return self.i2c.readfrom_mem(self.addr, 0, 1)[0]

3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the

Wrap each sensor in a class that owns its bus and address
py-emb-sen-class   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-sen-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-sen-id. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Module-level variables for the bus and address are enough for a driver.
A driver written with globals works for one sensor and breaks when you add a second chip with another address. A
class keeps the bus and address in the instance, so two sensors are two objects. Give it a small, honest API: read()
returns a value, and constants name the registers.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import I2C, Pin
i2c_g = I2C(0, scl=Pin(5), sda=Pin(4))
ADDR_G = 0x48
def read_bad():
    return i2c_g.readfrom_mem(ADDR_G, 0, 1)[0]
Correct:
 from machine import I2C, Pin
class Sensor:
    REG_TEMP = 0
    def __init__(self, i2c, addr=0x48):
        self.i2c = i2c
        self.addr = addr
    def read(self):
        return self.i2c.readfrom_mem(self.addr, self.REG_TEMP, 1)[0]
Sign-extend a 13-bit two's-complement temperature register
py-emb-sen-signed   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-sen-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-sen-ready. Follow-up: py-emb-sen-calib. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A 13-bit register value above 4095 is a large positive temperature.
The MCP9808 reports temperature in 13 bits with the sign in bit 12 and a resolution of 0.0625 degrees. A raw value of
0x1FFF means -1 step. Subtract 8192 when bit 12 is set, then multiply by 625 and divide by 10000 for degrees, or by
625 and keep the result in ten-thousandths to stay exact.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def temp_bad(raw13):
    return raw13 * 625
Correct:
 def temp_ten_thousandths(raw13):
    if raw13 & 0x1000:
        raw13 -= 0x2000
    return raw13 * 625

Check the chip ID in the constructor so a wrong or absent device fails early
py-emb-sen-id   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: py-emb-sen-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-sen-class. Follow-up: py-emb-sen-ready. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A driver can assume the right chip is at the address.
The same address can belong to different chips, and a loose wire gives OSError later in the program, far from the
cause. Read the identification register in __init__ and raise a clear error when it does not match.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

    def __init__(self, i2c, addr):
        self.i2c = i2c
        self.addr = addr
Correct:
 class Chip:
    WHO_AM_I = 0x0F
    CHIP_ID = 0x33
    def __init__(self, i2c, addr):
        self.i2c = i2c
        self.addr = addr
        found = i2c.readfrom_mem(addr, self.WHO_AM_I, 1)[0]
        if found != self.CHIP_ID:
            raise ValueError("unexpected chip id 0x%02x" % found)

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Wait for the data-ready flag with a timeout before reading a conversion
py-emb-sen-ready   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-sen-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-sen-id. Follow-up: py-emb-sen-signed. Complexity: O(timeout).
 Common misconception. A reading taken right after the start command is the new result.
Many sensors need milliseconds to convert. Reading too early returns the previous value or zeros. Poll the status
register for the ready bit, sleep a millisecond between polls and give up after a timeout so a dead sensor does not
hang the program.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def wait_bad(read_status):
    return read_status()
Correct:
 import time
def wait_ready(read_status, timeout_ms=50):
    start = time.ticks_ms()
    while not read_status():
        if time.ticks_diff(time.ticks_ms(), start) > timeout_ms:
            raise OSError("sensor timeout")
        time.sleep_ms(1)
    return True

Apply calibration as (raw - offset) * gain, in that order
py-emb-sen-calib   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: py-emb-sen-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-sen-signed. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. raw * gain - offset gives the same result.
A two-point calibration measures the raw value at a known zero and at a known span. The offset belongs to the raw
scale, so subtract it first and then scale. Applying the gain before the offset puts the offset on the wrong scale, and
the error grows with the gain. Store the two constants in the configuration, not in the code.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def calib_bad(raw, offset, gain_num, gain_den):
    return raw * gain_num // gain_den - offset
Correct:
 def calib(raw, offset, gain_num, gain_den):
    return (raw - offset) * gain_num // gain_den

Overview and mental model: Sensor drivers A sensor driver turns register reads into useful numbers. Good drivers are small classes that check the chip, wait for conversions, decode signed fields and apply calibration in the right order. 2. Overview and mental model: NeoPixel LED strips
WS2812 NeoPixel strips are addressable RGB LEDs on one data line. MicroPython neopixel.NeoPixel keeps a
colour per pixel in memory and sends all of them with write().
The usual mistakes are forgetting write(), overflowing a channel when dimming, wheel positions that are not wrapped,
indexes that run off the strip and ignoring the current the strip can draw.
Examples run against a simulated NeoPixel that records frames; real strips also need correct timing, a level shifter
and a supply that can deliver the current.
Toolbox
 from machine import Pin
from neopixel import NeoPixel
np = NeoPixel(Pin(5), 8)
np.fill((0, 0, 32))
np.write()

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
Setting pixels changes a buffer; the strip updates only when you call write()
py-emb-npx-write   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: py-emb-npx-mutation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-npx-brightness. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. np[0] = (255, 0, 0) lights the first pixel at once.
NeoPixel keeps the colours in memory and sends them to the strip in write(). Without it nothing changes on the LEDs.
Set all the pixels you want, then call write() once, because each write sends the whole strip and takes about 30
microseconds per pixel.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin
from neopixel import NeoPixel
np_bad = NeoPixel(Pin(4), 8)
np_bad[0] = (255, 0, 0)
Correct:
 from machine import Pin
from neopixel import NeoPixel
np = NeoPixel(Pin(5), 8)
np[0] = (255, 0, 0)
np.write()
Build a colour wheel from a position and wrap the position with modulo 256
py-emb-npx-wheel   lens: creation   level: L2   family: py-emb-npx-creation
Prerequisites: py-emb-npx-brightness. Follow-up: py-emb-npx-chase. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A position above 255 is a valid colour wheel input.
A colour wheel maps 0 to 255 onto red, green, blue and back to red. Animations add to the position every frame, so it
passes 255 quickly. Take pos % 256 first; without it the three segments do not apply and the channels go negative.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def wheel_bad(pos):
    if pos < 85:
        return (255 - pos * 3, pos * 3, 0)
    return (0, 0, 0)
Correct:
 def wheel(pos):
    pos %= 256
    if pos < 85:
        return (255 - pos * 3, pos * 3, 0)
    if pos < 170:
        pos -= 85
        return (0, 255 - pos * 3, pos * 3)
    pos -= 170
    return (pos * 3, 0, 255 - pos * 3)

Python on hardware, NeoPixel LED strips: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Scale brightness with integer maths and keep every channel between 0 and 255
py-emb-npx-brightness   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-npx-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-npx-write. Follow-up: py-emb-npx-wheel. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Multiplying a colour by the brightness gives a dimmer colour.
A channel is one byte. c * level with level up to 255 is far above 255 and raises ValueError. Scale with c * level // 255,
where level 255 means unchanged and 0 means off. Do it for each channel of the tuple.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def dim_bad(c, level):
    return tuple(v * level for v in c)
Correct:
 def dim(c, level):
    return tuple(v * level // 255 for v in c)

Move a lit pixel along the strip with the modulo operator and clear the old one first

 Common misconception. Adding one to the pixel index moves the light along.
The index passes the last pixel and raises IndexError. Use (i + 1) % n. Also clear the previous pixel before lighting the
next one, or the strip fills up with lit pixels instead of showing one that moves.

Estimate the current from the channel values and scale the frame to stay inside the supply
budget
py-emb-npx-power   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: py-emb-npx-complexity
Prerequisites: py-emb-npx-chase. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. The strip draws the same current whatever it shows.
Each lit channel of a WS2812 LED draws up to about 20 mA at full value, so a pixel at full white draws about 60 mA
and 100 white pixels would need 6 A. The current is roughly proportional to the sum of the channel values. Add the
values, compare with the budget and scale the whole frame down when it is exceeded. Check your LED datasheet
for the real figure.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def current_bad(frame):
    return len(frame) * 60

 def current_ma(frame):
    return sum(sum(p) for p in frame) * 20 // 255
def fit(frame, budget_ma):
    cur = current_ma(frame)
    if cur <= budget_ma:
        return frame
    return [tuple(v * budget_ma // cur for v in p) for p in frame]

2. Overview and mental model: asyncio on a microcontroller
MicroPython asyncio runs many tasks on one thread. Each task runs until it awaits, so blinking, button handling and
networking can share a board without interrupts or threads.
Typical mistakes are not awaiting a coroutine, running awaits one after another when they could overlap, calling
blocking functions, cancelling without cleanup, and waiting without a timeout.
Examples run on the MicroPython unix port with a virtual-time event loop: waits advance the simulated clock instead
of real time, and the stock event loop is otherwise unchanged.
Toolbox
 import asyncio
from machine import Pin
led = Pin(25, Pin.OUT)
async def blink():
    while True:
        led.toggle()
        await asyncio.sleep_ms(500)
asyncio.run(blink())

3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
Calling a coroutine function without await creates the coroutine and runs nothing
py-emb-aio-await   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-aio-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-aio-gather. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Calling tick() starts the work, the same as a normal function.
An async def function returns a coroutine object when called. The body runs only when it is awaited or scheduled with
asyncio.create_task or asyncio.run. A bare call silently does nothing, so the LED never blinks and no error appears.
Always await it, or create a task.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import asyncio
count_bad = [0]
async def tick_bad():
    count_bad[0] += 1
def start_bad():
    tick_bad()
Correct:
 import asyncio
count = [0]
async def tick():
    count[0] += 1
async def run_once():
    await tick()
Use gather to run waits side by side: the total time is the longest, not the sum
py-emb-aio-gather   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-aio-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-aio-await. Follow-up: py-emb-aio-blocking. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Awaiting two coroutines one after the other lets them run together.
await a() followed by await b() runs them one after another, so two 20 ms and 30 ms waits take 50 ms.
asyncio.gather(a(), b()) starts both and finishes after the longer one, 30 ms. Use it for independent sensors, or create
tasks when the results are not needed together.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import asyncio
async def work_bad(ms):
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(ms)
    return ms
async def sequential():
    a = await work_bad(20)
    b = await work_bad(30)
    return a + b

Page 4
Correct:
 import asyncio
async def work(ms):
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(ms)
    return ms
async def concurrent():
    r = await asyncio.gather(work(20), work(30))
    return sum(r)
Stop a task with cancel() and put the cleanup in a finally block
py-emb-aio-cancel   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: py-emb-aio-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: py-emb-aio-blocking. Follow-up: py-emb-aio-timeout. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Cancelling a task runs the code after its loop.
task.cancel() raises CancelledError inside the task at its next await. Code after an endless loop never runs, so a
motor stays on. Put the cleanup in a finally block: it runs on cancellation and on normal exit. Let the cancel propagate,
and yield once (await sleep_ms(0)) so the task finishes before you continue.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import asyncio
log_bad = []
async def worker_bad():
    log_bad.append("start")
    while True:
        await asyncio.sleep_ms(10)
    log_bad.append("cleanup")
Correct:
 import asyncio
log = []
async def worker():
    try:
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep_ms(10)
    finally:
        log.append("cleanup")
async def stop_after(ms):
    t = asyncio.create_task(worker())
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(ms)
    t.cancel()
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(0)

Never call time.sleep_ms inside a coroutine, because it stops every other task
py-emb-aio-blocking   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L2   family: py-emb-aio-fit-and-alternatives
Prerequisites: py-emb-aio-gather. Follow-up: py-emb-aio-cancel. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. time.sleep_ms and asyncio.sleep_ms are interchangeable inside a coroutine.
asyncio is cooperative: tasks switch only at an await. time.sleep_ms blocks the whole program, so a heartbeat task, a
button task and a network task all freeze for the delay. await asyncio.sleep_ms gives control back to the loop. The
same holds for any long loop without an await.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import asyncio, time
async def blocking_job():
    time.sleep_ms(55)
Correct:
 import asyncio
beats = [0]
async def heartbeat():
    while True:
        await asyncio.sleep_ms(10)
        beats[0] += 1
async def friendly_job():
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(55)
Bound every wait on hardware or a network with wait_for_ms
py-emb-aio-timeout   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-aio-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-aio-cancel. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Awaiting a sensor read is safe even if the sensor never answers.
If a device does not answer, a plain await waits forever and the task is stuck. asyncio.wait_for_ms(coro, ms) cancels
the coroutine after ms milliseconds and raises asyncio.TimeoutError, which the caller can catch to retry or report a
fault.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import asyncio
async def slow():
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(500)
    return "late"
async def read_bad():
    return await slow()
Correct:
 import asyncio
async def slow2():
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(500)
    return "late"
async def read_with_timeout(ms):
    try:
        return await asyncio.wait_for_ms(slow2(), ms)
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
        return None

Prompt. Why does a time.sleep call inside an async function freeze the other tasks, while await asyncio.sleep does

never returns control to the event loop, so no other task can run until it has finished. await asyncio.sleep suspends the
current task and lets the loop run the others until the delay is over.

Overview and mental model: asyncio on a microcontroller MicroPython asyncio runs many tasks on one thread. Each task runs until it awaits, so blinking, button handling and networking can share a board without interrupts or threads. Typical mistakes are not awaiting a coroutine, running awaits one after another when they could overlap, calling blocking functions, cancelling without cleanup, and waiting without a timeout. 2. Overview and mental model: Files and configuration
MicroPython boards keep a small flash file system. Configuration, logs and calibration data live there, and the file
system can be cut short by a reset at any moment.
Defensive habits are loading with defaults, writing through a temporary file, bounding logs, using fixed-size records
for random access, and remembering what JSON does to types.
Examples run on the MicroPython unix port with the host file system in a temporary directory; flash wear, power loss
and file system corruption are not simulated.

py-emb-fil-defaults   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: py-emb-fil-edge-cases
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-fil-atomic. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. The config file always exists and contains every key.
On first boot, after a file system reset, or after an interrupted write, config.json may be missing, empty or incomplete.
Start from a dictionary of defaults and update it with what you can read. Catch OSError for a missing file and
ValueError for invalid JSON, and keep the defaults in both cases.

Correct:
 import json
DEFAULTS = {"interval": 10, "name": "node"}
def load(path):
    cfg = dict(DEFAULTS)
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            cfg.update(json.load(f))
    except (OSError, ValueError):
        pass
    return cfg
Check the log size before appending and rotate it, because flash space is small
py-emb-fil-rotate   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: py-emb-fil-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: py-emb-fil-atomic. Follow-up: py-emb-fil-records. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Appending to a log file forever is fine.
A log that grows on a device with a few hundred kilobytes of flash fills the file system and breaks everything else.
Check the size with os.stat(path)[6] before each append. When it passes the limit, move the log to a backup name,
replacing the previous backup, and start a new file.

 import os
def log(path, line, limit=20):
    try:
        size = os.stat(path)[6]
    except OSError:
        size = 0
    if size + len(line) + 1 > limit:
        try:
            os.remove(path + ".1")
        except OSError:
            pass
        os.rename(path, path + ".1")
    with open(path, "a") as f:
        f.write(line + "\n")
Store fixed-size binary records so you can seek to record n without reading the file
py-emb-fil-records   lens: access   level: L3   family: py-emb-fil-access
Prerequisites: py-emb-fil-rotate. Follow-up: py-emb-fil-json. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Text lines can be read by index just as quickly as fixed-size records.
Finding line n of a text file needs a scan through the n lines before it. With fixed-size records, record n starts at n *
size, so seek and read one record. struct.pack with explicit sizes keeps the record width constant. Variable-width text
breaks this arithmetic.

Correct:
 import struct
REC = ">HH"
SIZE = struct.calcsize(REC)
def write_records(path, rows):
    with open(path, "wb") as f:
        for a, b in rows:
            f.write(struct.pack(REC, a, b))
def read_record(path, n):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        f.seek(n * SIZE)
        return struct.unpack(REC, f.read(SIZE))

2. Overview and mental model: State machines
Firmware is mostly a state machine: idle, running, error, with events such as a button press, a fault or a timeout. A
clear table of states and transitions keeps the code testable and avoids tangled flags.
Trouble comes from unhandled events that crash, actions that repeat on every event, indexes that run off the end,
timeouts that break at tick wrap-around and interrupts that change state directly.
The machines here are pure Python and run unchanged on a board; examples ran on the MicroPython unix port.

Describe transitions in a table and stay in the current state for unknown events
py-emb-fsm-table   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-fsm-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-fsm-actions. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Looking up the next state with brackets is enough.
A transition table maps (state, event) to the next state. An event that the state does not handle must not crash the
device: use .get(key, state) to stay where you are. Adding a state or event is then a one-line table change instead of
another branch in an if chain.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 TABLE_BAD = {("idle", "press"): "run", ("run", "press"): "idle"}
def step_bad(state, event):
    return TABLE_BAD[(state, event)]
Correct:
 TABLE = {("idle", "press"): "run", ("run", "press"): "idle", ("run", "fault"): "error"}
def step(state, event):
    return TABLE.get((state, event), state)
Run entry actions only when the state changes, not on every event
py-emb-fsm-actions   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-fsm-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-fsm-table. Follow-up: py-emb-fsm-cycle. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The action for a state can run whenever an event arrives in that state.
If the on-entry action (switch the motor on) runs for every event, a repeated press restarts it and a stuck sensor floods
the output. Compare the new state with the old one and call the action only for a real transition.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def feed_bad(machine, event, log):
    machine["state"] = step(machine["state"], event)
    log.append("enter " + machine["state"])
Correct:
 def feed(machine, event, log):
    new = step(machine["state"], event)
    if new != machine["state"]:
        machine["state"] = new
        log.append("enter " + new)

Python on hardware, State machines: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Cycle through a list of states with the modulo operator, not with an unchecked index
py-emb-fsm-cycle   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-fsm-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-fsm-actions. Follow-up: py-emb-fsm-timeout. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Adding 1 to the state index moves to the next phase.
A traffic light or a menu repeats a fixed sequence. index + 1 runs past the end of the list and raises IndexError. Use
(index + 1) % len(states) so the last state wraps to the first, and keep the sequence in one list or tuple.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

def next_bad(i):
    return i + 1
Correct:
 PHASES2 = ("green", "yellow", "red")
def next_phase(i):
    return (i + 1) % len(PHASES2)

Give a state a deadline and compare ticks with ticks_diff to leave it on timeout
py-emb-fsm-timeout   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-fsm-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-fsm-cycle. Follow-up: py-emb-fsm-queue. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A state can compare ticks_ms() with a stored end time using >=.
A door-open or pairing state needs a timeout. Store the time of entry and leave when ticks_diff(now, entered)
exceeds the limit. Plain subtraction or >= breaks when the tick counter wraps around, which happens after about 12
days on some ports.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def expired_bad(now, entered, limit):
    return now - entered > limit
Correct:
 import time
def expired(now, entered, limit):
    return time.ticks_diff(now, entered) > limit
Queue events from interrupts and let the main loop feed the state machine
py-emb-fsm-queue   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: py-emb-fsm-patterns
Prerequisites: py-emb-fsm-timeout. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Interrupt handlers should call the state machine directly.
A handler that changes state can interrupt the main loop in the middle of a transition. Put events into a small queue
and process them in the loop, in order. Bound the queue so a stuck input cannot exhaust memory, and drop the
newest event when it is full.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def handle_bad(machine, event):
    machine["state"] = step(machine["state"], event)
Correct:
 def post(queue, event, limit=8):
    if len(queue) < limit:
        queue.append(event)
def drain(machine, queue):
    while queue:
        machine["state"] = step(machine["state"], queue.pop(0))

Overview and mental model: State machines Firmware is mostly a state machine: idle, running, error, with events such as a button press, a fault or a timeout. A clear table of states and transitions keeps the code testable and avoids tangled flags. Trouble comes from unhandled events that crash, actions that repeat on every event, indexes that run off the end, timeouts that break at tick wrap-around and interrupts that change state directly. The machines here are pure Python and run unchanged on a board; examples ran on the MicroPython unix port. An event that the state does not handle must not crash the device: use .get(key, state) to stay where you are. Adding a state or event is then a one-line table change instead of another branch in an if chain. If the on-entry action (switch the motor on) runs for every event, a repeated press restarts it and a stuck sensor floods the output. Compare the new state with the old one and call the action only for a real transition. 2. Overview and mental model: OLED displays and framebuf
Small OLED and LCD screens are drawn through a frame buffer: the program draws into memory and a driver such
as ssd1306 sends the buffer over I2C or SPI.
Typical mistakes are expecting drawing to update the screen, using the wrong byte layout, leaving old pixels,
expecting text to wrap and drawing values that exceed the screen.
The examples draw into a real framebuf.FrameBuffer on the MicroPython unix port, and a send function records the
buffer instead of talking to an SSD1306.
Toolbox
 import framebuf
buf = bytearray(128 * 64 // 8)
fb = framebuf.FrameBuffer(buf, 128, 64, framebuf.MONO_VLSB)
fb.fill(0)
fb.text("Hello", 0, 0, 1)

3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
Draw into a frame buffer and send it to the display with one show() call
py-emb-dsp-show   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: py-emb-dsp-mutation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-dsp-layout. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Drawing functions change the screen right away.
framebuf.FrameBuffer draws into memory only. The OLED shows the new picture after you send the buffer, which the
SSD1306 driver does in show(). Draw the whole frame, then call show() once; calling it after every pixel is slow and
makes the screen flicker.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import framebuf
buf_bad = bytearray(32)
fb_bad = framebuf.FrameBuffer(buf_bad, 16, 16, framebuf.MONO_VLSB)
fb_bad.pixel(3, 3, 1)
Correct:
 import framebuf
sent = []
buf = bytearray(32)
fb = framebuf.FrameBuffer(buf, 16, 16, framebuf.MONO_VLSB)
def show():
    sent.append(bytes(buf))
fb.pixel(3, 3, 1)
show()
In MONO_VLSB each byte holds eight vertical pixels, so the byte index uses y // 8
py-emb-dsp-layout   lens: access   level: L2   family: py-emb-dsp-access
Prerequisites: py-emb-dsp-show. Follow-up: py-emb-dsp-clear. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The byte for pixel (x, y) is at y * width + x.
The SSD1306 stores the picture in pages of eight rows. A byte holds eight pixels of one column, with the least
significant bit on top. The pixel (x, y) is in byte (y // 8) * width + x, bit y % 8. A row-major formula points at the wrong
byte and is only correct for monochrome horizontal formats.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def index_bad(x, y, width):
    return y * width + x
Correct:
 def index_bit(x, y, width):
    return (y // 8) * width + x, y % 8

Python on hardware, OLED displays and framebuf: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Wrap text by the number of 8-pixel characters that fit in the display width
py-emb-dsp-wrap   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-dsp-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-dsp-clear. Follow-up: py-emb-dsp-bar. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Long text wraps to the next line by itself.
The built-in font is 8 pixels wide, so a 128 pixel display holds 16 characters per line. framebuf.text does not wrap: the
extra characters are cut off. Split the string into chunks of width // 8 characters and draw each chunk 8 pixels lower.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def lines_bad(s, width):
    return [s]
Correct:
 def lines(s, width):
    n = width // 8
    return [s[i:i + n] for i in range(0, len(s), n)]

Clear the buffer before redrawing, or old pixels stay on the screen
py-emb-dsp-clear   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: py-emb-dsp-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-dsp-layout. Follow-up: py-emb-dsp-wrap. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Drawing the new text over the old text replaces it.
Drawing sets pixels to the colour you give; it never erases the pixels that were set before. A shorter text leaves the tail
of the longer one visible. Call fill(0) at the start of each frame, or erase only the area you redraw with fill_rect.

py-emb-dsp-bar   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L3   family: py-emb-dsp-fit-and-alternatives
Prerequisites: py-emb-dsp-wrap. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The bar length can be the value itself.
A reading such as an ADC value of 40000 does not fit in 128 pixels. Map the value range to the bar range with integer
scaling, value * width // max_value, and clamp the result so a value above the maximum or below zero cannot draw
outside the display.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def bar_bad(value, max_value, width):

2. Overview and mental model: Bluetooth Low Energy
Bluetooth Low Energy lets a board advertise itself and exchange small values with a phone. MicroPython offers the
bluetooth module with an IRQ callback for events such as connect, disconnect and write.
The recurring errors are wrong advertising field lengths, an overflowing payload, big-endian UUIDs, notifications
larger than the MTU and not advertising again after a disconnect.
This chapter tests the byte-level code and the event logic only; the radio, pairing and the bluetooth module itself are
not simulated and need a real board.
Toolbox

Each advertising field is length, type, data, and the length counts the type byte
py-emb-ble-adv   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-ble-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-ble-limit. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. The first byte of a field is the length of the data.
An advertising payload is a sequence of fields: one byte of length, one byte of type, then the data. The length counts
the type byte and the data, so a field with n data bytes has length n + 1. A wrong length makes scanners stop parsing
the payload at that field.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import struct
def field_bad(adv_type, data):
    return bytes([len(data), adv_type]) + data
Correct:
 import struct
def field(adv_type, data):
    return bytes([len(data) + 1, adv_type]) + data
Put 16-bit UUIDs into advertising data in little-endian byte order
py-emb-ble-uuid   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-ble-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-ble-limit. Follow-up: py-emb-ble-chunk. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The UUID 0x181A is written as the bytes 18 1A.
Bluetooth sends multi-byte numbers least significant byte first. The service UUID 0x181A (Environmental Sensing) is
therefore the bytes 1A 18 in the payload. Build it with struct.pack("<H", uuid) and not with ">H".
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import struct
def uuid16_bad(u):
    return struct.pack(">H", u)
Correct:
 import struct
def uuid16(u):
    return struct.pack("<H", u)

Python on hardware, Bluetooth Low Energy: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
A legacy advertising packet holds 31 bytes, so shorten the name before it overflows
py-emb-ble-limit   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: py-emb-ble-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-ble-adv. Follow-up: py-emb-ble-uuid. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. The device name can be as long as you like.
The payload has room for 31 bytes, and the flags field already takes 3. The name field adds 2 bytes of overhead, so a
name has at most 26 characters if there is nothing else. Use the shortened-name type (0x08) when you have to cut it,
and the complete-name type (0x09) when it fits.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def name_field_bad(name):
    return bytes([len(name) + 1, 0x09]) + name
Correct:
 def name_field(name, room=26):
    if len(name) > room:
        return bytes([room + 1, 0x08]) + name[:room]
    return bytes([len(name) + 1, 0x09]) + name

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Split a notification into chunks of MTU minus 3 bytes
py-emb-ble-chunk   lens: iteration   level: L3   family: py-emb-ble-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-ble-uuid. Follow-up: py-emb-ble-irq. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Any payload can be sent in one notification.
The default ATT MTU is 23 bytes and 3 of them are the header, so a notification carries at most 20 bytes of data.
Larger values are cut off or rejected. Send a long message in slices of mtu - 3 bytes, and let the receiver join them.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def chunks_bad(data, mtu=23):
    return [data]
Correct:
 def chunks(data, mtu=23):
    n = mtu - 3
    return [data[i:i + n] for i in range(0, len(data), n)]
Handle connect and disconnect events and restart advertising after a disconnect
py-emb-ble-irq   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: py-emb-ble-patterns
Prerequisites: py-emb-ble-chunk. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The device keeps advertising after a central connects and disconnects.
The IRQ handler receives an event number and data. On a central connect the controller stops advertising, and after
the central disconnects it stays silent until you advertise again, so the device can never be found again. Track
connected handles in a set and restart advertising on the disconnect event.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

_DISCONNECT = 2
def irq_bad(ble, conns, event, handle):
    if event == _CONNECT:

    elif event == _DISCONNECT:
        conns.discard(handle)

_DISCONNECT = 2
def irq(ble, conns, event, handle):

    elif event == _DISCONNECT:
        conns.discard(handle)

2. Overview and mental model: Bytes, struct and bit operations
Registers and packets are bytes, and meaning lives in bit positions. MicroPython offers bytes, bytearray, the struct
module and Python integer operators, which cover nearly everything a driver needs.
The recurring errors are the wrong byte order, treating signed values as unsigned, mixing a bit number with a mask,
masking before shifting, and reading BCD as binary.
The helpers are pure Python and give the same answers on a board; the examples ran on the MicroPython unix port.
Toolbox
