Name the byte order in every struct format: ">" is big-endian and "<" is little-endian
py-emb-byt-endian   lens: access   level: L1   family: py-emb-byt-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-byt-signed. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. struct.unpack("<H", data) is the right way to read a 16-bit sensor value.
The prefix selects the byte order. Most I2C sensors send the high byte first, which is ">" (big-endian); the ESP32 and
ARM cores store integers little-endian ("<"). With the wrong prefix 0x1234 becomes 0x3412. Always write the prefix
explicitly and avoid the native default, whose alignment and size depend on the platform.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import struct
def read_u16_bad(data):
    return struct.unpack("<H", data)[0]
Correct:
 import struct
def read_u16(data):
    return struct.unpack(">H", data)[0]
Set, clear and test bits with masks built by shifting 1 left by the bit number
py-emb-byt-bits   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-byt-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-byt-signed. Follow-up: py-emb-byt-field. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. x | n sets bit number n.
The bit number and the bit mask are different things. To set bit 3 use x | (1 << 3). Clear it with x & ~(1 << 3) and test it
with (x >> 3) & 1. Writing x | 3 sets bits 0 and 1. Name the masks with constants such as LED_BIT = 3 to keep the
code readable.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def set_bit_bad(x, n):
    return x | n
Correct:
 def set_bit(x, n):
    return x | (1 << n)
def clear_bit(x, n):
    return x & ~(1 << n)
def test_bit(x, n):
    return (x >> n) & 1

Page 4
Use a lowercase format code for signed values: ">h" and not ">H"
py-emb-byt-signed   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: py-emb-byt-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-byt-endian. Follow-up: py-emb-byt-bits. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The format code H also returns negative numbers for readings below zero.
Uppercase codes (B, H, I) are unsigned and lowercase (b, h, i) are signed. A temperature of -2 degrees arrives as
0xFFFE; unpack with ">H" gives 65534. Use ">h" for signed 16-bit values. The same applies to one byte, where 0xFF
is 255 with B and -1 with b.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

def temp_bad(data):
    return struct.unpack(">H", data)[0]
Correct:
 import struct
def temp(data):
    return struct.unpack(">h", data)[0]

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Real-time clock chips store time as BCD, with a decimal digit in each nibble
py-emb-byt-bcd   lens: transformation   level: L3   family: py-emb-byt-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-byt-field. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The byte 0x59 means 89 seconds.
In binary-coded decimal the high nibble is the tens digit and the low nibble the ones digit, so 0x59 is 59, not 89.
Convert with (b >> 4) * 10 + (b & 0x0F) and back with ((n // 10) << 4) | (n % 10). Parsing it as a normal integer gives
out-of-range minutes and seconds.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def bcd_bad(b):
    return b
Correct:
 def bcd_to_int(b):
    return (b >> 4) * 10 + (b & 0x0F)
def int_to_bcd(n):
    return ((n // 10) << 4) | (n % 10)
Extract a bit field by shifting right and then masking with width ones
py-emb-byt-field   lens: transformation   level: L3   family: py-emb-byt-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-byt-bits. Follow-up: py-emb-byt-bcd. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Masking first and shifting later gives the field value.
To read width bits that start at bit shift, shift the register right by shift and then mask with (1 << width) - 1. Masking first
leaves the bits in place, so the result is multiplied by 2 to the power shift. Writing a field is the reverse: clear the field,
then OR in the shifted value.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def field_bad(reg, shift, width):
    return reg & (((1 << width) - 1) << shift)
Correct:
 def field(reg, shift, width):
    return (reg >> shift) & ((1 << width) - 1)
def set_field(reg, shift, width, value):
    mask = ((1 << width) - 1) << shift
    return (reg & ~mask) | ((value << shift) & mask)

2. Overview and mental model: Boot, main and modules
A MicroPython board runs boot.py and then main.py at power-up, and the REPL becomes available when they stop.
Good start-up code stays importable, survives missing modules and never locks you out.
Mistakes are hardware set-up at module level, unconditional imports of port-specific modules, no safe-mode escape,
bare excepts and ignoring why the board restarted.
Examples run on the MicroPython unix port; boot.py and main.py execution itself is not reproduced, only the code
patterns they use.
Toolbox
 import machine
from machine import Pin
def main():
    pass
if machine.reset_cause() == machine.WDT_RESET:
    pass
if Pin(14, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP).value():
    main()

Put start-up code in functions and run main() only under the __main__ guard
py-emb-boot-guard   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-boot-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-boot-optional. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Code at the top of a module runs only when the board starts.
Module-level statements run every time the module is imported, including when a test or another file imports it.
Hardware set-up there switches pins on and blocks the import. Define init() and main() and call main() under if
__name__ == "__main__" so the file can be imported safely.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin
led_bad = Pin(25, Pin.OUT)
led_bad.on()
Correct:
 from machine import Pin
led = None
def init():
    global led
    led = Pin(26, Pin.OUT)
def main():
    init()
    led.on()
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Check a safe-mode pin first so a bad main program cannot lock you out of the board
py-emb-boot-safe   lens: access   level: L2   family: py-emb-boot-access
Prerequisites: py-emb-boot-optional. Follow-up: py-emb-boot-recover. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. If main.py has a loop that never ends the board can still be reached over USB.
A main program that crashes, resets or blocks right away makes it hard to connect and fix it. Read a jumper or button
pin at the very start: if it is held low, return immediately and leave the REPL available. Decide it with a pull-up so a
missing jumper means normal start.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def should_run_bad(pin):
    return True
Correct:
 from machine import Pin
def should_run(pin):
    return pin.value() == 1

Import optional hardware modules inside try and except ImportError
py-emb-boot-optional   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: py-emb-boot-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-boot-guard. Follow-up: py-emb-boot-safe. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. import network works on every MicroPython board.
Ports differ: a board without Wi-Fi has no network module, and the unix port has none of the hardware ones. A plain
import then stops the program with ImportError. Wrap the import, store None when it is missing, and test it before
use, so the same file runs on a laptop for testing and on the board.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def wifi_bad():
    import network_missing_bad
    return network_missing_bad
Correct:
 try:
    import network_missing
except ImportError:
    network_missing = None
def has_wifi():
    return network_missing is not None

2. Overview and mental model: RPi.GPIO on the Raspberry Pi
RPi.GPIO is the long-standing library for GPIO on the Raspberry Pi. It is lower level than gpiozero: you choose the
numbering mode, set up each channel and release the pins yourself.
Typical errors are a missing setmode, writing to a channel that is not an output, reading a pull-up button as active
high, polling instead of edge callbacks and no cleanup.
Examples run against a simulated RPi.GPIO module that raises the same RuntimeError messages as the library for
these mistakes; newer Pi models and kernels may need a compatible replacement library such as rpi-lgpio.
Toolbox
 import RPi.GPIO as GPIO
GPIO.setmode(GPIO.BCM)
GPIO.setup(17, GPIO.OUT)
GPIO.output(17, GPIO.HIGH)
GPIO.cleanup()

Call GPIO.setmode before setup, and choose BCM or BOARD numbering once
py-emb-rg-mode   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-rg-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-rg-output. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. GPIO.setup(17, GPIO.OUT) works without any other call.
RPi.GPIO refuses to configure a channel until the numbering mode is set: GPIO.BCM uses the Broadcom GPIO
numbers, GPIO.BOARD uses the physical header position. Without setmode, setup raises RuntimeError. Pick one
mode for the whole program, since BCM 17 and BOARD 17 are different pins.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import RPi.GPIO as GPIO
def setup_bad(pin):
    GPIO.setup(pin, GPIO.OUT)
Correct:
 import RPi.GPIO as GPIO
def setup_ok(pin):
    GPIO.setmode(GPIO.BCM)
    GPIO.setup(pin, GPIO.OUT)
With pull_up_down=PUD_UP the pin reads 1 when released and 0 when pressed
py-emb-rg-pull   lens: access   level: L2   family: py-emb-rg-access
Prerequisites: py-emb-rg-output. Follow-up: py-emb-rg-edge. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. GPIO.input returns 1 when the button is pressed.
A button between the pin and ground with the pull-up enabled reads 1 at rest and 0 while pressed. The test for
pressed is GPIO.input(pin) == 0. Without a pull resistor the input floats, so always pass pull_up_down.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import RPi.GPIO as GPIO
def pressed_bad(pin):
    return GPIO.input(pin) == 1
Correct:
 import RPi.GPIO as GPIO
def pressed_ok(pin):
    GPIO.setup(pin, GPIO.IN, pull_up_down=GPIO.PUD_UP)
    return GPIO.input(pin) == 0

Only a channel set up as OUT can be written with GPIO.output
py-emb-rg-output   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-rg-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-rg-mode. Follow-up: py-emb-rg-pull. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. GPIO.output works on any channel after setmode.
A channel must be configured as an output first. GPIO.output on a channel that is an input, or was never set up,
raises RuntimeError. Use GPIO.setup(pin, GPIO.OUT, initial=GPIO.LOW) so the level is defined from the first
moment.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import RPi.GPIO as GPIO
def write_bad(pin, v):
    GPIO.output(pin, v)
Correct:
 import RPi.GPIO as GPIO
def write_ok(pin, v):
    GPIO.setup(pin, GPIO.OUT, initial=GPIO.LOW)
    GPIO.output(pin, v)
    return GPIO.input(pin)

Call GPIO.cleanup() in a finally block so the pins are released
py-emb-rg-cleanup   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-rg-edge-cases

    finally:

bounce. The callback gets the channel number, so one function can serve several buttons.

2. Overview and mental model: ADC analog input
An ADC turns a voltage into a number. MicroPython machine.ADC.read_u16() returns 0 to 65535 on every port, so
conversion code is the same across boards.
Mistakes come from scaling by the chip resolution, trusting single noisy samples, forgetting the divider ratio or the
sensor offset, and using a single switching threshold.
Examples run on the MicroPython unix port with a simulated ADC; real converters add noise, an offset and a
reference that varies with the supply.
Toolbox
 from machine import ADC, Pin
adc = ADC(Pin(26))
mv = adc.read_u16() * 3300 // 65535

read_u16 always returns 0 to 65535, so scale by 65535 and not by the chip resolution
py-emb-adc-scale   lens: access   level: L1   family: py-emb-adc-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-adc-median. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A 10-bit ADC returns 0 to 1023 from read_u16.
machine.ADC.read_u16() normalises every converter to 16 bits, so a 12-bit or 10-bit chip still returns values up to
65535. Convert to millivolts with raw * vref_mv // 65535. Dividing by 1023 or 4095 gives results that are 64 or 16
times too large. vref is the reference voltage, commonly 3300 mV.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import ADC
def to_mv_bad(raw):
    return raw * 3300 // 1023
Correct:
 from machine import ADC
def to_mv(raw, vref_mv=3300):
    return raw * vref_mv // 65535
Convert an analog temperature sensor with its datasheet offset, not just a scale factor
py-emb-adc-tmp36   lens: creation   level: L2   family: py-emb-adc-creation
Prerequisites: py-emb-adc-divider. Follow-up: py-emb-adc-hysteresis. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The TMP36 output is 10 mV per degree Celsius, so temperature is mV divided by 10.
The TMP36 outputs 750 mV at 25 degrees Celsius with a slope of 10 mV per degree and a 500 mV offset at 0
degrees. Subtract the offset before dividing: temp_tenths = (mv - 500). Without the offset every reading is 50 degrees
too high. Keep the result in tenths of a degree to stay in integers.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def tmp36_bad(mv):
    return mv // 10
Correct:
 def tmp36(mv):
    return (mv - 500) // 10

Undo a voltage divider by multiplying by (r1 + r2) / r2 to get the real battery voltage
py-emb-adc-divider   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-adc-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-adc-median. Follow-up: py-emb-adc-tmp36. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The pin voltage is the battery voltage.
A divider with r1 from the battery to the pin and r2 from the pin to ground gives v_pin = v_batt * r2 / (r1 + r2). To
recover the battery voltage multiply by (r1 + r2) / r2. Choose resistors so that the maximum battery voltage stays
below the ADC reference, and keep the arithmetic in integers (millivolts) to avoid float drift.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def battery_mv_bad(pin_mv, r1, r2):
    return pin_mv * r2 // (r1 + r2)
Correct:
 def battery_mv(pin_mv, r1, r2):
    return pin_mv * (r1 + r2) // r2

Take the median of a few samples to reject a spike that a mean would smear into the result
py-emb-adc-median   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-adc-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-adc-scale. Follow-up: py-emb-adc-divider. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. The mean of several readings is always the most robust value.
Noise on an analog line comes as small jitter and as occasional spikes. The mean moves with a spike, while the
median ignores it. Read an odd number of samples, sort them and take the middle one. Use a mean when the noise
is symmetric and small, and a median when single bad readings occur.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def mean_bad(samples):
    return sum(samples) // len(samples)
Correct:
 def median(samples):
    s = sorted(samples)
    return s[len(s) // 2]

2. Overview and mental model: MQTT messaging
MQTT is a light publish and subscribe protocol that many IoT devices use. On MicroPython, umqtt.simple gives a
small blocking client: connect, publish, subscribe and check_msg.
Typical errors are mixing bytes and strings, never calling check_msg, comparing topics with equality, forgetting the
keep-alive ping, and no last will.
Examples run against a simulated in-memory broker; real brokers add network delay, QoS handling, authentication
and TLS.
Toolbox
 from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
c = MQTTClient("dev1", "broker.local", keepalive=60)

MQTT topics and payloads are bytes: encode what you send and decode what you receive

Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-mqt-poll. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. The callback receives strings.
umqtt passes the topic and the payload to your callback as bytes, and publish expects bytes. Encode text with
.encode() before sending, and decode in the callback before comparing with a string. Comparing b"on" with "on" is
never true.

 from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
got_bad = []
def on_msg_bad(topic, msg):
    got_bad.append(msg == "on")
Correct:
 from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
got = []
def on_msg(topic, msg):
    got.append(msg.decode() == "on")
def send(client, topic, text):
    client.publish(topic.encode(), text.encode())
Call check_msg() regularly, because incoming messages are only handled when you do

Prerequisites: py-emb-mqt-bytes. Follow-up: py-emb-mqt-topics. Complexity: O(rounds).
 Common misconception. A subscribed callback is called by itself.
umqtt.simple has no background thread. A subscription only queues messages in the connection, and the callback
runs from check_msg() (non-blocking) or wait_msg() (blocking). Call check_msg() in every main loop iteration, and do
not let the loop block for longer than the keep-alive interval.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
def run_bad(client, cb):
    client.set_callback(cb)
    client.subscribe(b"cmd")
Correct:
 from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
def run(client, cb, rounds=3):
    client.set_callback(cb)
    client.subscribe(b"cmd")
    for _ in range(rounds):
        client.check_msg()

publishes rarely, call client.ping() on a schedule, for example every half of the keep-alive time. Compare times with
ticks_diff.

 import time
def ping_due(now, last, keepalive_s):
    return time.ticks_diff(now, last) >= keepalive_s * 500

Prerequisites: py-emb-mqt-poll. Follow-up: py-emb-mqt-ping. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A topic matches a subscription when the two strings are equal.
The filter sensors/+/temp matches any one level in the middle, and sensors/# matches everything below sensors.
Compare the filter and the topic level by level after splitting on the slash. A plain string comparison treats the

 def match(flt, topic):

    t = topic.split("/")

Prerequisites: py-emb-mqt-ping. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A device announces its own shutdown before it goes offline.
A device that loses power cannot send "offline". Set a last will with set_last_will before connect(): the broker
publishes it when the connection ends without a clean disconnect. Publish a retained "online" message after
connecting and make the will a retained "offline" on the same topic.

    c.connect()

 from umqtt.simple import MQTTClient
def start(c, topic=b"dev/1/status"):
    c.set_last_will(topic, b"offline", retain=True)
    c.connect()
    c.publish(topic, b"online", retain=True)

Prompt. What problem does an MQTT last-will message solve, and why is it retained?

2. Overview and mental model: Wi-Fi connectivity
Boards such as the ESP32 and the Pico W join a Wi-Fi network through network.WLAN. The connection is
asynchronous, can fail in several ways and can drop at any time.
The recurring problems are using the network before it is up, one handling for every failure, the RSSI sign, no
reconnect logic and leaving the radio on.
Examples run against a simulated WLAN with a configurable delay; real radios add scan time, DHCP delay, roaming
and country settings.
Toolbox

wlan = network.WLAN(network.STA_IF)
wlan.active(True)

connect() returns at once: wait for isconnected() with a timeout
py-emb-wif-wait   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: py-emb-wif-edge-cases
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-wif-status. Complexity: O(timeout).
 Common misconception. After wlan.connect() the device is online.
connect() only starts the association; the link is up some time later, and it may never come up. Poll
wlan.isconnected() with a short sleep and a deadline, and report failure when the deadline passes. Using the network
too early gives OSError on the first socket.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 import network
def connect_bad(ssid, pw):
    wlan = network.WLAN(network.STA_IF)
    wlan.active(True)
    wlan.connect(ssid, pw)
    return wlan
Correct:
 import time, network
def connect(ssid, pw, timeout_ms=10000):
    wlan = network.WLAN(network.STA_IF)
    wlan.active(True)
    wlan.connect(ssid, pw)
    start = time.ticks_ms()
    while not wlan.isconnected():
        if time.ticks_diff(time.ticks_ms(), start) > timeout_ms:
            return None
        time.sleep_ms(100)
    return wlan
Pick the strongest network by the largest RSSI, and decode the SSID bytes
py-emb-wif-scan   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: py-emb-wif-ordering
Prerequisites: py-emb-wif-status. Follow-up: py-emb-wif-reconnect. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. The smallest RSSI is the strongest signal.
scan() returns tuples (ssid, bssid, channel, rssi, security, hidden) where the SSID is bytes. RSSI is measured in dBm
and is negative, so -40 is stronger than -80. The strongest network has the largest value, which max() finds. Decode
the SSID before comparing it with a configured name.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def best_bad(nets):
    return min(nets, key=lambda n: n[3])[0]
Correct:
 def best(nets):
    top = max(nets, key=lambda n: n[3])
    return top[0].decode()

Read wlan.status() to tell a wrong password from a missing network
py-emb-wif-status   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L2   family: py-emb-wif-fit-and-alternatives
Prerequisites: py-emb-wif-wait. Follow-up: py-emb-wif-scan. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A failed connection always has the same cause and fix.
status() gives the reason while the link is not up. A wrong password (STAT_WRONG_PASSWORD) needs new
credentials and retrying will not help. A missing network (STAT_NO_AP_FOUND) may appear later, so waiting and
retrying makes sense. Compare with the named constants because the numeric values depend on the port.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

    return "failed"

 import network
def reason(status):
    if status == network.STAT_WRONG_PASSWORD:
        return "bad password"
    if status == network.STAT_NO_AP_FOUND:
        return "not found"
    return "other"

2. Overview and mental model: Cooperative scheduler
Many programs need several periodic jobs: read a sensor every 100 ms, blink an LED every 500 ms, send data every
minute. A small cooperative scheduler runs each job when its due time arrives, without threads.
Typical bugs are due-time comparisons that break at tick wrap-around, drift from basing the next run on the current
time, bursts after a long block, unfair ordering and one failing job stopping all of them.
The scheduler logic is plain Python on virtual ticks; real jitter depends on how long each job takes on the board.
Toolbox

A task is due when ticks_diff(now, due) is zero or positive
py-emb-sch-due   lens: ordering   level: L1   family: py-emb-sch-ordering
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-sch-drift. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. now >= due is a reliable test.
The tick counter wraps, so a due time that was computed just before the wrap is a small number afterwards and now
>= due is wrong. ticks_diff(now, due) >= 0 gives the right answer for any interval below half the counter range.
Compute due times with ticks_add.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def due_bad(now, due):
    return now >= due
Correct:
 import time
def due(now, due_at):
    return time.ticks_diff(now, due_at) >= 0
Schedule the next run from the previous due time, so late starts do not accumulate drift
py-emb-sch-drift   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: py-emb-sch-iteration
Prerequisites: py-emb-sch-due. Follow-up: py-emb-sch-catchup. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Add the period to the current time after each run.
If a task runs 3 ms late and the next due time is "now + period", every run shifts by a few milliseconds and the rate
slowly drifts. Adding the period to the previous due time keeps the long-term rate exact; only the single late run is late.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def next_bad(now, due_at, period):
    return now + period
Correct:
 import time
def next_due(now, due_at, period):
    return time.ticks_add(due_at, period)
If a task is far behind, skip the missed runs instead of running them in a burst
py-emb-sch-catchup   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-sch-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-sch-drift. Follow-up: py-emb-sch-order. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A task that missed five periods should run five times in a row.
After a long block, the due time is several periods in the past. Looping until it is in the future runs the task many times
back to back, which can starve other tasks and repeat stale work. Run it once and move the due time to the next slot
after now.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def reschedule_bad(due_at, now, period):
    return due_at + period
Correct:
 def reschedule(due_at, now, period):
    behind = now - due_at
    if behind >= period:
        due_at += (behind // period) * period
    return due_at + period

failing task can be disabled.

Correct:
 def run_all(tasks, errors):

Run the task with the earliest due time first

 Common misconception. Running tasks in list order is fair.
With a list order, a task near the end can wait while later-added tasks that are not due yet are examined first, and two
due tasks run in the order they were added and not in the order they became due. Pick the due task whose due time
is earliest, so the most overdue one goes first.

Correct:
 def pick(tasks, now):
    ready = [t for t in tasks if t["due"] <= now]
    if not ready:

Prompt. Why does computing the next run as "now + period" make a periodic task drift?

late. If the next run is based on the actual start time, every delay is added to all later runs and the lateness piles up, so

2. Overview and mental model: Serial framing and CRC
Serial links deliver a stream of bytes with no message boundaries and occasional corruption. A frame adds a start
marker, a length or end marker, and a checksum or CRC so the receiver can find messages and reject damaged
ones.
Bugs come from using the wrong checksum, forgetting to mask a CRC register, mismatched CRC parameters,
trusting an unchecked start byte, and payload bytes that look like markers.
The CRC check values are the standard ones for b"123456789". The code is pure Python, so it behaves the same on
a board; speed on a slow microcontroller is not measured.
Toolbox
 def checksum(data):
    c = 0
    for b in data:
        c ^= b
    return c
frame = bytes([0xAA, 2]) + b"hi"
frame += bytes([checksum(frame[1:])])

An XOR checksum folds every byte together with xor, and a sum is a different checksum
py-emb-frame-xor   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-frame-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-frame-crc8. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Adding the bytes gives the NMEA checksum.
NMEA 0183 sentences end with an XOR of every character between the dollar sign and the asterisk, written as two
hex digits. Addition gives a different value, so a correct message is rejected. Start from 0 and apply ^ to each byte,
and format with "%02X".
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def checksum_bad(data):
    s = 0
    for b in data:
        s = (s + b) & 0xFF
    return s
Correct:
 def checksum(data):
    c = 0
    for b in data:
        c ^= b
    return c
The same polynomial with a different start value is a different CRC-16
py-emb-frame-crc16   lens: equality   level: L2   family: py-emb-frame-equality
Prerequisites: py-emb-frame-crc8. Follow-up: py-emb-frame-parse. Complexity: O(8n).
 Common misconception. Any CRC-16 with polynomial 0x1021 is CRC-CCITT.
The polynomial 0x1021 is shared by several algorithms. CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE starts at 0xFFFF and gives 0x29B1
for b"123456789"; starting at 0x0000 gives the XMODEM variant, 0x31C3. Both ends must agree on initial value,
polynomial, bit order and final xor, so write the parameters into the protocol description.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def crc16_xmodem(data):
    crc = 0x0000
    for b in data:
        crc ^= b << 8
        for _ in range(8):
            crc = ((crc << 1) ^ 0x1021) & 0xFFFF if crc & 0x8000 else (crc << 1) & 0xFFFF
    return crc

Page 4
Correct:
 def crc16_ccitt(data, init=0xFFFF):
    crc = init
    for b in data:
        crc ^= b << 8
        for _ in range(8):
            if crc & 0x8000:
                crc = ((crc << 1) ^ 0x1021) & 0xFFFF
            else:
                crc = (crc << 1) & 0xFFFF
    return crc
Compute CRC-8 bit by bit and mask to eight bits after every shift
py-emb-frame-crc8   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-frame-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-frame-xor. Follow-up: py-emb-frame-crc16. Complexity: O(8n).
 Common misconception. The shift can be left unmasked, since Python integers grow.
A CRC register is eight bits wide. Python integers are unbounded, so an unmasked left shift keeps the high bits and
the result is wrong. Use polynomial 0x07: for each byte xor it into the register, then eight times shift left, xor with the
polynomial when the top bit was set and mask with 0xFF. The check value for b"123456789" is 0xF4.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def crc8_bad(data, poly=0x07):
    crc = 0
    for b in data:
        crc ^= b
        for _ in range(8):
            crc = (crc << 1) ^ poly if crc & 0x80 else crc << 1
    return crc
Correct:
 def crc8(data, poly=0x07):
    crc = 0
    for b in data:
        crc ^= b
        for _ in range(8):
            if crc & 0x80:
                crc = ((crc << 1) ^ poly) & 0xFF
            else:
                crc = (crc << 1) & 0xFF
    return crc

Prerequisites: py-emb-frame-crc16. Follow-up: py-emb-frame-slip. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A frame that starts with the start byte is valid.
A frame here is 0xAA, a length byte, the payload and an XOR checksum of the length and payload. A parser that
trusts the start byte returns garbage when bytes are lost. Check that the buffer is long enough, that the length fits, and
that the checksum matches; return None for anything else so the caller can resynchronise.

Correct:

    if len(buf) < 3 or buf[0] != 0xAA:
        return None
    n = buf[1]
    if len(buf) < 3 + n:
        return None
    payload = bytes(buf[2:2 + n])
    if checksum(buf[1:2 + n]) != buf[2 + n]:
        return None
    return payload
def build(payload):
    body = bytes([len(payload)]) + payload
    return bytes([0xAA]) + body + bytes([checksum(body)])
Escape the end marker inside the payload with byte stuffing
py-emb-frame-slip   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-frame-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-frame-parse. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A payload can contain any byte without special treatment.
If a frame ends at byte 0xC0, a payload that contains 0xC0 ends it early. SLIP replaces 0xC0 inside the data with
0xDB 0xDC and 0xDB with 0xDB 0xDD. Escape 0xDB first or the escape bytes are escaped twice, and decode by
reversing the pairs.

    return bytes(data) + b"\xc0"

Page 7
Correct:
 def slip(data):
    out = bytearray()
    for b in data:
        if b == 0xC0:
            out.extend(b"\xdb\xdc")
        elif b == 0xDB:
            out.extend(b"\xdb\xdd")
        else:
            out.append(b)
    out.append(0xC0)
    return bytes(out)
def unslip(frame):
    out = bytearray()
    i = 0
    while i < len(frame) and frame[i] != 0xC0:
        if frame[i] == 0xDB:
            i += 1
            out.append(0xC0 if frame[i] == 0xDC else 0xDB)
        else:
            out.append(frame[i])
        i += 1
    return bytes(out)

2. Overview and mental model: Hardware timers
A machine.Timer calls a function after a delay or at a regular rate while the main program does something else. The
program can also keep its own deadlines with time.ticks_ms, ticks_add and ticks_diff.
Mistakes include forgetting PERIODIC mode, mixing frequency and period, leaving timers running, blocking with
sleep, and comparing wrapped tick values with plain operators.
Examples run on the MicroPython unix port with a virtual clock: sleep_ms advances simulated time and fires due
timers, so no real time passes.
Toolbox
 import time
from machine import Timer
t = Timer(mode=Timer.PERIODIC, freq=2, callback=lambda t: print("tick"))
time.sleep_ms(1000)

A Timer repeats only in PERIODIC mode; the default one-shot mode fires once
py-emb-tim-periodic   lens: creation   level: L1   family: py-emb-tim-creation

 Common misconception. Timer(period=100, callback=f) calls f every 100 ms.
A machine.Timer has two modes. ONE_SHOT calls the callback once after the period, PERIODIC repeats it. Pass
mode=Timer.PERIODIC explicitly, because the default differs between ports and a missing mode is a silent bug. The
callback receives the timer object and runs in interrupt context on many ports, so keep it short.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

from machine import Timer
ticks_bad = []
def cb_bad(t):
    ticks_bad.append(1)
tim_bad = Timer(mode=Timer.ONE_SHOT, period=100, callback=cb_bad)
Correct:
 import time
from machine import Timer
ticks = []
def cb(t):
    ticks.append(1)
tim = Timer(mode=Timer.PERIODIC, period=100, callback=cb)
freq is in hertz and period is in milliseconds, so do not mix them
py-emb-tim-freq   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: py-emb-tim-transformation
Prerequisites: py-emb-tim-oneshot. Follow-up: py-emb-tim-deinit. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Timer(freq=10) and Timer(period=10) mean the same.
freq=10 means 10 times per second, a period of 100 ms. period=10 means every 10 ms, which is 100 times per
second. Mixing them changes the rate by a factor of ten. Convert explicitly with period_ms = 1000 // hz so the unit is
visible in the code.

from machine import Timer
n10_bad = []
def cb10_bad(t):
    n10_bad.append(1)
tim10_bad = Timer(mode=Timer.PERIODIC, period=10, callback=cb10_bad)

from machine import Timer

 Common misconception. Dropping the variable stops the timer.

running. Call deinit() when you no longer need it, for example before entering a different mode of operation or before
a soft reset, and create the timer again when needed.

Use a one-shot timer for a delayed action instead of blocking with sleep
py-emb-tim-oneshot   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: py-emb-tim-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: py-emb-tim-periodic. Follow-up: py-emb-tim-freq. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. time.sleep_ms(200) before turning the LED off is the simplest way to delay.
Sleeping blocks the program, so buttons and sensors are ignored for the whole delay. A one-shot timer lets the main
loop carry on and runs the action once when the time is up. Re-arming the timer on every new event restarts the
delay, which is how a light stays on for 200 ms after the last motion.

from machine import Pin
lamp_bad = Pin(40, Pin.OUT)
def pulse_bad():
    lamp_bad.on()
    time.sleep_ms(200)
    lamp_bad.off()
Correct:
 import time
from machine import Pin, Timer
lamp = Pin(41, Pin.OUT)
off_timer = Timer()
def lamp_off(t):
    lamp.off()
def pulse():
    lamp.on()
    off_timer.init(mode=Timer.ONE_SHOT, period=200, callback=lamp_off)

Prerequisites: py-emb-tim-deinit. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. now >= deadline tells you that a deadline has passed.
ticks_ms() counts up to a limit and then wraps to zero, so a deadline computed near the end can be a small number.
Plain comparison then says the deadline has already passed. ticks_add computes the deadline with wrapping and
ticks_diff(now, deadline) >= 0 compares correctly as long as the interval is under half the range.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

    return now >= deadline
Correct:
 import time
def due(now, deadline):
    return time.ticks_diff(now, deadline) >= 0

2. Overview and mental model: Filters and PID control
Raw sensor values are noisy, and a controller that reacts to every wiggle is unstable. Filters smooth the signal and a
PID controller turns an error into an actuator command.
Typical errors are averaging forever, starting an exponential filter at zero, an integral that winds up, a derivative that
spikes on a setpoint change, and ignoring the real loop time.
Everything here is integer arithmetic so it runs on chips without an FPU; tuning constants must be found on the real
system, since the examples run only against numbers.
Toolbox
 class Ema:
    def __init__(self):
        self.y = None
    def add(self, x):
        self.y = x if self.y is None else self.y + (x - self.y) // 4
        return self.y

A moving average keeps a fixed window and divides by the window size
py-emb-flt-window   lens: iteration   level: L1   family: py-emb-flt-iteration
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-flt-ema. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Averaging every reading since start-up smooths the signal best.
An average over all readings reacts more and more slowly and its sum grows without limit. A moving average keeps
only the last n values. Add the new value, drop the oldest when the window is full and divide by the number of values
held. Dividing by the window size before it fills gives values that are too low.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class AvgBad:
    def __init__(self):
        self.vals = []
    def add(self, v):
        self.vals.append(v)
        return sum(self.vals) // len(self.vals)
Correct:
 class MovingAvg:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.vals = []
    def add(self, v):
        self.vals.append(v)
        if len(self.vals) > self.n:
            self.vals.pop(0)
        return sum(self.vals) // len(self.vals)
An exponential filter needs no history, but it must start from the first sample

Clamp the PID integral term so it cannot wind up while the output is saturated
py-emb-flt-windup   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: py-emb-flt-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-flt-ema. Follow-up: py-emb-flt-kick. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The integral term can grow without limit and the controller still behaves.
If the output is at its maximum and the error stays positive, the integral keeps growing. When the error finally changes
sign the integral is huge and the output stays saturated for a long time (windup). Clamp the integral to the range that
can still matter, or stop integrating while the output is saturated.

    def __init__(self, kp, ki):

Correct:

    def __init__(self, kp, ki, imax=100):
        self.kp, self.ki, self.imax, self.integral = kp, ki, imax, 0

        self.integral = max(-self.imax, min(self.imax, self.integral + error))
        return self.kp * error + self.ki * self.integral

Prerequisites: py-emb-flt-kick. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Loops run at exactly the same interval every time.

ms and sometimes 30 ms gives wrong results if the code assumes a constant step. Measure dt with ticks_diff and
scale: integral += error * dt, derivative = delta / dt.

2. Overview and mental model: Pin interrupts
A pin interrupt calls a handler when the level changes, so the program reacts to a button or a pulse without polling. In
MicroPython Pin.irq(handler, trigger) registers a function for IRQ_RISING, IRQ_FALLING or both.
The mistakes are the wrong edge for the wiring, handlers that do too much, events lost between a read and a clear,
and closures that all see the last loop value.
Examples run on the MicroPython unix port; the simulator calls the handler immediately when a test drives the pin,
whereas hardware interrupts can arrive at any instruction.
Toolbox
 from machine import Pin
n = [0]
def on_press(p):
    n[0] += 1
btn = Pin(14, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
btn.irq(on_press, Pin.IRQ_FALLING)

Choose the edge that matches the wiring: a pull-up button presses on the falling edge
py-emb-irq-edge   lens: access   level: L1   family: py-emb-irq-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: py-emb-irq-counter. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. IRQ_RISING detects a button press.
With the internal pull-up a button reads 1 when released and 0 when pressed, so the press is a falling edge and the
release is a rising edge. Register the handler with Pin.IRQ_FALLING to count presses. Using IRQ_RISING counts
the releases, and using both edges counts every press twice.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin

py-emb-irq-closure   lens: creation   level: L2   family: py-emb-irq-creation
Prerequisites: py-emb-irq-counter. Follow-up: py-emb-irq-atomic. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A lambda created in a loop remembers the value the variable had at that moment.
A closure captures the variable and not its value, so after the loop every handler sees the last value. A default
argument is evaluated when the lambda is created, so lambda p, i=i: freezes the current index. The same applies to
callbacks given to Timer and to asyncio tasks.

for i in range(3):

py-emb-irq-atomic   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: py-emb-irq-edge-cases
Prerequisites: py-emb-irq-closure. Follow-up: py-emb-irq-gate. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Reading the counter and then setting it to zero is safe.
An interrupt can fire between reading n = count and writing count = 0. The event it counted is then erased and never
processed. Wrap the pair in machine.disable_irq() and enable_irq(state) so it cannot be interrupted, and keep the
protected section as short as possible.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

def take_bad(between=None):
    n = count_bad[0]
    if between:

    count_bad[0] = 0

 from machine import disable_irq, enable_irq

def take_ok():
    state = disable_irq()
    n = count_ok[0]
    count_ok[0] = 0
    enable_irq(state)
    return n

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Count events in the handler and consume the count in the main loop, so no event is lost
py-emb-irq-counter   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: py-emb-irq-mutation
Prerequisites: py-emb-irq-edge. Follow-up: py-emb-irq-closure. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A boolean flag set by the handler records every event.
A flag only says that something happened since it was last cleared. Two events before the main loop looks give one
flag and one handled event. A counter that the handler increments keeps the number of events, and the main loop
subtracts what it processed. Keep the handler short: no printing, no allocation, no waiting.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 from machine import Pin
flag_bad = [False]
src_bad = Pin(12, Pin.IN)
def on_flag(pin):
    flag_bad[0] = True
src_bad.irq(on_flag, Pin.IRQ_RISING)
Correct:
 from machine import Pin
count = [0]
src = Pin(13, Pin.IN)
def on_edge(pin):
    count[0] += 1
src.irq(on_edge, Pin.IRQ_RISING)
def take():
    n = count[0]
    count[0] -= n
    return n

Measure frequency by counting rising edges in a fixed gate time
py-emb-irq-gate   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: py-emb-irq-complexity
Prerequisites: py-emb-irq-atomic. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Counting both edges gives the frequency of the signal.
A signal at f Hz has f rising edges and f falling edges per second. Counting both doubles the result. Count one edge
type for a gate time of gate_ms milliseconds and compute freq = edges * 1000 // gate_ms. A longer gate improves
resolution to 1000 / gate_ms Hz but delays the answer.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def freq_bad(edges, gate_ms):
    return edges * 1000 // gate_ms
Correct:
 def freq_hz(rising_edges, gate_ms):
    return rising_edges * 1000 // gate_ms

py-emb-irq-counter-ex2   format: explain-why   level: L2   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Why should an interrupt handler be short and only update a counter or flag, with the real work done in the
main loop?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). While a handler runs, other interrupts may be delayed and the main
program is stopped, so long handlers add latency and lose events. Printing, allocating memory or waiting inside a
handler can also fail or block, because the runtime may be in the middle of its own work. A counter or flag is a tiny
update, and the main loop can then process the events at a safe time.

Concept: Switch both inputs of an H-bridge off before changing direction
Misconception: Setting the new direction pin high and the old one low in any order is safe.
Explanation: If both inputs of one half of an H-bridge are high for even an instant, the supply is shorted through the transistors (shoot-through). Always turn the old input off first, wait the dead time that the driver needs, and only then turn the new one on.
Incorrect:
def reverse_bad(a, b):
    b.value(1)
    a.value(0)
Correct:
import time
def reverse(a, b, dead_ms=1):
    a.value(0)
    b.value(0)
    time.sleep_ms(dead_ms)
    b.value(1)
Complexity: O(1)

Prompt: Why must both H-bridge inputs be turned off before reversing a motor?

payload.answer: Each half of the bridge has a high-side and a low-side transistor. If both inputs are on at once, both transistors conduct and the supply is shorted to ground through them, which can destroy the driver. Switching everything off, waiting the dead time and then enabling the new input prevents the overlap.

Concept: Accelerate a stepper with shrinking step delays instead of starting at full speed
Misconception: The motor can start at its top speed.
Explanation: A stepper that starts at its maximum rate cannot pick up its load and loses steps or stalls. Start with a long delay between steps and shorten it a little each step until the cruise delay is reached. The list of delays can be computed once and reused.
Incorrect:
def delays_bad(n, cruise):
    return [cruise] * n
Correct:
def delays(n, start, cruise):
    out = []
    d = start
    for _ in range(n):
        out.append(d)

Concept: Step through the coil patterns with modulo so the index wraps in both directions
Misconception: Adding the direction to the index is enough to keep stepping.
Explanation: A full-step sequence of four coil patterns repeats forever. index + 1 runs off the end of the table at the fourth step. (index + direction) % 4 wraps both forward and backward, because Python gives a non-negative remainder for a positive divisor. Write the pattern to the four coil pins as one value.
Incorrect:
SEQ = (0b1000, 0b0100, 0b0010, 0b0001)
def advance_bad(i, d):
    return SEQ[i + d]
Correct:
SEQ2 = (0b1000, 0b0100, 0b0010, 0b0001)
def advance(i, d):
    return (i + d) % len(SEQ2)
Complexity: O(1)

Python (embedded) · actuator control on MicroPython boards · mutation · L2
Concept: Limit how far a servo or motor setpoint can move per update (slew rate)
Misconception: Jumping straight to the target angle is fine.
Explanation: A big instant change draws a surge of current and can jerk the mechanism or reset the board. Move toward the target by at most max_step per update. The move is a clamp on the difference, so it works in both directions and stops exactly at the target.
Incorrect:
def move_bad(cur, target, max_step):
    return target
Correct:
def move(cur, target, max_step):
    diff = target - cur
    diff = max(-max_step, min(max_step, diff))
    return cur + diff
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: Convert an angle to steps with the steps per revolution of your motor
Misconception: A stepper always has 200 steps per revolution.
Explanation: The common 28BYJ-48 geared stepper needs 2048 full steps (4096 half steps) for one turn of the output shaft, while a plain NEMA 17 motor has 200. Compute steps = angle * steps_per_rev // 360 and keep the motor value as a parameter. Integer division drops the remainder, so track the exact position to avoid drift.
Incorrect:
def steps_bad(angle):
    return angle * 200 // 360
Correct:
def steps_for(angle, steps_per_rev=2048):
    return angle * steps_per_rev // 360
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: Undo a voltage divider by multiplying by (r1 + r2) / r2 to get the real battery voltage
Misconception: The pin voltage is the battery voltage.
Explanation: A divider with r1 from the battery to the pin and r2 from the pin to ground gives v_pin = v_batt * r2 / (r1 + r2). To recover the battery voltage multiply by (r1 + r2) / r2. Choose resistors so that the maximum battery voltage stays below the ADC reference, and keep the arithmetic in integers (millivolts) to avoid float drift.
Incorrect:
def battery_mv_bad(pin_mv, r1, r2):
    return pin_mv * r2 // (r1 + r2)
Correct:
def battery_mv(pin_mv, r1, r2):
    return pin_mv * (r1 + r2) // r2
Complexity: O(1)

payload.answer: The ADC reference is usually 3.3 V and a pin above it can be damaged, so a divider scales the battery voltage down into range. With r1 on the battery side and r2 on the ground side the pin sees v_batt * r2 / (r1 + r2). The code multiplies the measured pin voltage by (r1 + r2) / r2 to recover the real battery voltage.

Explanation: A reading that hovers around a single threshold flips the output on every sample. A Schmitt trigger uses a high threshold to switch on and a lower one to switch off, so the band between them keeps the previous state. Keep the state in the function arguments or an object so the decision depends on history.
Incorrect:
def heater_bad(temp, limit):
    return temp < limit
Correct:
def heater(temp, was_on, low, high):
    if temp < low:
        return True
    if temp > high:
        return False
    return was_on
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: Take the median of a few samples to reject a spike that a mean would smear into the result
Misconception: The mean of several readings is always the most robust value.
Explanation: Noise on an analog line comes as small jitter and as occasional spikes. The mean moves with a spike, while the median ignores it. Read an odd number of samples, sort them and take the middle one. Use a mean when the noise is symmetric and small, and a median when single bad readings occur.
Incorrect:
def mean_bad(samples):
    return sum(samples) // len(samples)
Correct:
def median(samples):
    s = sorted(samples)
    return s[len(s) // 2]
Complexity: O(n log n)

Concept: read_u16 always returns 0 to 65535, so scale by 65535 and not by the chip resolution
Misconception: A 10-bit ADC returns 0 to 1023 from read_u16.
Explanation: machine.ADC.read_u16() normalises every converter to 16 bits, so a 12-bit or 10-bit chip still returns values up to 65535. Convert to millivolts with raw * vref_mv // 65535. Dividing by 1023 or 4095 gives results that are 64 or 16 times too large. vref is the reference voltage, commonly 3300 mV.

from machine import ADC
def to_mv_bad(raw):
    return raw * 3300 // 1023
Correct:
from machine import ADC
def to_mv(raw, vref_mv=3300):
    return raw * vref_mv // 65535
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: Convert an analog temperature sensor with its datasheet offset, not just a scale factor
Misconception: The TMP36 output is 10 mV per degree Celsius, so temperature is mV divided by 10.
Explanation: The TMP36 outputs 750 mV at 25 degrees Celsius with a slope of 10 mV per degree and a 500 mV offset at 0 degrees. Subtract the offset before dividing: temp_tenths = (mv - 500). Without the offset every reading is 50 degrees too high. Keep the result in tenths of a degree to stay in integers.
Incorrect:
def tmp36_bad(mv):
    return mv // 10
Correct:
def tmp36(mv):
    return (mv - 500) // 10
Complexity: O(1)

Python (embedded) · asyncio for cooperative tasks on MicroPython · creation · L1
Concept: Calling a coroutine function without await creates the coroutine and runs nothing
Misconception: Calling tick() starts the work, the same as a normal function.
Explanation: An async def function returns a coroutine object when called. The body runs only when it is awaited or scheduled with asyncio.create_task or asyncio.run. A bare call silently does nothing, so the LED never blinks and no error appears. Always await it, or create a task.
Incorrect:
import asyncio
count_bad = [0]
async def tick_bad():
    count_bad[0] += 1
def start_bad():
    tick_bad()
Correct:
import asyncio
count = [0]
async def tick():
    count[0] += 1
async def run_once():
    await tick()
Complexity: O(1)

Explanation: asyncio is cooperative: tasks switch only at an await. time.sleep_ms blocks the whole program, so a heartbeat task, a button task and a network task all freeze for the delay. await asyncio.sleep_ms gives control back to the loop. The same holds for any long loop without an await.
Incorrect:
import asyncio, time
async def blocking_job():
    time.sleep_ms(55)
Correct:
import asyncio
beats = [0]
async def heartbeat():
    while True:
        await asyncio.sleep_ms(10)
        beats[0] += 1
async def friendly_job():
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(55)
Complexity: O(1)

Python (embedded) · asyncio for cooperative tasks on MicroPython · insertion-and-deletion · L3
Concept: Stop a task with cancel() and put the cleanup in a finally block
Misconception: Cancelling a task runs the code after its loop.
Explanation: task.cancel() raises CancelledError inside the task at its next await. Code after an endless loop never runs, so a motor stays on. Put the cleanup in a finally block: it runs on cancellation and on normal exit. Let the cancel propagate, and yield once (await sleep_ms(0)) so the task finishes before you continue.
Incorrect:
import asyncio
log_bad = []
async def worker_bad():
    log_bad.append("start")
    while True:
        await asyncio.sleep_ms(10)
    log_bad.append("cleanup")
Correct:
import asyncio
log = []
async def worker():
    try:
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep_ms(10)
    finally:
        log.append("cleanup")
async def stop_after(ms):
    t = asyncio.create_task(worker())
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(ms)
    t.cancel()
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(0)
Complexity: O(1)

Python (embedded) · asyncio for cooperative tasks on MicroPython · iteration · L2
Concept: Use gather to run waits side by side: the total time is the longest, not the sum
Misconception: Awaiting two coroutines one after the other lets them run together.
Explanation: await a() followed by await b() runs them one after another, so two 20 ms and 30 ms waits take 50 ms. asyncio.gather(a(), b()) starts both and finishes after the longer one, 30 ms. Use it for independent sensors, or create tasks when the results are not needed together.
Incorrect:
import asyncio
async def work_bad(ms):
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(ms)
    return ms
async def sequential():
    a = await work_bad(20)
    b = await work_bad(30)
    return a + b
Correct:
import asyncio
async def work(ms):
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(ms)
    return ms
async def concurrent():
    r = await asyncio.gather(work(20), work(30))
    return sum(r)
Complexity: O(n)

Python (embedded) · asyncio for cooperative tasks on MicroPython · edge-cases · L3
Concept: Bound every wait on hardware or a network with wait_for_ms
Misconception: Awaiting a sensor read is safe even if the sensor never answers.
Explanation: If a device does not answer, a plain await waits forever and the task is stuck. asyncio.wait_for_ms(coro, ms) cancels the coroutine after ms milliseconds and raises asyncio.TimeoutError, which the caller can catch to retry or report a fault.
Incorrect:
import asyncio
async def slow():
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(500)
    return "late"
async def read_bad():
    return await slow()
Correct:
import asyncio
async def slow2():
    await asyncio.sleep_ms(500)
    return "late"
async def read_with_timeout(ms):
    try:
        return await asyncio.wait_for_ms(slow2(), ms)
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
        return None
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: Each advertising field is length, type, data, and the length counts the type byte
Misconception: The first byte of a field is the length of the data.
Explanation: An advertising payload is a sequence of fields: one byte of length, one byte of type, then the data. The length counts the type byte and the data, so a field with n data bytes has length n + 1. A wrong length makes scanners stop parsing the payload at that field.
Incorrect:
import struct
def field_bad(adv_type, data):
    return bytes([len(data), adv_type]) + data
Correct:
import struct
def field(adv_type, data):
    return bytes([len(data) + 1, adv_type]) + data
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: Split a notification into chunks of MTU minus 3 bytes
Misconception: Any payload can be sent in one notification.
Explanation: The default ATT MTU is 23 bytes and 3 of them are the header, so a notification carries at most 20 bytes of data. Larger values are cut off or rejected. Send a long message in slices of mtu - 3 bytes, and let the receiver join them.
Incorrect:
def chunks_bad(data, mtu=23):
    return [data]
Correct:
def chunks(data, mtu=23):
    n = mtu - 3
    return [data[i:i + n] for i in range(0, len(data), n)]
Complexity: O(n)

Prompt: Why is the usable payload of a default BLE notification only 20 bytes?

payload.answer: The default ATT MTU is 23 bytes. Three of them belong to the ATT header (the opcode and the attribute handle), which leaves 20 bytes for data. A larger value needs a negotiated bigger MTU, so a long message has to be split into slices of at most mtu minus 3 bytes.

Concept: Handle connect and disconnect events and restart advertising after a disconnect
Misconception: The device keeps advertising after a central connects and disconnects.
Explanation: The IRQ handler receives an event number and data. On a central connect the controller stops advertising, and after the central disconnects it stays silent until you advertise again, so the device can never be found again. Track connected handles in a set and restart advertising on the disconnect event.
Incorrect:
_CONNECT = 1
_DISCONNECT = 2
def irq_bad(ble, conns, event, handle):
    if event == _CONNECT:
        conns.add(handle)
    elif event == _DISCONNECT:
        conns.discard(handle)
Correct:
_CONNECT = 1
_DISCONNECT = 2
def irq(ble, conns, event, handle):
    if event == _CONNECT:
        conns.add(handle)
    elif event == _DISCONNECT:
        conns.discard(handle)
        ble.advertise()
Complexity: O(1)

Python (embedded) · BLE peripherals on MicroPython boards · edge-cases · L2
Concept: A legacy advertising packet holds 31 bytes, so shorten the name before it overflows
Misconception: The device name can be as long as you like.
Explanation: The payload has room for 31 bytes, and the flags field already takes 3. The name field adds 2 bytes of overhead, so a name has at most 26 characters if there is nothing else. Use the shortened-name type (0x08) when you have to cut it, and the complete-name type (0x09) when it fits.
Incorrect:
def name_field_bad(name):
    return bytes([len(name) + 1, 0x09]) + name
Correct:
def name_field(name, room=26):
    if len(name) > room:
        return bytes([room + 1, 0x08]) + name[:room]
    return bytes([len(name) + 1, 0x09]) + name
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: Read machine.reset_cause() at start-up to tell a power-on from a watchdog or deep-sleep reset
Misconception: Every start-up should run the same set-up code.
Explanation: After a watchdog reset the program should assume something went wrong and start safely, while after deep sleep it may restore saved state. machine.reset_cause() returns a constant such as PWRON_RESET, WDT_RESET or DEEPSLEEP_RESET. Compare it with the named constants, because the numbers differ between ports.
Incorrect:
def start_kind_bad(cause):
    return "cold"

import machine
def start_kind():
    c = machine.reset_cause()
    if c == machine.WDT_RESET:
        return "recover"
    if c == machine.DEEPSLEEP_RESET:
        return "resume"
    return "cold"
Complexity: O(1)

Python (embedded) · start-up structure on MicroPython boards · creation · L1
Concept: Put start-up code in functions and run main() only under the __main__ guard
Misconception: Code at the top of a module runs only when the board starts.
Explanation: Module-level statements run every time the module is imported, including when a test or another file imports it. Hardware set-up there switches pins on and blocks the import. Define init() and main() and call main() under if __name__ == "__main__" so the file can be imported safely.
Incorrect:
from machine import Pin
led_bad = Pin(25, Pin.OUT)
led_bad.on()
Correct:
from machine import Pin
led = None
def init():
    global led
    led = Pin(26, Pin.OUT)
def main():
    init()
    led.on()
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: Import optional hardware modules inside try and except ImportError
Misconception: import network works on every MicroPython board.
Explanation: Ports differ: a board without Wi-Fi has no network module, and the unix port has none of the hardware ones. A plain import then stops the program with ImportError. Wrap the import, store None when it is missing, and test it before use, so the same file runs on a laptop for testing and on the board.
Incorrect:
def wifi_bad():
    import network_missing_bad
    return network_missing_bad
Correct:
try:
    import network_missing
except ImportError:
    network_missing = None
def has_wifi():
    return network_missing is not None
Complexity: O(1)

payload.answer: A bare except catches every exception including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit. Then Ctrl-C and a deliberate exit cannot stop the program, which makes the board hard to debug. Concept: Check a safe-mode pin first so a bad main program cannot lock you out of the board
Misconception: If main.py has a loop that never ends the board can still be reached over USB.
Explanation: A main program that crashes, resets or blocks right away makes it hard to connect and fix it. Read a jumper or button pin at the very start: if it is held low, return immediately and leave the REPL available. Decide it with a pull-up so a missing jumper means normal start.
Incorrect:
def should_run_bad(pin):
    return True
Correct:
from machine import Pin
def should_run(pin):
    return pin.value() == 1
Complexity: O(1)

def bcd_bad(b):
    return b
payload.explanation: In binary-coded decimal the high nibble is the tens digit and the low nibble the ones digit, so 0x59 is 59, not 89. Convert with (b >> 4) * 10 + (b & 0x0F) and back with ((n // 10) << 4) | (n % 10). Parsing it as a normal integer gives out-of-range minutes and seconds.
payload.misconception: The byte 0x59 means 89 seconds.

Python (embedded) · bytes, struct and bit manipulation for devices · access · L1
Concept: Name the byte order in every struct format: ">" is big-endian and "<" is little-endian
Misconception: struct.unpack("<H", data) is the right way to read a 16-bit sensor value.
Explanation: The prefix selects the byte order. Most I2C sensors send the high byte first, which is ">" (big-endian); the ESP32 and ARM cores store integers little-endian ("<"). With the wrong prefix 0x1234 becomes 0x3412. Always write the prefix explicitly and avoid the native default, whose alignment and size depend on the platform.
Incorrect:
import struct
def read_u16_bad(data):
    return struct.unpack("<H", data)[0]
Correct:
import struct
def read_u16(data):
    return struct.unpack(">H", data)[0]
Complexity: O(1)

Prompt: Why should you always write the byte-order prefix in a struct format when reading from a sensor?

metadata.data_structure: bytes, struct and bit manipulation for devices

payload.answer: Without a prefix struct uses the native byte order, size and alignment of the machine that runs it, which differ between platforms. A sensor datasheet defines the order of its bytes, big-endian for most I2C chips, and the code must match that order whatever the board does. An explicit ">" or "<" makes the program portable and shows the reader what the device sends.

metadata.concept: Extract a bit field by shifting right and then masking with width ones
metadata.data_structure: bytes, struct and bit manipulation for devices

payload.concept: Extract a bit field by shifting right and then masking with width ones
payload.data_structure: bytes, struct and bit manipulation for devices
payload.example_bad:
def field_bad(reg, shift, width):
    return reg & (((1 << width) - 1) << shift)
payload.explanation: To read width bits that start at bit shift, shift the register right by shift and then mask with (1 << width) - 1. Masking first leaves the bits in place, so the result is multiplied by 2 to the power shift. Writing a field is the reverse: clear the field, then OR in the shifted value.
payload.misconception: Masking first and shifting later gives the field value.

Python (embedded) · bytes, struct and bit manipulation for devices · edge-cases · L2
Concept: Use a lowercase format code for signed values: ">h" and not ">H"
Misconception: The format code H also returns negative numbers for readings below zero.
Explanation: Uppercase codes (B, H, I) are unsigned and lowercase (b, h, i) are signed. A temperature of -2 degrees arrives as 0xFFFE; unpack with ">H" gives 65534. Use ">h" for signed 16-bit values. The same applies to one byte, where 0xFF is 255 with B and -1 with b.
Incorrect:
import struct
def temp_bad(data):
    return struct.unpack(">H", data)[0]
Correct:
import struct
def temp(data):
    return struct.unpack(">h", data)[0]
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: Convert AnalogIn.value to volts with the reference voltage and 65536
Misconception: The value is the voltage in millivolts.
Explanation: AnalogIn.value is a 16-bit number from 0 to 65535 whatever the real converter resolution. The voltage is value * reference_voltage / 65536. A value of 32768 is half of the reference, 1.65 V at 3.3 V. Use the reference_voltage attribute and not a number that is hard-coded for one board.
Incorrect:
import board, analogio
adc_bad = analogio.AnalogIn(board.A0)
def volts_bad():
    return adc_bad.value / 1000
Correct:
import board, analogio
adc = analogio.AnalogIn(board.A1)
def volts():
    return adc.value * adc.reference_voltage / 65536
Complexity: O(1)

Python (embedded) · CircuitPython on Adafruit and Pico boards · mutation · L2
Concept: Lock the I2C bus with try_lock before using it and unlock it in finally
Misconception: busio.I2C can be used directly after it is created.
Explanation: On CircuitPython an I2C bus can be shared by several libraries, so scan, readfrom_into and writeto raise RuntimeError unless you hold the lock. Loop on try_lock() until it returns True, do the transfer in try, and call unlock() in finally. Libraries that take the bus object do this for you.
Incorrect:
import board, busio
i2c_bad = busio.I2C(board.SCL, board.SDA)
def scan_bad():
    return i2c_bad.scan()
Correct:
import board, busio
i2c = busio.I2C(board.SCL, board.SDA)
def scan():
    while not i2c.try_lock():
        pass
    try:
        return i2c.scan()
    finally:
        i2c.unlock()
Complexity: O(1)

payload.answer: A bus can be shared by several drivers, and their transactions must not interleave. The lock makes one piece of code the owner for the length of a transaction: try_lock returns False if someone else holds it. Holding it in a try and releasing it in finally also frees the bus when an error occurs.

Concept: With Pull.UP a button reads True when released and False when pressed
Misconception: A pressed button reads True.
Explanation: For an input wired between the pin and ground, enable the pull-up with pull = Pull.UP. Python (embedded) · CircuitPython on Adafruit and Pico boards · mutation · L3
Concept: Configure the SPI bus while holding the lock, and write only after configure
Misconception: busio.SPI works with its default settings.
Explanation: Like I2C, an SPI bus needs a lock, and its speed and mode are set with configure() while the lock is held. Libraries do this for each transaction because several devices can share the bus with different settings. Release the lock when the transfer is complete.
Incorrect:
import board, busio
spi_bad = busio.SPI(board.SCK, board.MOSI, board.MISO)
def send_bad(data):
    spi_bad.write(data)
Correct:
import board, busio
spi = busio.SPI(board.SCK, board.MOSI, board.MISO)
def send(data, baud=1000000):
    while not spi.try_lock():
        pass
    try:
        spi.configure(baudrate=baud, polarity=0, phase=0)
        spi.write(data)
    finally:
        spi.unlock()
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: Keep the last eight samples in one byte and detect a clean press as a bit pattern
Misconception: A press is detected when the latest sample is 0.
Explanation: Shift each new sample into an integer: h = ((h << 1) | bit) & 0xFF. With a pull-up, the pattern 0b11110000 means four released samples followed by four pressed ones. The test fires once on the transition, because the pattern cannot match again until the pins go high and low again. It needs no timers and no per-button objects.
Incorrect:
def pressed_bad(h, bit):
    return bit == 0
Correct:
def push(h, bit):
    return ((h << 1) | bit) & 0xFF
def pressed(h):
    return h == 0xF0
Complexity: O(1)

Python (embedded) · button debouncing on microcontrollers · testing · L3
Concept: Test a debouncer by driving a bouncing pin in simulated time
Misconception: A debouncer is correct if it works with one clean edge.
Explanation: The failure only appears with bursts. Drive the pin high and low several times a millisecond apart, then once more after the lockout, and assert that exactly two presses were counted. In a handler use the tick time at the moment of the interrupt, not the time the main loop looks at it.
Incorrect:
import time
from machine import Pin
raw_hits = []
bounce_pin_bad = Pin(60, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
bounce_pin_bad.irq(lambda p: raw_hits.append(1), Pin.IRQ_FALLING)
Correct:
import time
from machine import Pin
good_hits = []
last_t = [None]
def on_fall(pin):
    now = time.ticks_ms()
    if last_t[0] is None or time.ticks_diff(now, last_t[0]) >= 50:
        last_t[0] = now
        good_hits.append(now)
bounce_pin = Pin(61, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
bounce_pin.irq(on_fall, Pin.IRQ_FALLING)
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: Tell a short press from a long press by the time between press and release

import time

    return 'long' if held >= 800 else 'short'

Python (embedded) · button debouncing on microcontrollers · iteration · L2
Concept: Require several identical samples in a row before the state changes
Misconception: One reading tells whether the button is pressed.
Explanation: A sampling debouncer reads the pin at a fixed rate and changes its output only after the input has been the same for N consecutive samples. A single glitch resets the count. This works in a timer callback or a polling loop and needs no timestamps.
Incorrect:
def stable_bad(samples):
    return samples[-1]
Correct:
def stable(samples, need, start=0):
    out = start
    run = 0
    last = start
    for s in samples:
        run = run + 1 if s == last else 1
        last = s
        if run >= need:
            out = s
    return out
Complexity: O(n)

Python (embedded) · button debouncing on microcontrollers · edge-cases · L1
Concept: Ignore edges that arrive within a lockout time after the last accepted one
Misconception: Every edge a mechanical button produces is a separate press.
Explanation: A mechanical contact bounces: one press produces a burst of edges over a few milliseconds. Accept the first edge, remember its time and ignore edges closer than a lockout of about 20 to 50 ms. Compare times with ticks_diff so the check survives counter wrap-around.
Incorrect:
import time
class RawCounter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.n = 0
    def edge(self, now):
        self.n += 1
Correct:
import time
class Lockout:
    def __init__(self, ms):
        self.ms = ms
        self.last = None
        self.n = 0
    def edge(self, now):
        if self.last is None or time.ticks_diff(now, self.last) >= self.ms:
            self.last = now
            self.n += 1
Complexity: O(1)

Python (embedded) · OLED displays on MicroPython boards · fit-and-alternatives · L3
Concept: Scale a value to a bar width in pixels and clamp it so it never leaves the screen
Misconception: The bar length can be the value itself.
Explanation: A reading such as an ADC value of 40000 does not fit in 128 pixels. Map the value range to the bar range with integer scaling, value * width // max_value, and clamp the result so a value above the maximum or below zero cannot draw outside the display.
Incorrect:
def bar_bad(value, max_value, width):
    return value
Correct:
def bar(value, max_value, width):
    n = value * width // max_value
    return max(0, min(width, n))
Complexity: O(1)

Python (embedded) · OLED displays on MicroPython boards · edge-cases · L2
Concept: Clear the buffer before redrawing, or old pixels stay on the screen
Misconception: Drawing the new text over the old text replaces it.
Explanation: Drawing sets pixels to the colour you give; it never erases the pixels that were set before. A shorter text leaves the tail of the longer one visible. Call fill(0) at the start of each frame, or erase only the area you redraw with fill_rect.
Incorrect:
import framebuf
buf_a = bytearray(32)
fa = framebuf.FrameBuffer(buf_a, 16, 16, framebuf.MONO_VLSB)
def draw_bad(fb, text):
    fb.text(text, 0, 0, 1)
Correct:
import framebuf
buf_b = bytearray(32)
fbb = framebuf.FrameBuffer(buf_b, 16, 16, framebuf.MONO_VLSB)
def draw(fb, text):
    fb.fill(0)
    fb.text(text, 0, 0, 1)
Complexity: O(n)

payload.answer: Drawing only writes pixels with the colour you ask for. It does not know about the pixels already set, so the old text remains wherever the new text does not cover it. Concept: In MONO_VLSB each byte holds eight vertical pixels, so the byte index uses y // 8
Misconception: The byte for pixel (x, y) is at y * width + x.
Explanation: The SSD1306 stores the picture in pages of eight rows. A byte holds eight pixels of one column, with the least significant bit on top. The pixel (x, y) is in byte (y // 8) * width + x, bit y % 8. A row-major formula points at the wrong byte and is only correct for monochrome horizontal formats.
Incorrect:
def index_bad(x, y, width):
    return y * width + x
Correct:
def index_bit(x, y, width):
    return (y // 8) * width + x, y % 8
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: Draw into a frame buffer and send it to the display with one show() call
Misconception: Drawing functions change the screen right away.
Explanation: framebuf.FrameBuffer draws into memory only. The OLED shows the new picture after you send the buffer, which the SSD1306 driver does in show(). Draw the whole frame, then call show() once; calling it after every pixel is slow and makes the screen flicker.
Incorrect:
import framebuf
buf_bad = bytearray(32)
fb_bad = framebuf.FrameBuffer(buf_bad, 16, 16, framebuf.MONO_VLSB)
fb_bad.pixel(3, 3, 1)
Correct:
import framebuf
sent = []
buf = bytearray(32)
fb = framebuf.FrameBuffer(buf, 16, 16, framebuf.MONO_VLSB)
def show():
    sent.append(bytes(buf))
fb.pixel(3, 3, 1)
show()
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: Wrap text by the number of 8-pixel characters that fit in the display width
Misconception: Long text wraps to the next line by itself.
Explanation: The built-in font is 8 pixels wide, so a 128 pixel display holds 16 characters per line. framebuf.text does not wrap: the extra characters are cut off. Split the string into chunks of width // 8 characters and draw each chunk 8 pixels lower.
Incorrect:
def lines_bad(s, width):
    return [s]
Correct:
def lines(s, width):
    n = width // 8
    return [s[i:i + n] for i in range(0, len(s), n)]
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: Write to a temporary file and rename it, so a failed write cannot destroy the old file
Misconception: Opening the file with "w" and writing is a safe way to save.
Explanation: open(path, "w") truncates the file immediately. A power cut or an exception during the write leaves an empty or partial file and the old content is gone. Write the new data to path + ".tmp", then os.rename it over the original after the write has succeeded.
Incorrect:
def save_bad(path, text):
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        f.write(text)
Correct:
import os
def save(path, text):
    tmp = path + ".tmp"
    with open(tmp, "w") as f:
        f.write(text)
    os.rename(tmp, path)
Complexity: O(n)

Python (embedded) · file storage and configuration on MicroPython boards · edge-cases · L1
Concept: Load settings with defaults, because the file or a key can be missing
Misconception: The config file always exists and contains every key.
Explanation: On first boot, after a file system reset, or after an interrupted write, config.json may be missing, empty or incomplete. Start from a dictionary of defaults and update it with what you can read. Catch OSError for a missing file and ValueError for invalid JSON, and keep the defaults in both cases.
Incorrect:
import json
def load_bad(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return json.load(f)
Correct:
import json
DEFAULTS = {"interval": 10, "name": "node"}
def load(path):
    cfg = dict(DEFAULTS)
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            cfg.update(json.load(f))
    except (OSError, ValueError):
        pass
    return cfg
Complexity: O(n)

Python (embedded) · file storage and configuration on MicroPython boards · equality · L3
Concept: JSON round trips change types: tuples become lists and integer keys become strings
Misconception: json.loads(json.dumps(x)) == x for any x.
Explanation: JSON has arrays and objects with string keys. A tuple is written as an array and read back as a list, and the key 1 comes back as "1". The round trip is then not equal to the original and lookups by the integer key fail. Convert explicitly after loading, or use string keys from the start.
Incorrect:
import json
def roundtrip_bad(x):
    return json.loads(json.dumps(x)) == x
Correct:
import json
def roundtrip(x):
    y = json.loads(json.dumps(x))
    return {int(k): tuple(v) for k, v in y.items()}
Complexity: O(n)

Python (embedded) · file storage and configuration on MicroPython boards · access · L3
Concept: Store fixed-size binary records so you can seek to record n without reading the file
Misconception: Text lines can be read by index just as quickly as fixed-size records.
Explanation: Finding line n of a text file needs a scan through the n lines before it. With fixed-size records, record n starts at n * size, so seek and read one record. struct.pack with explicit sizes keeps the record width constant. Variable-width text breaks this arithmetic.
Incorrect:
def read_line_bad(path, n):
    with open(path) as f:
        return f.read().split("\n")[n]
Correct:
import struct
REC = ">HH"
SIZE = struct.calcsize(REC)
def write_records(path, rows):
    with open(path, "wb") as f:
        for a, b in rows:
            f.write(struct.pack(REC, a, b))
def read_record(path, n):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        f.seek(n * SIZE)
        return struct.unpack(REC, f.read(SIZE))
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: Check the log size before appending and rotate it, because flash space is small
Misconception: Appending to a log file forever is fine.
Explanation: A log that grows on a device with a few hundred kilobytes of flash fills the file system and breaks everything else. Check the size with os.stat(path)[6] before each append. When it passes the limit, move the log to a backup name, replacing the previous backup, and start a new file.
Incorrect:
def log_bad(path, line):
    with open(path, "a") as f:
        f.write(line + "\n")
Correct:
import os
def log(path, line, limit=20):
    try:
        size = os.stat(path)[6]
    except OSError:
        size = 0
    if size + len(line) + 1 > limit:
        try:
            os.remove(path + ".1")
        except OSError:
            pass
        os.rename(path, path + ".1")
    with open(path, "a") as f:
        f.write(line + "\n")
Complexity: O(1)

Python (embedded) · signal filtering and PID control for microcontrollers · complexity · L3
Concept: Scale the integral and the derivative by the measured time step
Misconception: Loops run at exactly the same interval every time.
Explanation: An integral accumulates error times time, and a derivative is a change per unit time. A loop that sometimes takes 10 ms and sometimes 30 ms gives wrong results if the code assumes a constant step. Measure dt with ticks_diff and scale: integral += error * dt, derivative = delta / dt.
Incorrect:
def integrate_bad(integral, error, dt_ms):
    return integral + error
Correct:
def integrate(integral, error, dt_ms):
    return integral + error * dt_ms // 1000
Complexity: O(1)

    return (setpoint - meas) - (prev_setpoint - prev_meas)
