ruby-adjmatrix-create-ex2   format: explain-why   level: L1   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Why does Array.new(3, Array.new(3, 0)) give a broken adjacency matrix?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). The default value argument is evaluated once and the same Array object
is used for every row. All rows are therefore aliases of one row, so setting m[0][1] = 1 changes m[1][1] and m[2][1] too,
and the matrix shows edges that were never added. The block form Array.new(3) { Array.new(3, 0) } builds a separate
row for each index.

2. Overview and mental model: Queue and SizedQueue
Thread::Queue (Queue) is a thread-safe, unbounded FIFO queue; Thread::SizedQueue (SizedQueue) adds a
capacity. Both are in the core language, so require "thread" is not needed. push and pop are O(1).
pop blocks while the queue is empty, pop(true) raises ThreadError, and pop(timeout: s) returns nil on timeout. close
wakes all waiting consumers: pop returns nil once the closed queue is empty, and push raises ClosedQueueError.
SizedQueue gives back-pressure: push blocks while the queue is full. Results arrive in completion order, so tag them
with an index to restore the input order.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
pop blocks on an empty Queue; pop(true) raises ThreadError and pop(timeout:) returns nil
ruby-threadqueue-poll   lens: access   level: L1   family: ruby-threadqueue-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-threadqueue-close. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. q.pop(true) waits politely for an item.
Queue#pop blocks until an item arrives. With non_block = true it never waits and raises ThreadError (queue empty)
when there is nothing to take. Since Ruby 3.2 pop(timeout: seconds) waits up to the limit and returns nil if nothing
arrived. Use the timeout form for polling loops.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def poll_bad(q)
  q.pop(true)
end
Correct:
 def poll(q)
  q.pop(timeout: 0.05)
end
Queue.new takes initial items, not a capacity; use SizedQueue.new(n) for a limit
ruby-threadqueue-init   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-threadqueue-creation
Prerequisites: ruby-threadqueue-order. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Queue.new(5) creates a queue with room for five items.
Queue.new accepts an enumerable of initial items (Ruby 3.1+), so Queue.new(5) raises TypeError (can't convert
Integer into Array). A plain Queue is unbounded. A capacity needs SizedQueue.new(5). Both live in the core as
Thread::Queue and Thread::SizedQueue; require "thread" is no longer needed.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  Queue.new(5)
end
Correct:
 def limited
  SizedQueue.new(5)
end
def preloaded
  Queue.new([1, 2, 3])
end

Page 5
A SizedQueue blocks the producer when full; a non-blocking push raises ThreadError
ruby-threadqueue-sized   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: ruby-threadqueue-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-threadqueue-close. Follow-up: ruby-threadqueue-order. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Pushing more items than the SizedQueue limit just waits for room.
SizedQueue.new(n) limits the queue to n items and gives back-pressure: push blocks while the queue is full, so a fast
producer cannot outrun a slow consumer. push(x, true) never waits and raises ThreadError (queue full); push(x,
timeout: s) returns nil on timeout. A consumer thread must be running, or the blocking push never returns.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def fill_bad(items, cap)
  q = SizedQueue.new(cap)
  items.each { |x| q.push(x, true) }
  q.size
end
Correct:
 def pipeline(items, cap)
  q = SizedQueue.new(cap)
  producer = Thread.new do
    items.each { |x| q << x }
    q.close
  end
  out = []
  while (x = q.pop)
    out << x
  end
  producer.join
  out
end
Results arrive in completion order; tag each result with its index and sort
ruby-threadqueue-order   lens: ordering   level: L3   family: ruby-threadqueue-ordering
Prerequisites: ruby-threadqueue-sized. Follow-up: ruby-threadqueue-init. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. Results pushed by worker threads come out in the order the jobs were started.
A Queue is FIFO by arrival, not by job start. A thread that finishes first pushes first, so slow jobs appear late. Tag
each result with its job index, collect all of them and sort by index to restore the submission order.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def run_bad(delays)
  out = Queue.new
  ts = delays.each_with_index.map { |d, i| Thread.new { sleep d; out << i } }
  ts.each(&:join)
  Array.new(out.size) { out.pop }
end
Correct:
 def run(delays)
  out = Queue.new
  ts = delays.each_with_index.map { |d, i| Thread.new { sleep d; out << [i, d] } }
  ts.each(&:join)
  Array.new(out.size) { out.pop }.sort.map(&:last)
end

Close the queue to stop all workers; a single sentinel value stops only one of them
ruby-threadqueue-close   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-threadqueue-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-threadqueue-poll. Follow-up: ruby-threadqueue-sized. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Pushing one :done value shuts down every worker.
Each :done is consumed by exactly one worker, so with two workers one sentinel leaves the other blocked forever in
pop. Queue#close wakes every waiting consumer: pop returns nil once a closed queue is empty, so workers can loop
with while (job = q.pop). After close, push raises ClosedQueueError.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def finished_bad(workers)
  q = Queue.new
  threads = Array.new(workers) { Thread.new { while (j = q.pop) != :done; end } }
  3.times { |i| q << i }
  q << :done
  count = threads.count { |t| t.join(0.2) }
  threads.each(&:kill)
  count
end
Correct:
 def finished(workers)
  q = Queue.new
  threads = Array.new(workers) { Thread.new { while (j = q.pop); end } }
  3.times { |i| q << i }
  q.close
  count = threads.count { |t| t.join(0.2) }
  threads.each(&:kill)
  count
end

Prompt. Why does closing a Queue stop all workers while a single sentinel value does not?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). A sentinel is an ordinary item and is taken by exactly one consumer, so
the others stay blocked in pop. Closing the queue changes its state: every blocked pop wakes up and returns nil once the
remaining items are gone, and later pops return nil immediately. Each worker sees the nil and exits its loop, whatever the
number of workers.

2. Overview and mental model: Adjacency list
An adjacency list stores, for every vertex, the list of its neighbours. In Ruby a Hash of Arrays keeps the space at O(V
+ E) and makes neighbour iteration proportional to the degree.
Use it for sparse graphs. Edge lookup between two given vertices is O(degree); use a Hash of Sets or an adjacency
matrix when that matters.
Depth-first search with an explicit stack, breadth-first search with a queue, Kahn's topological sort and component
counting all run in O(V + E).
Toolbox

g.add_edge(1, 2)
g.add_edge(2, 3)
g.neighbors(2)

4.4 Algorithm chunks
An undirected edge must be stored in both adjacency lists, and both endpoints must exist as
vertices
ruby-adjlist-edge   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-adjlist-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-adjlist-dfs. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Adding v to the list of u is enough to connect the two vertices in an undirected graph.
With only u -> v stored, v has no way back to u, so searches that start at v miss u and degree counts are wrong. An
undirected edge adds v to u's list and u to v's list; a directed edge adds only one. Creating both vertices first keeps
isolated endpoints in the vertex list, and neighbors uses fetch so that reading an unknown vertex does not create it.
Adding an edge is O(1); space is O(V + E).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def add_edge_bad(adj, u, v)
  (adj[u] ||= []) << v
  adj[v] ||= []
end
Correct:
 class Graph
  def initialize(directed: false)
    @directed = directed
    @adj = {}
  end
  def add_vertex(v)
    @adj[v] ||= []
    self
  end
  def add_edge(u, v)
    add_vertex(u)
    add_vertex(v)
    @adj[u] << v
    @adj[v] << u unless @directed
    self
  end
  def neighbors(v)
    @adj.fetch(v, [])
  end
  def vertices
    @adj.keys
  end
end

Page 5
Use an explicit stack for depth-first search; recursion overflows the Ruby stack on long paths
ruby-adjlist-dfs   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ruby-adjlist-iteration
Prerequisites: ruby-adjlist-edge. Follow-up: ruby-adjlist-path. Complexity: O(V+E).
 Common misconception. A recursive depth-first search is fine for any graph that fits in memory.
Each recursive call uses a stack frame, and Ruby raises SystemStackError after roughly ten thousand nested calls,
which a path-shaped graph with hundreds of thousands of vertices easily reaches. Keep your own stack in an Array,
mark vertices when they are popped, and push neighbours in reverse to keep the natural order. Time O(V + E),
space O(V).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def dfs_bad(g, v, seen = {}, order = [])
  seen[v] = true
  order << v
  g.neighbors(v).each { |n| dfs_bad(g, n, seen, order) unless seen[n] }
  order
end
Correct:
 def dfs_order(g, start)
  seen = {}
  stack = [start]
  order = []
  until stack.empty?
    v = stack.pop
    next if seen[v]
    seen[v] = true
    order << v
    g.neighbors(v).reverse_each { |n| stack.push(n) unless seen[n] }
  end
  order
end
Count connected components by starting a search only from vertices not yet seen
ruby-adjlist-components   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-adjlist-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-adjlist-topo. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(V+E).
 Common misconception. Start a search from every vertex and count the searches.
Starting from every vertex counts each vertex as its own component. Keep a seen set shared by all searches and
start a new search only from an unseen vertex. The number of searches is the number of components. Mark vertices
when they are pushed so none enters the stack twice. O(V + E).

    end

end
Correct:
 def components(g)
  seen = {}
  out = []
  g.vertices.each do |s|
    next if seen[s]
    seen[s] = true
    comp = []
    stack = [s]
    until stack.empty?
      v = stack.pop
      comp << v
      g.neighbors(v).each do |n|
        next if seen[n]
        seen[n] = true
        stack.push(n)
      end
    end
    out << comp.sort
  end
  out
end
Rebuild a BFS path by following parents back from the target, then reverse it
ruby-adjlist-path   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-adjlist-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-adjlist-dfs. Follow-up: ruby-adjlist-topo. Complexity: O(V+E).
 Common misconception. Following parent links from the target to the source already gives the path in order.
The parent links lead backwards: target, its parent, and so on up to the source, so the collected list runs from target to
source. Reverse it before returning. Breadth-first search finds a path with the fewest edges in an unweighted graph,
in O(V + E). Return nil when the target was never reached.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def path_bad(parent, src, dst)
  return nil unless parent.key?(dst)
  path = [dst]
  path << parent[path.last] until path.last == src
  path
end

Correct:
 def shortest_path(g, src, dst)
  parent = { src => nil }
  queue = [src]
  until queue.empty?
    v = queue.shift
    break if v == dst
    g.neighbors(v).each do |n|
      next if parent.key?(n)
      parent[n] = v
      queue.push(n)
    end
  end
  return nil unless parent.key?(dst)
  path = [dst]
  path << parent[path.last] until path.last == src
  path.reverse
end
Kahn's topological sort must compare the output size with the vertex count to detect cycles
ruby-adjlist-topo   lens: ordering   level: L3   family: ruby-adjlist-ordering
Prerequisites: ruby-adjlist-path. Follow-up: ruby-adjlist-components. Complexity: O(V+E).
 Common misconception. If the queue empties, the order produced is a complete topological order.
Vertices on a cycle never reach in-degree zero, so they are never queued and silently missing from the output. If the
result has fewer vertices than the graph, a cycle exists and no topological order does. Count in-degrees, queue the
zero ones, remove them one by one, and return nil on a cycle. O(V + E).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def topo_bad(g)
  indeg = Hash.new(0)
  g.vertices.each { |v| g.neighbors(v).each { |n| indeg[n] += 1 } }
  queue = g.vertices.select { |v| indeg[v].zero? }
  order = []
  until queue.empty?
    v = queue.shift
    order << v
    g.neighbors(v).each do |n|
      indeg[n] -= 1
      queue.push(n) if indeg[n].zero?
    end
  end
  order
end
Correct:
 def topo_sort(g)
  indeg = Hash.new(0)
  g.vertices.each { |v| g.neighbors(v).each { |n| indeg[n] += 1 } }
  queue = g.vertices.select { |v| indeg[v].zero? }
  order = []
  until queue.empty?
    v = queue.shift
    order << v
    g.neighbors(v).each do |n|
      indeg[n] -= 1
      queue.push(n) if indeg[n].zero?
    end
  end
  order.size == g.vertices.size ? order : nil
end

ruby-adjlist-dfs-ex2   format: explain-why   level: L2   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Why can a recursive depth-first search fail on a large graph in Ruby, and how does an explicit stack avoid
that?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Every recursive call adds a frame to the interpreter's call stack, which
has a fixed size, so a path-like graph with many thousands of vertices raises SystemStackError. An explicit stack is an
Array on the heap that grows with available memory, so the search depth is not limited by the call stack. The visiting
order stays the same if neighbours are pushed in reverse.

Overview and mental model: Adjacency list An adjacency list stores, for every vertex, the list of its neighbours. In Ruby a Hash of Arrays keeps the space at O(V + E) and makes neighbour iteration proportional to the degree. Use it for sparse graphs. Edge lookup between two given vertices is O(degree); use a Hash of Sets or an adjacency matrix when that matters. Depth-first search with an explicit stack, breadth-first search with a queue, Kahn's topological sort and component counting all run in O(V + E). 2. Overview and mental model: String
A String is a mutable sequence of characters with an encoding, UTF-8 by default. It has built-in search, slicing,
splitting and transformation methods. Indexing by character is O(1) for ASCII-only strings and O(n) otherwise.
Methods that end in ! and << mutate the object; + and the non-bang forms return a new string. == compares content,
equal? compares identity, and a string used as a hash key is copied and frozen.
length counts characters, bytesize counts bytes. Build large strings with << or join, not +=.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
<< and bang methods mutate the receiver, so a method that appends to its argument
changes the caller's string
ruby-string-mutation   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ruby-string-mutation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-string-unicode. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A method can append to its string parameter without affecting the caller.
Ruby strings are mutable objects passed by reference value. s << "!" changes the object everyone holds. s + "!" and
the non-bang methods return a new string. Use dup or the non-mutating form inside methods that should not change
their arguments.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def shout_bad(s)
  s << "!"
end
Correct:
 def shout(s)
  s + "!"
end
== compares content, equal? compares object identity; two equal literals are different objects
ruby-string-equality   lens: equality   level: L1   family: ruby-string-equality
Prerequisites: ruby-string-unicode. Follow-up: ruby-string-build. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. a.equal?(b) is true whenever a and b hold the same text.
equal? asks whether two variables point at the same object, so two separately created strings with the same text are
not equal?. Use == (or eql? for hash-key equality) to compare content. Symbols are different: the same symbol is
always the same object.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def same_text_bad?(a, b)
  a.equal?(b)
end
Correct:
 def same_text?(a, b)
  a == b
end

Ruby String: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 5
length counts characters but bytesize counts bytes; byteslice can cut a character in half
ruby-string-unicode   lens: access   level: L2   family: ruby-string-access
Prerequisites: ruby-string-mutation. Follow-up: ruby-string-equality. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A string's length is its size in bytes.
In a UTF-8 string "héllo" has 5 characters and 6 bytes. s[0, n] slices by characters and is safe. byteslice(0, n) slices
by bytes and can end in the middle of a multi-byte character, giving a string whose valid_encoding? is false. Indexing
a character is O(n) for non-ASCII strings.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def head_bad(s, n)
  s.byteslice(0, n)
end
Correct:
 def head(s, n)
  s[0, n]
end
split(" ") treats runs of whitespace as one separator, split(/ /) keeps empty strings
ruby-string-split   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ruby-string-iteration
Prerequisites: ruby-string-build. Follow-up: ruby-string-palindrome. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. split(/ /) and split(" ") give the same words.
split(" ") is awk-style: it ignores leading whitespace and splits on runs of spaces and tabs. split(/ /) splits at every
single space, so double spaces produce empty strings. Trailing empty strings are dropped unless you pass a
negative limit.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def word_count_bad(s)
  s.split(/ /).size
end
Correct:
 def word_count(s)
  s.split(" ").size
end

Ruby String: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
Build strings with << or join; += creates a new string object every iteration
ruby-string-build   lens: transformation   level: L3   family: ruby-string-transformation
Prerequisites: ruby-string-equality. Follow-up: ruby-string-split. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. s += piece appends to the same string in a loop.
s += x is s = s + x: it allocates a new string and copies the old one each time, so a loop is O(n^2) in the total length.
<< appends in place, and Array#join builds the result in one pass. Use << on a string you own.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def build_bad(parts)
  s = ""
  ids = []
  parts.each { |x| s += x; ids << s.object_id }
  [s, ids.uniq.size]
end
Correct:
 def build(parts)
  s = +""
  ids = []
  parts.each { |x| s << x; ids << s.object_id }
  [s, ids.uniq.size]
end
Normalise with downcase and gsub before comparing to its reverse for a palindrome check
ruby-string-palindrome   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-string-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-string-split. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. s == s.reverse is a correct palindrome test for sentences.
Case, spaces and punctuation break a direct comparison. Normalise first: downcase, then delete everything that is
not a letter or digit with gsub(/[^a-z0-9]/, ""), then compare with the reverse. This is O(n) time and space; two pointers
do it in O(1) extra space.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def palindrome_bad?(s)
  s == s.reverse
end
Correct:
 def palindrome?(s)
  t = s.downcase.gsub(/[^a-z0-9]/, "")
  t == t.reverse
end

Prompt. Why is building a long string with += in a loop slower than with <<?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Each s += x evaluates s + x, which allocates a new string and copies all
of s plus x, then rebinds s. Over n appends the copying adds up to O(n^2) characters and creates garbage. << appends
into the existing buffer, which grows geometrically, so the loop is O(n) overall.

2. Overview and mental model: Binary search tree
A binary search tree keeps smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right subtree, so an in-order walk
yields the keys in sorted order.
Search, insert and delete are O(h): O(log n) when balanced and O(n) when keys arrive sorted. Self-balancing trees
such as AVL and red-black trees keep h at O(log n).
Include Enumerable and define each as an in-order walk to get sort, min, max, first and more.

A recursive insert must assign the returned subtree back to the child link
ruby-bst-insert   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-bst-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-bst-validate. Complexity: O(h).
 Common misconception. A recursive insert can just call itself on the child and ignore the result.
Inserting into an empty subtree creates a new node, but that node only becomes part of the tree if the caller stores it
in node.left or node.right. Without the assignment the new node is discarded. Return the subtree root from every call
and assign it. Duplicates are ignored here. Insert is O(h) where h is the height: O(log n) for a balanced tree and O(n)
for a degenerate one.

  else

  end
  node
end

 class BSTNode
  attr_accessor :key, :left, :right
  def initialize(key)

class BST
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :root, :size
  def initialize
    @root = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def insert(key)
    @root = insert_at(@root, key)
    self
  end
  def include?(key)
    node = @root
    while node
      return true if key == node.key
      node = key < node.key ? node.left : node.right
    end
    false
  end
  def each(&block)
    return to_enum(:each) unless block
    walk(@root, &block)
    self
  end
  private
  def insert_at(node, key)
    if node.nil?
      @size += 1
      return BSTNode.new(key)
    end
    if key < node.key
      node.left = insert_at(node.left, key)
    elsif key > node.key
      node.right = insert_at(node.right, key)
    end
    node
  end
  def walk(node, &block)
    return unless node
    walk(node.left, &block)
    block.call(node.key)
    walk(node.right, &block)
  end
end

Validate a BST by passing lower and upper bounds down, not by comparing parent and child
only
ruby-bst-validate   lens: equality   level: L2   family: ruby-bst-equality
Prerequisites: ruby-bst-insert. Follow-up: ruby-bst-delete. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A tree is a BST if every node is greater than its left child and smaller than its right child.
The BST rule applies to the whole subtree, not just the children. A node can satisfy its parent and still violate a distant
ancestor, for example a 6 in the left subtree of 5. Carry an open interval (lo, hi) down the recursion and require lo <
key < hi. Checking all nodes is O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def valid_bad?(node)
  return true unless node
  return false if node.left && node.left.key >= node.key
  return false if node.right && node.right.key <= node.key
  valid_bad?(node.left) && valid_bad?(node.right)
end
Correct:
 def valid_bst?(node, lo = nil, hi = nil)
  return true unless node
  return false if lo && node.key <= lo
  return false if hi && node.key >= hi
  valid_bst?(node.left, lo, node.key) && valid_bst?(node.right, node.key, hi)
end
The lowest common ancestor in a BST is the first node where the keys split or one equals the
node
ruby-bst-lca   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-bst-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-bst-kth. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(h).
 Common misconception. Move left if either key is smaller than the node, and right if either is larger.
With || the walk goes left as soon as one key is smaller, even when the other key is larger and the node is already the
split point. Go left only if both keys are smaller, right only if both are larger, otherwise the current node is the answer.
O(h) time, O(1) space.

    if p < node.key || q < node.key
      node = node.left
    elsif p > node.key || q > node.key
      node = node.right
    else
      return node.key
    end
  end
  nil
end

  node = root
  while node
    if p < node.key && q < node.key
      node = node.left
    elsif p > node.key && q > node.key

Deleting a node with two children replaces its key with the in-order successor
ruby-bst-delete   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: ruby-bst-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-bst-validate. Follow-up: ruby-bst-kth. Complexity: O(h).
 Common misconception. A node with two children can be replaced by its left child.
Replacing the node by one child drops the other child's whole subtree. Copy the in-order successor (the minimum of
the right subtree) into the node and remove that minimum from the right subtree. Zero or one child is simpler: return
the other child. Delete returns the new subtree root, like insert. O(h).

    node.right = delete_bad(node.right, key)
  else
    return node.right unless node.left
    return node.left
  end
  node
end

 class BST
  def delete(key)
    @root = delete_at(@root, key)
    self
  end
  private
  def delete_at(node, key)
    return nil unless node
    if key < node.key
      node.left = delete_at(node.left, key)
    elsif key > node.key
      node.right = delete_at(node.right, key)
    else
      @size -= 1
      return node.right unless node.left
      return node.left unless node.right
      succ = node.right
      succ = succ.left while succ.left
      node.key = succ.key
      node.right = remove_min(node.right)
    end
    node
  end
  def remove_min(node)
    return node.right unless node.left
    node.left = remove_min(node.left)
    node
  end
end
The kth smallest key is the kth node of an in-order walk; ranks start at 1
ruby-bst-kth   lens: ordering   level: L3   family: ruby-bst-ordering
Prerequisites: ruby-bst-delete. Follow-up: ruby-bst-lca. Complexity: O(h+k).
 Common misconception. The kth smallest key is at index k of the sorted keys.
Ranks are 1-based while Array indexes are 0-based, so keys[k] returns the (k+1)th smallest. An iterative in-order
walk with an explicit stack can stop at the kth node without visiting the rest: O(h + k) time. Return nil when k is out of
range.

end

  keys_bad(root)[k]

 def kth_smallest(root, k)
  stack = []
  node = root
  while node || !stack.empty?
    while node
      stack.push(node)
      node = node.left
    end
    node = stack.pop
    k -= 1
    return node.key if k.zero?
    node = node.right
  end
  nil
end

Prompt. Why must a recursive BST insert assign the result of the recursive call back to node.left or node.right?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). When the recursion reaches an empty subtree it builds a new node and
returns it. Only the caller can link that node into the tree by storing it in its left or right reference. If the result is ignored,
the new node is garbage and the tree never changes. Returning the subtree root from every call and assigning it also
keeps the code correct when a rebalancing step replaces the root of a subtree.

2. Overview and mental model: Fenwick tree
A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) keeps prefix sums in an Array of n + 1 cells. Cell i stores the sum of the range of
length i & -i that ends at i, so both point updates and prefix queries take O(log n).
Updates climb with i += i & -i and queries descend with i -= i & -i. It needs less memory and code than a segment tree
but supports only invertible operations such as sum.
Ruby's Integer bit operators are unbounded, so i & -i is exact for any positive index.

A range sum is prefix(r + 1) - prefix(l) for inclusive indexes
ruby-fenwicktree-range   lens: access   level: L2   family: ruby-fenwicktree-access
Prerequisites: ruby-fenwicktree-update. Follow-up: ruby-fenwicktree-build. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. The sum of elements l through r is prefix(r) - prefix(l).
prefix(k) is the sum of the first k elements, indexes 0 to k - 1. The difference prefix(r) - prefix(l) therefore covers l
through r - 1 and drops the last element. For an inclusive range use prefix(r + 1) - prefix(l). The prefix of 0 elements is
0, so a range starting at index 0 needs no special case. O(log n).

An update climbs with i += i & -i and a query descends with i -= i & -i
ruby-fenwicktree-update   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ruby-fenwicktree-mutation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-fenwicktree-range. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Both update and query can walk with i -= i & -i.
Cell i of a Fenwick tree holds the sum of the range of length lowbit(i) ending at i, where lowbit(i) = i & -i. A change at
position i affects the cells found by repeatedly adding the lowest set bit, while a prefix sum collects cells by repeatedly
removing it. Using the same direction for both double counts or misses cells. Ruby integers are unbounded, so i & -i
works for any positive i. Each loop is O(log n).

 class Fenwick
  attr_reader :size, :tree
  def initialize(n)
    @size = n
    @tree = Array.new(n + 1, 0)
  end
  def add(i, delta)
    i += 1
    while i <= @size
      @tree[i] += delta
      i += i & -i
    end
    self
  end
  def prefix(count)
    total = 0
    i = count
    while i > 0
      total += @tree[i]
      i -= i & -i
    end
    total
  end
end

ruby-fenwicktree-build   lens: creation   level: L3   family: ruby-fenwicktree-creation
Prerequisites: ruby-fenwicktree-range. Follow-up: ruby-fenwicktree-kth. Complexity: O(n).

Each cell must hold the sum of a whole range, not just its own element. Place every value in its cell, then for i from 1
to n add cell i to its parent cell i + (i & -i) when that exists. Cells are processed in increasing order, so cell i is complete
before it is pushed. This is O(n); n calls to add would be O(n log n).

  def self.from(arr)
    f = new(arr.size)
    t = f.tree
    arr.each_with_index { |v, i| t[i + 1] += v }
    (1..arr.size).each do |i|
      j = i + (i & -i)
      t[j] += t[i] if j <= arr.size
    end
    f
  end
end

  def lower_bound(target)
    pos = 0
    step = @size.zero? ? 0 : 1 << (@size.bit_length - 1)
    while step > 0
      nxt = pos + step
      if nxt <= @size && @tree[nxt] < target

      step >>= 1

Prompt. Why does i & -i give the lowest set bit of a positive integer, and why does a Fenwick tree use it?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). In two's complement, -i is the bitwise complement of i plus one. The
complement flips every bit, and adding one carries through the trailing zeros up to the lowest set bit, so only that bit (and
the zeros below it) match in i and -i. The and keeps exactly the lowest set bit. A Fenwick cell i covers a range whose
length is that value, so adding it moves to the next cell that covers i and subtracting it moves to the previous disjoint
range.

2. Overview and mental model: Deque
A deque supports push and pop at both ends. A Ruby Array already behaves as one (push, pop, shift, unshift are
amortised O(1)); a ring buffer makes the mechanics and the fixed capacity explicit.

order. Ruby's modulo of a negative number is non-negative, which makes push_front simple.
Deques power sliding-window algorithms, palindrome checks and work-stealing schedulers.

After the head has moved, head + size - 1 can exceed the last slot and the Array read returns nil instead of wrapping

 class RingDeque
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :size
  def initialize(cap = 4)
    @buf = Array.new(cap)
    @head = 0
    @size = 0
  end
  def capacity
    @buf.size
  end
  def full?
    @size == @buf.size
  end
  def empty?
    @size.zero?
  end
  def push_back(v)
    return false if full?
    @buf[(@head + @size) % @buf.size] = v
    @size += 1
    true
  end
  def push_front(v)
    return false if full?
    @head = (@head - 1) % @buf.size
    @buf[@head] = v
    @size += 1
    true
  end
  def pop_front
    return nil if empty?
    v = @buf[@head]
    @buf[@head] = nil
    @head = (@head + 1) % @buf.size
    @size -= 1
    v
  end
  def pop_back
    return nil if empty?
    i = (@head + @size - 1) % @buf.size
    v = @buf[i]
    @buf[i] = nil
    @size -= 1
    v
  end
  def front
    empty? ? nil : @buf[@head]
  end
  def back
    empty? ? nil : @buf[(@head + @size - 1) % @buf.size]
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    @size.times { |i| yield @buf[(@head + i) % @buf.size] }
  end
end

Array#rotate returns a new array; rotate! changes the receiver
ruby-deque-rotate   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ruby-deque-transformation
Prerequisites: ruby-deque-palindrome. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Calling a.rotate(k) rotates the array a.
rotate builds and returns a rotated copy and leaves the receiver unchanged, so discarding the result does nothing.
Use rotate! to change the array in place. Positive counts move the front items to the back; negative counts do the
reverse. Both are O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def rotate_bad(a, k)
  a.rotate(k)
  a
end
Correct:
 def rotate_in_place(a, k)
  a.rotate!(k)
  a
end
A deque palindrome check compares both ends and stops with one or zero items left
ruby-deque-palindrome   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-deque-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-deque-slidingmax. Follow-up: ruby-deque-rotate. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Loop while the deque is not empty, popping a front and a back item each time.
With an odd length the last item is both front and back. After the front pop there is nothing left, so pop returns nil and
the comparison fails for a real palindrome like "aba". Loop while more than one item remains. In Ruby an Array
already supports shift and pop in amortised O(1), so it works as a deque.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  dq = s.chars
  until dq.empty?
    return false unless dq.shift == dq.pop
  end
  true
end
Correct:
 def pal?(s)
  dq = s.chars
  while dq.size > 1
    return false unless dq.shift == dq.pop
  end
  true
end

When a ring buffer grows it must copy elements in logical order, not physical order
ruby-deque-growth   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-deque-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-deque-ring. Follow-up: ruby-deque-slidingmax. Complexity: O(1) amortised.
 Common misconception. Appending empty slots to the buffer is enough to double the capacity.
If the contents have wrapped around, extending the Array leaves the head and tail in the middle of the old region, and
reading from head crosses empty slots. Copy the elements in logical order into a bigger buffer and reset head to 0.
Growth costs O(n) but happens rarely, so push is O(1) amortised.

    @head = 0
    @size = 0

    @size += 1

    v = @buf[@head]
    @head = (@head + 1) % @buf.size
    @size -= 1

  def to_a

Correct:
 class AutoDeque < RingDeque
  def push_back(v)
    grow! if full?
    super
  end
  def push_front(v)
    grow! if full?
    super
  end
  private
  def grow!
    items = to_a
    @buf = items + Array.new([items.size, 1].max)
    @head = 0
  end
end

A sliding-window maximum keeps a decreasing deque and drops expired indexes from the
front
ruby-deque-slidingmax   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-deque-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-deque-growth. Follow-up: ruby-deque-palindrome. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Keeping only decreasing values in the deque is enough; old indexes never matter.
A maximum that has left the window must be removed, or it keeps being reported. Store indexes, pop smaller values
from the back, and pop from the front when its index is outside the window. The front is then always the window
maximum. Each index enters and leaves once, so the scan is O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def window_max_bad(nums, k)
  dq = []
  out = []
  nums.each_with_index do |x, i|
    dq.pop while !dq.empty? && nums[dq.last] <= x
    dq.push(i)
    out << nums[dq.first] if i >= k - 1
  end
  out
end
Correct:
 def window_max(nums, k)
  dq = []
  out = []
  nums.each_with_index do |x, i|
    dq.shift if !dq.empty? && dq.first <= i - k
    dq.pop while !dq.empty? && nums[dq.last] <= x
    dq.push(i)
    out << nums[dq.first] if i >= k - 1
  end
  out
end

Prompt. Why must a growing ring-buffer deque copy its elements in logical order instead of just enlarging the array?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Elements can wrap around the end of the array, so the logical order
differs from the physical order. If the array is only extended, the wrapped part stays in the old slots while head and the
modulo arithmetic now use the larger capacity, so reads cross empty slots and the order is corrupted. Copying from head
onward into a new array and resetting head to 0 restores a contiguous, correctly ordered buffer.

2. Overview and mental model: Hash
A Hash is a hash table of key-value pairs. Lookup, insert and delete are O(1) on average. Since Ruby 1.9 it iterates in
insertion order, which makes a Hash usable as an ordered map and as the core of an LRU cache.
A missing key reads as nil unless the hash has a default. Hash.new(0) is the counter idiom, the block form builds
independent defaults, and fetch raises KeyError. Keys are compared with eql? and hash, so mutable keys must not
change after insertion.
A hash cannot gain keys while it is being iterated, and merge keeps the argument's value unless a block combines
them.

h[:c] = 3
h.fetch(:d, 0)
h.delete("a")
h.each { |k, v| puts k }
h.transform_values { |v| v * 2 }

4.4 Algorithm chunks
h[key] returns nil for a missing key; count with Hash.new(0) or fetch when absence is an error
ruby-hash-missing-key   lens: access   level: L1   family: ruby-hash-access
Prerequisites: ruby-hash-default-shared. Follow-up: ruby-hash-iteration-add. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. counts[word] += 1 works on an empty hash.
A missing key reads as nil, and nil + 1 raises NoMethodError. Give the hash a default of 0 for counters, use fetch(key)
to raise KeyError when a key must exist, or fetch(key, default) for an explicit fallback. Lookup is O(1) on average.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def tally_bad(words)
  c = {}
  words.each { |w| c[w] += 1 }
  c
end
Correct:
 def tally(words)
  c = Hash.new(0)
  words.each { |w| c[w] += 1 }
  c
end

Ruby Hash: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 5
Hash.new([]) shares one default array and never stores the key; use the block form
ruby-hash-default-shared   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-hash-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-hash-missing-key. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Hash.new([]) gives every missing key its own empty array.
The default value is a single object returned for every missing key. h[:a] << 1 mutates that shared default and stores
nothing, so h.keys stays empty and h[:b] also sees the 1. The block form Hash.new { |hash, key| hash[key] = [] }
creates and stores a fresh array on first access.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def group_bad(pairs)
  h = Hash.new([])
  pairs.each { |k, v| h[k] << v }
  h
end
Correct:
 def group(pairs)
  h = Hash.new { |hash, key| hash[key] = [] }
  pairs.each { |k, v| h[k] << v }
  h
end
Mutating an array used as a key breaks lookup until rehash; freeze or copy the key
ruby-hash-mutable-key   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-hash-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-hash-order. Follow-up: ruby-hash-merge. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A key can be changed after it is stored and still be found.
A hash stores each key under its hash code at insertion time. If the key object is mutated afterwards, its code
changes and h[key] no longer finds the entry, although the entry is still there. Strings are copied and frozen when
used as keys, arrays are not. Use frozen keys (key.dup.freeze) or call rehash after a deliberate change.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def lookup_bad
  key = [1]
  h = { key => :found }
  key << 2
  h[key]
end
Correct:
 def lookup
  key = [1].freeze
  h = { key => :found }
  h[[1]]
end

Page 6
Adding a key while iterating a hash raises; iterate over a snapshot or build a new hash
ruby-hash-iteration-add   lens: iteration   level: L3   family: ruby-hash-iteration
Prerequisites: ruby-hash-missing-key. Follow-up: ruby-hash-order. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. You can add keys to a hash inside its own each loop.
A hash cannot grow during iteration: the insertion raises RuntimeError (can't add a new key into hash during
iteration). Updating the value of an existing key is allowed. Iterate over h.to_a or h.keys, or build the result with
transform_values, each_with_object or merge.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def double_keys_bad(h)
  h.each { |k, v| h[k.to_s * 2] = v }
  h
end
Correct:
 def double_keys(h)
  out = h.dup
  h.each { |k, v| out[k.to_s * 2] = v }
  out
end
A hash keeps insertion order; reassigning a key keeps its place, delete then insert moves it to
the end
ruby-hash-order   lens: ordering   level: L3   family: ruby-hash-ordering
Prerequisites: ruby-hash-iteration-add. Follow-up: ruby-hash-mutable-key. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. h[key] = value moves the key to the end of the hash.
Since Ruby 1.9 a Hash iterates in insertion order. Assigning to an existing key only changes its value and leaves its
position. To mark a key as most recently used, delete it and insert it again. That gives an LRU cache from one Hash:
evict h.first (the oldest) when the capacity is exceeded. All operations are O(1) on average.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def touch_bad(h, key)
  h[key] = h[key]
  h
end
Correct:
 def touch(h, key)
  value = h.delete(key)
  h[key] = value
  h
end
def evict_oldest(h)
  h.delete(h.first[0])
end

Ruby Hash: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
merge keeps the second hash's value on conflicts; pass a block to combine them
ruby-hash-merge   lens: transformation   level: L3   family: ruby-hash-transformation
Prerequisites: ruby-hash-mutable-key. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(m).
 Common misconception. a.merge(b) adds up values for keys present in both hashes.
Without a block, merge lets the argument win and the first value is lost. With a block { |key, old, new| ... } you decide
how conflicts combine, for example by summing counters. merge returns a new hash; merge! updates the receiver.
Cost is O(size of the argument).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def combine_bad(a, b)
  a.merge(b)
end
Correct:
 def combine(a, b)
  a.merge(b) { |_key, x, y| x + y }
end

Prompt. Why does h = Hash.new([]); h[:a] << 1 leave h empty?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Hash.new([]) creates one empty array and returns that same array for
every missing key. The expression h[:a] reads the default and pushes onto it, but a read never stores the key, so the
hash itself stays empty and every other missing key now returns the modified default. The block form creates a new array
and assigns it to the key on first access.

2. Overview and mental model: Singly linked list
A singly linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a reference to the next node. Ruby arrays are
contiguous buffers, so a custom list is useful when you splice nodes in O(1) given a reference, or keep a stable node
identity.
push_front is O(1); push_back is O(1) with a tail pointer; remove and search are O(n); reversal is O(n) time and O(1)
space. Always handle the empty list, the head and the tail separately.
Fast and slow pointers solve cycle detection and the middle node in one pass. Including Enumerable and defining
each gives map, select, to_a, include? and more for free.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Keep a tail pointer so push_back is O(1), and handle the empty list separately
ruby-singlylinkedlist-append   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-singlylinkedlist-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-singlylinkedlist-remove. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Appending can always start with head.next, even when the list is empty.
An empty list has no head node, so head.next raises NoMethodError on nil. push_back must set both head and tail
when the list is empty, and otherwise link the new node after the tail and move the tail. With a tail pointer append is
O(1); walking from the head to find the end is O(n). push_front is O(1) with or without a tail.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def append_bad(list, v)
  node = list.head
  node = node.next while node.next
  node.next = SLNode.new(v)
end

Correct:
 class SLNode
  attr_accessor :value, :next
  def initialize(value, nxt = nil)
    @value = value
    @next = nxt
  end
end
class SinglyList
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :head, :tail, :size
  def initialize
    @head = @tail = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def push_front(v)
    node = SLNode.new(v, @head)
    @head = node
    @tail ||= node
    @size += 1
    self
  end
  def push_back(v)
    node = SLNode.new(v)
    if @tail
      @tail.next = node
    else
      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
    @size += 1
    self
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    node = @head
    while node
      yield node.value
      node = node.next
    end
  end
end
Removing a node needs the previous node; also update head when removing the first node
and tail when removing the last
ruby-singlylinkedlist-remove   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ruby-singlylinkedlist-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-singlylinkedlist-append. Follow-up: ruby-singlylinkedlist-reverse. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Deleting the first node whose value matches only needs prev.next = node.next.
The first node has no previous node, so removing it must move head instead. Removing the last node must move tail
to the previous node, otherwise later push_back calls attach to a node that is no longer in the list. Finding the node
costs O(n); unlinking is O(1).

Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def remove_bad(list, v)
  prev = nil
  node = list.head
  while node && node.value != v
    prev = node
    node = node.next
  end
  prev.next = node.next if node
  node

Correct:
 class SinglyList
  def remove(v)
    prev = nil
    node = @head
    while node && node.value != v
      prev = node
      node = node.next
    end
    return false unless node
    if prev
      prev.next = node.next
    else
      @head = node.next
    end
    @tail = prev if node.equal?(@tail)
    @size -= 1
    true
  end
end
Reverse in place by saving node.next before redirecting it
ruby-singlylinkedlist-reverse   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-singlylinkedlist-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-singlylinkedlist-remove. Follow-up: ruby-singlylinkedlist-cycle. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Setting node.next = prev and then moving to node.next walks the old list.
After node.next = prev the old successor is unreachable, so the walk stops after one node and the rest of the list is
lost. Save nxt = node.next first, redirect, then advance prev and node. Reversal is O(n) time and O(1) extra space;
head and tail swap roles.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def reverse_bad(list)
  prev = nil
  node = list.head
  while node
    node.next = prev
    prev = node
    node = node.next
  end
  prev
end

 class SinglyList
  def reverse!
    prev = nil
    node = @head
    @tail = @head
    while node
      nxt = node.next
      node.next = prev
      prev = node
      node = nxt
    end
    @head = prev
    self
  end
end
Floyd cycle detection moves the pointers first and compares afterwards
ruby-singlylinkedlist-cycle   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-singlylinkedlist-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-singlylinkedlist-reverse. Follow-up: ruby-singlylinkedlist-middle. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Comparing slow and fast before moving them detects a cycle.
Both pointers start at the head, so comparing them before the first step is always true and reports a cycle in every list.
Advance slow by one and fast by two, then compare. If fast reaches nil the list ends. Floyd's method uses O(n) time
and O(1) space; a Set of visited nodes needs O(n) space.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def cycle_bad?(head)
  slow = fast = head
  while fast && fast.next
    return true if slow.equal?(fast)
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
  end
  false
end
Correct:
 def cycle?(head)
  slow = fast = head
  while fast && fast.next
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
    return true if slow.equal?(fast)
  end
  false
end

Find the middle with slow and fast pointers; the loop test must be fast && fast.next
ruby-singlylinkedlist-middle   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-singlylinkedlist-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-singlylinkedlist-cycle. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. while fast.next is a sufficient loop condition for the fast pointer.
With an even number of nodes, fast.next.next becomes nil after the last step and the next test fast.next calls a
method on nil. Test fast && fast.next so both fast and its successor exist. The slow pointer ends on the second middle
node for even lengths and on the middle node for odd lengths. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def middle_bad(head)
  slow = fast = head
  while fast.next
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
  end
  slow.value
end
Correct:
 def middle(head)
  return nil unless head
  slow = fast = head
  while fast && fast.next
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
  end
  slow.value
end

ruby-singlylinkedlist-remove-ex2   format: explain-why   level: L2   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Why must a singly linked list remove method update the tail pointer when it removes the last node?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). The tail pointer is used by push_back to attach the next node in O(1). If
the last node is unlinked but the tail still points to it, the next push_back links the new node after a node that is no longer
reachable from the head, so the new element silently disappears from the list. The remove method must move the tail to
the previous node.

2. Overview and mental model: Classes and Modules
Classes model data and behaviour; modules provide namespacing and mixins. A class has one superclass and any
number of included modules, which appear in its ancestors list. Method lookup walks the ancestors in order.
include adds a module's methods to instances, extend adds them to the class itself. Comparable (needs <=>) and
Enumerable (needs each) give a whole family of methods from one definition.
@@ class variables are shared with subclasses, class-level instance variables are not. private applies to instance
methods only, so class methods need private_class_method. A subclass initialize must call super, and hash-key
objects need ==, eql? and hash.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
@@ class variables are shared with every subclass; a class-level instance variable belongs
to one class
ruby-classmodule-class-state   lens: mental-model   level: L2   family: ruby-classmodule-mental-model
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-classmodule-mixin. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Each subclass gets its own copy of a @@ class variable.
A @@variable is a single slot shared by a class and all its subclasses, so counting instances of a subclass also
changes the parent's count. A class-level instance variable (@count set in the class body, exposed with class << self;
attr_accessor) belongs to exactly one class object. Initialise it for each subclass in the inherited hook.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class CounterBad
  @@count = 0
  def self.count = @@count
  def initialize = @@count += 1
end
class SubCounterBad < CounterBad; end
Correct:
 class Counter
  @count = 0
  class << self
    attr_accessor :count
    def inherited(sub)
      super
      sub.count = 0
    end
  end
  def initialize = self.class.count += 1
end
class SubCounter < Counter; end

include adds module methods to instances; extend adds them to the class itself
ruby-classmodule-mixin   lens: mental-model   level: L2   family: ruby-classmodule-composition
Prerequisites: ruby-classmodule-class-state. Follow-up: ruby-classmodule-comparable. Complexity: O(1).

include inserts the module into the ancestors of the class, so its methods become instance methods. To call them on
the class object, use extend, which adds them to the class's singleton. Calling an instance method on the class raises
NoMethodError.

A subclass initialize must call super, or the parent never sets its fields
ruby-classmodule-super   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-classmodule-creation
Prerequisites: ruby-classmodule-private. Follow-up: ruby-classmodule-hash-key. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A subclass inherits the parent's initialize automatically even when it defines its own.
Defining initialize in the subclass replaces the parent's. Without super the parent's instance variables stay unset (nil).
Call super(name) with the arguments the parent expects, or super() for none. Bare super forwards the same
arguments.

private does not apply to def self.; use private_class_method
ruby-classmodule-private   lens: access   level: L3   family: ruby-classmodule-access
Prerequisites: ruby-classmodule-comparable. Follow-up: ruby-classmodule-super. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Writing private above def self.helper makes the class method private.
The private keyword affects instance methods defined after it. Methods defined with def self.name are singleton
methods and stay public. Hide them with private_class_method :name, which makes calls with an explicit receiver
raise NoMethodError (private method called).

end

To use objects as Hash keys define ==, eql? and hash together
ruby-classmodule-hash-key   lens: equality   level: L3   family: ruby-classmodule-equality
Prerequisites: ruby-classmodule-super. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Defining == is enough for objects to work as Hash keys.
A Hash finds keys with hash and eql?, not ==. A class that only defines == makes two equal-looking objects different
keys. Define eql? (usually calling ==) and hash built from the same fields, for example [self.class, x, y].hash. The
fields used must not change while the object is a key.

  def initialize(x) = @x = x
  def ==(other) = other.is_a?(KeyBad) && x == other.x
end
def lookup_bad = { KeyBad.new(1) => :found }[KeyBad.new(1)]

  def initialize(x) = @x = x
  def ==(other) = other.is_a?(Key) && x == other.x
  alias eql? ==
  def hash = [self.class, x].hash
end

Define <=> and include Comparable to get sorting, comparison operators and between?
ruby-classmodule-comparable   lens: ordering   level: L3   family: ruby-classmodule-ordering
Prerequisites: ruby-classmodule-mixin. Follow-up: ruby-classmodule-private. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. An object can be sorted without defining <=>.
sort, min and max compare elements with <=>. A class that does not define it raises ArgumentError (comparison of
Version with Version failed). Define <=> and include Comparable to get <, <=, ==, >=, > and between?, clamp.
Similarly, define each and include Enumerable to get map, select, sort_by and min_by.

  def initialize(n) = @n = n
end
def sorted_versions_bad(ns)
  ns.map { |n| VersionBad.new(n) }.sort.map(&:n)
end
Correct:
 class Version
  include Comparable
  attr_reader :n
  def initialize(n) = @n = n
  def <=>(other) = n <=> other.n
end
def sorted_versions(ns)
  ns.map { |n| Version.new(n) }.sort.map(&:n)
end

Prompt. Why does a @@count in a parent class change when you create instances of a subclass?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). A class variable is stored once in the class hierarchy where it was first
defined, and every subclass reads and writes that same slot. Creating a subclass instance that runs @@count += 1
therefore updates the one shared value. A class-level instance variable (@count in the class body) is stored on each
class object separately, so each class keeps its own count.

2. Overview and mental model: Trie
A trie (prefix tree) stores strings character by character. Shared prefixes share nodes, so lookups cost O(L) in the
word length and do not depend on how many words are stored.
Each node holds a Hash from character to child node, a terminal flag marking the end of a word, and optionally a
pass count of words through it.
Typical uses are autocomplete, spell-check, prefix counting and longest-common-prefix problems.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Each trie node needs its own children Hash; Hash.new({}) shares one default Hash between
all nodes
ruby-trie-insert   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ruby-trie-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-trie-search. Complexity: O(L).
 Common misconception. Hash.new({}) is a convenient way to give every node an empty children Hash that fills itself
in.
The default value of Hash.new({}) is a single shared Hash object, and reading a missing key returns it without storing
anything, so children[ch] ||= is never true and the code walks into a bare Hash that has no node methods. Writes
through the default would be visible from every node. Use a plain {} per node and create children with ||=. Insert costs
O(L) for a word of length L.

 class TrieNode
  attr_reader :children
  attr_accessor :terminal, :pass
  def initialize
    @children = {}
    @terminal = false
    @pass = 0
  end
end
class Trie
  attr_reader :root, :size
  def initialize
    @root = TrieNode.new
    @size = 0
  end
  def insert(word)
    existing = find(word)
    return false if existing && existing.terminal
    node = @root
    word.each_char do |ch|
      node = (node.children[ch] ||= TrieNode.new)
      node.pass += 1
    end
    node.terminal = true
    @size += 1
    true
  end
  private
  def find(str)
    node = @root
    str.each_char do |ch|
      node = node.children[ch]
      return nil unless node
    end
    node
  end
end
A word exists only if its last node is terminal; a prefix exists if the path exists
ruby-trie-search   lens: access   level: L2   family: ruby-trie-access
Prerequisites: ruby-trie-insert. Follow-up: ruby-trie-autocomplete. Complexity: O(L).
 Common misconception. A word is in the trie when its path of characters exists.
The path for "app" exists as soon as "apple" is inserted, but "app" was never added as a word. Words need a terminal
flag on the last node, while a prefix check only needs the path. Both walk L nodes, O(L), independent of how many
words are stored.

Autocomplete walks the subtree and builds each word with prefix + ch, never by mutating a
shared string
ruby-trie-autocomplete   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ruby-trie-iteration
Prerequisites: ruby-trie-search. Follow-up: ruby-trie-delete. Complexity: O(L+k).
 Common misconception. Appending the character with << to the prefix as the recursion descends builds the words.
The same String object is passed to every recursive call, so << keeps lengthening it and siblings see the leftovers of
earlier branches, producing words like "abc" for "ac". Build a new string with prefix + ch for each child. Sort the results
for a deterministic order. Cost is O(L + size of the subtree).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

end
Correct:
 class Trie
  def words_with_prefix(prefix)
    node = find(prefix)
    return [] unless node
    out = []
    collect(node, prefix, out)
    out.sort
  end
  private
  def collect(node, prefix, out)
    out << prefix if node.terminal
    node.children.each { |ch, child| collect(child, prefix + ch, out) }
  end
end

Counting words with a prefix reads one pass counter instead of traversing the subtree
ruby-trie-count   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-trie-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-trie-delete. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(L).
 Common misconception. The number of words with a prefix is 1 if the prefix node is terminal, otherwise 0.
That only counts the prefix itself. Every node stores how many inserted words pass through it, so the count for a
prefix is the pass counter of its node, or 0 when the path is missing. Duplicate inserts must be ignored or the counters
inflate. The query is O(L), independent of the number of matches.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def count_bad(trie, prefix)
  node = trie.send(:find, prefix)
  node && node.terminal ? 1 : 0
end
Correct:
 class Trie
  def count_prefix(prefix)
    node = find(prefix)
    node ? node.pass : 0
  end
end
Deleting a word must not remove longer words that share its path
ruby-trie-delete   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: ruby-trie-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-trie-autocomplete. Follow-up: ruby-trie-count. Complexity: O(L).
 Common misconception. Deleting a word means removing the last character's node from its parent.
Removing that node also removes every longer word below it, so deleting "app" would delete "apple". Keep a pass
count on each node (how many words go through it). Decrement along the path, delete the first child whose count
reaches zero, and otherwise just clear the terminal flag. Delete costs O(L).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def delete_bad(trie, word)
  node = trie.root
  parent = nil
  word.each_char do |ch|
    parent = node
    node = node.children[ch]
    return false unless node
  end
  parent.children.delete(word[-1])
  true
end

Page 8
Correct:
 class Trie
  def delete(word)
    existing = find(word)
    return false unless existing && existing.terminal
    node = @root
    word.each_char do |ch|
      child = node.children[ch]
      child.pass -= 1
      if child.pass.zero?
        node.children.delete(ch)
        @size -= 1
        return true
      end
      node = child
    end
    node.terminal = false
    @size -= 1
    true
  end
end

Prompt. Why is Hash.new({}) a bug when it is used for the children of a trie node?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). The empty Hash given to Hash.new is one shared default object.

creates a node because the shared Hash is truthy. Any write made through the default would also appear in every other
node. Each node needs its own {} and nodes must be created explicitly.

2. Overview and mental model: Disjoint set
A disjoint-set (union-find) structure tracks a partition of elements into sets. find returns a set representative and union
merges two sets; both are nearly constant time with path compression and union by rank.
The classic array form stores parent[i] with parent[i] == i for roots. For arbitrary keys use a Hash whose default block
makes each new key its own root.
Typical uses are Kruskal's minimum spanning tree, cycle detection in undirected graphs, connected components and
grouping equivalent items.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Every element starts as its own parent: parent[i] = i, not a repeated default
ruby-disjointset-create   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ruby-disjointset-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-disjointset-compress. Complexity: O(h).
 Common misconception. Array.new(n, 0) is a fine initial parent array.
With every parent set to 0, all elements start in the set of element 0, so every pair looks connected before any union.
A root is defined by parent[x] == x, so the initial array must be the identity: Array.new(n) { |i| i }. Then n elements form
n sets, find walks parents up to the root, and union links one root to the other. The count of sets starts at n and drops
by one per successful union.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def find_bad(parent, x)
  x = parent[x] while parent[x] != x
  x
end
Correct:
 class DisjointSet
  attr_reader :parent, :rank, :count
  def initialize(n)
    @parent = Array.new(n) { |i| i }
    @rank = Array.new(n, 0)
    @count = n
  end
  def find(x)
    x = @parent[x] while @parent[x] != x
    x
  end
  def union(a, b)
    ra = find(a)
    rb = find(b)
    return false if ra == rb
    @parent[ra] = rb
    @count -= 1
    true
  end
  def connected?(a, b)
    find(a) == find(b)
  end
end

Ruby Disjoint set: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 5
For arbitrary keys use a Hash whose default block stores the key as its own parent
ruby-disjointset-named   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-disjointset-creation
Prerequisites: ruby-disjointset-kruskal. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(α(n)).
 Common misconception. A plain Hash of parents works for strings and symbols, since missing keys can be added
later.
find on an unseen key returns nil with a plain Hash, so union of two new keys compares nil with nil, decides they are
already connected and merges nothing. A Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = k } default block stores each new key as its own
root on first access. Keep sizes in a Hash.new(1) for union by size. Group the keys by their root to list the sets.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class NamedBad
  def initialize
    @parent = {}
  end
  def find(x)
    x = @parent[x] while @parent[x] != x
    x
  end
  def union(a, b)
    ra = find(a)
    rb = find(b)
    return false if ra == rb
    @parent[ra] = rb
    true
  end
end
Correct:
 class NamedSets
  def initialize
    @parent = Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = k }
    @size = Hash.new(1)
  end
  def find(x)
    root = x
    root = @parent[root] while @parent[root] != root
    while @parent[x] != root
      nxt = @parent[x]
      @parent[x] = root
      x = nxt
    end
    root
  end
  def union(a, b)
    ra = find(a)
    rb = find(b)
    return false if ra == rb
    ra, rb = rb, ra if @size[ra] < @size[rb]
    @parent[rb] = ra
    @size[ra] += @size[rb]
    true
  end
  def groups
    @parent.keys.group_by { |k| find(k) }.values.map(&:sort).sort
  end
  def sets_count
    groups.size
  end
end

Path compression must repoint every node on the path, saving the next node before
changing the link
ruby-disjointset-compress   lens: access   level: L2   family: ruby-disjointset-access
Prerequisites: ruby-disjointset-create. Follow-up: ruby-disjointset-rank. Complexity: O(α(n)).
 Common misconception. After finding the root, setting parent[x] = root for the starting node is enough.
Only the first node would then skip ahead; the nodes in the middle of the path keep long chains, so repeated finds
stay slow. Walk the path again from the start and set each node to the root, reading the old parent before overwriting
it. With compression, find is nearly constant on average (inverse Ackermann amortised with union by rank).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def compress_bad(parent, x)
  root = x
  root = parent[root] while parent[root] != root
  parent[x] = root
  root
end
Correct:
 class DisjointSet
  def find(x)
    root = x
    root = @parent[root] while @parent[root] != root
    while @parent[x] != root
      nxt = @parent[x]
      @parent[x] = root
      x = nxt
    end
    root
  end
end
Union by rank attaches the shorter tree under the taller one to keep trees shallow
ruby-disjointset-rank   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ruby-disjointset-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-disjointset-compress. Follow-up: ruby-disjointset-kruskal. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Always attach the first root under the second root.
Sequential unions such as (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3) then build a single long chain, and find becomes O(n). Attach the root
with the smaller rank (an upper bound of the height) under the other, and increase the rank only when both ranks are
equal. Trees then have height O(log n); with path compression the amortised cost per operation is nearly constant.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  ra = a
  ra = parent[ra] while parent[ra] != ra
  rb = b
  rb = parent[rb] while parent[rb] != rb
  parent[ra] = rb unless ra == rb
end
def depth_of(parent, x)
  d = 0
  while parent[x] != x
    x = parent[x]
    d += 1
  end
  d
end

 class DisjointSet
  def union(a, b)
    ra = find(a)
    rb = find(b)
    return false if ra == rb

Union returns false for an edge inside one set, which is how cycles are detected and Kruskal
skips edges
ruby-disjointset-kruskal   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-disjointset-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-disjointset-rank. Follow-up: ruby-disjointset-named. Complexity: O(E log E).
 Common misconception. Kruskal can union every sorted edge and add its weight.
An edge whose endpoints are already connected would close a cycle and must be skipped, so the weight is added
only when union reports that it merged two different sets. Sort the edges by weight, take the cheapest edges that do
not form a cycle, and stop when the forest is connected. Sorting dominates: O(E log E). The same test finds cycles in
an undirected graph.

    w
  end

 def mst_weight(n, edges)
  ds = DisjointSet.new(n)
  edges.sort_by { |e| e[2] }.sum { |u, v, w| ds.union(u, v) ? w : 0 }
end
def has_cycle?(n, edges)
  ds = DisjointSet.new(n)
  edges.any? { |u, v| !ds.union(u, v) }
end

Prompt. Why do union by rank and path compression together make a disjoint-set forest nearly constant time per

Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Union by rank keeps every tree shallow, with height at most logarithmic
in its size, so a single find is already cheap. Path compression flattens the nodes it visits so later finds on the same
elements reach the root in one step. Together the amortised cost per operation is bounded by the inverse Ackermann
function, which is at most 4 for any practical input size.

A stack pops from the same end it pushes to, and popping an empty stack must be handled
ruby-stack-pushpop   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-stack-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-stack-balanced. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Array#pop on an empty array is a safe way to read the top of a stack.
Array#pop and Array#last return nil on an empty array instead of raising, so a missing element travels onward until a
later call such as nil + nil fails far from the cause. A Stack class can raise a clear error on pop and peek of an empty
stack. push, pop and peek are O(1). Iterating from the top gives last-in, first-out order.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

end
Correct:
 class EmptyStackError < StandardError; end
class Stack
  include Enumerable
  def initialize
    @items = []
  end
  def push(v)
    @items.push(v)
    self
  end
  def pop
    raise EmptyStackError, "pop from empty stack" if @items.empty?
    @items.pop
  end
  def peek
    raise EmptyStackError, "peek at empty stack" if @items.empty?
    @items.last
  end
  def empty?
    @items.empty?
  end
  def size
    @items.size
  end
  def each(&block)
    return to_enum(:each) unless block
    @items.reverse_each(&block)
    self
  end
end

Balanced brackets need a stack because a counter cannot check the order of different kinds
ruby-stack-balanced   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-stack-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-stack-pushpop. Follow-up: ruby-stack-minstack. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Counting opening and closing brackets of each kind is enough to validate a string.
Equal counts do not mean proper nesting: "([)]" has one of each kind and ")(" has equal counts but closes before it
opens. Push each opener, and on a closer pop and compare with the matching opener. The string is balanced only if
no mismatch occurs and the stack ends empty. One pass, O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

end
Correct:
 PAIRS = { ")" => "(", "]" => "[", "}" => "{" }
def balanced?(s)
  stack = Stack.new
  s.each_char do |ch|
    if PAIRS.value?(ch)
      stack.push(ch)
    elsif PAIRS.key?(ch)
      return false if stack.empty? || stack.pop != PAIRS[ch]
    end
  end
  stack.empty?
end
In reverse Polish evaluation the first pop is the right operand
ruby-stack-rpn   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-stack-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-stack-minstack. Follow-up: ruby-stack-nextgreater. Complexity: O(n).

The stack holds operands in the order they appeared, so the first pop returns the right operand and the second the
left one. Swapping them is harmless for + and * but reverses - and /. Pop b, pop a, then compute a op b. Evaluation is
O(n).

A min-stack keeps a second stack of running minimums so pop can restore the previous
minimum

Prerequisites: ruby-stack-balanced. Follow-up: ruby-stack-rpn. Complexity: O(1).

When the current minimum is popped the single variable is stale and the previous minimum is lost. Store with each
value the minimum at that depth, or keep a parallel stack of minimums. Then push, pop and min are all O(1), at the
cost of O(n) extra space.

  def initialize
    @items = []
    @mins = []

  def push(v)

    @mins.push(@mins.empty? ? v : [@mins.last, v].min)

    @items.pop

Prerequisites: ruby-stack-rpn. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Popping while arr[top] <= x gives the next greater element.
With <= an equal value is popped and gets an equal value as its next greater element, but "greater" means strictly
larger. Keep a stack of indexes whose answer is still unknown and pop while arr[top] < x. Each index is pushed and
popped once, so the total is O(n), not O(n squared).

2. Overview and mental model: Set
A Set holds unique elements. It is built on a Hash whose values are ignored, so add, delete and include? are O(1) on
average. Set is autoloaded in current Ruby, but require "set" keeps older versions working.
Set#add? signals whether the element was new. Set == ignores order, and <=, <, disjoint? and intersect? express
subset relations. Union (|), intersection (&), difference (-) and symmetric difference (^) return new sets.
Elements are hashed like Hash keys, so do not mutate them after insertion. A Set keeps insertion order but has no
sorted variant; use set.sort for order.

s.sort

Set.new takes an enumerable; Set.new(5) raises, so convert a scalar or string with to_a or

ruby-set-create   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ruby-set-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-set-add-q. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Set.new accepts any value and wraps it as one element.
Set.new(enum) iterates its argument, so an Integer raises ArgumentError (value must be enumerable) and a String is
not enumerable either. Use Set[1, 2, 3] for literal members, enum.to_set for a collection, and "abc".chars.to_set for
characters. A Set is backed by a Hash, so add and include? are O(1) on average.

end
Correct:

def letters(word)
  word.chars.to_set
end

add always returns the set; add? returns nil when the element was already present
ruby-set-add-q   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ruby-set-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-set-create. Follow-up: ruby-set-equality. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. seen.add(x) returns false for a duplicate.
Set#add returns the set itself, which is always truthy, so it cannot tell you whether the element was new. Set#add?
returns the set when it inserted the element and nil when it was already there. That makes duplicate detection a
single O(1) call per element.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "set"
def first_dup_bad(items)
  seen = Set.new
  items.each { |x| return x unless seen.add(x) }
  nil
end
Correct:
 require "set"
def first_dup(items)
  seen = Set.new
  items.each { |x| return x unless seen.add?(x) }
  nil
end
Sets are equal when they hold the same elements, in any order; arrays also compare order
ruby-set-equality   lens: equality   level: L2   family: ruby-set-equality
Prerequisites: ruby-set-add-q. Follow-up: ruby-set-mutable. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Set[1, 2] and [1, 2] behave the same when compared with their reversed versions.
Set#== ignores order, so Set[1, 2] == Set[2, 1], while [1, 2] == [2, 1] is false. Use <= (subset?), < (proper_subset?),
disjoint? and intersect? for relations. Comparing a Set with an Array is never equal, even with the same elements.

end
Correct:

def same_items?(a, b)

end

Changing an element after it was added makes a Set lose it; add frozen elements
ruby-set-mutable   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-set-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-set-equality. Follow-up: ruby-set-sorted. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. An array stored in a Set can be modified and still be found.
A Set stores each element under its hash code, like Hash keys. If an element such as an array is mutated afterwards,
its hash code changes and include? returns false, although the element is still in the set. Add frozen copies
(item.dup.freeze) or immutable values such as Data.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

def lost_bad
  s = Set.new
  item = [1]
  s << item
  item << 2
  s.include?(item)
end
Correct:
 require "set"
def kept
  s = Set.new
  item = [1].freeze
  s << item
  s.include?([1])
end
A Set iterates in insertion order and has no sorting; SortedSet was removed, so call sort
ruby-set-sorted   lens: ordering   level: L3   family: ruby-set-ordering
Prerequisites: ruby-set-mutable. Follow-up: ruby-set-pair. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. SortedSet.new keeps the elements ordered.
SortedSet was extracted from the standard library in Ruby 3.0 and raises on use. A Set keeps insertion order and
offers no ordered access, so sort the elements into an Array when you need order: set.sort (O(n log n)). For a sorted
structure with fast insertion use a balanced tree or a heap.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

def ordered_bad(items)
  SortedSet.new(items).to_a
end
Correct:
 require "set"
def ordered(items)

2. Overview and mental model: AVL tree
An AVL tree is a binary search tree that keeps the heights of every node's two subtrees within one. Rotations restore
the balance after an insert or a delete while preserving the in-order sequence.
Search, insert and delete are O(log n); the height is at most about 1.44 log2(n + 2). Each node stores its height so
balance factors are O(1).
Recursive insert and delete return the new subtree root, and the caller assigns it to the child link.

After rotate_right the old root y becomes the child of x. x's height depends on y's height, so y must be updated first.

  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :root, :size

  def height_of(node)
    node ? node.height : 0

  def update(node)
    node.height = 1 + [height_of(node.left), height_of(node.right)].max

    height_of(node.left) - height_of(node.right)

    x = y.left
    y.left = x.right
    x.right = y
    update(y)
    update(x)

  def rotate_left(x)
    y = x.right
    x.right = y.left
    y.left = x
    update(x)
    update(y)

Prerequisites: ruby-avltree-delete. Follow-up: ruby-avltree-check. Complexity: O(log n).

A plain BST fed sorted keys becomes a chain of height n and each operation is O(n). An AVL tree rebalances after
each insert, so its height never exceeds about 1.44 log2(n + 2). Inserting 1..15 in order gives height 4, the minimum
possible. Search, insert and delete are all O(log n).

A left-right or right-left imbalance needs a double rotation, not a single one
ruby-avltree-double   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-avltree-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-avltree-rotate. Follow-up: ruby-avltree-delete. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Whenever a node is left-heavy, one right rotation restores balance.
If the heavy left child is itself right-heavy (the zig-zag case), a single right rotation just moves the imbalance to the
other side. First rotate the child left, then rotate the node right. The mirror case rotates the right child right and then
the node left. The balance factors of the node and of the heavy child pick the case.

    child_balance < 0 ? [:rotate_child_left, :rotate_right] : [:rotate_right]

Deletion can unbalance every ancestor, so rebalance on the way back up
ruby-avltree-delete   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: ruby-avltree-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-avltree-double. Follow-up: ruby-avltree-height. Complexity: O(log n).

Removing a node from one side makes the other side relatively taller and can break the balance factor of the parent
or a higher ancestor. Call rebalance on every node of the recursion path as it returns. A node with two children takes
