Checking the AVL property means testing every node, not only the root
ruby-avltree-check   lens: equality   level: L3   family: ruby-avltree-equality
Prerequisites: ruby-avltree-height. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).

failure marker as soon as any node has a balance factor outside -1..1. One pass, O(n). Checking recomputed heights

 def avl_height(node)
  return 0 unless node
  l = avl_height(node.left)
  return nil unless l
  r = avl_height(node.right)
  return nil unless r
  return nil if (l - r).abs > 1
  1 + [l, r].max

2. Overview and mental model: Heap
A binary min-heap stores a complete binary tree in an Array: node i has children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 and parent (i - 1) / 2.
The smallest element is always at index 0.
push and pop are O(log n), peek is O(1) and bottom-up build is O(n). Ruby has no built-in heap; a small class or an
array with min and delete is the usual choice.
Ruby division and negative array indexes hide off-by-one bugs: (0 - 1) / 2 is -1 and @a[-1] is the last element, so
guard the loop with i > 0.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Sift-up must stop at index 0, because in Ruby (0 - 1) / 2 is -1 and -1 indexes the last element
ruby-heap-pushsift   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-heap-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-heap-pop. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. The loop can end naturally when the parent is not larger than the value.
A binary heap stores node i's parent at (i - 1) / 2. Ruby integer division rounds toward negative infinity, so for i = 0 the
parent index is -1, and @a[-1] is the last element of the array, not an error. Without an i > 0 guard the root is
compared with the last element and the two can be swapped, corrupting the heap. push is O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def sift_up_bad(a, i)
  parent = (i - 1) / 2
  while a[parent] > a[i]
    a[parent], a[i] = a[i], a[parent]
    i = parent
    parent = (i - 1) / 2
  end
  a
end

Correct:
 class MinHeap
  attr_reader :size
  def initialize
    @a = []
  end
  def size
    @a.size
  end
  def empty?
    @a.empty?
  end
  def peek
    @a.first
  end
  def push(v)
    @a.push(v)
    sift_up(@a.size - 1)
    self
  end
  def pop
    return nil if @a.empty?
    top = @a[0]
    last = @a.pop
    unless @a.empty?
      @a[0] = last
      sift_down(0)
    end
    top
  end
  private
  def sift_up(i)
    while i > 0
      parent = (i - 1) / 2
      break if @a[parent] <= @a[i]
      @a[parent], @a[i] = @a[i], @a[parent]
      i = parent
    end
  end
  def sift_down(i)
    n = @a.size
    loop do
      l = 2 * i + 1
      r = l + 1
      small = i
      small = l if l < n && @a[l] < @a[small]
      small = r if r < n && @a[r] < @a[small]
      break if small == i
      @a[small], @a[i] = @a[i], @a[small]
      i = small
    end
  end
end

Build a heap in O(n) by sifting down from the last parent to the root
ruby-heap-heapify   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-heap-creation
Prerequisites: ruby-heap-pop. Follow-up: ruby-heap-kth. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Sifting down from index 0 upward to the last parent builds the heap.
Sift-down assumes both child subtrees are already heaps, so the work must start at the bottom: from index n / 2 - 1
down to 0. Going from the root downwards fixes the root before its subtrees are ordered and leaves violations behind.
Most nodes are near the leaves and move little, so the total is O(n), better than n pushes at O(n log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def build_bad(items)
  a = items.dup
  n = a.size
  (0...(n / 2)).each do |start|
    i = start
    while 2 * i + 1 < n
      l = 2 * i + 1
      r = l + 1
      s = i
      s = l if a[l] < a[s]
      s = r if r < n && a[r] < a[s]
      break if s == i
      a[s], a[i] = a[i], a[s]
      i = s
    end
  end
  a
end
Correct:
 class MinHeap
  def build(items)
    @a = items.dup
    (@a.size / 2 - 1).downto(0) { |i| sift_down(i) }
    self
  end
end
Sift-down swaps with the smaller of the two children, not always the left one
ruby-heap-pop   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ruby-heap-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-heap-pushsift. Follow-up: ruby-heap-heapify. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. After moving the last element to the root, swapping it with the left child when it is larger is
enough.
If the right child is smaller than the left one, swapping with the left child leaves the right child smaller than its new
parent, which breaks the heap order. Compare with both children and swap with the smallest. Children of i are 2i + 1
and 2i + 2, and each must be checked against the array size. pop is O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def sift_down_bad(a, i)
  n = a.size
  while 2 * i + 1 < n
    l = 2 * i + 1
    break if a[l] >= a[i]
    a[l], a[i] = a[i], a[l]
    i = l
  end
  a
end

 def sift_down_ok(a, i)
  n = a.size
  loop do
    l = 2 * i + 1
    r = l + 1
    small = i
    small = l if l < n && a[l] < a[small]
    small = r if r < n && a[r] < a[small]
    break if small == i
    a[small], a[i] = a[i], a[small]
    i = small
  end
  a
end
A max-heap can reuse a min-heap by negating keys, and must negate again on the way out
ruby-heap-maxheap   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: ruby-heap-ordering
Prerequisites: ruby-heap-kth. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Pushing negated values is enough; pop and peek already return the right numbers.
The negation trick turns the smallest negated value into the largest original one, but the heap stores and returns
negated numbers. Negate on push and negate again on pop and peek. It works for numeric keys only; for other types
pass a comparator or store an ordering key. Operations stay O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class MaxHeapBad
  def initialize
    @h = MinHeap.new
  end
  def push(v)
    @h.push(-v)
    self
  end
  def pop
    @h.pop
  end
end
Correct:
 class MaxHeap
  def initialize
    @h = MinHeap.new
  end
  def push(v)
    @h.push(-v)
    self
  end
  def pop
    v = @h.pop
    v && -v
  end
  def peek
    v = @h.peek
    v && -v
  end
  def size
    @h.size
  end
end

The kth largest element comes from a min-heap capped at k items, trimmed after each push
ruby-heap-kth   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-heap-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-heap-heapify. Follow-up: ruby-heap-maxheap. Complexity: O(n log k).
 Common misconception. Trim the heap before adding the new value to keep it at k items.
Trimming before the push evicts the smallest stored value even when the new value is smaller still, so a small
newcomer displaces a larger value that belongs in the top k. Push first, then pop while the size exceeds k; the root is
then the smallest of the k largest values, which is the kth largest. Time O(n log k) and O(k) space, better than sorting
when k is small.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def kth_largest_bad(nums, k)
  h = MinHeap.new
  nums.each do |x|
    h.pop if h.size >= k
    h.push(x)
  end
  h.peek
end
Correct:
 def kth_largest(nums, k)
  h = MinHeap.new
  nums.each do |x|
    h.push(x)
    h.pop if h.size > k
  end
  h.peek
end

Prompt. Why is building a heap bottom-up with sift-down O(n) although each sift-down can cost O(log n)?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Sift-down from a node costs at most the height of its subtree. Half of the
nodes are leaves and need no work, a quarter have height 1, an eighth have height 2, and so on. The total work is the
sum of height times the number of nodes at that height, which converges to a constant times n. Only the few nodes near
the root pay the full logarithmic cost.

2. Overview and mental model: Enumerator
An Enumerator wraps an iteration. Most iterator methods return one when called without a block (each, map,
each_slice, each_cons). It supports external iteration with next, peek and rewind, internal iteration with a block, and
chaining such as map.with_index(1).
enum.lazy makes a chain that processes one element at a time and stops early, so it can work with infinite sources
like (1..) or Enumerator.new { |y| loop { y << x } }. Eager chains build an intermediate array per step.
next raises StopIteration at the end; loop rescues it. each_cons(k) gives overlapping windows, each_slice(k) gives
disjoint chunks.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Enumerator#next raises StopIteration at the end; loop rescues it, while and until do not
ruby-enumerator-next   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ruby-enumerator-iteration
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-enumerator-lazy. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. e.next returns nil when the enumerator is exhausted.
External iteration with next hands out one element per call and raises StopIteration when the sequence is over.
Kernel#loop rescues StopIteration and ends quietly, so loop { out << e.next } is the idiom. A while true loop lets the
exception escape. peek looks ahead without consuming, and rewind starts again.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def drain_bad(arr)
  e = arr.each
  out = []
  while true
    out << e.next
  end
  out
end
Correct:
 def drain(arr)
  e = arr.each
  out = []
  loop { out << e.next }
  out
end

Ruby Enumerator: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 5
map.with_index(1) numbers from 1; each_with_index starts at 0
ruby-enumerator-index   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ruby-enumerator-transformation
Prerequisites: ruby-enumerator-generator. Follow-up: ruby-enumerator-window. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. each_with_index numbers the elements from 1.
each_with_index and with_index default to a zero-based offset. Pass an argument to start elsewhere:
map.with_index(1). The enumerator returned by map without a block carries the method with it, so with_index
decides the offset and map decides what is collected.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def numbered_bad(items)
  items.each_with_index.map { |x, i| "#{i}. #{x}" }
end
Correct:
 def numbered(items)
  items.map.with_index(1) { |x, i| "#{i}. #{x}" }
end
Enumerator.new generates values with yielder << x; a generator without loop is finite
ruby-enumerator-generator   lens: creation   level: L3   family: ruby-enumerator-creation
Prerequisites: ruby-enumerator-lazy. Follow-up: ruby-enumerator-index. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. An Enumerator.new block keeps producing values by itself.
The block runs once and ends when it returns. To produce an infinite stream, wrap the yielding in loop { y << value }.
The stream is consumed on demand: take(8), first(8) or lazy chains stop it. Without loop the block yields its single
value and finishes, so take(8) returns one element.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def fib_bad
  Enumerator.new do |y|
    a, b = 0, 1
    y << a
  end
end
Correct:
 def fib
  Enumerator.new do |y|
    a, b = 0, 1
    loop do
      y << a
      a, b = b, a + b
    end
  end
end

Page 6
lazy evaluates elements one at a time and stops early; eager map and select process the
whole collection first
ruby-enumerator-lazy   lens: iteration   level: L3   family: ruby-enumerator-iteration
Prerequisites: ruby-enumerator-next. Follow-up: ruby-enumerator-generator. Complexity: O(k).
 Common misconception. map.select.first(n) only processes as many elements as it needs.
Eager methods build a full intermediate array at every step, so (1..1000).map { }.select { }.first(2) calls the map block
1000 times. enum.lazy passes each element through the whole chain before taking the next, and first(n) stops once n
results exist. Lazy chains also work on infinite sources such as (1..).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def eager(n)
  calls = 0
  r = (1..1000).map { |x| calls += 1; x * 2 }.select { |x| (x % 3).zero? }.first(n)
  [r, calls]
end
Correct:
 def lazily(n)
  calls = 0
  r = (1..1000).lazy.map { |x| calls += 1; x * 2 }.select { |x| (x % 3).zero? }.first(n)
  [r, calls]
end
each_cons gives overlapping windows; each_slice gives disjoint chunks
ruby-enumerator-window   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-enumerator-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-enumerator-index. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n * k).
 Common misconception. each_slice(k) visits every window of size k.
each_slice(k) cuts the collection into non-overlapping groups, so a sliding-window maximum sees only n / k windows.
each_cons(k) yields every consecutive window of size k: n - k + 1 of them. Summing each window is O(n * k), or O(n)
with a running sum.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def best_window_bad(nums, k)
  nums.each_slice(k).map(&:sum).max
end
Correct:
 def best_window(nums, k)
  nums.each_cons(k).map(&:sum).max
end

Prompt. Why does lazy make map and select over a large range cheaper when you only need the first few results?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). An eager chain finishes each step for the whole collection before the
next step starts, so map runs on every element and builds an array even though only a few results are used. A lazy chain
sends one element at a time through map and select and stops as soon as first(n) has n results, so only the elements up
to that point are ever processed, and no full intermediate arrays are created.

2. Overview and mental model: Segment tree
A segment tree stores an aggregate (sum, minimum, maximum, gcd) for every segment of an array, so any range
query and any point update take O(log n) after an O(n) build.
The recursive layout keeps node i's children at 2i and 2i + 1 and uses a 4n-slot Array. A bottom-up version with
leaves at n..2n-1 is shorter for associative operations. Lazy propagation adds O(log n) range updates.
Pick the identity of the operation for out-of-range segments: 0 for sum, Float::INFINITY for min.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Split a segment into [l, mid] and [mid + 1, r] so the halves never overlap
ruby-segmenttree-build   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-segmenttree-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-query. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Splitting a range at mid into [l, mid] and [mid, r] is the natural way to divide it.
The two halves share the element at mid, so it is counted twice, and a range of two elements recurses on itself
forever (SystemStackError). Use [l, mid] and [mid + 1, r]. Store node i's children at 2i and 2i + 1 and allocate 4n slots,
which always suffices for the recursive layout. Building is O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def build_bad(arr, l, r)
  return arr[l] if l == r
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  build_bad(arr, l, mid) + build_bad(arr, mid, r)
end
Correct:
 class SegTree
  attr_reader :tree, :size
  def initialize(arr)
    @size = arr.size
    @tree = Array.new(4 * [@size, 1].max, 0)
    build(arr, 1, 0, @size - 1) if @size > 0
  end
  def total
    @tree[1]
  end
  private
  def build(arr, node, l, r)
    if l == r
      @tree[node] = arr[l]
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    build(arr, 2 * node, l, mid)
    build(arr, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r)
    @tree[node] = @tree[2 * node] + @tree[2 * node + 1]
  end
end

A point update must recompute every ancestor on the path from the leaf to the root
ruby-segmenttree-update   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ruby-segmenttree-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-query. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-min. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Changing the leaf value is enough, because queries read from the leaves.
Queries use the stored sums of inner nodes, so an ancestor that is not recomputed keeps answering with the old
value. After changing the leaf, recompute each ancestor as the sum of its children while the recursion unwinds. Only
one root-to-leaf path changes, so an update is O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  if l == r
    t[node] = v
    return
  end

  if i <= mid
    update_bad(t, 2 * node, l, mid, i, v)
  else
    update_bad(t, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, i, v)
  end
end
Correct:
 class SegTree
  def update(i, v)
    update_at(1, 0, @size - 1, i, v)
    self
  end
  private
  def update_at(node, l, r, i, v)
    if l == r
      @tree[node] = v
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    if i <= mid
      update_at(2 * node, l, mid, i, v)
    else
      update_at(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, i, v)
    end
    @tree[node] = @tree[2 * node] + @tree[2 * node + 1]
  end
end

A range query returns the identity for disjoint segments, the stored value for covered ones,
and combines otherwise
ruby-segmenttree-query   lens: access   level: L3   family: ruby-segmenttree-access
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-build. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-update. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. A query can return the stored value whenever the segment is covered, and recurse
otherwise, without a disjoint case.
Without the disjoint check the recursion reaches leaves that lie outside the query and adds their values. For a sum
the identity is 0: return 0 when the node range does not intersect the query, return the stored sum when it is fully
inside, and otherwise add the answers from both children. At most about 2 log n nodes are expanded, so a query is
O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  return t[node] if l == r || (ql <= l && r <= qr)
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  query_bad(t, 2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) +
    query_bad(t, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
end
Correct:
 class SegTree
  def query(ql, qr)
    query_at(1, 0, @size - 1, ql, qr)
  end
  private
  def query_at(node, l, r, ql, qr)
    return 0 if qr < l || r < ql
    return @tree[node] if ql <= l && r <= qr
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    query_at(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) + query_at(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
  end
end
Lazy propagation must push pending additions to the children before descending into them
ruby-segmenttree-lazy   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-segmenttree-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-min. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. A pending range addition stored on a node can stay there until the whole node is queried.
A partial query or update descends into the children, which do not yet know about the addition stored on their parent,
so they return stale values. Push the pending value down (apply it to both children and clear it) before recursing.
Then range add and range sum are both O(log n) instead of O(n) per update.

 class LazySeg
  def initialize(arr)
    @n = arr.size
    @sum = Array.new(4 * @n, 0)
    @lazy = Array.new(4 * @n, 0)
    build(1, 0, @n - 1, arr)
  end
  def add(l, r, v)
    range_add(1, 0, @n - 1, l, r, v)
  end
  def sum(l, r)
    range_sum(1, 0, @n - 1, l, r)
  end
  private
  def build(node, l, r, arr)
    if l == r
      @sum[node] = arr[l]
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    build(2 * node, l, mid, arr)
    build(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, arr)
    @sum[node] = @sum[2 * node] + @sum[2 * node + 1]
  end
  def apply(node, l, r, v)
    @sum[node] += v * (r - l + 1)
    @lazy[node] += v
  end
  def push(node, l, r)
    return if @lazy[node].zero?
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    apply(2 * node, l, mid, @lazy[node])
    apply(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, @lazy[node])
    @lazy[node] = 0
  end
  def range_add(node, l, r, ql, qr, v)
    return if qr < l || r < ql
    if ql <= l && r <= qr
      apply(node, l, r, v)
      return
    end
    push(node, l, r)
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    range_add(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr, v)
    range_add(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr, v)
    @sum[node] = @sum[2 * node] + @sum[2 * node + 1]
  end
  def range_sum(node, l, r, ql, qr)
    return 0 if qr < l || r < ql
    return @sum[node] if ql <= l && r <= qr
    push(node, l, r)
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    range_sum(2 * node, l, mid, ql, qr) + range_sum(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
  end
end

The identity element must match the operation: Float::INFINITY for minimum, not 0
ruby-segmenttree-min   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-segmenttree-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-segmenttree-update. Follow-up: ruby-segmenttree-lazy. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Starting the running result at 0 works for any combine operation.
Zero is the identity for sum, but for minimum any positive value is larger than 0, so every query returns 0. The identity
of min is Float::INFINITY and of max is -Float::INFINITY. This bottom-up version stores the leaves at n..2n-1 and
answers half-open ranges [l, r) by climbing; build is O(n) and query O(log n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

  def initialize(arr)

    @t = Array.new(2 * @n, 0)

  end

    l += @n
    r += @n

        res = [res, @t[l]].min

end
Correct:
 class MinSegTree
  def initialize(arr)
    @n = arr.size
    @t = Array.new(2 * @n, Float::INFINITY)
    arr.each_with_index { |v, i| @t[@n + i] = v }
    (@n - 1).downto(1) { |i| @t[i] = [@t[2 * i], @t[2 * i + 1]].min }
  end
  def query(l, r)
    res = Float::INFINITY
    l += @n
    r += @n
    while l < r
      if l.odd?
        res = [res, @t[l]].min
        l += 1
      end
      if r.odd?
        r -= 1
        res = [res, @t[r]].min
      end
      l /= 2
      r /= 2
    end
    res
  end
end

Prompt. Why is a recursive segment tree usually stored in an array of 4n slots?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). The recursive layout puts the children of node i at 2i and 2i + 1 and splits
ranges in the middle, so for sizes that are not powers of two the tree is not complete and some indexes are skipped. The
deepest level can reach an index of almost 4n, so 4n slots are a simple safe upper bound. A power-of-two padded size of
2 * 2^ceil(log2 n) would also work.

2. Overview and mental model: Bloom filter
A Bloom filter is a compact probabilistic set. add sets k bits chosen by hashing; include? returns false only if the item
was never added, and true if the item was added or by chance collides (a false positive). It never gives false
negatives.
In Ruby one arbitrarily large Integer can hold the whole bit array: set with |= 1 << i, read with bits[i]. Positions come
from double hashing with Zlib.crc32 and Digest::MD5; String#hash is randomised per process and must not be used.
Size it with m = -n ln p / (ln 2)^2 bits and k = (m / n) ln 2 hashes. Standard filters cannot delete; use a counting filter
when removal is needed.

ruby-bloomfilter-bits   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ruby-bloomfilter-mutation

Addition carries: if bit i is already set, adding 1 << i clears it and sets bit i + 1, silently corrupting a neighbour. OR is

String#hash
ruby-bloomfilter-hash   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ruby-bloomfilter-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-bloomfilter-bits. Complexity: O(k).
 Common misconception. item.hash is a quick way to get the hash value for a Bloom filter.
String#hash is seeded randomly for every Ruby process, so the same string hashes differently after a restart. A filter
that was saved, shared or rebuilt elsewhere then answers wrongly. Use deterministic hashes: Zlib.crc32 and
Digest::MD5 give two independent values h1 and h2, and double hashing derives all k positions as (h1 + i * h2) % m.
Keep h2 non-zero so positions differ. Each add or lookup costs O(k).

 require "digest"
require "zlib"
class BloomFilter
  attr_reader :m, :k, :bits
  def initialize(m, k)
    @m = m
    @k = k
    @bits = 0
  end
  def positions(item)
    s = item.to_s
    h1 = Zlib.crc32(s)
    h2 = Digest::MD5.hexdigest(s).to_i(16) % (@m - 1) + 1
    Array.new(@k) { |i| (h1 + i * h2) % @m }
  end
  def add(item)
    positions(item).each { |i| @bits |= 1 << i }
    self
  end
  def include?(item)
    positions(item).all? { |i| @bits[i] == 1 }
  end
end

A Bloom filter cannot delete; clearing bits breaks other items, so use counters
ruby-bloomfilter-remove   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: ruby-bloomfilter-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-bloomfilter-size. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(k).
 Common misconception. Removing an item means clearing its k bits.
Those bits may also belong to other items, which would then be reported absent: false negatives, which a Bloom filter
must never produce. A counting Bloom filter keeps a small counter per position, increments on add and decrements
on remove, and treats a position as set when its counter is above zero. It uses several times the memory. Only
remove items that were added.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

    positions(item).each { |i| @bits &= ~(1 << i) }
    self
  end
end
Correct:
 class CountingBloom < BloomFilter
  def initialize(m, k)
    super
    @counts = Array.new(m, 0)
  end
  def add(item)
    positions(item).each { |i| @counts[i] += 1 }
    self
  end
  def include?(item)
    positions(item).all? { |i| @counts[i] > 0 }
  end
  def remove(item)
    return false unless include?(item)
    positions(item).each { |i| @counts[i] -= 1 }
    true
  end
end
Size the filter with m = -n ln p / (ln 2)^2 and k = (m / n) ln 2
ruby-bloomfilter-size   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: ruby-bloomfilter-complexity
Prerequisites: ruby-bloomfilter-query. Follow-up: ruby-bloomfilter-remove. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Take m = n * ln(p) / (ln 2)^2 for n items and a false-positive rate p.
For p < 1, ln(p) is negative, so the formula needs a minus sign or m comes out negative. The optimal number of hash
functions is (m / n) ln 2, rounded. For one thousand items at one percent this gives about 9586 bits and 7 hashes,
roughly 9.6 bits per item. Memory is independent of the size of the items.

Prompt. Why can a standard Bloom filter not remove items without creating false negatives?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Each item sets k bits and different items may share bits. Clearing the bits
of a removed item also clears bits that other stored items rely on, so those items would no longer have all of their bits set
and would be reported absent, a false negative. A counting Bloom filter stores a counter per position so that a shared
position only reaches zero when every item using it has been removed.

2. Overview and mental model: Date, Time and DateTime
Date (require "date") models calendar days; Time models an instant with a time zone; DateTime is a legacy class that
the Ruby documentation discourages in favour of Time. Date arithmetic is O(1): + adds days, >> adds months with
clamping, and subtracting two dates gives a Rational number of days.
Date.new raises Date::Error for impossible dates; valid_date? checks first. wday is 0 for Sunday, cwday follows ISO
(Monday 1 to Sunday 7). Date.parse guesses the field order, so use strptime or Date.iso8601 for external text.
Time.utc(...) and Time.at(...).utc avoid dependence on the machine time zone. Time subtraction returns Float
seconds.

2. Overview and mental model: Matrix and Vector
Matrix and Vector (require "matrix", a bundled gem since Ruby 3.1) provide linear algebra on arrays of numbers.
They work with Integer, Rational and Float entries, and many operations are exact: the inverse of an integer matrix
has Rational entries.
Matrix[[1, 2], [3, 4]] builds from rows; rows must have equal length. * is the matrix product (O(n^3) for square
matrices), hadamard_product is element-wise, determinant and inverse are O(n^3), and ** uses repeated squaring.
Shapes must match: A * B needs A.column_count == B.row_count. Vector * Vector is undefined; use inner_product.
A 2D Array of Arrays is often enough for grids; use Matrix for algebra.

* is the matrix product; use hadamard_product for element-wise multiplication
ruby-matrix-multiply   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ruby-matrix-transformation
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-ragged. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-shape. Complexity: O(n^3).
 Common misconception. Multiplying two matrices with * multiplies matching elements.
* computes the row-by-column matrix product, so [[1, 2], [3, 4]] squared is [[7, 10], [15, 22]]. Element-wise
multiplication is hadamard_product (also called entrywise_product). The product of an r x k and a k x c matrix takes
O(r * k * c) operations.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def square_bad(m)
  Matrix.build(m.row_count, m.column_count) { |r, c| m[r, c] * m[r, c] }
end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def square(m)
  m * m
end
def entrywise(m)
  m.hadamard_product(m)
end
Multiplying needs left columns equal to right rows; otherwise ErrDimensionMismatch is
raised
ruby-matrix-shape   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: ruby-matrix-edge-cases
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-multiply. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-inverse. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Any two matrices can be multiplied.
The product A * B requires A.column_count == B.row_count. A 1 x 2 matrix times a 1 x 2 matrix raises
ExceptionForMatrix::ErrDimensionMismatch. Check the shapes before multiplying, or transpose one operand: A *
B.transpose is 1 x 1 here.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def product_bad(a, b)
  a * b
end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def product(a, b)
  return nil unless a.column_count == b.row_count
  a * b
end

inverse of an integer matrix has Rational entries and a singular matrix raises ErrNotRegular
ruby-matrix-inverse   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: ruby-matrix-edge-cases
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-shape. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-fib. Complexity: O(n^3).
 Common misconception. The inverse of an integer matrix is made of floats, and every square matrix has one.
Matrix#inverse uses exact arithmetic: integer input gives Rational entries such as (3/2). A matrix with determinant 0
has no inverse and raises ExceptionForMatrix::ErrNotRegular. Test determinant.zero? first, or use rescue.
Determinant and inverse are O(n^3).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def invert_bad(m)
  m.inverse
end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def invert(m)
  return nil if m.determinant.zero?
  m.inverse
end
Use inner_product for the dot product; Vector * Vector is not defined
ruby-matrix-vector   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-matrix-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-fib. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. v * w computes the dot product of two vectors.
Vector * Vector raises ExceptionForMatrix::ErrOperationNotDefined; * with a number scales the vector and * with a
Matrix multiplies. The dot product is v.inner_product(w) (also dot), the length is v.norm (also magnitude). Both are
O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 require "matrix"
def dot_bad(v, w)
  v * w
end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def dot(v, w)
  v.inner_product(w)
end

ruby-matrix-fib   lens: patterns   level: L4   family: ruby-matrix-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-matrix-inverse. Follow-up: ruby-matrix-vector. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Any 2x2 matrix of ones gives Fibonacci numbers.
The matrix [[1, 1], [1, 0]] raised to n has F(n) in its top-right cell. Matrix#** uses repeated squaring, so it takes O(log n)
2x2 multiplications. A matrix of all ones, [[1, 1], [1, 1]], grows as powers of 2 instead, because its rows are identical.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

end
Correct:
 require "matrix"
def fib(n)
  (Matrix[[1, 1], [1, 0]] ** n)[0, 1]
end

Prompt. Why does raising [[1, 1], [1, 0]] to the n-th power compute Fibonacci numbers in O(log n) steps?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Multiplying the vector (F(k+1), F(k)) by the matrix gives (F(k+2), F(k+1)),
so the n-th power of the matrix applies the Fibonacci recurrence n times at once and its top-right cell is F(n). Matrix
exponentiation uses repeated squaring, which needs only about log2(n) matrix multiplications of a fixed 2x2 size, instead
of n additions.

2. Overview and mental model: Range
A Range represents an interval with a beginning and an end: 1..10 includes 10, 1...10 stops before it, and "a".."z"
works for anything with a successor and a comparison. Ranges are lazy: they store only the two ends.
A range can be endless (1..) or beginless (..5), which makes them useful as slice bounds (a[1..]) and with lazy
enumeration. cover? is O(1), while size and include? on non-numeric ranges may iterate.
Iteration needs a successor, so Float ranges use step. Range#bsearch does binary search over an integer range
when the block is monotone.

ruby-range-exclusive   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ruby-range-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-range-endless. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. (0..a.size) is the right range for visiting every index of an array.
The two-dot range includes its end, the three-dot range stops before it. The valid indexes of an array are 0...a.size, so
(0..a.size) visits one extra index, where a[i] is nil. (1..5).size is 5 and (1...5).size is 4. For simple loops prefer

Prerequisites: ruby-range-endless. Follow-up: ruby-range-float. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. include? and cover? give the same answer for every range.
For numeric ranges both compare against the bounds. For a string range ("a".."z"), include? checks whether the
value is one of the generated elements, while cover? only checks begin <= value <= end by string comparison, so
"bb" is covered but not included. cover? is O(1); include? on a string range may iterate.

end

Range#bsearch needs a monotone block: false then true; testing == is not monotone
ruby-range-bsearch   lens: patterns   level: L4   family: ruby-range-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-range-float. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. bsearch { |x| x * x == n } finds the square root.
In find-minimum mode the block must be false for small values and true from some point on. The test x * x == n is
false again after the root, so it is not monotone and the search may return nil even though a root exists. Search for
the first x with x * x > n and subtract one to get the floor of the square root. Binary search over an integer range is
O(log n).

end
Correct:

  (0..n + 1).bsearch { |x| x * x > n } - 1
end

Prompt. Why must a Range#bsearch block in find-minimum mode be monotone?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Binary search discards half of the range after each probe, assuming that
if the block is true at some x it stays true for every larger x, and false for every smaller one. A block such as x * x == n is
true at one point only, so a probe on the wrong side of it throws away the part that contains the answer. A condition like x
* x > n is false then true, so each probe is safe.

2. Overview and mental model: Red-Black tree
A red-black tree is a binary search tree whose nodes are colored so that the root is black, no red node has a red child
and every path to a nil leaf has the same number of black nodes. These rules bound the height by 2 log2(n + 1).
The left-leaning variant implemented here stores a 2-3 tree and needs only three fix-up rules (rotate left, rotate right,
flip colors). It supports insert and search in O(log n); deletion is more involved and is omitted.
Include Enumerable with an in-order each to get sort, min, max and friends. Production libraries typically use a
different red-black variant.

 Common misconception. The root can keep whatever color the fix-up left it with.

color flip can turn the root red, which would break the rule that the root is black. Set root.red = false after every insert.

A rotation hands the old parent's color to the new subtree root and makes the old parent red
ruby-redblacktree-rotate   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ruby-redblacktree-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-redblacktree-insert. Follow-up: ruby-redblacktree-fixup. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A rotation only moves links; the colors can stay where they are.
The subtree root keeps the color that the parent link expects, so the new root must take the old root's color and the
demoted node becomes red. Leaving the colors alone can create a red node with a red child or a black node where a
red one was expected. A rotation is O(1) and keeps the key order.

ruby-redblacktree-height   lens: complexity   level: L2   family: ruby-redblacktree-complexity
Prerequisites: ruby-redblacktree-fixup. Follow-up: ruby-redblacktree-check. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Sorted insertions make any binary search tree as deep as the number of keys.
Every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes and red nodes never touch, so the longest path is at
most twice the shortest and the height is at most about 2 log2(n + 1). Search, insert and delete stay O(log n) in the
worst case. Without the fix-ups the same code is a plain BST with height n.

The three fix-up rules run one after another with separate ifs, not as an elsif chain
ruby-redblacktree-fixup   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-redblacktree-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-redblacktree-rotate. Follow-up: ruby-redblacktree-height. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The three fix-up rules are mutually exclusive, so elsif is equivalent.
A single insert can need several fixes on the same node: a right rotation can produce a node with two red children
that must then be flipped. With elsif the flip is skipped and two red children stay in the tree. Apply the three rules in
order with independent ifs: rotate left if only the right child is red, rotate right if two reds are in a row on the left, flip if
both children are red.

Verifying a red-black tree requires equal black heights, not only local color rules
ruby-redblacktree-check   lens: equality   level: L3   family: ruby-redblacktree-equality
Prerequisites: ruby-redblacktree-height. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. If the root is black and no red node has a red child, the tree is a valid red-black tree.
The third rule says every path from a node to its nil leaves has the same number of black nodes. A tree of black
nodes with one side deeper passes the local rules but violates it. Compute the black height recursively, count nil as
one, and return nil on any mismatch or red-red pair. In this left-leaning variant a red right child is also invalid. O(n).

end
def rb_bad?(root)
  root.nil? || (!root.red && local_ok?(root))

 def black_height(node)
  return 1 unless node
  return nil if node.right && node.right.red
  return nil if node.red && node.left && node.left.red
  l = black_height(node.left)
  r = black_height(node.right)
  return nil unless l && r && l == r
  l + (node.red ? 0 : 1)
end
def rb_valid?(root)
  return true unless root
  !root.red && !black_height(root).nil?

2. Overview and mental model: Queue
A queue is a first-in, first-out structure. Ruby's Array can act as one through push and shift, and shift is O(1)
amortised in CRuby. A custom queue shows what happens underneath and fixes capacity when needed.
enqueue and dequeue are O(1) in a linked queue, a ring buffer and an amortised two-stack queue. Typical uses are
breadth-first search, task scheduling and sliding windows.
Watch the empty-to-nonempty transitions: reset the tail in a linked queue, wrap indexes with modulo in a ring buffer,
and move between stacks only when the output side is empty.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
A linked queue must reset its tail when the last node is dequeued
ruby-queue-linked   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-queue-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-queue-twostack. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. dequeue only needs to move the head pointer.
When the last node is removed the head becomes nil but the tail still points to the removed node. The next enqueue
then links the new node behind the dead node, and the queue looks empty or loses elements. Reset the tail to nil
whenever the head becomes nil. enqueue and dequeue are O(1).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):

    @head = @tail = nil
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    node = [v, nil]
    if @tail
      @tail[1] = node
    else
      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil unless @head
    v = @head[0]
    @head = @head[1]
    v
  end
  def to_a
    out = []
    node = @head
    while node
      out << node[0]
      node = node[1]
    end
    out
  end
end

class LinkedQueue
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :size
  def initialize
    @head = @tail = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    node = QNode.new(v)
    if @tail
      @tail.next = node
    else
      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
    @size += 1
    self
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil unless @head
    v = @head.value
    @head = @head.next
    @tail = nil unless @head
    @size -= 1
    v
  end
  def front
    @head && @head.value
  end
  def empty?
    @size.zero?
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    node = @head
    while node
      yield node.value
      node = node.next
    end
  end
end

Breadth-first search marks a node as seen when it is enqueued, not when it is dequeued
ruby-queue-bfs   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-queue-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-queue-ring. Follow-up: ruby-queue-movingavg. Complexity: O(V+E).
 Common misconception. Marking a node visited when it is dequeued avoids repeats.
A node reachable by two paths is enqueued twice if it is only marked on dequeue, producing duplicates in the visiting
order and wasted work. Mark on enqueue so each node enters the queue once. An Array works as the queue
because shift is O(1) amortised in CRuby. BFS is O(V + E).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def bfs_bad(graph, start)
  order = []
  seen = {}
  queue = [start]
  until queue.empty?
    node = queue.shift
    seen[node] = true
    order << node
    graph[node].each { |n| queue.push(n) unless seen[n] }
  end
  order
end
Correct:
 def bfs(graph, start)
  order = []
  seen = { start => true }
  queue = [start]
  until queue.empty?
    node = queue.shift
    order << node
    graph[node].each do |n|
      next if seen[n]
      seen[n] = true
      queue.push(n)
    end
  end
  order
end
A moving average keeps a queue of the window and divides by its current length
ruby-queue-movingavg   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ruby-queue-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-queue-bfs. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Dividing the running sum by the window size is right from the first value.
Until the window fills, the queue holds fewer values than the window size, so dividing by the size understates the
average. Add the new value, subtract the value that leaves the queue, and divide by the queue length. fdiv avoids
integer division. Each update is O(1).

A ring buffer queue wraps its indexes with modulo so storage stays fixed
ruby-queue-ring   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-queue-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-queue-twostack. Follow-up: ruby-queue-bfs. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Advancing head and tail with += 1 is enough for a fixed-size queue.
Without modulo the indexes grow forever, and assigning past the end of a Ruby Array silently extends it, so the
supposedly fixed buffer keeps growing. Wrap with (i + 1) % capacity. Track size separately to tell full from empty.
enqueue and dequeue are O(1) with constant memory.

 class RingQueue
  def initialize(cap)
    @buf = Array.new(cap)
    @head = @tail = @size = 0
  end
  def slots
    @buf.size
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    return false if @size == @buf.size
    @buf[@tail] = v
    @tail = (@tail + 1) % @buf.size
    @size += 1
    true
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil if @size.zero?
    v = @buf[@head]
    @buf[@head] = nil
    @head = (@head + 1) % @buf.size
    @size -= 1
    v
  end
  def to_a
    Array.new(@size) { |i| @buf[(@head + i) % @buf.size] }
  end
end

A queue from two stacks moves items across only when the output stack is empty
ruby-queue-twostack   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-queue-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-queue-linked. Follow-up: ruby-queue-ring. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. dequeue can always move everything from the input stack to the output stack first.
Moving every time puts newer items on top of older ones that are still waiting in the output stack, so the order is
wrong. Transfer only when the output stack is empty. Each element moves at most once, so dequeue is O(1)
amortised.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class TwoStackBad
  def initialize
    @in = []
    @out = []
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    @in.push(v)
    self
  end
  def dequeue
    @out.push(@in.pop) until @in.empty?
    @out.pop
  end
end
Correct:
 class TwoStackQueue
  def initialize
    @in = []
    @out = []
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    @in.push(v)
    self
  end
  def dequeue
    @out.push(@in.pop) until @in.empty? if @out.empty?
    @out.pop
  end
  def size
    @in.size + @out.size
  end
end

ruby-queue-twostack-ex2   format: explain-why   level: L3   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Why is dequeue O(1) amortised in a queue built from two stacks even though one call can move many
elements?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Each element is pushed onto the input stack once, moved to the output
stack at most once, and popped once. A single dequeue may transfer many elements, but the transfer only happens
when the output stack is empty, so across n operations the total number of moves is at most n. The cost spread over all
operations is constant per operation.

2. Overview and mental model: Doubly linked list
A doubly linked list stores prev and next links in every node. With head and tail sentinels, insertion and removal given
a node are O(1) with no special cases for the ends.
It is the structure behind LRU caches: a Hash maps keys to nodes and the list orders them by recency. Positional
access is O(n); use an Array when you index often.
Including Enumerable and defining each and reverse_each gives forward and backward traversal plus map, select,
sort and more.

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Inserting between two nodes rewires four pointers, and sentinels remove the edge cases
ruby-doublylinkedlist-insert   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-doublylinkedlist-remove. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Inserting after a node only needs node.next and the new node's prev.
A doubly linked list has two links per edge. Inserting between a and b must set the new node's prev and next and also
a.next and b.prev. Forgetting b.prev leaves the backward chain skipping the new node, so forward and backward
traversal disagree. Head and tail sentinel nodes mean every real node has both neighbours, so push_front,
push_back and middle inserts share one code path in O(1).

 class DNode
  attr_accessor :value, :prev, :next
  def initialize(value = nil)
    @value = value

end
class DList
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :head, :tail, :size
  def initialize
    @head = DNode.new
    @tail = DNode.new
    @head.next = @tail
    @tail.prev = @head
    @size = 0
  end
  def link_after(node, fresh)
    fresh.prev = node
    fresh.next = node.next
    node.next.prev = fresh
    node.next = fresh
    @size += 1
    fresh
  end
  def insert_after(node, v)
    link_after(node, DNode.new(v))
  end
  def push_front(v)
    insert_after(@head, v)
  end
  def push_back(v)
    insert_after(@tail.prev, v)
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    node = @head.next
    until node.equal?(@tail)
      yield node.value
      node = node.next
    end
  end
  def reverse_each
    return to_enum(:reverse_each) unless block_given?
    node = @tail.prev
    until node.equal?(@head)
      yield node.value
      node = node.prev
    end
  end
end

Index from the nearer end, and normalise negative indexes before walking
ruby-doublylinkedlist-at   lens: access   level: L2   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-access
Prerequisites: ruby-doublylinkedlist-reverse. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Walking i times from the head also handles negative indexes.
Integer#times does nothing for a negative count, so a negative index silently returns the first element. Normalise it by
adding the size, reject out-of-range values with nil, then walk from whichever end is closer, at most size/2 steps.
Access by position is still O(n); a list is not a replacement for an Array when you index a lot.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def at_bad(list, i)
  node = list.head.next
  i.times { node = node.next }
  node.value
end
Correct:
 class DList
  def at(i)
    i += @size if i < 0
    return nil unless i >= 0 && i < @size
    if i < @size / 2
      node = @head.next
      i.times { node = node.next }
    else
      node = @tail.prev
      (@size - 1 - i).times { node = node.prev }
    end
    node.value
  end
end
Removing a node you already hold is O(1) because it knows both neighbours
ruby-doublylinkedlist-remove   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-insertion-and-deletion
Prerequisites: ruby-doublylinkedlist-insert. Follow-up: ruby-doublylinkedlist-lru. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Unlinking a node only needs prev.next = node.next.
The node after the removed one still points back to it through prev unless node.next.prev is updated too. Backward
traversal then visits a node that forward traversal no longer sees. With both links fixed, removal given a node
reference is O(1); a singly linked list must first find the previous node in O(n).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def remove_bad(node)
  node.prev.next = node.next
  node.value
end
Correct:
 class DList
  def remove(node)
    node.prev.next = node.next
    node.next.prev = node.prev
    @size -= 1
    node.value
  end
end

Reverse a doubly linked list by swapping prev and next in every node, sentinels included
ruby-doublylinkedlist-reverse   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-mutation
Prerequisites: ruby-doublylinkedlist-lru. Follow-up: ruby-doublylinkedlist-at. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. After swapping a node's links, node.next still leads to the next node to visit.
Once node.next and node.prev are swapped, node.next points to the old previous node, so advancing with it walks
backwards and stops at once. Save the old next first, swap, then move on. Swap the two sentinels too, then
exchange the head and tail references. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 def reverse_bad(list)
  node = list.head
  while node
    node.next, node.prev = node.prev, node.next
    node = node.next
  end
  list
end
Correct:
 class DList
  def reverse!
    node = @head
    while node
      nxt = node.next
      node.next, node.prev = node.prev, node.next
      node = nxt
    end
    @head, @tail = @tail, @head
    self
  end
end
An LRU cache pairs a Hash for lookup with a doubly linked list for recency order
ruby-doublylinkedlist-lru   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ruby-doublylinkedlist-patterns
Prerequisites: ruby-doublylinkedlist-remove. Follow-up: ruby-doublylinkedlist-reverse. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A Hash alone can evict the least recently used key, even if get never refreshes it.
A Hash keeps insertion order, not usage order, so get must move the entry to the most recent end. A list gives O(1)
unlink and relink, and the Hash maps each key to its node, so get and put are both O(1). Evict the node before the tail
sentinel and delete its key from the Hash as well.

 class LRU
  def initialize(cap)
    @cap = cap
    @map = {}
    @list = DList.new
  end
  def get(k)
    node = @map[k]
    return nil unless node
    @list.remove(node)
    @list.link_after(@list.head, node)
    node.value[1]
  end
  def put(k, v)
    if (node = @map[k])
      @list.remove(node)
      @list.link_after(@list.head, node)
      node.value = [k, v]
      return v
    end
    if @map.size >= @cap
      old = @list.tail.prev
      @list.remove(old)
      @map.delete(old.value[0])
    end
    @map[k] = @list.push_front([k, v])
    v
  end
end

Prompt. Why do head and tail sentinel nodes simplify a doubly linked list?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). With sentinels every real node always has a previous and a next node,
so insert and remove never have to test for the first or last node or update separate head and tail references. push_front,
push_back and middle inserts all use the same four pointer updates, and an empty list is just two linked sentinels, which
removes a whole class of nil bugs.

2. Overview and mental model: Data
Data.define(:x, :y) (Ruby 3.2+) creates an immutable value class. Instances are frozen, have readers but no setters,
compare by value and have a stable hash. with(x: 5) returns a modified copy.
Construction is strict: every member is required (positionally or by keyword) and extra arguments raise
ArgumentError. Defaults come from overriding initialize with keyword defaults and calling super.
Immutability is shallow: mutable members such as arrays can still change unless you copy and freeze them. Use
Data for keys, set elements and values passed between layers; use Struct when you need mutation.

Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ruby-data-args. Complexity: O(1).

instance_variable_set raises FrozenError. with(x: 5) returns a new object with the changed field and leaves the

Ruby · graphs stored as adjacency lists · patterns · L2
Concept: Count connected components by starting a search only from vertices not yet seen
Misconception: Start a search from every vertex and count the searches.
Explanation: Starting from every vertex counts each vertex as its own component. Keep a seen set shared by all searches and start a new search only from an unseen vertex. The number of searches is the number of components. Mark vertices when they are pushed so none enters the stack twice. O(V + E).
Incorrect:
def components_bad(g)
  count = 0
  g.vertices.each do |s|
    seen = { s => true }
    stack = [s]
    until stack.empty?
      v = stack.pop
      g.neighbors(v).each do |n|
        next if seen[n]
        seen[n] = true
        stack.push(n)
      end
    end
    count += 1
  end
  count
end
Correct:
def components(g)
  seen = {}
  out = []
  g.vertices.each do |s|
    next if seen[s]
    seen[s] = true
    comp = []
    stack = [s]
    until stack.empty?
      v = stack.pop
      comp << v
      g.neighbors(v).each do |n|
        next if seen[n]
        seen[n] = true
        stack.push(n)
      end
    end
    out << comp.sort
  end
  out
end
Complexity: O(V+E)

Ruby · graphs stored as adjacency lists · iteration · L2
Concept: Use an explicit stack for depth-first search; recursion overflows the Ruby stack on long paths
Misconception: A recursive depth-first search is fine for any graph that fits in memory.
Explanation: Each recursive call uses a stack frame, and Ruby raises SystemStackError after roughly ten thousand nested calls, which a path-shaped graph with hundreds of thousands of vertices easily reaches. Keep your own stack in an Array, mark vertices when they are popped, and push neighbours in reverse to keep the natural order. Time O(V + E), space O(V).
Incorrect:
def dfs_bad(g, v, seen = {}, order = [])
  seen[v] = true
  order << v
  g.neighbors(v).each { |n| dfs_bad(g, n, seen, order) unless seen[n] }
  order
end
Correct:
def dfs_order(g, start)
  seen = {}
  stack = [start]
  order = []
  until stack.empty?
    v = stack.pop
    next if seen[v]
    seen[v] = true
    order << v
    g.neighbors(v).reverse_each { |n| stack.push(n) unless seen[n] }
  end
  order
end
Complexity: O(V+E)

Prompt: Why can a recursive depth-first search fail on a large graph in Ruby, and how does an explicit stack avoid that?

payload.answer: Every recursive call adds a frame to the interpreter's call stack, which has a fixed size, so a path-like graph with many thousands of vertices raises SystemStackError. An explicit stack is an Array on the heap that grows with available memory, so the search depth is not limited by the call stack. The visiting order stays the same if neighbours are pushed in reverse.

Ruby · graphs stored as adjacency lists · patterns · L2
Concept: Rebuild a BFS path by following parents back from the target, then reverse it
Misconception: Following parent links from the target to the source already gives the path in order.
Explanation: The parent links lead backwards: target, its parent, and so on up to the source, so the collected list runs from target to source. Reverse it before returning. Breadth-first search finds a path with the fewest edges in an unweighted graph, in O(V + E). Return nil when the target was never reached.
Incorrect:
def path_bad(parent, src, dst)
  return nil unless parent.key?(dst)
  path = [dst]
  path << parent[path.last] until path.last == src
  path
end
Correct:
def shortest_path(g, src, dst)
  parent = { src => nil }
  queue = [src]
  until queue.empty?
    v = queue.shift
    break if v == dst
    g.neighbors(v).each do |n|
      next if parent.key?(n)
      parent[n] = v
      queue.push(n)
    end
  end
  return nil unless parent.key?(dst)
  path = [dst]
  path << parent[path.last] until path.last == src
  path.reverse
end
Complexity: O(V+E)

Ruby · graphs stored as adjacency lists · ordering · L3
Concept: Kahn's topological sort must compare the output size with the vertex count to detect cycles
Misconception: If the queue empties, the order produced is a complete topological order.
Explanation: Vertices on a cycle never reach in-degree zero, so they are never queued and silently missing from the output. If the result has fewer vertices than the graph, a cycle exists and no topological order does. Count in-degrees, queue the zero ones, remove them one by one, and return nil on a cycle. O(V + E).
Incorrect:
def topo_bad(g)
  indeg = Hash.new(0)
  g.vertices.each { |v| g.neighbors(v).each { |n| indeg[n] += 1 } }
  queue = g.vertices.select { |v| indeg[v].zero? }
  order = []
  until queue.empty?
    v = queue.shift
    order << v
    g.neighbors(v).each do |n|
      indeg[n] -= 1
      queue.push(n) if indeg[n].zero?
    end
  end
  order
end
Correct:
def topo_sort(g)
  indeg = Hash.new(0)
  g.vertices.each { |v| g.neighbors(v).each { |n| indeg[n] += 1 } }
  queue = g.vertices.select { |v| indeg[v].zero? }
  order = []
  until queue.empty?
    v = queue.shift
    order << v
    g.neighbors(v).each do |n|
      indeg[n] -= 1
      queue.push(n) if indeg[n].zero?
    end
  end
  order.size == g.vertices.size ? order : nil
end
Complexity: O(V+E)

Ruby · graphs stored as adjacency matrices · patterns · L3
Concept: Floyd-Warshall needs the intermediate vertex k in the outermost loop and infinity for missing edges
Misconception: The three loops of Floyd-Warshall can be nested in any order.
Explanation: The algorithm builds shortest paths using only the first k vertices as stops, so k must be the outermost loop. With k innermost, a path that needs several intermediates is never assembled. Missing edges must be Float::INFINITY, not 0, otherwise they look like free edges; the diagonal starts at 0. Time O(V cubed), space O(V squared).
Incorrect:
def floyd_bad(w)
  n = w.size
  inf = Float::INFINITY
  d = Array.new(n) do |i|
    Array.new(n) { |j| i == j ? 0 : (w[i][j].zero? ? inf : w[i][j]) }
  end
  n.times do |i|
    n.times do |j|
      n.times do |k|
        d[i][j] = [d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]].min
      end
    end
  end
  d
end
Correct:
def floyd(w)
  inf = Float::INFINITY
  n = w.size
  d = Array.new(n) do |i|
    Array.new(n) { |j| i == j ? 0 : (w[i][j].zero? ? inf : w[i][j]) }
  end
  n.times do |k|
    n.times do |i|
      n.times do |j|
        d[i][j] = [d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]].min
      end
    end
  end
  d
end
Complexity: O(V^3)

def floyd(w)
  inf = Float::INFINITY
  n = w.size
  d = Array.new(n) do |i|
    Array.new(n) { |j| i == j ? 0 : (w[i][j].zero? ? inf : w[i][j]) }
  end
  n.times do |k|
    n.times do |i|
      n.times do |j|
        d[i][j] = [d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]].min
      end
    end
  end
  d
end
payload.explanation: The algorithm builds shortest paths using only the first k vertices as stops, so k must be the outermost loop. With k innermost, a path that needs several intermediates is never assembled. Missing edges must be Float::INFINITY, not 0, otherwise they look like free edges; the diagonal starts at 0. Ruby · graphs stored as adjacency matrices · transformation · L3
Concept: Powers of the adjacency matrix count walks, and Matrix ** k is a matrix product, not an element-wise power
Misconception: Squaring every entry of the matrix counts the walks of length two.
Explanation: Entry (i, j) of A to the power k is the number of walks of length k from i to j, using the matrix product. Squaring each entry is a different operation (the Hadamard product) and counts nothing useful. The standard library class Matrix defines ** as the repeated matrix product. Each multiplication is O(V cubed).
Incorrect:
require "matrix"
def walks_bad(a)
  a.hadamard_product(a)
end
Correct:
require "matrix"
def walk_count(a, k, i, j)
  (a ** k)[i, j]
end
Complexity: O(V^3 log k)

Concept: Bang methods such as uniq! and compact! return nil when nothing changed, so do not chain on them
Misconception: a.uniq!.sort works whether or not the array had duplicates.
Explanation: Array#uniq!, compact!, flatten!, reject! and similar methods mutate the receiver and return nil when no change was made. Chaining another call on the result then raises NoMethodError for nil. Use the non-bang version when you want a return value (uniq, compact) or call the bang method as a statement and use the array afterwards.
Incorrect:
def tidy_bad(a)
  a.uniq!.sort
end
Correct:
def tidy(a)
  a.uniq.sort
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Array · iteration · L3
Concept: Deleting from an array while iterating it with each skips elements; use reject! or delete_if
Misconception: Calling delete inside each removes every matching element.
Explanation: each walks by index. Deleting the current element shifts the rest left, so the element that moved into the current slot is skipped. Remove elements with delete_if or reject!, which handle the shifting correctly in a single pass, or build a new array with reject or select. A single pass costs O(n).
Incorrect:
def drop_evens_bad(a)
  a.each { |x| a.delete(x) if x.even? }
  a
end
Correct:
def drop_evens(a)
  a.delete_if(&:even?)
end
Complexity: O(n)

payload.answer: each steps through the array by index. When an element is deleted, everything after it moves one slot to the left, so the next element now sits at the index that was just visited. The iterator then advances to the following index and never looks at it. delete_if and reject! avoid this by compacting the array in a single pass instead of deleting while a separate loop is walking it.

Ruby · Array · patterns · L3
Concept: push/pop make a stack and push/shift make a queue; mixing pop into a FIFO loop reverses the order
Misconception: pop removes the oldest element, like a queue.
Explanation: pop removes from the end, so push + pop is LIFO (stack). shift removes from the front, so push + shift is FIFO (queue). In CRuby both ends are amortised O(1) on large arrays because the array can become a shared view of its buffer, so a plain Array works as a queue for most programs; use a custom class or Thread::Queue only when you need other guarantees.
Incorrect:
def process_bad(items)
  q = items.dup
  out = []
  out << q.pop until q.empty?
  out
end
Correct:
def process(items)
  q = items.dup
  out = []
  out << q.shift until q.empty?
  out
end
Complexity: O(1) amortised

Concept: dup and clone copy only the outer array; nested arrays are still shared
Misconception: grid.dup gives a fully independent copy of a 2D array.
Explanation: dup creates a new outer array whose elements are the same objects as before. Changing a nested row through the copy changes the original. Copy each level you intend to mutate, for example grid.map(&:dup), or use Marshal.load(Marshal.dump(grid)) for arbitrary depth. The cost is O(total elements).
Incorrect:
def copy_bad(grid)
  grid.dup
end
Correct:
def copy_grid(grid)
  grid.map(&:dup)
end
Complexity: O(n * m)

Concept: a[start, len] returns [] when start equals size but nil when start is past the end
Misconception: A slice that starts past the end returns an empty array.
Explanation: For an array of size n, a[n, k] is [] but a[n + 1, k] is nil, and a[i] outside the range is nil. Calling a method on the nil result raises NoMethodError. Guard a slice with || [] when the start may exceed the size, or use take/drop, which never return nil. Negative indexes count from the end: a[-1] is the last element.
Incorrect:
def slice_sum_bad(a, start, len)
  a[start, len].sum
end
Correct:
def slice_sum(a, start, len)
  (a[start, len] || []).sum
end
Complexity: O(k)

Ruby · AVL trees · equality · L3
Concept: Checking the AVL property means testing every node, not only the root
Misconception: A tree is AVL if the heights of the root's two subtrees differ by at most one.
Explanation: A subtree deep inside can be badly unbalanced while the root looks fine. Compute heights recursively and return a failure marker as soon as any node has a balance factor outside -1..1. One pass, O(n). Checking recomputed heights also catches stale stored height fields.
Incorrect:
def naive_height(node)
  return 0 unless node
  1 + [naive_height(node.left), naive_height(node.right)].max
end
def avl_bad?(node)
  return true unless node
  (naive_height(node.left) - naive_height(node.right)).abs <= 1
end
Correct:
def avl_height(node)
  return 0 unless node
  l = avl_height(node.left)
  return nil unless l
  r = avl_height(node.right)
  return nil unless r
  return nil if (l - r).abs > 1
  1 + [l, r].max
end
def avl?(node)
  !avl_height(node).nil?
end
Complexity: O(n)

Misconception: A tree is AVL if the heights of the root's two subtrees differ by at most one.
Explanation: A subtree deep inside can be badly unbalanced while the root looks fine. Compute heights recursively and return a failure marker as soon as any node has a balance factor outside -1..1. One pass, O(n). Checking recomputed heights also catches stale stored height fields.

def naive_height(node)
  return 0 unless node
  1 + [naive_height(node.left), naive_height(node.right)].max
end
def avl_bad?(node)
  return true unless node
  (naive_height(node.left) - naive_height(node.right)).abs <= 1
end
Correct:
def avl_height(node)
  return 0 unless node
  l = avl_height(node.left)
  return nil unless l
  r = avl_height(node.right)
  return nil unless r
  return nil if (l - r).abs > 1
  1 + [l, r].max
end
def avl?(node)
  !avl_height(node).nil?
end

Imported reference; not locally executed. Subject: ruby
Ruby · AVL trees · insertion-and-deletion · L3
Concept: Deletion can unbalance every ancestor, so rebalance on the way back up
Misconception: Deleting a key can only shorten a subtree, so no rebalancing is needed.
Explanation: Removing a node from one side makes the other side relatively taller and can break the balance factor of the parent or a higher ancestor. Call rebalance on every node of the recursion path as it returns. A node with two children takes its in-order successor and the minimum is removed from the right subtree, also with rebalancing. O(log n).
Incorrect:
class AVLNoRebalance < AVL
  def delete(key)
    @root = del(@root, key)
    self
  end
  private
  def del(node, key)
    return nil unless node
    if key < node.key
      node.left = del(node.left, key)
    elsif key > node.key
      node.right = del(node.right, key)
    else
      @size -= 1
      return node.right || node.left
    end
    update(node)
    node
  end
end
Correct:
class AVL
  def delete(key)
    @root = delete_at(@root, key)
    self
  end
  private
  def delete_at(node, key)
    return nil unless node
    if key < node.key
      node.left = delete_at(node.left, key)
    elsif key > node.key
      node.right = delete_at(node.right, key)
    else
      @size -= 1
      return node.right unless node.left
      return node.left unless node.right
      succ = node.right
      succ = succ.left while succ.left
      node.key = succ.key
      node.right = remove_min(node.right)
    end
    rebalance(node)
  end
  def remove_min(node)
    return node.right unless node.left
    node.left = remove_min(node.left)
    rebalance(node)
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · AVL trees · mutation · L3
Concept: A left-right or right-left imbalance needs a double rotation, not a single one
Misconception: Whenever a node is left-heavy, one right rotation restores balance.
Explanation: If the heavy left child is itself right-heavy (the zig-zag case), a single right rotation just moves the imbalance to the other side. First rotate the child left, then rotate the node right. The mirror case rotates the right child right and then the node left. The balance factors of the node and of the heavy child pick the case.
Incorrect:
class AVLNoDouble < AVL
  private
  def rebalance(node)
    update(node)
    b = balance(node)
    return rotate_right(node) if b > 1
    return rotate_left(node) if b < -1
    node
  end
end
Correct:
def rotation_plan(balance, child_balance)
  if balance > 1
    child_balance < 0 ? [:rotate_child_left, :rotate_right] : [:rotate_right]
  elsif balance < -1
    child_balance > 0 ? [:rotate_child_right, :rotate_left] : [:rotate_left]
  else
    []
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

Prompt: Why does a left-right imbalance in an AVL tree need two rotations?

payload.answer: When the left child of an unbalanced node is itself right-heavy, a single right rotation moves that child's heavy right subtree to the other side, so the new root is still unbalanced by the same amount. Rotating the left child left first makes the heavy side the outer left side, and the second rotation right then lifts the middle node to the root and balances both sides.

Ruby · AVL trees · complexity · L2
Concept: Sorted insertions keep an AVL tree at height O(log n) while a plain BST degenerates to a list
Misconception: Inserting keys in sorted order is the worst case for every search tree.
Explanation: A plain BST fed sorted keys becomes a chain of height n and each operation is O(n). An AVL tree rebalances after each insert, so its height never exceeds about 1.44 log2(n + 2). Inserting 1..15 in order gives height 4, the minimum possible. Search, insert and delete are all O(log n).
Incorrect:
class AVLNoBalance < AVL
  private
  def rebalance(node)
    update(node)
    node
  end
end
Correct:
def height_after(keys)
  t = AVL.new
  keys.each { |k| t.insert(k) }
  t.height
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · AVL trees · mutation · L2
Concept: A rotation must recompute the lower node's height before the new subtree root's height
Misconception: After a rotation the two heights can be updated in either order.
Explanation: After rotate_right the old root y becomes the child of x. x's height depends on y's height, so y must be updated first. Updating x first uses y's stale height and the error spreads to every ancestor. A rotation changes only a constant number of links, so it is O(1), and it preserves the in-order sequence of keys.
Incorrect:
BN = Struct.new(:key, :left, :right, :height)
def hgt_bad(n)
  n ? n.height : 0
end
def rotate_right_bad(y)
  x = y.left
  y.left = x.right
  x.right = y
  x.height = 1 + [hgt_bad(x.left), hgt_bad(x.right)].max
  y.height = 1 + [hgt_bad(y.left), hgt_bad(y.right)].max
  x
end
Correct:
class AVLNode
  attr_accessor :key, :left, :right, :height
  def initialize(key)
    @key = key
    @height = 1
  end
end
class AVL
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :root, :size
  def initialize
    @root = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def insert(key)
    @root = insert_at(@root, key)
    self
  end
  def height
    height_of(@root)
  end
  def each(&block)
    return to_enum(:each) unless block
    walk(@root, &block)
    self
  end
  private
  def height_of(node)
    node ? node.height : 0
  end
  def update(node)
    node.height = 1 + [height_of(node.left), height_of(node.right)].max
  end
  def balance(node)
    height_of(node.left) - height_of(node.right)
  end
  def rotate_right(y)
    x = y.left
    y.left = x.right
    x.right = y
    update(y)
    update(x)
    x
  end
  def rotate_left(x)
    y = x.right
    x.right = y.left
    y.left = x
    update(x)
    update(y)
    y
  end
  def rebalance(node)
    update(node)
    b = balance(node)
    if b > 1
      node.left = rotate_left(node.left) if balance(node.left) < 0
      return rotate_right(node)
    elsif b < -1
      node.right = rotate_right(node.right) if balance(node.right) > 0
      return rotate_left(node)
    end
    node
  end
  def insert_at(node, key)
    if node.nil?
      @size += 1
      return AVLNode.new(key)
    end
    if key < node.key
      node.left = insert_at(node.left, key)
    elsif key > node.key
      node.right = insert_at(node.right, key)
    else
      return node
    end
    rebalance(node)
  end
  def walk(node, &block)
    return unless node
    walk(node.left, &block)
    block.call(node.key)
    walk(node.right, &block)
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Bloom filters · mutation · L1
Concept: Set a bit with OR, not addition; setting an already-set bit must change nothing
Misconception: bits + (1 << i) sets bit i just like bits | (1 << i).
Explanation: Addition carries: if bit i is already set, adding 1 << i clears it and sets bit i + 1, silently corrupting a neighbour. OR is idempotent. Ruby Integers have arbitrary size, so one Integer can serve as the whole bit array, and Integer#[] reads a bit (0 or 1). Integers are immutable, so store the new value back in the instance variable. Memory is m / 8 bytes.
Incorrect:
def set_bit_bad(bits, i)
  bits + (1 << i)
end
Correct:
def set_bit(bits, i)
  bits | (1 << i)
end
def bit_set?(bits, i)
  bits[i] == 1
end
def popcount(bits)
  bits.to_s(2).count("1")
end
Complexity: O(m/64)

def process_hash(word)
  IO.popen([RbConfig.ruby, "-e", "print #{word.inspect}.hash"], &:read)

payload.explanation: String#hash is seeded randomly for every Ruby process, so the same string hashes differently after a restart. A filter that was saved, shared or rebuilt elsewhere then answers wrongly. Use deterministic hashes: Zlib.crc32 and Digest::MD5 give two independent values h1 and h2, and double hashing derives all k positions as (h1 + i * h2) % m. Keep h2 non-zero so positions differ. Each add or lookup costs O(k).

Ruby · Bloom filters · exercise · explain-why · L3
Prompt: Why can a standard Bloom filter not remove items without creating false negatives?

payload.answer: Each item sets k bits and different items may share bits. Clearing the bits of a removed item also clears bits that other stored items rely on, so those items would no longer have all of their bits set and would be reported absent, a false negative. A counting Bloom filter stores a counter per position so that a shared position only reaches zero when every item using it has been removed.

Ruby · Bloom filters · complexity · L3
Concept: Size the filter with m = -n ln p / (ln 2)^2 and k = (m / n) ln 2
Misconception: Take m = n * ln(p) / (ln 2)^2 for n items and a false-positive rate p.
Explanation: For p < 1, ln(p) is negative, so the formula needs a minus sign or m comes out negative. The optimal number of hash functions is (m / n) ln 2, rounded. For one thousand items at one percent this gives about 9586 bits and 7 hashes, roughly 9.6 bits per item. Memory is independent of the size of the items.
Incorrect:
def bloom_params_bad(n, p)
  m = (n * Math.log(p) / (Math.log(2)**2)).ceil
  k = (m.to_f / n * Math.log(2)).round
  [m, k]
end
Correct:
def bloom_params(n, p)
  m = (-n * Math.log(p) / (Math.log(2)**2)).ceil
  k = (m.to_f / n * Math.log(2)).round
  [m, k]
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · binary search trees · insertion-and-deletion · L3
Concept: Deleting a node with two children replaces its key with the in-order successor
Misconception: A node with two children can be replaced by its left child.
Explanation: Replacing the node by one child drops the other child's whole subtree. Copy the in-order successor (the minimum of the right subtree) into the node and remove that minimum from the right subtree. Zero or one child is simpler: return the other child. Delete returns the new subtree root, like insert. O(h).
Incorrect:
def delete_bad(node, key)
  return nil unless node
  if key < node.key
    node.left = delete_bad(node.left, key)
  elsif key > node.key
    node.right = delete_bad(node.right, key)
  else
    return node.right unless node.left
    return node.left
  end
  node
end
Correct:
class BST
  def delete(key)
    @root = delete_at(@root, key)
    self
  end
  private
  def delete_at(node, key)
    return nil unless node
    if key < node.key
      node.left = delete_at(node.left, key)
    elsif key > node.key
      node.right = delete_at(node.right, key)
    else
      @size -= 1
      return node.right unless node.left
      return node.left unless node.right
      succ = node.right
      succ = succ.left while succ.left
      node.key = succ.key
      node.right = remove_min(node.right)
    end
    node
  end
  def remove_min(node)
    return node.right unless node.left
    node.left = remove_min(node.left)
    node
  end
end
Complexity: O(h)

Imported reference; not locally executed. Subject: ruby
Ruby · binary search trees · insertion-and-deletion · L1
Concept: A recursive insert must assign the returned subtree back to the child link
Misconception: A recursive insert can just call itself on the child and ignore the result.
Explanation: Inserting into an empty subtree creates a new node, but that node only becomes part of the tree if the caller stores it in node.left or node.right. Without the assignment the new node is discarded. Return the subtree root from every call and assign it. Duplicates are ignored here. Insert is O(h) where h is the height: O(log n) for a balanced tree and O(n) for a degenerate one.
Incorrect:
def insert_bad(node, key)
  return BSTNode.new(key) if node.nil?
  if key < node.key
    insert_bad(node.left, key)
  else
    insert_bad(node.right, key)
  end
  node
end
Correct:
class BSTNode
  attr_accessor :key, :left, :right
  def initialize(key)
    @key = key
  end
end
class BST
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :root, :size
  def initialize
    @root = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def insert(key)
    @root = insert_at(@root, key)
    self
  end
  def include?(key)
    node = @root
    while node
      return true if key == node.key
      node = key < node.key ? node.left : node.right
    end
    false
  end
  def each(&block)
    return to_enum(:each) unless block
    walk(@root, &block)
    self
  end
  private
  def insert_at(node, key)
    if node.nil?
      @size += 1
      return BSTNode.new(key)
    end
    if key < node.key
      node.left = insert_at(node.left, key)
    elsif key > node.key
      node.right = insert_at(node.right, key)
    end
    node
  end
  def walk(node, &block)
    return unless node
    walk(node.left, &block)
    block.call(node.key)
    walk(node.right, &block)
  end
end
Complexity: O(h)

Ruby · binary search trees · ordering · L3
Concept: The kth smallest key is the kth node of an in-order walk; ranks start at 1
Misconception: The kth smallest key is at index k of the sorted keys.
Explanation: Ranks are 1-based while Array indexes are 0-based, so keys[k] returns the (k+1)th smallest. An iterative in-order walk with an explicit stack can stop at the kth node without visiting the rest: O(h + k) time. Return nil when k is out of range.
Incorrect:
def keys_bad(node)
  return [] unless node
  keys_bad(node.left) + [node.key] + keys_bad(node.right)
end
def kth_bad(root, k)
  keys_bad(root)[k]
end
Correct:
def kth_smallest(root, k)
  stack = []
  node = root
  while node || !stack.empty?
    while node
      stack.push(node)
      node = node.left
    end
    node = stack.pop
    k -= 1
    return node.key if k.zero?
    node = node.right
  end
  nil
end
Complexity: O(h+k)
