Ruby · binary search trees · patterns · L2
Concept: The lowest common ancestor in a BST is the first node where the keys split or one equals the node
Misconception: Move left if either key is smaller than the node, and right if either is larger.
Explanation: With || the walk goes left as soon as one key is smaller, even when the other key is larger and the node is already the split point. Go left only if both keys are smaller, right only if both are larger, otherwise the current node is the answer. O(h) time, O(1) space.
Incorrect:
def lca_bad(root, p, q)
  node = root
  while node
    if p < node.key || q < node.key
      node = node.left
    elsif p > node.key || q > node.key
      node = node.right
    else
      return node.key
    end
  end
  nil
end
Correct:
def lca(root, p, q)
  node = root
  while node
    if p < node.key && q < node.key
      node = node.left
    elsif p > node.key && q > node.key
      node = node.right
    else
      return node.key
    end
  end
  nil
end
Complexity: O(h)

Ruby · binary search trees · equality · L2
Concept: Validate a BST by passing lower and upper bounds down, not by comparing parent and child only
Misconception: A tree is a BST if every node is greater than its left child and smaller than its right child.
Explanation: The BST rule applies to the whole subtree, not just the children. A node can satisfy its parent and still violate a distant ancestor, for example a 6 in the left subtree of 5. Carry an open interval (lo, hi) down the recursion and require lo < key < hi. Checking all nodes is O(n).
Incorrect:
def valid_bad?(node)
  return true unless node
  return false if node.left && node.left.key >= node.key
  return false if node.right && node.right.key <= node.key
  valid_bad?(node.left) && valid_bad?(node.right)
end
Correct:
def valid_bst?(node, lo = nil, hi = nil)
  return true unless node
  return false if lo && node.key <= lo
  return false if hi && node.key >= hi
  valid_bst?(node.left, lo, node.key) && valid_bst?(node.right, node.key, hi)
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Classes and Modules · mental-model · L2
Concept: @@ class variables are shared with every subclass; a class-level instance variable belongs to one class
Misconception: Each subclass gets its own copy of a @@ class variable.
Explanation: A @@variable is a single slot shared by a class and all its subclasses, so counting instances of a subclass also changes the parent's count. A class-level instance variable (@count set in the class body, exposed with class << self; attr_accessor) belongs to exactly one class object. Initialise it for each subclass in the inherited hook.
Incorrect:
class CounterBad
  @@count = 0
  def self.count = @@count
  def initialize = @@count += 1
end
class SubCounterBad < CounterBad; end
Correct:
class Counter
  @count = 0
  class << self
    attr_accessor :count
    def inherited(sub)
      super
      sub.count = 0
    end
  end
  def initialize = self.class.count += 1
end
class SubCounter < Counter; end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Classes and Modules · ordering · L3
Concept: Define <=> and include Comparable to get sorting, comparison operators and between?
Misconception: An object can be sorted without defining <=>.
Explanation: sort, min and max compare elements with <=>. A class that does not define it raises ArgumentError (comparison of Version with Version failed). Define <=> and include Comparable to get <, <=, ==, >=, > and between?, clamp. Similarly, define each and include Enumerable to get map, select, sort_by and min_by.
Incorrect:
class VersionBad
  attr_reader :n
  def initialize(n) = @n = n
end
def sorted_versions_bad(ns)
  ns.map { |n| VersionBad.new(n) }.sort.map(&:n)
end

Ruby · Classes and Modules · equality · L3
Concept: To use objects as Hash keys define ==, eql? and hash together
Misconception: Defining == is enough for objects to work as Hash keys.
Explanation: A Hash finds keys with hash and eql?, not ==. A class that only defines == makes two equal-looking objects different keys. Define eql? (usually calling ==) and hash built from the same fields, for example [self.class, x, y].hash. The fields used must not change while the object is a key.
Incorrect:
class KeyBad
  attr_reader :x
  def initialize(x) = @x = x
  def ==(other) = other.is_a?(KeyBad) && x == other.x
end
def lookup_bad = { KeyBad.new(1) => :found }[KeyBad.new(1)]
Correct:
class Key
  attr_reader :x
  def initialize(x) = @x = x
  def ==(other) = other.is_a?(Key) && x == other.x
  alias eql? ==
  def hash = [self.class, x].hash
end
def lookup_good = { Key.new(1) => :found }[Key.new(1)]
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Classes and Modules · mental-model · L2
Concept: include adds module methods to instances; extend adds them to the class itself
Misconception: include Greeter lets you call Service.hello on the class.
Explanation: include inserts the module into the ancestors of the class, so its methods become instance methods. To call them on the class object, use extend, which adds them to the class's singleton. Calling an instance method on the class raises NoMethodError.
Incorrect:
module Greeter
  def hello = "hi"
end
class ServiceBad
  include Greeter
end
def class_call_bad = ServiceBad.hello
Correct:
module Hello
  def hello = "hi"
end
class Service
  extend Hello
end
class Person
  include Hello
end
def class_call = Service.hello
def instance_call = Person.new.hello
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: private does not apply to def self.; use private_class_method
Misconception: Writing private above def self.helper makes the class method private.

  def self.run = secret + 1
  def self.secret = 42
  private_class_method :secret
end

Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Classes and Modules · creation · L2
Concept: A subclass initialize must call super, or the parent never sets its fields
Misconception: A subclass inherits the parent's initialize automatically even when it defines its own.
Explanation: Defining initialize in the subclass replaces the parent's. Without super the parent's instance variables stay unset (nil). Call super(name) with the arguments the parent expects, or super() for none. Bare super forwards the same arguments.
Incorrect:
class AnimalBad
  attr_reader :name
  def initialize(name) = @name = name
end
class DogBad < AnimalBad
  def initialize(name, tricks)
    @tricks = tricks
  end
end
Correct:
class Animal
  attr_reader :name
  def initialize(name) = @name = name
end
class Dog < Animal
  attr_reader :tricks
  def initialize(name, tricks)
    super(name)
    @tricks = tricks
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

end

Ruby · Data (Ruby 3.2+) · equality · L2
Concept: Data compares by value and is safe as a Set element or hash key because it is frozen
Misconception: Two plain objects with the same fields are equal.
Explanation: Data defines ==, eql? and hash from its members, and instances cannot change, so their hash code stays valid in a Set or as a Hash key. A plain class compares by identity, so a Set keeps duplicates. This makes Data a good fit for visited-set coordinates in a grid search.
Incorrect:
class Spot
  attr_reader :row, :col
  def initialize(row, col)
    @row = row
    @col = col
  end
end
def visited_bad(moves)
  moves.map { |r, c| Spot.new(r, c) }.to_set.size
end
Correct:
Cell = Data.define(:row, :col)
def visited(moves)
  moves.map { |r, c| Cell.new(row: r, col: c) }.to_set.size
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Data (Ruby 3.2+) · mutation · L1
Concept: Data instances have no setters; use with to get a changed copy
Misconception: A Data object can be changed with a setter like a Struct.
Explanation: Data.define(:x, :y) creates readers only, and instances are frozen. Assigning pt.x = 5 raises NoMethodError, and instance_variable_set raises FrozenError. with(x: 5) returns a new object with the changed field and leaves the original untouched.
Incorrect:
Pt = Data.define(:x, :y)
def move_bad(pt)
  pt.x = 5
  pt
end
Correct:
Vec = Data.define(:x, :y)
def move(vec, dx)
  vec.with(x: vec.x + dx)
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Data (Ruby 3.2+) · exercise · explain-why · L2
Prompt: Why is Data a better fit than Struct for a value used as a Hash key?

payload.answer: A Hash stores each key under its hash code at insertion time. A Struct can be changed after it was stored, which changes its hash code and makes the entry unreachable. A Data instance is frozen, so its members cannot change and its hash code stays valid. Data also defines equality by value, so equal instances find the same entry.

Ruby · Data (Ruby 3.2+) · mutation · L3
Concept: Data is shallowly immutable: a mutable member can still change; freeze or copy it on the way in
Misconception: A frozen Data object cannot change at all.
Explanation: Freezing applies to the Data object, not to the objects it refers to. A Data with an array member lets callers push into that array, and the same array may also be shared with the caller. Copy and freeze mutable members in initialize or at construction, for example items.dup.freeze.
Incorrect:
Box = Data.define(:items)
def box_bad(items)
  Box.new(items: items)
end
Correct:
Box2 = Data.define(:items) do
  def initialize(items:)
    super(items: items.dup.freeze)
  end
end
def box(items)
  Box2.new(items: items)
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Data (Ruby 3.2+) · transformation · L2
Concept: with returns a new Data; ignoring its result leaves the original unchanged
Misconception: pt.with(x: 1) updates pt.
Explanation: Because Data is immutable, with builds and returns a new instance. Calling it as a statement and then using the original gives the old values. Assign the result or return it. Chained updates (a.with(x: 1).with(y: 2)) create one object per step.
Incorrect:
Pos = Data.define(:x, :y)
def bump_bad(pos)
  pos.with(x: pos.x + 1)
  pos
end
Correct:
def bump(pos)
  pos.with(x: pos.x + 1)
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Date, Time and DateTime (require "date") · creation · L1
Concept: Date.new raises Date::Error for an impossible date; check with valid_date? first
Misconception: Date.new(2024, 2, 30) rolls over into March.
Explanation: Date.new validates its arguments and raises Date::Error (invalid date) for February 30. Date.valid_date?(y, m, d) returns false instead of raising, which suits user input. Leap years are handled by the calendar: 2024 has February 29, 2100 does not.
Incorrect:
require "date"
def make_bad(y, m, d)
  Date.new(y, m, d)
end
Correct:
require "date"
def make(y, m, d)
  return nil unless Date.valid_date?(y, m, d)
  Date.new(y, m, d)
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Date, Time and DateTime (require "date") · mutation · L2
Concept: date + n adds days, date >> n adds months and clamps to the month end
Misconception: Adding 30 days is the same as adding one month.
Explanation: Date#+ adds days, so Jan 31 + 30 is Mar 1 in a leap year. Date#>> adds months and clamps the day to the last day of the target month: Jan 31 >> 1 is Feb 29 (2024). Use >> for calendar months and + for exact day counts. Both return new objects and are O(1).
Incorrect:
require "date"
def next_month_bad(d)
  d + 30
end
Correct:
require "date"
def next_month(d)
  d >> 1
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Date, Time and DateTime (require "date") · exercise · explain-why · L2
Prompt: Why can date >> 1 give a day number that differs from the original, while date + 30 never does?

payload.answer: Months have different lengths. Date#>> moves to the same day in the next month and, when that day does not exist, clamps to the last day of the month, so Jan 31 becomes Feb 29 or 28. Date#+ adds an exact number of days, which keeps the arithmetic uniform but ignores month boundaries.

Ruby · Date, Time and DateTime (require "date") · transformation · L3
Concept: Date.parse guesses the field order; strptime with an explicit format does not
Misconception: Date.parse("03/04/2024") reads month first.
Explanation: Date.parse accepts many styles and reads "03/04/2024" as day/month, April 3. That is correct for some locales and wrong for others. Date.strptime(text, "%m/%d/%Y") states the format, and raises Date::Error when the text does not match. Prefer strptime or ISO 8601 (Date.iso8601) for external data.
Incorrect:
require "date"
def parse_bad(text)
  Date.parse(text)
end
Correct:
require "date"
def parse_us(text)
  Date.strptime(text, "%m/%d/%Y")
end
Complexity: O(1)

Concept: wday counts from Sunday = 0 while cwday follows ISO with Monday = 1 and Sunday = 7
Misconception: wday numbers Monday as 1 and Sunday as 7.
Explanation: Date#wday returns 0 for Sunday through 6 for Saturday. Date#cwday follows ISO 8601: Monday is 1 and Sunday is 7. Mixing them shifts a weekday check by one. Use cwday > 5 for a weekend test, or saturday? and sunday?.
Incorrect:
require "date"
def weekend_bad?(d)
  d.wday > 5
end
Correct:
require "date"
def weekend?(d)
  d.cwday > 5
end
Complexity: O(1)

payload.concept: When a ring buffer grows it must copy elements in logical order, not physical order
payload.example_good:
class AutoDeque < RingDeque
  def push_back(v)
    grow! if full?
    super
  end
  def push_front(v)
    grow! if full?
    super
  end
  private
  def grow!
    items = to_a
    @buf = items + Array.new([items.size, 1].max)
    @head = 0
  end
end
payload.explanation: If the contents have wrapped around, extending the Array leaves the head and tail in the middle of the old region, and reading from head crosses empty slots. Copy the elements in logical order into a bigger buffer and reset head to 0. Growth costs O(n) but happens rarely, so push is O(1) amortised.
payload.misconception: Appending empty slots to the buffer is enough to double the capacity.

Ruby · deques · exercise · explain-why · L3
Prompt: Why must a growing ring-buffer deque copy its elements in logical order instead of just enlarging the array?

payload.answer: Elements can wrap around the end of the array, so the logical order differs from the physical order. If the array is only extended, the wrapped part stays in the old slots while head and the modulo arithmetic now use the larger capacity, so reads cross empty slots and the order is corrupted. Copying from head onward into a new array and resetting head to 0 restores a contiguous, correctly ordered buffer.

Ruby · deques · patterns · L2
Concept: A deque palindrome check compares both ends and stops with one or zero items left
Misconception: Loop while the deque is not empty, popping a front and a back item each time.
Explanation: With an odd length the last item is both front and back. After the front pop there is nothing left, so pop returns nil and the comparison fails for a real palindrome like "aba". Loop while more than one item remains. In Ruby an Array already supports shift and pop in amortised O(1), so it works as a deque.
Incorrect:
def pal_bad?(s)
  dq = s.chars
  until dq.empty?
    return false unless dq.shift == dq.pop
  end
  true
end
Correct:
def pal?(s)
  dq = s.chars
  while dq.size > 1
    return false unless dq.shift == dq.pop
  end
  true
end
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: Array#rotate returns a new array; rotate! changes the receiver
Misconception: Calling a.rotate(k) rotates the array a.
Explanation: rotate builds and returns a rotated copy and leaves the receiver unchanged, so discarding the result does nothing. Use rotate! to change the array in place. Positive counts move the front items to the back; negative counts do the reverse. Both are O(n).

def rotate_bad(a, k)
  a.rotate(k)
  a
end

def rotate_in_place(a, k)
  a.rotate!(k)
  a
end

Ruby · deques · patterns · L3
Concept: A sliding-window maximum keeps a decreasing deque and drops expired indexes from the front
Misconception: Keeping only decreasing values in the deque is enough; old indexes never matter.
Explanation: A maximum that has left the window must be removed, or it keeps being reported. Store indexes, pop smaller values from the back, and pop from the front when its index is outside the window. The front is then always the window maximum. Each index enters and leaves once, so the scan is O(n).
Incorrect:
def window_max_bad(nums, k)
  dq = []
  out = []
  nums.each_with_index do |x, i|
    dq.pop while !dq.empty? && nums[dq.last] <= x
    dq.push(i)
    out << nums[dq.first] if i >= k - 1
  end
  out
end
Correct:
def window_max(nums, k)
  dq = []
  out = []
  nums.each_with_index do |x, i|
    dq.shift if !dq.empty? && dq.first <= i - k
    dq.pop while !dq.empty? && nums[dq.last] <= x
    dq.push(i)
    out << nums[dq.first] if i >= k - 1
  end
  out
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · disjoint sets (union-find) · access · L2
Concept: Path compression must repoint every node on the path, saving the next node before changing the link
Misconception: After finding the root, setting parent[x] = root for the starting node is enough.
Explanation: Only the first node would then skip ahead; the nodes in the middle of the path keep long chains, so repeated finds stay slow. Walk the path again from the start and set each node to the root, reading the old parent before overwriting it. With compression, find is nearly constant on average (inverse Ackermann amortised with union by rank).
Incorrect:
def compress_bad(parent, x)
  root = x
  root = parent[root] while parent[root] != root
  parent[x] = root
  root
end
Correct:
class DisjointSet
  def find(x)
    root = x
    root = @parent[root] while @parent[root] != root
    while @parent[x] != root
      nxt = @parent[x]
      @parent[x] = root
      x = nxt
    end
    root
  end
end
Complexity: O(α(n))

Ruby · disjoint sets (union-find) · patterns · L3
Concept: Union returns false for an edge inside one set, which is how cycles are detected and Kruskal skips edges
Misconception: Kruskal can union every sorted edge and add its weight.
Explanation: An edge whose endpoints are already connected would close a cycle and must be skipped, so the weight is added only when union reports that it merged two different sets. Sort the edges by weight, take the cheapest edges that do not form a cycle, and stop when the forest is connected. Sorting dominates: O(E log E). The same test finds cycles in an undirected graph.
Incorrect:
def mst_bad(n, edges)
  ds = DisjointSet.new(n)
  edges.sort_by { |e| e[2] }.sum do |u, v, w|
    ds.union(u, v)
    w
  end
end
Correct:
def mst_weight(n, edges)
  ds = DisjointSet.new(n)
  edges.sort_by { |e| e[2] }.sum { |u, v, w| ds.union(u, v) ? w : 0 }
end
def has_cycle?(n, edges)
  ds = DisjointSet.new(n)
  edges.any? { |u, v| !ds.union(u, v) }
end
Complexity: O(E log E)

Imported reference; not locally executed. Subject: ruby
Ruby · disjoint sets (union-find) · creation · L2
Concept: For arbitrary keys use a Hash whose default block stores the key as its own parent
Misconception: A plain Hash of parents works for strings and symbols, since missing keys can be added later.
Explanation: find on an unseen key returns nil with a plain Hash, so union of two new keys compares nil with nil, decides they are already connected and merges nothing. A Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = k } default block stores each new key as its own root on first access. Keep sizes in a Hash.new(1) for union by size. Group the keys by their root to list the sets.
Incorrect:
class NamedBad
  def initialize
    @parent = {}
  end
  def find(x)
    x = @parent[x] while @parent[x] != x
    x
  end
  def union(a, b)
    ra = find(a)
    rb = find(b)
    return false if ra == rb
    @parent[ra] = rb
    true
  end
end
Correct:
class NamedSets
  def initialize
    @parent = Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = k }
    @size = Hash.new(1)
  end
  def find(x)
    root = x
    root = @parent[root] while @parent[root] != root
    while @parent[x] != root
      nxt = @parent[x]
      @parent[x] = root
      x = nxt
    end
    root
  end
  def union(a, b)
    ra = find(a)
    rb = find(b)
    return false if ra == rb
    ra, rb = rb, ra if @size[ra] < @size[rb]
    @parent[rb] = ra
    @size[ra] += @size[rb]
    true
  end
  def groups
    @parent.keys.group_by { |k| find(k) }.values.map(&:sort).sort
  end
  def sets_count
    groups.size
  end
end
Complexity: O(α(n))

Ruby · disjoint sets (union-find) · insertion-and-deletion · L2
Concept: Union by rank attaches the shorter tree under the taller one to keep trees shallow
Misconception: Always attach the first root under the second root.
Explanation: Sequential unions such as (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3) then build a single long chain, and find becomes O(n). Attach the root with the smaller rank (an upper bound of the height) under the other, and increase the rank only when both ranks are equal. Trees then have height O(log n); with path compression the amortised cost per operation is nearly constant.
Incorrect:
def union_bad(parent, a, b)
  ra = a
  ra = parent[ra] while parent[ra] != ra
  rb = b
  rb = parent[rb] while parent[rb] != rb
  parent[ra] = rb unless ra == rb
end
def depth_of(parent, x)
  d = 0
  while parent[x] != x
    x = parent[x]
    d += 1
  end
  d
end
Correct:
class DisjointSet
  def union(a, b)
    ra = find(a)
    rb = find(b)
    return false if ra == rb
    ra, rb = rb, ra if @rank[ra] < @rank[rb]
    @parent[rb] = ra
    @rank[ra] += 1 if @rank[ra] == @rank[rb]
    @count -= 1
    true
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · doubly linked lists · access · L2
Concept: Index from the nearer end, and normalise negative indexes before walking
Misconception: Walking i times from the head also handles negative indexes.
Explanation: Integer#times does nothing for a negative count, so a negative index silently returns the first element. Normalise it by adding the size, reject out-of-range values with nil, then walk from whichever end is closer, at most size/2 steps. Access by position is still O(n); a list is not a replacement for an Array when you index a lot.
Incorrect:
def at_bad(list, i)
  node = list.head.next
  i.times { node = node.next }
  node.value
end
Correct:
class DList
  def at(i)
    i += @size if i < 0
    return nil unless i >= 0 && i < @size
    if i < @size / 2
      node = @head.next
      i.times { node = node.next }
    else
      node = @tail.prev
      (@size - 1 - i).times { node = node.prev }
    end
    node.value
  end
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · doubly linked lists · insertion-and-deletion · L1
Concept: Inserting between two nodes rewires four pointers, and sentinels remove the edge cases
Misconception: Inserting after a node only needs node.next and the new node's prev.
Explanation: A doubly linked list has two links per edge. Inserting between a and b must set the new node's prev and next and also a.next and b.prev. Forgetting b.prev leaves the backward chain skipping the new node, so forward and backward traversal disagree. Head and tail sentinel nodes mean every real node has both neighbours, so push_front, push_back and middle inserts share one code path in O(1).
Incorrect:
def insert_bad(node, v)
  fresh = DNode.new(v)
  fresh.next = node.next
  fresh.prev = node
  node.next = fresh
  fresh
end
Correct:
class DNode
  attr_accessor :value, :prev, :next
  def initialize(value = nil)
    @value = value
  end
end
class DList
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :head, :tail, :size
  def initialize
    @head = DNode.new
    @tail = DNode.new
    @head.next = @tail
    @tail.prev = @head
    @size = 0
  end
  def link_after(node, fresh)
    fresh.prev = node
    fresh.next = node.next
    node.next.prev = fresh
    node.next = fresh
    @size += 1
    fresh
  end
  def insert_after(node, v)
    link_after(node, DNode.new(v))
  end
  def push_front(v)
    insert_after(@head, v)
  end
  def push_back(v)
    insert_after(@tail.prev, v)
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    node = @head.next
    until node.equal?(@tail)
      yield node.value
      node = node.next
    end
  end
  def reverse_each
    return to_enum(:reverse_each) unless block_given?
    node = @tail.prev
    until node.equal?(@head)
      yield node.value
      node = node.prev
    end
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

payload.answer: With sentinels every real node always has a previous and a next node, so insert and remove never have to test for the first or last node or update separate head and tail references. push_front, push_back and middle inserts all use the same four pointer updates, and an empty list is just two linked sentinels, which removes a whole class of nil bugs.

Ruby · doubly linked lists · insertion-and-deletion · L2
Concept: Removing a node you already hold is O(1) because it knows both neighbours
Misconception: Unlinking a node only needs prev.next = node.next.
Explanation: The node after the removed one still points back to it through prev unless node.next.prev is updated too. Backward traversal then visits a node that forward traversal no longer sees. With both links fixed, removal given a node reference is O(1); a singly linked list must first find the previous node in O(n).
Incorrect:
def remove_bad(node)
  node.prev.next = node.next
  node.value
end
Correct:
class DList
  def remove(node)
    node.prev.next = node.next
    node.next.prev = node.prev
    @size -= 1
    node.value
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · doubly linked lists · mutation · L3
Concept: Reverse a doubly linked list by swapping prev and next in every node, sentinels included
Misconception: After swapping a node's links, node.next still leads to the next node to visit.
Explanation: Once node.next and node.prev are swapped, node.next points to the old previous node, so advancing with it walks backwards and stops at once. Save the old next first, swap, then move on. Swap the two sentinels too, then exchange the head and tail references. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
Incorrect:
def reverse_bad(list)
  node = list.head
  while node
    node.next, node.prev = node.prev, node.next
    node = node.next
  end
  list
end
Correct:
class DList
  def reverse!
    node = @head
    while node
      nxt = node.next
      node.next, node.prev = node.prev, node.next
      node = nxt
    end
    @head, @tail = @tail, @head
    self
  end
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Enumerator and lazy evaluation · creation · L3
Concept: Enumerator.new generates values with yielder << x; a generator without loop is finite
Misconception: An Enumerator.new block keeps producing values by itself.
Explanation: The block runs once and ends when it returns. To produce an infinite stream, wrap the yielding in loop { y << value }. The stream is consumed on demand: take(8), first(8) or lazy chains stop it. Without loop the block yields its single value and finishes, so take(8) returns one element.
Incorrect:
def fib_bad
  Enumerator.new do |y|
    a, b = 0, 1
    y << a
  end
end
Correct:
def fib
  Enumerator.new do |y|
    a, b = 0, 1
    loop do
      y << a
      a, b = b, a + b
    end
  end
end
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: map.with_index(1) numbers from 1; each_with_index starts at 0
Misconception: each_with_index numbers the elements from 1.
Explanation: each_with_index and with_index default to a zero-based offset. Pass an argument to start elsewhere: map.with_index(1). The enumerator returned by map without a block carries the method with it, so with_index decides the offset and map decides what is collected.

def numbered_bad(items)
  items.each_with_index.map { |x, i| "#{i}. #{x}" }
end
Correct:
def numbered(items)
  items.map.with_index(1) { |x, i| "#{i}. #{x}" }
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Enumerator and lazy evaluation · iteration · L3
Concept: lazy evaluates elements one at a time and stops early; eager map and select process the whole collection first
Misconception: map.select.first(n) only processes as many elements as it needs.
Explanation: Eager methods build a full intermediate array at every step, so (1..1000).map { }.select { }.first(2) calls the map block 1000 times. enum.lazy passes each element through the whole chain before taking the next, and first(n) stops once n results exist. Lazy chains also work on infinite sources such as (1..).
Incorrect:
def eager(n)
  calls = 0
  r = (1..1000).map { |x| calls += 1; x * 2 }.select { |x| (x % 3).zero? }.first(n)
  [r, calls]
end
Correct:
def lazily(n)
  calls = 0
  r = (1..1000).lazy.map { |x| calls += 1; x * 2 }.select { |x| (x % 3).zero? }.first(n)
  [r, calls]
end
Complexity: O(k)

Ruby · Enumerator and lazy evaluation · iteration · L2
Concept: Enumerator#next raises StopIteration at the end; loop rescues it, while and until do not
Misconception: e.next returns nil when the enumerator is exhausted.
Explanation: External iteration with next hands out one element per call and raises StopIteration when the sequence is over. Kernel#loop rescues StopIteration and ends quietly, so loop { out << e.next } is the idiom. A while true loop lets the exception escape. peek looks ahead without consuming, and rewind starts again.
Incorrect:
def drain_bad(arr)
  e = arr.each
  out = []
  while true
    out << e.next
  end
  out
end
Correct:
def drain(arr)
  e = arr.each
  out = []
  loop { out << e.next }
  out
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Enumerator and lazy evaluation · patterns · L3
Concept: each_cons gives overlapping windows; each_slice gives disjoint chunks
Misconception: each_slice(k) visits every window of size k.
Explanation: each_slice(k) cuts the collection into non-overlapping groups, so a sliding-window maximum sees only n / k windows. each_cons(k) yields every consecutive window of size k: n - k + 1 of them. Summing each window is O(n * k), or O(n) with a running sum.
Incorrect:
def best_window_bad(nums, k)
  nums.each_slice(k).map(&:sum).max
end
Correct:
def best_window(nums, k)
  nums.each_cons(k).map(&:sum).max
end
Complexity: O(n * k)

Ruby · Fenwick trees · creation · L3
Concept: Build a Fenwick tree in O(n) by pushing each finished cell into its parent
Misconception: Copying the array into the tree cells gives a ready Fenwick tree.
Explanation: Each cell must hold the sum of a whole range, not just its own element. Place every value in its cell, then for i from 1 to n add cell i to its parent cell i + (i & -i) when that exists. Cells are processed in increasing order, so cell i is complete before it is pushed. This is O(n); n calls to add would be O(n log n).
Incorrect:
def build_bad(arr)
  [0] + arr
end
Correct:
class Fenwick
  def self.from(arr)
    f = new(arr.size)
    t = f.tree
    arr.each_with_index { |v, i| t[i + 1] += v }
    (1..arr.size).each do |i|
      j = i + (i & -i)
      t[j] += t[i] if j <= arr.size
    end
    f
  end
end
Complexity: O(n)

    arr.each_with_index { |v, i| t[i + 1] += v }

      j = i + (i & -i)
      t[j] += t[i] if j <= arr.size

    f

Place every value in its cell, then for i from 1 to n add cell i to its parent cell i + (i & -i) when that exists. Cells are processed in increasing order, so cell i is complete before it is pushed. Concept: Counting inversions with a Fenwick tree treats equal values as non-inversions
Misconception: For each element, count the earlier elements that are not smaller.
Explanation: An inversion is a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j], strictly greater. Counting earlier elements that are greater than or equal to the current one counts equal pairs as inversions. Compress the values to ranks, and for each element subtract the count of earlier elements with rank at most its own: earlier - prefix(rank + 1). Overall O(n log n).
Incorrect:
def inversions_bad(arr)
  ranks = arr.uniq.sort.each_with_index.to_h
  f = Fenwick.new(ranks.size)
  inv = 0
  arr.each_with_index do |x, i|
    r = ranks[x]
    inv += i - f.prefix(r)
    f.add(r, 1)
  end
  inv
end
Correct:
def count_inversions(arr)
  ranks = arr.uniq.sort.each_with_index.to_h
  f = Fenwick.new(ranks.size)
  inv = 0
  arr.each_with_index do |x, i|
    r = ranks[x]
    inv += i - f.prefix(r + 1)
    f.add(r, 1)
  end
  inv
end
Complexity: O(n log n)

Ruby · Fenwick trees · patterns · L3
Concept: Binary descent finds the first index whose prefix sum reaches a target; the comparison must be strict
Misconception: Descend while the cell value is less than or equal to the remaining target.
Explanation: With <= the walk also skips a cell whose sum equals the target, so the answer lands one position too late. To find the first position where the prefix sum is at least the target, skip a cell only when its value is strictly less than the remaining target, subtract it, and halve the step. Start the step at the highest power of two not above n, available as 1 << (n.bit_length - 1). Works for non-negative values; O(log n).
Incorrect:
def lower_bound_bad(t, n, target)
  pos = 0
  step = 1 << (n.bit_length - 1)
  while step > 0
    nxt = pos + step
    if nxt <= n && t[nxt] <= target
      pos = nxt
      target -= t[nxt]
    end
    step >>= 1
  end
  pos
end
Correct:
class Fenwick
  def lower_bound(target)
    pos = 0
    step = @size.zero? ? 0 : 1 << (@size.bit_length - 1)
    while step > 0
      nxt = pos + step
      if nxt <= @size && @tree[nxt] < target
        pos = nxt
        target -= @tree[nxt]
      end
      step >>= 1
    end
    pos
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Misconception: The sum of elements l through r is prefix(r) - prefix(l).
Explanation: prefix(k) is the sum of the first k elements, indexes 0 to k - 1. The difference prefix(r) - prefix(l) therefore covers l through r - 1 and drops the last element. end

  def range_sum(l, r)
    prefix(r + 1) - prefix(l)
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · Fenwick trees · mutation · L2
Concept: An update climbs with i += i & -i and a query descends with i -= i & -i
Misconception: Both update and query can walk with i -= i & -i.
Explanation: Cell i of a Fenwick tree holds the sum of the range of length lowbit(i) ending at i, where lowbit(i) = i & -i. A change at position i affects the cells found by repeatedly adding the lowest set bit, while a prefix sum collects cells by repeatedly removing it. Using the same direction for both double counts or misses cells. Ruby integers are unbounded, so i & -i works for any positive i. Each loop is O(log n).
Incorrect:
def add_bad(t, i, delta)
  while i > 0
    t[i] += delta
    i -= i & -i
  end
end
def sum_bad(t, i)
  total = 0
  while i > 0
    total += t[i]
    i -= i & -i
  end
  total
end
Correct:
class Fenwick
  attr_reader :size, :tree
  def initialize(n)
    @size = n
    @tree = Array.new(n + 1, 0)
  end
  def add(i, delta)
    i += 1
    while i <= @size
      @tree[i] += delta
      i += i & -i
    end
    self
  end
  def prefix(count)
    total = 0

Ruby · Fenwick trees · exercise · explain-why · L2
Prompt: Why does i & -i give the lowest set bit of a positive integer, and why does a Fenwick tree use it?

payload.answer: In two's complement, -i is the bitwise complement of i plus one. The complement flips every bit, and adding one carries through the trailing zeros up to the lowest set bit, so only that bit (and the zeros below it) match in i and -i. The and keeps exactly the lowest set bit. A Fenwick cell i covers a range whose length is that value, so adding it moves to the next cell that covers i and subtracting it moves to the previous disjoint range.

Concept: Mutating an array used as a key breaks lookup until rehash; freeze or copy the key
Misconception: A key can be changed after it is stored and still be found.
Explanation: A hash stores each key under its hash code at insertion time.   h[key]
end

  key = [1].freeze
  h = { key => :found }
  h[[1]]
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Hash · ordering · L3
Concept: A hash keeps insertion order; reassigning a key keeps its place, delete then insert moves it to the end
Misconception: h[key] = value moves the key to the end of the hash.
Explanation: Since Ruby 1.9 a Hash iterates in insertion order. Assigning to an existing key only changes its value and leaves its position. To mark a key as most recently used, delete it and insert it again. That gives an LRU cache from one Hash: evict h.first (the oldest) when the capacity is exceeded. All operations are O(1) on average.
Incorrect:
def touch_bad(h, key)
  h[key] = h[key]
  h
end
Correct:
def touch(h, key)
  value = h.delete(key)
  h[key] = value
  h
end
def evict_oldest(h)
  h.delete(h.first[0])
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · heaps · creation · L2
Concept: Build a heap in O(n) by sifting down from the last parent to the root
Misconception: Sifting down from index 0 upward to the last parent builds the heap.
Explanation: Sift-down assumes both child subtrees are already heaps, so the work must start at the bottom: from index n / 2 - 1 down to 0. Going from the root downwards fixes the root before its subtrees are ordered and leaves violations behind. Most nodes are near the leaves and move little, so the total is O(n), better than n pushes at O(n log n).
Incorrect:
def build_bad(items)
  a = items.dup
  n = a.size
  (0...(n / 2)).each do |start|
    i = start
    while 2 * i + 1 < n
      l = 2 * i + 1
      r = l + 1
      s = i
      s = l if a[l] < a[s]
      s = r if r < n && a[r] < a[s]
      break if s == i
      a[s], a[i] = a[i], a[s]
      i = s
    end
  end
  a
end
Correct:
class MinHeap
  def build(items)
    @a = items.dup
    (@a.size / 2 - 1).downto(0) { |i| sift_down(i) }
    self
  end
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · heaps · exercise · explain-why · L3
Prompt: Why is building a heap bottom-up with sift-down O(n) although each sift-down can cost O(log n)?

payload.answer: Sift-down from a node costs at most the height of its subtree. Half of the nodes are leaves and need no work, a quarter have height 1, an eighth have height 2, and so on. The total work is the sum of height times the number of nodes at that height, which converges to a constant times n. Only the few nodes near the root pay the full logarithmic cost.

Ruby · heaps · patterns · L3
Concept: The kth largest element comes from a min-heap capped at k items, trimmed after each push
Misconception: Trim the heap before adding the new value to keep it at k items.
Explanation: Trimming before the push evicts the smallest stored value even when the new value is smaller still, so a small newcomer displaces a larger value that belongs in the top k. Push first, then pop while the size exceeds k; the root is then the smallest of the k largest values, which is the kth largest. Time O(n log k) and O(k) space, better than sorting when k is small.
Incorrect:
def kth_largest_bad(nums, k)
  h = MinHeap.new
  nums.each do |x|
    h.pop if h.size >= k
    h.push(x)
  end
  h.peek
end
Correct:
def kth_largest(nums, k)
  h = MinHeap.new
  nums.each do |x|
    h.push(x)
    h.pop if h.size > k
  end
  h.peek
end
Complexity: O(n log k)

Imported reference; not locally executed. Subject: ruby
Ruby · heaps · ordering · L2
Concept: A max-heap can reuse a min-heap by negating keys, and must negate again on the way out
Misconception: Pushing negated values is enough; pop and peek already return the right numbers.
Explanation: The negation trick turns the smallest negated value into the largest original one, but the heap stores and returns negated numbers. Negate on push and negate again on pop and peek. It works for numeric keys only; for other types pass a comparator or store an ordering key. Operations stay O(log n).
Incorrect:
class MaxHeapBad
  def initialize
    @h = MinHeap.new
  end
  def push(v)
    @h.push(-v)
    self
  end
  def pop
    @h.pop
  end
end
Correct:
class MaxHeap
  def initialize
    @h = MinHeap.new
  end
  def push(v)
    @h.push(-v)
    self
  end
  def pop
    v = @h.pop
    v && -v
  end
  def peek
    v = @h.peek
    v && -v
  end
  def size
    @h.size
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · heaps · insertion-and-deletion · L2
Concept: Sift-down swaps with the smaller of the two children, not always the left one
Misconception: After moving the last element to the root, swapping it with the left child when it is larger is enough.
Explanation: If the right child is smaller than the left one, swapping with the left child leaves the right child smaller than its new parent, which breaks the heap order. Compare with both children and swap with the smallest. Children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and each must be checked against the array size. pop is O(log n).
Incorrect:
def sift_down_bad(a, i)
  n = a.size
  while 2 * i + 1 < n
    l = 2 * i + 1
    break if a[l] >= a[i]
    a[l], a[i] = a[i], a[l]
    i = l
  end
  a
end
Correct:
def sift_down_ok(a, i)
  n = a.size
  loop do
    l = 2 * i + 1
    r = l + 1
    small = i
    small = l if l < n && a[l] < a[small]
    small = r if r < n && a[r] < a[small]
    break if small == i
    a[small], a[i] = a[i], a[small]
    i = small
  end
  a
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · heaps · insertion-and-deletion · L1
Concept: Sift-up must stop at index 0, because in Ruby (0 - 1) / 2 is -1 and -1 indexes the last element
Misconception: The loop can end naturally when the parent is not larger than the value.
Explanation: A binary heap stores node i's parent at (i - 1) / 2. Ruby integer division rounds toward negative infinity, so for i = 0 the parent index is -1, and @a[-1] is the last element of the array, not an error. Without an i > 0 guard the root is compared with the last element and the two can be swapped, corrupting the heap. push is O(log n).
Incorrect:
def sift_up_bad(a, i)
  parent = (i - 1) / 2
  while a[parent] > a[i]
    a[parent], a[i] = a[i], a[parent]
    i = parent
    parent = (i - 1) / 2
  end
  a
end
Correct:
class MinHeap
  attr_reader :size
  def initialize
    @a = []
  end
  def size
    @a.size
  end
  def empty?
    @a.empty?
  end
  def peek
    @a.first
  end
  def push(v)
    @a.push(v)
    sift_up(@a.size - 1)
    self
  end
  def pop
    return nil if @a.empty?
    top = @a[0]
    last = @a.pop
    unless @a.empty?
      @a[0] = last
      sift_down(0)
    end
    top
  end
  private
  def sift_up(i)
    while i > 0
      parent = (i - 1) / 2
      break if @a[parent] <= @a[i]
      @a[parent], @a[i] = @a[i], @a[parent]
      i = parent
    end
  end
  def sift_down(i)
    n = @a.size
    loop do
      l = 2 * i + 1
      r = l + 1
      small = i
      small = l if l < n && @a[l] < @a[small]
      small = r if r < n && @a[r] < @a[small]
      break if small == i
      @a[small], @a[i] = @a[i], @a[small]
      i = small
    end
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Explanation: The matrix [[1, 1], [1, 0]] raised to n has F(n) in its top-right cell. Matrix#** uses repeated squaring, so it takes O(log n) 2x2 multiplications. A matrix of all ones, [[1, 1], [1, 1]], grows as powers of 2 instead, because its rows are identical.

end

Concept: inverse of an integer matrix has Rational entries and a singular matrix raises ErrNotRegular
Misconception: The inverse of an integer matrix is made of floats, and every square matrix has one.
Explanation: Matrix#inverse uses exact arithmetic: integer input gives Rational entries such as (3/2). A matrix with determinant 0 has no inverse and raises ExceptionForMatrix::ErrNotRegular. Test determinant.zero? first, or use rescue. Determinant and inverse are O(n^3).
Incorrect:
require "matrix"
def invert_bad(m)
  m.inverse
end
Correct:
require "matrix"
def invert(m)
  return nil if m.determinant.zero?
  m.inverse
end
Complexity: O(n^3)

Ruby · Matrix and Vector (require "matrix") · transformation · L2
Concept: * is the matrix product; use hadamard_product for element-wise multiplication
Misconception: Multiplying two matrices with * multiplies matching elements.
Explanation: * computes the row-by-column matrix product, so [[1, 2], [3, 4]] squared is [[7, 10], [15, 22]]. Element-wise multiplication is hadamard_product (also called entrywise_product). The product of an r x k and a k x c matrix takes O(r * k * c) operations.
Incorrect:
require "matrix"
def square_bad(m)
  Matrix.build(m.row_count, m.column_count) { |r, c| m[r, c] * m[r, c] }
end
Correct:
require "matrix"
def square(m)
  m * m
end
def entrywise(m)
  m.hadamard_product(m)
end
Complexity: O(n^3)

Ruby · Matrix and Vector (require "matrix") · edge-cases · L2
Concept: Multiplying needs left columns equal to right rows; otherwise ErrDimensionMismatch is raised
Misconception: Any two matrices can be multiplied.
Explanation: The product A * B requires A.column_count == B.row_count. A 1 x 2 matrix times a 1 x 2 matrix raises ExceptionForMatrix::ErrDimensionMismatch. Check the shapes before multiplying, or transpose one operand: A * B.transpose is 1 x 1 here.
Incorrect:
require "matrix"
def product_bad(a, b)
  a * b
end
Correct:
require "matrix"
def product(a, b)
  return nil unless a.column_count == b.row_count
  a * b
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Matrix and Vector (require "matrix") · patterns · L3
Concept: Use inner_product for the dot product; Vector * Vector is not defined
Misconception: v * w computes the dot product of two vectors.
Explanation: Vector * Vector raises ExceptionForMatrix::ErrOperationNotDefined; * with a number scales the vector and * with a Matrix multiplies. The dot product is v.inner_product(w) (also dot), the length is v.norm (also magnitude). Both are O(n).
Incorrect:
require "matrix"
def dot_bad(v, w)
  v * w
end
Correct:
require "matrix"
def dot(v, w)
  v.inner_product(w)

Ruby · priority queues · ordering · L2
Concept: A priority queue comparator must return an Integer like <=>, not true or false
Misconception: The ordering block can return a boolean such as a > b.
Explanation: The heap needs to know less than, equal and greater than, which is what <=> returns as -1, 0 or 1. A block returning true or false cannot be tested with < 0 and raises NoMethodError, or silently misorders if it is used as a truthy value. For a max-first queue swap the operands: { |a, b| b <=> a }. Without a block the queue is a min-queue on <=>. push and pop are O(log n).
Incorrect:
def less_bad?(cmp, x, y)
  cmp.call(x, y) < 0
end
Correct:
class PQ
  def initialize(&cmp)
    @cmp = cmp || proc { |a, b| a <=> b }
    @a = []
  end
  def size
    @a.size
  end
  def empty?
    @a.empty?
  end
  def peek
    @a.first
  end
  def push(v)
    @a.push(v)
    sift_up(@a.size - 1)
    self
  end
  def pop
    return nil if @a.empty?
    top = @a[0]
    last = @a.pop
    unless @a.empty?
      @a[0] = last
      sift_down(0)
    end
    top
  end
  private
  def before?(i, j)
    @cmp.call(@a[i], @a[j]) < 0
  end
  def sift_up(i)
    while i > 0
      parent = (i - 1) / 2
      break unless before?(i, parent)
      @a[i], @a[parent] = @a[parent], @a[i]
      i = parent
    end
  end
  def sift_down(i)
    n = @a.size
    loop do
      l = 2 * i + 1
      r = l + 1
      first = i
      first = l if l < n && before?(l, first)
      first = r if r < n && before?(r, first)
      break if first == i
      @a[first], @a[i] = @a[i], @a[first]
      i = first
    end
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Imported reference; not locally executed. Subject: ruby
Ruby · priority queues · patterns · L3
Concept: Dijkstra finalises a node when it is popped, so skip stale entries instead of marking on push
Misconception: Mark a node as done when it is first pushed, as in breadth-first search.
Explanation: With weights the first path found to a node is not necessarily the shortest. Marking on push freezes the first, possibly longer, distance. Push every improvement, and when popping skip entries whose distance is larger than the best known. The queue has no decrease-key, so duplicates are allowed. O((V + E) log V).
Incorrect:
def dijkstra_bad(graph, src)
  dist = { src => 0 }
  seen = { src => true }
  q = PQ.new { |a, b| a[0] <=> b[0] }
  q.push([0, src])
  until q.empty?
    d, u = q.pop
    graph[u].each do |v, w|
      next if seen[v]
      seen[v] = true
      dist[v] = d + w
      q.push([d + w, v])
    end
  end
  dist
end
Correct:
def dijkstra(graph, src)
  dist = Hash.new(Float::INFINITY)
  dist[src] = 0
  q = PQ.new { |a, b| a[0] <=> b[0] }
  q.push([0, src])
  until q.empty?
    d, u = q.pop
    next if d > dist[u]
    graph[u].each do |v, w|
      nd = d + w
      next unless nd < dist[v]
      dist[v] = nd
      q.push([nd, v])
    end
  end
  dist
end
Complexity: O((V+E) log V)

Ruby · priority queues · patterns · L3
Concept: When merging with a heap, tied keys must not fall through to comparing non-comparable objects
Misconception: Pushing [value, node] pairs is enough because the value decides the order.
Explanation: Array#<=> moves to the next element when the first elements are equal. Two different node objects have no ordering, so <=> returns nil and the heap raises when two lists have equal values. Add a unique, comparable tie-breaker such as the list index before the node. Merging k sorted lists of n items in total costs O(n log k).
Incorrect:
BNode = Struct.new(:val, :nxt)
def merge_bad(heads)
  q = PQ.new
  heads.each { |h| q.push([h.val, h]) if h }
  out = []
  until q.empty?
    _, node = q.pop
    out << node.val
    q.push([node.nxt.val, node.nxt]) if node.nxt
  end
  out
end
Correct:
LNode = Struct.new(:val, :nxt)
def build_list(values)
  head = nil
  values.reverse_each { |v| head = LNode.new(v, head) }
  head
end
def merge_lists(heads)
  q = PQ.new
  heads.each_with_index { |h, i| q.push([h.val, i, h]) if h }
  out = []
  until q.empty?
    _, i, node = q.pop
    out << node.val
    q.push([node.nxt.val, i, node.nxt]) if node.nxt
  end
  out
end
Complexity: O(n log k)

Prompt: Why does a heap-based priority queue not return equal-priority items in insertion order, and how does a sequence number fix that?

payload.answer: Sifting swaps elements between distant positions in the array, so the relative order of items with equal keys is not preserved. Storing a strictly increasing sequence number with each item and comparing it after the priority makes every key unique, so ties are resolved in insertion order. The value itself is never compared.

Ruby · queues · patterns · L2
Concept: Breadth-first search marks a node as seen when it is enqueued, not when it is dequeued
Misconception: Marking a node visited when it is dequeued avoids repeats.
Explanation: A node reachable by two paths is enqueued twice if it is only marked on dequeue, producing duplicates in the visiting order and wasted work. Mark on enqueue so each node enters the queue once. An Array works as the queue because shift is O(1) amortised in CRuby. BFS is O(V + E).
Incorrect:
def bfs_bad(graph, start)
  order = []
  seen = {}
  queue = [start]
  until queue.empty?
    node = queue.shift
    seen[node] = true
    order << node
    graph[node].each { |n| queue.push(n) unless seen[n] }
  end
  order
end
Correct:
def bfs(graph, start)
  order = []
  seen = { start => true }
  queue = [start]
  until queue.empty?
    node = queue.shift
    order << node
    graph[node].each do |n|
      next if seen[n]
      seen[n] = true
      queue.push(n)
    end
  end
  order
end
Complexity: O(V+E)

Imported reference; not locally executed. Subject: ruby
Ruby · queues · insertion-and-deletion · L1
Concept: A linked queue must reset its tail when the last node is dequeued
Misconception: dequeue only needs to move the head pointer.
Explanation: When the last node is removed the head becomes nil but the tail still points to the removed node. The next enqueue then links the new node behind the dead node, and the queue looks empty or loses elements. Reset the tail to nil whenever the head becomes nil. enqueue and dequeue are O(1).
Incorrect:
class QueueBad
  def initialize
    @head = @tail = nil
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    node = [v, nil]
    if @tail
      @tail[1] = node
    else
      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil unless @head
    v = @head[0]
    @head = @head[1]
    v
  end
  def to_a
    out = []
    node = @head
    while node
      out << node[0]
      node = node[1]
    end
    out
  end
end
Correct:
class QNode
  attr_accessor :value, :next
  def initialize(value)
    @value = value
  end
end
class LinkedQueue
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :size
  def initialize
    @head = @tail = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def enqueue(v)
    node = QNode.new(v)
    if @tail
      @tail.next = node
    else
      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
    @size += 1
    self
  end
  def dequeue
    return nil unless @head
    v = @head.value
    @head = @head.next
    @tail = nil unless @head
    @size -= 1
    v
  end
  def front
    @head && @head.value
  end
  def empty?
    @size.zero?
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    node = @head
    while node
      yield node.value
      node = node.next
    end
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · queues · exercise · explain-why · L3
Prompt: Why is dequeue O(1) amortised in a queue built from two stacks even though one call can move many elements?

payload.answer: Each element is pushed onto the input stack once, moved to the output stack at most once, and popped once. A single dequeue may transfer many elements, but the transfer only happens when the output stack is empty, so across n operations the total number of moves is at most n. The cost spread over all operations is constant per operation.

Ruby · Range · patterns · L4
Concept: Range#bsearch needs a monotone block: false then true; testing == is not monotone
Misconception: bsearch { |x| x * x == n } finds the square root.
Explanation: In find-minimum mode the block must be false for small values and true from some point on. The test x * x == n is false again after the root, so it is not monotone and the search may return nil even though a root exists. Search for the first x with x * x > n and subtract one to get the floor of the square root. Binary search over an integer range is O(log n).
Incorrect:
def isqrt_bad(n)
  (0..n).bsearch { |x| x * x == n }
end
Correct:
def isqrt(n)
  (0..n + 1).bsearch { |x| x * x > n } - 1
end
Complexity: O(log n)

payload.document:
Ruby · Range · exercise · explain-why · L4
Prompt: Why must a Range#bsearch block in find-minimum mode be monotone?

payload.answer: Binary search discards half of the range after each probe, assuming that if the block is true at some x it stays true for every larger x, and false for every smaller one. A block such as x * x == n is true at one point only, so a probe on the wrong side of it throws away the part that contains the answer. A condition like x * x > n is false then true, so each probe is safe.

Ruby · Range · iteration · L2
Concept: An endless range cannot be turned into an array; take from it or use lazy
Misconception: (1..).to_a returns the numbers from 1 upwards.
Explanation: An endless range (1..) has no last element, so to_a raises RangeError (cannot convert endless range to an array). Use first(n), take_while, find, or lazy to consume only what you need. The same range works as a slice end: a[1..] is the array without its first element.
Incorrect:
def first_squares_bad(n)
  (1..).to_a.first(n).map { |x| x * x }
end
Correct:
def first_squares(n)
  (1..).lazy.map { |x| x * x }.first(n)
end
Complexity: O(n)

Misconception: (0..a.size) is the right range for visiting every index of an array.

def doubled_bad(a)
  (0..a.size).map { |i| a[i] * 2 }
end
Correct:
def doubled(a)
  (0...a.size).map { |i| a[i] * 2 }
end

Ruby · red-black trees · equality · L3
Concept: Verifying a red-black tree requires equal black heights, not only local color rules
Misconception: If the root is black and no red node has a red child, the tree is a valid red-black tree.
Explanation: The third rule says every path from a node to its nil leaves has the same number of black nodes. A tree of black nodes with one side deeper passes the local rules but violates it. Compute the black height recursively, count nil as one, and return nil on any mismatch or red-red pair. In this left-leaning variant a red right child is also invalid. O(n).
Incorrect:
def local_ok?(node, parent_red = false)
  return true unless node
  return false if node.red && parent_red
  return false if node.right && node.right.red
  local_ok?(node.left, node.red) && local_ok?(node.right, node.red)
end
def rb_bad?(root)
  root.nil? || (!root.red && local_ok?(root))
end
Correct:
def black_height(node)
  return 1 unless node
  return nil if node.right && node.right.red
  return nil if node.red && node.left && node.left.red
  l = black_height(node.left)
  r = black_height(node.right)
  return nil unless l && r && l == r
  l + (node.red ? 0 : 1)
end
def rb_valid?(root)
  return true unless root
  !root.red && !black_height(root).nil?
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · red-black trees · mutation · L3
Concept: The three fix-up rules run one after another with separate ifs, not as an elsif chain
Misconception: The three fix-up rules are mutually exclusive, so elsif is equivalent.
Explanation: A single insert can need several fixes on the same node: a right rotation can produce a node with two red children that must then be flipped. With elsif the flip is skipped and two red children stay in the tree. Apply the three rules in order with independent ifs: rotate left if only the right child is red, rotate right if two reds are in a row on the left, flip if both children are red.
Incorrect:
class RBElsif < RBTree
  private
  def insert_at(h, key)
    if h.nil?
      @size += 1
      return RBNode.new(key)
    end
    if key < h.key
      h.left = insert_at(h.left, key)
    elsif key > h.key
      h.right = insert_at(h.right, key)
    end
    if red?(h.right) && !red?(h.left)
      h = rotate_left(h)
    elsif red?(h.left) && red?(h.left.left)
      h = rotate_right(h)
    elsif red?(h.left) && red?(h.right)
      flip_colors(h)
    end
    h
  end
end
Correct:
class RBTree
  private
  def fixup(h)
    h = rotate_left(h) if red?(h.right) && !red?(h.left)
    h = rotate_right(h) if red?(h.left) && red?(h.left.left)
    flip_colors(h) if red?(h.left) && red?(h.right)
    h
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · red-black trees · complexity · L2
Concept: Color rules bound the height by 2 log2(n + 1), so sorted input stays logarithmic
Misconception: Sorted insertions make any binary search tree as deep as the number of keys.
Explanation: Every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes and red nodes never touch, so the longest path is at most twice the shortest and the height is at most about 2 log2(n + 1). Search, insert and delete stay O(log n) in the worst case. Without the fix-ups the same code is a plain BST with height n.
Incorrect:
class RBNoFix < RBTree
  private
  def insert_at(h, key)
    if h.nil?
      @size += 1
      return RBNode.new(key)
    end
    if key < h.key
      h.left = insert_at(h.left, key)
    elsif key > h.key
      h.right = insert_at(h.right, key)
    end
    h
  end
end
Correct:
def within_bound?(tree)
  tree.height <= 2 * Math.log2(tree.size + 1)
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Imported reference; not locally executed. Subject: ruby
Ruby · red-black trees · insertion-and-deletion · L1
Concept: New nodes are red, and the root is recolored black after every insert
Misconception: The root can keep whatever color the fix-up left it with.
Explanation: Inserting a red node keeps the black height unchanged, so fixing red violations is cheaper than fixing black ones. A color flip can turn the root red, which would break the rule that the root is black. Set root.red = false after every insert. This left-leaning variant, which stores 2-3 trees as binary trees, supports insert and search; deletion is considerably more complex and is omitted. Insert is O(log n).
Incorrect:
RBN = Struct.new(:key, :left, :right, :red)
class RedRootBad
  attr_reader :root
  def insert(key)
    @root ||= RBN.new(key, nil, nil, true)
    self
  end
end
Correct:
class RBNode
  attr_accessor :key, :left, :right, :red
  def initialize(key, red = true)
    @key = key
    @red = red
  end
end
class RBTree
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :root, :size
  def initialize
    @root = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def insert(key)
    @root = insert_at(@root, key)
    @root.red = false
    self
  end
  def height(node = @root)
    node ? 1 + [height(node.left), height(node.right)].max : 0
  end
  def each(&block)
    return to_enum(:each) unless block
    walk(@root, &block)
    self
  end
  private
  def red?(node)
    !node.nil? && node.red
  end
  def rotate_left(h)
    x = h.right
    h.right = x.left
    x.left = h
    x.red = h.red
    h.red = true
    x
  end
  def rotate_right(h)
    x = h.left
    h.left = x.right
    x.right = h
    x.red = h.red
    h.red = true
    x
  end
  def flip_colors(h)
    h.red = true
    h.left.red = false
    h.right.red = false
  end
  def insert_at(h, key)
    if h.nil?
      @size += 1
      return RBNode.new(key)
    end
    if key < h.key
      h.left = insert_at(h.left, key)
    elsif key > h.key
      h.right = insert_at(h.right, key)
    end
    h = rotate_left(h) if red?(h.right) && !red?(h.left)
    h = rotate_right(h) if red?(h.left) && red?(h.left.left)
    flip_colors(h) if red?(h.left) && red?(h.right)
    h
  end
  def walk(node, &block)
    return unless node
    walk(node.left, &block)
    block.call(node.key)
    walk(node.right, &block)
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Misconception: The root can keep whatever color the fix-up left it with.
Explanation: Inserting a red node keeps the black height unchanged, so fixing red violations is cheaper than fixing black ones. A color flip can turn the root red, which would break the rule that the root is black. Set root.red = false after every insert. This left-leaning variant, which stores 2-3 trees as binary trees, supports insert and search; deletion is considerably more complex and is omitted. Insert is O(log n).
Incorrect:
RBN = Struct.new(:key, :left, :right, :red)
class RedRootBad
  attr_reader :root
  def insert(key)
    @root ||= RBN.new(key, nil, nil, true)
    self
  end
end
Correct:
class RBNode
  attr_accessor :key, :left, :right, :red
  def initialize(key, red = true)
    @key = key
    @red = red
  end
end
class RBTree
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :root, :size
  def initialize
    @root = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def insert(key)
    @root = insert_at(@root, key)
    @root.red = false
    self
  end
  def height(node = @root)
    node ? 1 + [height(node.left), height(node.right)].max : 0
  end
  def each(&block)
    return to_enum(:each) unless block
    walk(@root, &block)
    self
  end
  private
  def red?(node)
    !node.nil? && node.red
  end
  def rotate_left(h)
    x = h.right
    h.right = x.left
    x.left = h
    x.red = h.red
    h.red = true
    x
  end
  def rotate_right(h)
    x = h.left
    h.left = x.right
    x.right = h
    x.red = h.red
    h.red = true
    x
  end
  def flip_colors(h)
    h.red = true
    h.left.red = false
    h.right.red = false
  end
  def insert_at(h, key)
    if h.nil?
      @size += 1
      return RBNode.new(key)
    end
    if key < h.key
      h.left = insert_at(h.left, key)
    elsif key > h.key
      h.right = insert_at(h.right, key)
    end
    h = rotate_left(h) if red?(h.right) && !red?(h.left)
    h = rotate_right(h) if red?(h.left) && red?(h.left.left)
    flip_colors(h) if red?(h.left) && red?(h.right)
    h
  end
  def walk(node, &block)
    return unless node
    walk(node.left, &block)
    block.call(node.key)
    walk(node.right, &block)
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · Regexp (regular expressions) · equality · L2
Concept: ^ and $ match at every line; use \A and \z to anchor the whole string
Misconception: /^\w+$/ only matches a string that is one word.
Explanation: In Ruby ^ and $ are line anchors, always on. A string with a newline matches if any line matches, so "abc\nDROP TABLE" passes /^\w+$/. \A matches the start of the string and \z the end (\Z allows a final newline). Use \A...\z for validating input.
Incorrect:
def valid_bad?(s)
  s.match?(/^\w+$/)
end
Correct:
def valid?(s)
  s.match?(/\A\w+\z/)
end
Complexity: O(n)

payload.answer: In Ruby ^ and $ always match at the start and end of any line, not of the whole string. An input such as "abc\nDROP TABLE" has a first line that matches, so the check passes although the string contains more than one line. \A and \z anchor to the start and end of the whole string and cannot be fooled by embedded newlines.

Ruby · Regexp (regular expressions) · creation · L3
Concept: Interpolating user text into a pattern needs Regexp.escape
Misconception: /#{input}/ searches for the literal text of input.
Explanation: Interpolation inserts the text as pattern syntax. A "." matches any character and an unbalanced "(" raises RegexpError. Regexp.escape(input) quotes every metacharacter so the pattern matches the literal text. For substring tests use include? or start_with? and avoid a regular expression.
Incorrect:
def contains_bad?(text, input)
  text.match?(/#{input}/)
end
Correct:
def contains?(text, input)
  text.match?(/#{Regexp.escape(input)}/)
end
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: match returns nil when there is no match, so check it before indexing the result
Misconception: s.match(/(\d{4})/)[1] always returns the year.
Explanation: String#match returns a MatchData or nil. Indexing nil raises NoMethodError. Assign the result and test it: if (m = s.match(re)). Named groups (?<year>\d{4}) make m[:year] readable. match? returns only true or false and allocates nothing, so use it when you do not need the captures.
Incorrect:
def year_bad(s)
  s.match(/(\d{4})/)[1]
end
Correct:
def year(s)
  m = s.match(/(?<year>\d{4})/)
  m && m[:year]
end
Complexity: O(n)

A Regexp is a regular expression object written /pattern/. It is matched with match, match?, =~, scan, gsub and case/when. Ruby · Regexp (regular expressions) · transformation · L3
Concept: scan with groups returns an array of arrays, one inner array per match
Misconception: scan always returns a flat array of strings.
Explanation: Without groups, scan returns the matched strings. With capture groups it returns one array of captures per match, so [["a", "1"], ["b", "2"]]. Calling a String method on each element then fails because the element is an Array. Destructure in the block or build a hash with to_h { |k, v| ... }.
Incorrect:
def counts_bad(s)
  s.scan(/([a-z])(\d)/).map(&:to_i)
end
Correct:
def counts(s)
  s.scan(/([a-z])(\d)/).map { |k, v| [k, v.to_i] }
end
Complexity: O(n)

document:
Imported reference; not locally executed. Subject: ruby
Ruby · segment trees · creation · L2
Concept: Split a segment into [l, mid] and [mid + 1, r] so the halves never overlap
Misconception: Splitting a range at mid into [l, mid] and [mid, r] is the natural way to divide it.
Explanation: The two halves share the element at mid, so it is counted twice, and a range of two elements recurses on itself forever (SystemStackError). Use [l, mid] and [mid + 1, r]. Store node i's children at 2i and 2i + 1 and allocate 4n slots, which always suffices for the recursive layout. Building is O(n).
Incorrect:
def build_bad(arr, l, r)
  return arr[l] if l == r
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  build_bad(arr, l, mid) + build_bad(arr, mid, r)
end
Correct:
class SegTree
  attr_reader :tree, :size
  def initialize(arr)
    @size = arr.size
    @tree = Array.new(4 * [@size, 1].max, 0)
    build(arr, 1, 0, @size - 1) if @size > 0
  end
  def total
    @tree[1]
  end
  private
  def build(arr, node, l, r)
    if l == r
      @tree[node] = arr[l]
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    build(arr, 2 * node, l, mid)
    build(arr, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r)
    @tree[node] = @tree[2 * node] + @tree[2 * node + 1]
  end
end
Complexity: O(n)

Misconception: Starting the running result at 0 works for any combine operation.

  end
  def query(l, r)

    l += @n
    r += @n
    while l < r

        res = [res, @t[l]].min
        l += 1
      end
      if r.odd?
        r -= 1

      end

      r /= 2
    end
    res
  end

Ruby · segment trees · mutation · L2
Concept: A point update must recompute every ancestor on the path from the leaf to the root
Misconception: Changing the leaf value is enough, because queries read from the leaves.
Explanation: Queries use the stored sums of inner nodes, so an ancestor that is not recomputed keeps answering with the old value. After changing the leaf, recompute each ancestor as the sum of its children while the recursion unwinds. Only one root-to-leaf path changes, so an update is O(log n).
Incorrect:
def update_bad(t, node, l, r, i, v)
  if l == r
    t[node] = v
    return
  end
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  if i <= mid
    update_bad(t, 2 * node, l, mid, i, v)
  else
    update_bad(t, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, i, v)
  end
end
Correct:
class SegTree
  def update(i, v)
    update_at(1, 0, @size - 1, i, v)
    self
  end
  private
  def update_at(node, l, r, i, v)
    if l == r
      @tree[node] = v
      return
    end
    mid = (l + r) / 2
    if i <= mid
      update_at(2 * node, l, mid, i, v)
    else
      update_at(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, r, i, v)
    end
    @tree[node] = @tree[2 * node] + @tree[2 * node + 1]
  end
end
Complexity: O(log n)

Ruby · Set (require "set") · insertion-and-deletion · L2
Concept: add always returns the set; add? returns nil when the element was already present
Misconception: seen.add(x) returns false for a duplicate.
Explanation: Set#add returns the set itself, which is always truthy, so it cannot tell you whether the element was new. Set#add? returns the set when it inserted the element and nil when it was already there. That makes duplicate detection a single O(1) call per element.
Incorrect:
require "set"
def first_dup_bad(items)
  seen = Set.new
  items.each { |x| return x unless seen.add(x) }
  nil
end
Correct:
require "set"
def first_dup(items)
  seen = Set.new
  items.each { |x| return x unless seen.add?(x) }
  nil
end
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: Set.new takes an enumerable; Set.new(5) raises, so convert a scalar or string with to_a or chars first
Misconception: Set.new accepts any value and wraps it as one element.
Explanation: Set.new(enum) iterates its argument, so an Integer raises ArgumentError (value must be enumerable) and a String is not enumerable either. Use Set[1, 2, 3] for literal members, enum.to_set for a collection, and "abc".chars.to_set for characters. A Set is backed by a Hash, so add and include? are O(1) on average.

require "set"
def letters_bad(word)
  Set.new(word)
end
Correct:
require "set"
def letters(word)
  word.chars.to_set
end
Complexity: O(n)

Misconception: Set[1, 2] and [1, 2] behave the same when compared with their reversed versions.
Explanation: Set#== ignores order, so Set[1, 2] == Set[2, 1], while [1, 2] == [2, 1] is false. Use <= (subset?), < (proper_subset?), disjoint? and intersect? for relations. Comparing a Set with an Array is never equal, even with the same elements.

  a.to_set == b.to_set
end

Ruby · Set (require "set") · mutation · L3
Concept: Changing an element after it was added makes a Set lose it; add frozen elements
Misconception: An array stored in a Set can be modified and still be found.
Explanation: A Set stores each element under its hash code, like Hash keys. If an element such as an array is mutated afterwards, its hash code changes and include? returns false, although the element is still in the set. Add frozen copies (item.dup.freeze) or immutable values such as Data.
Incorrect:
require "set"
def lost_bad
  s = Set.new
  item = [1]
  s << item
  item << 2
  s.include?(item)
end
Correct:
require "set"
def kept
  s = Set.new
  item = [1].freeze
  s << item
  s.include?([1])
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · Set (require "set") · patterns · L3
Concept: Check for the complement before adding the current number in a two-sum search
Misconception: Adding x to the seen set first and then testing target - x is fine.
Explanation: If x is added before the check, a number can pair with itself: with target 6 and the list [3], 6 - 3 = 3 is already in the set. Test target - x against the elements seen so far, then add x. One pass with a Set is O(n) time and space.
Incorrect:
require "set"
def pair_bad?(nums, target)
  seen = Set.new
  nums.each do |x|
    seen << x
    return true if seen.include?(target - x)
  end
  false
end
Correct:
require "set"
def pair?(nums, target)
  seen = Set.new
  nums.each do |x|
    return true if seen.include?(target - x)
    seen << x
  end
  false
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · Set (require "set") · ordering · L3
Concept: A Set iterates in insertion order and has no sorting; SortedSet was removed, so call sort
Misconception: SortedSet.new keeps the elements ordered.
Explanation: SortedSet was extracted from the standard library in Ruby 3.0 and raises on use. A Set keeps insertion order and offers no ordered access, so sort the elements into an Array when you need order: set.sort (O(n log n)). For a sorted structure with fast insertion use a balanced tree or a heap.
Incorrect:
require "set"
def ordered_bad(items)
  SortedSet.new(items).to_a
end
Correct:
require "set"
def ordered(items)
  items.to_set.sort
end
Complexity: O(n log n)

Imported reference; not locally executed. Subject: ruby
Ruby · singly linked lists · insertion-and-deletion · L1
Concept: Keep a tail pointer so push_back is O(1), and handle the empty list separately
Misconception: Appending can always start with head.next, even when the list is empty.
Explanation: An empty list has no head node, so head.next raises NoMethodError on nil. push_back must set both head and tail when the list is empty, and otherwise link the new node after the tail and move the tail. With a tail pointer append is O(1); walking from the head to find the end is O(n). push_front is O(1) with or without a tail.
Incorrect:
def append_bad(list, v)
  node = list.head
  node = node.next while node.next
  node.next = SLNode.new(v)
end
Correct:
class SLNode
  attr_accessor :value, :next
  def initialize(value, nxt = nil)
    @value = value
    @next = nxt
  end
end
class SinglyList
  include Enumerable
  attr_reader :head, :tail, :size
  def initialize
    @head = @tail = nil
    @size = 0
  end
  def push_front(v)
    node = SLNode.new(v, @head)
    @head = node
    @tail ||= node
    @size += 1
    self
  end
  def push_back(v)
    node = SLNode.new(v)
    if @tail
      @tail.next = node
    else
      @head = node
    end
    @tail = node
    @size += 1
    self
  end
  def each
    return to_enum(:each) unless block_given?
    node = @head
    while node
      yield node.value
      node = node.next
    end
  end
end
Complexity: O(1)

Ruby · singly linked lists · patterns · L3
Concept: Floyd cycle detection moves the pointers first and compares afterwards
Misconception: Comparing slow and fast before moving them detects a cycle.
Explanation: Both pointers start at the head, so comparing them before the first step is always true and reports a cycle in every list. Advance slow by one and fast by two, then compare. If fast reaches nil the list ends. Floyd's method uses O(n) time and O(1) space; a Set of visited nodes needs O(n) space.
Incorrect:
def cycle_bad?(head)
  slow = fast = head
  while fast && fast.next
    return true if slow.equal?(fast)
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
  end
  false
end
Correct:
def cycle?(head)
  slow = fast = head
  while fast && fast.next
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
    return true if slow.equal?(fast)
  end
  false
end
Complexity: O(n)

Ruby · singly linked lists · insertion-and-deletion · L2
Concept: Removing a node needs the previous node; also update head when removing the first node and tail when removing the last
Misconception: Deleting the first node whose value matches only needs prev.next = node.next.
Explanation: The first node has no previous node, so removing it must move head instead. Removing the last node must move tail to the previous node, otherwise later push_back calls attach to a node that is no longer in the list. Finding the node costs O(n); unlinking is O(1).
Incorrect:
def remove_bad(list, v)
  prev = nil
  node = list.head
  while node && node.value != v
    prev = node
    node = node.next
  end
  prev.next = node.next if node
  node
end
Correct:
class SinglyList
  def remove(v)
    prev = nil
    node = @head
    while node && node.value != v
      prev = node
      node = node.next
    end
    return false unless node
    if prev
      prev.next = node.next
    else
      @head = node.next
    end
    @tail = prev if node.equal?(@tail)
    @size -= 1
    true
  end
end
Complexity: O(n)

payload.answer: The tail pointer is used by push_back to attach the next node in O(1). Ruby · singly linked lists · mutation · L3
Concept: Reverse in place by saving node.next before redirecting it
Misconception: Setting node.next = prev and then moving to node.next walks the old list.
Explanation: After node.next = prev the old successor is unreachable, so the walk stops after one node and the rest of the list is lost. Save nxt = node.next first, redirect, then advance prev and node. Reversal is O(n) time and O(1) extra space; head and tail swap roles.
Incorrect:
def reverse_bad(list)
  prev = nil
  node = list.head
  while node
    node.next = prev
    prev = node
    node = node.next
  end
  prev
end
Correct:
class SinglyList
  def reverse!
    prev = nil
    node = @head
    @tail = @head
    while node
      nxt = node.next
      node.next = prev
      prev = node
      node = nxt
    end
    @head = prev
    self
  end
end
Complexity: O(n)

    while node
      nxt = node.next
      node.next = prev
      prev = node
      node = nxt
    end
    @head = prev
    self
  end
end

Ruby · stacks · patterns · L2
Concept: Balanced brackets need a stack because a counter cannot check the order of different kinds
Misconception: Counting opening and closing brackets of each kind is enough to validate a string.
Explanation: Equal counts do not mean proper nesting: "([)]" has one of each kind and ")(" has equal counts but closes before it opens. Push each opener, and on a closer pop and compare with the matching opener. The string is balanced only if no mismatch occurs and the stack ends empty. One pass, O(n).
Incorrect:
def balanced_bad?(s)
  s.count("([{") == s.count(")]}")
end
Correct:
PAIRS = { ")" => "(", "]" => "[", "}" => "{" }
def balanced?(s)
  stack = Stack.new
  s.each_char do |ch|
    if PAIRS.value?(ch)
      stack.push(ch)
    elsif PAIRS.key?(ch)
      return false if stack.empty? || stack.pop != PAIRS[ch]
    end
  end
  stack.empty?
end
Complexity: O(n)

Concept: A monotonic stack finds each next greater element in one pass; use a strict comparison
Misconception: Popping while arr[top] <= x gives the next greater element.
Explanation: With <= an equal value is popped and gets an equal value as its next greater element, but "greater" means strictly larger. Keep a stack of indexes whose answer is still unknown and pop while arr[top] < x. Each index is pushed and popped once, so the total is O(n), not O(n squared).
Incorrect:
def next_greater_bad(arr)
  res = Array.new(arr.size, -1)
  st = []
  arr.each_with_index do |x, i|
    res[st.pop] = x while !st.empty? && arr[st.last] <= x
    st.push(i)
  end
  res
end

def next_greater(arr)
  res = Array.new(arr.size, -1)
  st = []
  arr.each_with_index do |x, i|
    res[st.pop] = x while !st.empty? && arr[st.last] < x
    st.push(i)
  end
  res
end
Complexity: O(n)
