Edition: 16 October 2026. Separate framework sections share a common foundation, practice model and verification register. 1 Purpose, boundaries and learning routes This curriculum follows the earlier HTML and CSS/Sass/Bootstrap material: mental model first, mechanism second, complete implementation third, then failure diagnosis and evidence. It teaches how to reason about a framework rather than memorize attractive snippets. Readers should already understand semantic HTML, the cascade, flex/grid, JavaScript events and basic React before the React-specific chapters. Tailwind CSS is a utility compiler and design-token interface. Bulma is a CSS component and layout framework whose interaction code belongs to the application. shadcn/ui distributes source-owned components and supporting tooling; its behavioral dependencies and chosen primitive base remain essential. Calling all three interchangeable CSS libraries obscures these differences. “Comprehensive” here means a structured treatment of the major shipped concepts, utility families, Bulma modules and shadcn component categories, with focused API records and working labs. Arbitrary values, generated permutations, third-party registries, commercial products and future releases cannot form a finite exhaustive list. The catalogue explains their grammar and extension points. Verify the installed source before accepting an unlisted prop or class. A complete beginner follows chapters in order after the HTML/CSS prerequisites. A framework switcher starts with the comparison and reproduces the same study dashboard in each system. An experienced interview candidate completes the debugging cases and explains the underlying CSS/DOM behavior without relying on framework vocabulary. All routes use the same acceptance criteria; experience changes pacing, not correctness. Each topic should be learned through fourteen lenses: purpose, mental model, setup, syntax, composition, state, layout, responsive behavior, tokens, accessibility, performance, failure modes, appropriate use and verification. A visual match alone cannot demonstrate a correct component. This is candidate reference and practice material. It has not been ingested into the application or approved as an automatically graded curriculum. Tested examples are explicitly separated from conceptual exercises. Browser checks cover the recorded Chrome environment; manual screen-reader and cross-browser checks remain necessary. FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 4 2 Version contract and architectural comparison Package metadata and official documentation were observed on 16 October 2026. Package versions below are a reproducibility snapshot, not a promise that every future registry item has the same API. The shadcn CLI version is not a runtime component version; copied files and primitive dependencies must be tracked separately. Package Observed version tailwindcss 4.3.3 @tailwindcss/cli 4.3.3 bulma 1.0.4 shadcn 4.22.0 @base-ui/react 1.9.0 react 19.3.1 react-dom 19.3.1 vite 8.3.4 @vitejs/plugin-react 6.1.2 typescript 7.0.2 class-variance-authority 0.7.1 clsx 2.1.1 tailwind-merge 3.7.0 lucide-react 1.58.0 The runnable examples pin Tailwind CSS 4.3.3, Bulma 1.0.4, Base UI 1.9.0 and React 19.3.1. Their compiler deliberately pins TypeScript 5.9.3 and esbuild 0.25.12 rather than assuming that the newest tools work on every local Node installation. The complete dependency graph is in examples/package-lock.json. A clean install should use npm ci. System Ownership and execution model Tailwind CSS Build-time scanning and utility generation; ordinary CSS in the browser; no interaction runtime required. Bulma Prebuilt CSS or modular Sass compiled to CSS; semantic class conventions; application supplies menus, dialogs and state. shadcn/ui Local React component source plus chosen primitives, utility compiler and token CSS; updates require reviewing owned code. Shared responsibility HTML semantics, data validation, accessible content, application state, persistence and product policy. For Tailwind v4, teach CSS-first configuration and the package-specific CLI/PostCSS/Vite adapters. Do not copy a v3 setup using only @tailwind directives and assume it is current. Bulma v1 introduces CSS-variable-driven themes and a modular Sass structure. shadcn/ui's July 2026 documentation makes Base UI the default while preserving Radix support; older tutorials commonly assume Radix. Record base, style, registry URL, copied-source hash and dependency versions for each installation. https://tailwindcss.com/docs/upgrade-guide https://bulma.io/documentation/start/overview/ https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/changelog/2026-07-base-ui-default FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 5 3 Common platform contract Start with meaningful elements: links navigate, buttons act, forms collect data, headings structure content and tables express two-dimensional relationships. Framework styling does not change those contracts. Use type="button" for controls that must not submit their containing form. An anchor styled as a button still navigates. Never nest a button inside another button by composing two triggers incorrectly. The cascade resolves origin, importance, layers, specificity and order; the order of class tokens inside className is not a general CSS priority mechanism. A class-merging helper can remove known conflicts, but cannot prove the computed cascade across arbitrary CSS, inline styles, pseudo-elements and plugins. Inspect the matched rules when a utility appears ineffective. Keep the state owner explicit. React state or native DOM state should determine both the visible style and accessibility attributes. Changing aria-expanded alone does not hide a menu. Adding is-active alone does not trap dialog focus. CSS can react to a state but cannot implement every interaction protocol. Accessibility acceptance includes keyboard operation, visible focus, correct names and relationships, logical source order, zoom/reflow, error recovery, reduced-motion preferences, forced-color behavior and sufficient contrast in every theme. Automated axe checks catch a useful subset. A zero-violation scan is not a WCAG conformance certificate. Build responsive behavior from content constraints. Test at 320 CSS pixels, intermediate widths and large text, not merely five named devices. Let long translated labels wrap. A grid track with minmax(0, 1fr) and min-width: 0 children often prevents overflow that width: 100% alone cannot fix. Preserve reading order when rearranging layouts. https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/ FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 6 4 Tailwind CSS - compiler, installation and source detection Tailwind reads source text, recognizes complete candidate class names, resolves utilities and variants against the theme, then emits CSS. It does not run your JavaScript or infer the eventual result of arbitrary interpolation. The browser receives selectors and declarations, not a Tailwind layout engine. A reproducible CLI workflow is useful for understanding the pipeline before adopting a framework adapter: npm install -D tailwindcss@4.3.3 @tailwindcss/cli@4.3.3 npx @tailwindcss/cli -i ./src/app.css -o ./dist/app.css --minify @import "tailwindcss" source(none); @source "./index.html"; @source "./components"; Automatic detection is convenient, but repository boundaries, ignored paths and external packages matter. Explicit sources make teaching examples reproducible. Paths in @source are relative to the stylesheet. Monorepos need intentional source roots; scanning the entire workspace can bloat output and obscure which package owns a candidate. const toneClasses = { success: "bg-emerald-700 text-white", danger: "bg-red-700 text-white", }; function Notice({ tone }: { tone: keyof typeof toneClasses }) { return

Build completed

; } The complete strings above are visible to the scanner. A construction such as bg-${tone}-700 is not a reliable source of CSS. Do not solve the problem by accepting arbitrary user-supplied classes. Map domain values to a bounded approved vocabulary. For genuinely continuous data, set a custom property and use a static utility such as w-[var(--progress)], validating the numeric input separately. @source inline("...") can deliberately include candidates not otherwise present. Keep the list narrow and document why it exists. It is not a substitute for a coherent component API. Build a production bundle in CI and inspect the emitted selectors for important dynamic states; development rendering alone can hide missing candidates. Vite uses @tailwindcss/vite; PostCSS uses @tailwindcss/postcss; the CLI uses @tailwindcss/cli. Install the adapter actually used by the build. Browser CDN/playground tooling is useful for exploration but is not the pinned production workflow taught here. Tailwind v4 depends on modern CSS; check the official compatibility baseline and your product browser matrix before migration. https://tailwindcss.com/docs/installation/tailwind-cli https://tailwindcss.com/docs/detecting-classes-in-source-files https://tailwindcss.com/docs/compatibility FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 7 5 Tailwind CSS - utility grammar and layout reasoning A candidate usually combines optional variants, a utility family and a value: md:hover:bg-slate-800. The colon separates variants, not CSS declarations. A bracketed arbitrary value supplies an escape hatch, for example grid-cols-[16rem_1fr]; underscores represent spaces where the class token cannot contain literal whitespace. A negative modifier is supported only by suitable utilities, such as -mt-2. A slash often supplies a modifier, such as text-base/6 or bg-black/50; its meaning depends on the family. The spacing scale is a system rather than a list of pixel constants. With the default spacing unit, p-4 is 1rem. The result depends on the theme and the root font size. Utilities that use CSS properties such as color or font-family can participate in inheritance; width, margin, borders and display normally do not inherit. A class is not itself “inherited.” The property it sets determines inheritance. Flexbox is appropriate for a navigation row or a one-dimensional action group. Grid expresses two-dimensional alignment and track constraints. flex-1 cannot fix every overflowing child: use min-w-0 where the automatic minimum size is the issue. A gap-* class sets space between children; it does not create edge padding. space-y-* uses sibling relationships and is less suitable for wrapped or reordered layouts.

Practice pathways

  • JavaScript fundamentals

    Arrays, functions and objects.

    Open JavaScript pathway
This is a focused structural example; the runnable dashboard supplies real local actions. Semantic list structure survives the grid layout. Adding md:grid-cols-3 does not create or reorder content. Use span and start/end utilities for deliberate placement; avoid visual ordering that makes keyboard navigation appear to jump unpredictably. Absolute positioning removes an element from normal flow and requires a containing-block strategy. z-50 is not a universal “above everything” guarantee: stacking contexts, transforms, opacity, isolation and the browser top layer can dominate. Debug the ancestor chain rather than escalating z-index without a model. FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 8 6 Tailwind CSS - responsive, container and state variants Unprefixed utilities form the baseline. A breakpoint variant applies at its minimum width and above unless constrained by a maximum variant. Default viewport breakpoints are sm 40rem, md 48rem, lg 64rem, xl 80rem and 2xl 96rem. These values are theme configuration, not a taxonomy of physical devices. Use md:max-lg:* for an interval when that expresses the actual design requirement. Container queries respond to an ancestor's available size. Mark the container with @container and apply @md:* to descendants. Named containers prevent a deeply nested component from accidentally observing the wrong ancestor. Container breakpoint names refer to the container-size scale, not automatically to viewport breakpoint values. A study card can therefore adapt inside a sidebar without treating the entire viewport as small. State variants describe selectors and media conditions. hover:* is appropriate for enhancement, focus-visible:* for keyboard focus indication, disabled:* for a genuinely disabled control and aria-expanded:* for the declared expanded state. The data-[state=open]:* spelling targets a specific attribute value; a Base UI component might instead expose data-open, so inspect its actual DOM before choosing a selector. JavaScript must update the associated panel and aria-expanded together. A group parent enables group-hover:* and group-focus-within:* reactions on descendants; a peer usually affects suitable following siblings. Named groups/peers reduce ambiguity in nested components. Neither mechanism replaces a proper label, a correct tab order or application state. Use motion-reduce:* or motion-safe:* to respect reduced-motion preferences. Use forced-colors:* and system colors where necessary to retain borders and focus indicators. print:* should preserve essential content and avoid printing hidden answer panels merely because a display utility was overridden carelessly. https://tailwindcss.com/docs/responsive-design https://tailwindcss.com/docs/hover-focus-and-other-states FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 9 7 Tailwind CSS - design tokens, dark mode and extensions Separate primitive tokens from semantic roles. A blue palette entry describes a color; --action describes an application purpose. A semantic foreground/background pair should be evaluated together in every theme. A token name is not evidence that its contrast is acceptable. @import "tailwindcss"; @custom-variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *)); :root { --action: #1d4ed8; --surface: #ffffff; --ink: #172033; } .dark { --action: #93c5fd; --surface: #111827; --ink: #f8fafc; } @theme inline { --color-action: var(--action); --color-surface: var(--surface); --color-ink: var(--ink); } @theme { --breakpoint-wide: 90rem; --radius-panel: 0.8rem; } @utility content-auto { content-visibility: auto; } @theme makes tokens participate in utility generation. Ordinary :root variables remain normal CSS variables. @theme inline is useful when a theme token aliases another variable and the utility should resolve that alias at the point of use. @theme static requests emission of theme variables even when their associated utilities are not used. Resetting a namespace to initial intentionally removes its default token-driven utilities, so treat that as a compatibility change. @utility registers a utility that can participate in variants. @custom-variant names a reusable selector/media condition. @variant applies variants inside authored CSS. @apply expands existing utility declarations inside a selector; it does not turn CSS into a general programming language or remove the need to understand the cascade. @reference provides context to independently processed styles without importing a second copy of all CSS. @config and @plugin support compatibility/plugin workflows; read their v4 limitations instead of assuming every old configuration option is supported. Custom CSS belongs in an intentional cascade layer. Tailwind's layer order is theme, base, components, utilities. Normal unlayered author CSS can outrank normal layered utilities even at lower specificity. Importing Bulma unlayered beside Tailwind can therefore change expectations dramatically. Scope or separate the systems rather than assuming class names alone isolate them. A dark-mode selector must reach portaled overlays. If the theme exists only on a nested app div while a dialog portal renders under body, the overlay may inherit different tokens. Put the theme on an appropriate common ancestor or provide a supported portal container. Persist user preference defensively and consider the OS preference when no explicit choice exists; storage can fail and server rendering can flash the wrong theme. https://tailwindcss.com/docs/theme https://tailwindcss.com/docs/functions-and-directives https://tailwindcss.com/docs/dark-mode FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 10 8 Tailwind CSS - production architecture and debugging Extract a component when a domain concept or repeated behavior deserves an API. Repetition of three utility tokens alone is weak evidence for abstraction. A CourseCard component can own a heading relationship, progress semantics and loading state; a class string cannot enforce those contracts. Keep finite variants in a lookup or a variant helper. Reject contradictory domain states such as simultaneously busy and ready-to-submit. Do not remove focus styles because a default ring clashes with a theme; replace them with an equally usable indicator. A disabled button prevents an action but may make an explanation unreachable, so offer nearby text when the user needs to understand why. Tailwind is not automatically “smaller” than every alternative. Measure the production CSS, repeated markup, component JavaScript and user-perceived rendering costs. Excessive arbitrary values dilute design consistency; broad source inclusion can inflate CSS. Conversely, deleting every repeated utility through @apply can make the system harder to trace. Optimize a measured bottleneck. Debug in this order: confirm candidate text exists; confirm the compiler saw that file; confirm the emitted selector exists; confirm its variant condition matches; inspect cascade precedence; inspect layout constraints; then inspect browser feature support. Reordering classes at random skips the causal chain. A v3-to-v4 migration should inventory build adapters, configuration, custom plugins, renamed utilities, default border/ring behavior, variant stacking and browser support. Upgrade in a branch, compare representative screens and interactions, and inspect generated CSS. Do not run a migration tool against an unrelated application merely to illustrate a curriculum. https://tailwindcss.com/docs/adding-custom-styles FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 11 9 Bulma - CSS architecture, installation and naming Bulma provides visual building blocks through ordinary class names. It can style server-rendered HTML, React, Vue, static pages or Web Components with appropriate CSS scope. It does not ship a JavaScript interaction engine. A navbar burger, dropdown, tab set or modal must be wired to real state and accessibility behavior by the application. npm install bulma@1.0.4 The base class identifies the component, child classes identify its anatomy, and is-*/has-* modifiers describe variants or helper behavior. A modifier only works where the CSS defines it. is-large does not resize every arbitrary element; has-text-centered sets alignment but does not give a control an accessible name. Bulma's reset/base rules have global effects. Loading only the classes you think you need is not always sufficient because component modules depend on shared utilities, variables and themes. Begin with a working full build, then reduce imports with measured visual and behavior checks. Do not combine two global resets blindly. Use the source package as the authoritative list for the pinned release. Documentation can evolve independently. The reference chapters below cover layout, elements, forms, components, helpers and theme architecture; they do not treat every generated color/spacing permutation as a separate concept. FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 12 10 Bulma - columns, grid, containers and responsive layout columns is the row-like wrapper and column its children. Equal columns share available space; fractional and twelve-part width modifiers express explicit proportions. Mobile stacking is the usual baseline. is-mobile requests a horizontal column arrangement even at small widths, which can be inappropriate for long forms. is-multiline allows wrapping; is-gapless removes gutters; is-vcentered changes alignment rather than the semantic reading order.

Arrays

Practice indexing and iteration before two-pointer problems.

Bulma's default breakpoints are mobile through 768px, tablet from 769px, desktop from 1024px, widescreen from 1216px and fullhd from 1408px, subject to Sass customization and feature switches. Width helpers and visibility helpers may support different suffix sets. A rule that works at desktop-and-above differs from one constrained to desktop-only. The v1 smart grid uses grid with cell children and minimum-column-width/gap helpers, allowing the number of columns to follow available space. fixed-grid provides explicit column-count control. A grid is still CSS Grid; spanning cells, intrinsic minimums and source order follow platform behavior. Choose columns for familiar flex-based composition and grid for track-based constraints rather than nesting columns to imitate every grid pattern. container constrains and centers content; section supplies page spacing; hero composes a prominent content region; level aligns compact horizontal groups; media aligns a figure with text. None defines landmarks automatically. Use header/main/section/article according to document meaning and add headings where appropriate. https://bulma.io/documentation/columns/basics/ https://bulma.io/documentation/grid/smart-grid/ FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 13 11 Bulma - forms, validation and feedback The field wrapper groups a label, control and help text. control handles the input layout, including icons or loading decoration. input, textarea and select style the underlying native elements. A styled select wrapper still requires an actual select element; a decorative icon must not replace a visible or programmatic label.

We use this for progress reminders.

For an error, add is-danger to the appropriate control, set aria-invalid="true", attach an error description and explain how to recover. Do not rely on red alone. Clear the error when validation succeeds and keep help/error identifiers stable. Native required/type/min/max constraints provide useful behavior, but authoritative validation remains necessary wherever data is persisted. Grouped fields, addons and horizontal forms solve visual arrangements. They do not create a label relationship or keyboard group automatically. A radio group needs a fieldset and legend when a shared question must be conveyed. Native disabled and readonly have different submission and interaction semantics; is-static is presentation, not an authorization control. A loading spinner should accompany a clear busy label or status. is-loading does not prevent repeated submission. Set the actual disabled property where appropriate and preserve understandable feedback. Async errors must reach the relevant control or summary without moving focus unpredictably after every keystroke. https://bulma.io/documentation/form/general/ FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 14 12 Bulma - interactive components and application-owned behavior A Bulma navbar contains navbar-brand, navbar-burger and navbar-menu; menu sections contain navbar-start/navbar-end and navbar-item. Use a real button for the burger with aria-controls and aria-expanded, then toggle is-active on both the button and menu. Preserve normal link semantics. A desktop hover menu needs an equivalent keyboard/touch interaction if it contains essential navigation. A modal is more than .modal.is-active. An accessible implementation must move focus inside, keep background interaction unavailable, support an appropriate Escape policy, expose a name/description and restore focus on close. The runnable lab uses a native dialog with Bulma visual parts, relying on showModal() for top-layer modality. Do not add a second, conflicting focus trap around native dialog. Dropdown menus need deliberate semantics. A simple disclosure of navigation links can remain ordinary links inside a region. An ARIA menu requires the full menu keyboard model, not just role="menu". Tabs similarly require selected state, panel relationships and correct keyboard interaction if implemented as an ARIA tab widget; a row of navigation links styled as tabs is a different valid pattern. Message and notification components communicate status; choose live regions only when updates need announcement. A static explanation need not interrupt assistive technology. A delete-style close button needs an explicit name such as “Dismiss progress notice.” Pagination should identify the navigation region and mark the current page; disabled-looking anchors must not keep navigating. https://bulma.io/documentation/components/navbar/ https://bulma.io/documentation/components/modal/ FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 15 13 Bulma - modular Sass, CSS variables and themes Sass configuration determines what CSS is built. CSS custom properties determine values at runtime. Use Sass to select modules and establish foundational scales; use scoped custom properties for supported runtime adjustments. Changing a Sass variable in a browser does nothing because Sass no longer exists there. @use "bulma/sass" with ( $family-primary: 'Arial, sans-serif', $primary: #2456a6 ); Use @use configuration before a module is loaded; Sass modules are evaluated once per compilation. Reconfiguring an already-loaded module can fail. A modular build can import utilities, base/themes and selected elements/components, but exact dependencies must be checked against the installed version. Preserve ordering and compare compiled output after reducing modules. Bulma's CSS variables use a --bulma- prefix by default. Many colors are represented through hue/saturation/lightness and derived role values; overriding a single final color can leave hover, border or contrast variables inconsistent. Inspect the component's local variables and derived properties before designing a custom theme. [data-theme="dark"] { color-scheme: dark; } .practice-scope { --bulma-primary-h: 218deg; } The hue example affects descendants using that token; it does not guarantee every component becomes a coherent new theme. Themes can follow system preference or explicit data-theme/class selectors. Scope overrides deliberately and inspect both light and dark states. Do not treat a theme switch as permission to discard contrast, disabled-state readability or focus indication. Spacing helpers cover margin and padding directions and scale values; typography/color/flex/visibility helpers provide targeted overrides. Helpers can clash with component styles or each other. Prefer one intentional rule over accumulating opposing modifiers and then depending on stylesheet order accidentally. https://bulma.io/documentation/customize/with-modular-sass/ https://bulma.io/documentation/features/css-variables/ https://bulma.io/documentation/features/dark-mode/ FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 16 14 shadcn/ui - source ownership, primitive bases and installation shadcn/ui supplies source that becomes part of your project, together with CLI/registry conventions. You own the resulting customization and review burden. A package update to a primitive dependency does not automatically merge improvements into copied component source. A registry refresh may change both visuals and behavioral composition, so review the diff like application code. The current default base is Base UI. Radix remains relevant for existing projects and explicit installations. A Base UI trigger commonly composes through a render prop; Radix examples often use asChild. These are distinct APIs. Inspect the copied component's imports and type signature before translating a tutorial. // Base UI composition through a source-owned wrapper: }>Open learning plan // Radix-only counterpart; do not pass asChild to an unrelated wrapper: The examples are API contrasts, not interchangeable components. The complete lab uses Base UI throughout. Render composition must preserve forwarded props, event handlers, refs and native element semantics; a custom component that swallows a ref or onClick can break focus restoration and activation. A normal project setup establishes a React-capable build, Tailwind CSS, token CSS, aliases and components.json, then initializes the CLI and adds selected components. Use a pinned CLI in a reproducible workflow: npx shadcn@4.22.0 init npx shadcn@4.22.0 add button dialog accordion These commands mutate the selected project and may install dependencies. Run them in the intended clean project, inspect generated files and commit the lockfile. CLI options and generated style defaults can change; inspect --help and the project configuration rather than treating this pair of commands as a complete universal installation recipe. https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/installation/vite https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/cli FRONT-END ARCHITECTURE / TAILWIND - BULMA - SHADCN/UI Technical training reference | Sources observed October 16, 2026 17 15 shadcn/ui - component anatomy, variants and data contracts A source-owned component often combines a primitive, a utility class recipe, a merging helper and a typed public interface. The primitive manages interaction state and accessibility mechanics; the wrapper supplies design-system defaults; the application supplies content and domain behavior. The boundaries matter when a bug appears: a missing label belongs to the application even if focus trapping belongs to the primitive. class-variance-authority maps finite variant values to class strings. clsx assembles conditional classes; tailwind-merge resolves known utility conflicts. Neither validates accessibility or computes browser styles. Extend the merge configuration if your custom utility families require it, and test the extension rather than assuming every arbitrary class is recognized. import { clsx, type ClassValue } from "clsx"; import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge"; export function cn(...values: ClassValue[]) { return twMerge(clsx(values)); } A local Button should expose a small semantic variant set such as primary, secondary and destructive. Size is independent of purpose. A danger-looking button should describe the destructive action in text, not only by color. An icon-only control needs an accessible name and adequate target size. A tooltip is useful supplementary help, not a reliable replacement for the name. Use data-slot and component-specific data attributes as styling hooks where actually provided. Do not infer that Base UI and Radix emit identical attributes. Controlled state uses a value/open prop with the corresponding change callback; uncontrolled state uses a default value. Do not switch modes unintentionally when async data first arrives. A compound component needs its full anatomy. Tailwind CSS is a utility compiler and design-token interface. Resetting a namespace to initial intentionally removes its default token-driven utilities, so treat that as a compatibility change. @utility registers a utility that can participate in variants. @custom-variant names a reusable selector/media condition. @variant applies variants inside authored CSS. @apply expands existing utility declarations inside a selector; it does not turn CSS into a general programming language or remove the need to understand the cascade. @reference provides context to independently processed styles without importing a second copy of all CSS. @config and @plugin support compatibility/plugin workflows; read their v4 limitations instead of assuming every old configuration option is supported. Custom CSS belongs in an intentional cascade layer. Tailwind's layer order is theme, base, components, utilities. Repetition of three utility tokens alone is weak evidence for abstraction. A CourseCard component can own a heading relationship, progress semantics and loading state; a class string cannot enforce those contracts. Keep finite variants in a lookup or a variant helper. Reject contradictory domain states such as simultaneously busy and ready-to-submit. Do not remove focus styles because a default ring clashes with a theme; replace them with an equally usable indicator. A disabled button prevents an action but may make an explanation unreachable, so offer nearby text when the user needs to understand why. Tailwind is not automatically “smaller” than every alternative. Measure the production CSS, repeated markup, component JavaScript and user-perceived rendering costs. Excessive arbitrary values dilute design consistency; broad source inclusion can inflate CSS. Conversely, deleting every repeated utility through @apply can make the system harder to trace. Optimize a measured bottleneck. Debug in this order: confirm candidate text exists; confirm the compiler saw that file; confirm the emitted selector exists; confirm its variant condition matches; inspect cascade precedence; inspect layout constraints; then inspect browser feature support. Reordering classes at random skips the causal chain. A v3-to-v4 migration should inventory build adapters, configuration, custom plugins, renamed utilities, default border/ring behavior, variant stacking and browser support. Upgrade in a branch, compare representative screens and interactions, and inspect generated CSS.

1. How to use this document
This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

2. Overview and mental model: Binary Tree
A binary tree is a set of nodes where each node has a value and at most two children, called left and right. In
TypeScript a node is an interface with TreeNode | null links.
Depth first traversals (preorder, inorder, postorder) use recursion or an explicit stack; breadth first (level order) uses a
queue or a level array.
Use plain binary trees for expression trees, hierarchies and as the base for search trees. Add ordering rules to get a
BST, and balance rules to get AVL or red-black trees.
Toolbox
 const t = node(1, node(2, node(4), node(5)), node(3));
inorder(t);        // [4, 2, 5, 1, 3]
preorder(t);       // [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]
levels(t);         // [[1], [2, 3], [4, 5]]
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
2 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

TypeScript Binary Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
Child links are TreeNode | null, so strict mode rejects access that skips the null check
ts-binarytree-null-checks   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-bt-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-binarytree-height. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. n.left.val is safe once the tree is built.
A leaf has no children, so left and right are typed TreeNode<T> | null. With strictNullChecks the compiler rejects
n.left.val (TS18047) because the link may be null. Use optional chaining with a fallback, or test the link before reading
it.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS18047):
 interface NodeB {
  val: number;
  left: NodeB | null;
}
function leftBad(n: NodeB): number {
  return n.left.val;
}
Correct:
 interface TreeNode<T> {
  val: T;
  left: TreeNode<T> | null;
  right: TreeNode<T> | null;
}
function node<T>(
  val: T, left: TreeNode<T> | null = null, right: TreeNode<T> | null = null,
): TreeNode<T> {
  return { val, left, right };
}
function leftVal(n: TreeNode<number>): number {
  return n.left?.val ?? -1;
}
Height adds one for the current node; taking the max of the children alone never grows
ts-binarytree-height   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: ts-bt-complexity
Prerequisites: ts-binarytree-null-checks. Follow-up: ts-binarytree-traversal-concat. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. height(n) = max(height(left), height(right)).
The height of a node is one more than the taller child. Without the + 1 every call returns the base case value. Define
the empty tree as -1 so a leaf has height 0 (edges), and state the convention because node-count heights use 0 for
an empty tree.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function heightBad<T>(n: TreeNode<T> | null): number {
  return n === null ? -1 : Math.max(heightBad(n.left), heightBad(n.right));
}
Correct:
 function height<T>(n: TreeNode<T> | null): number {
  return n === null ? -1 : 1 + Math.max(height(n.left), height(n.right));
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Level order processes one level at a time; one flat queue loop mixes the levels
ts-binarytree-levels   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ts-bt-iteration
Prerequisites: ts-binarytree-dfs-order. Follow-up: ts-binarytree-equality. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A single loop over a growing queue gives the levels.
A queue loop visits nodes in level order but does not say where a level ends, so everything lands in one row. Keep
the current level in an array, read its values, then build the next level from its children, and repeat until a level is
empty.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function levelsBad<T>(root: TreeNode<T> | null): T[][] {
  const out: T[][] = [];
  if (root === null) return out;
  const queue: Array<TreeNode<T>> = [root];
  const row: T[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < queue.length; i++) {
    const n = queue[i] as TreeNode<T>;
    row.push(n.val);
    if (n.left) queue.push(n.left);
    if (n.right) queue.push(n.right);
  }
  out.push(row);
  return out;
}
Correct:
 function levels<T>(root: TreeNode<T> | null): T[][] {
  const out: T[][] = [];
  let level: Array<TreeNode<T>> = root ? [root] : [];
  while (level.length > 0) {
    out.push(level.map((n) => n.val));
    level = level.flatMap((n) => [n.left, n.right])
      .filter((c): c is TreeNode<T> => c !== null);
  }
  return out;
}

TypeScript Binary Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
Array.prototype.concat returns a new array; calling it for its side effect loses the subtree
ts-binarytree-traversal-concat   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ts-bt-iteration
Prerequisites: ts-binarytree-height. Follow-up: ts-binarytree-dfs-order. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. out.concat(inorder(n.left)) appends the left subtree to out.
concat does not modify the array it is called on, it returns a new one. A traversal that calls it and ignores the result
returns only the root value. Spread the results into a new array, or push into one shared array.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function inorderBad<T>(n: TreeNode<T> | null): T[] {
  if (n === null) return [];
  const out: T[] = [];
  out.concat(inorderBad(n.left));
  out.push(n.val);
  out.concat(inorderBad(n.right));
  return out;
}
Correct:
 function inorder<T>(n: TreeNode<T> | null): T[] {
  if (n === null) return [];
  return [...inorder(n.left), n.val, ...inorder(n.right)];
}
Two trees are equal when shape and values match; === compares object identity
ts-binarytree-equality   lens: equality   level: L2   family: ts-bt-equality
Prerequisites: ts-binarytree-levels. Follow-up: ts-binarytree-lca. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. a === b tells whether two trees are the same.
Objects are compared by reference. Two separately built trees with the same shape and values are not === equal.
Compare structurally: both null, or both present with equal values and equal left and right subtrees.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function isSameBad<T>(a: TreeNode<T> | null, b: TreeNode<T> | null): boolean {
  return a === b;
}
Correct:
 function isSame<T>(a: TreeNode<T> | null, b: TreeNode<T> | null): boolean {
  if (a === null || b === null) return a === b;
  return a.val === b.val && isSame(a.left, b.left) && isSame(a.right, b.right);
}

An iterative preorder pushes the right child first so the left child pops first
ts-binarytree-dfs-order   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: ts-bt-ordering
Prerequisites: ts-binarytree-traversal-concat. Follow-up: ts-binarytree-levels. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Push left then right to visit left first.
A stack pops the last item pushed. To visit left before right, push right first. Pushing left first visits the right subtree
first, which produces a mirrored preorder. The same reasoning applies to every stack based depth first search.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function preorderBad<T>(root: TreeNode<T> | null): T[] {
  const out: T[] = [];
  const stack: Array<TreeNode<T>> = root ? [root] : [];
  while (stack.length > 0) {
    const n = stack.pop() as TreeNode<T>;
    out.push(n.val);
    if (n.left) stack.push(n.left);
    if (n.right) stack.push(n.right);
  }
  return out;
}
Correct:
 function preorder<T>(root: TreeNode<T> | null): T[] {
  const out: T[] = [];
  const stack: Array<TreeNode<T>> = root ? [root] : [];
  while (stack.length > 0) {
    const n = stack.pop() as TreeNode<T>;
    out.push(n.val);
    if (n.right) stack.push(n.right);
    if (n.left) stack.push(n.left);
  }
  return out;
}
The diameter may avoid the root, so track a best value at every node
ts-binarytree-diameter   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-bt-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-binarytree-lca. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. The longest path goes through the root: height(left) + height(right).
The longest path between two nodes may lie entirely inside one subtree. Compute depths bottom up and, at every
node, update a running best with leftDepth + rightDepth, while returning 1 + the larger depth to the parent. A closure
variable holds the best.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function diameterBad<T>(root: TreeNode<T> | null): number {
  const depth = (n: TreeNode<T> | null): number =>
    n === null ? 0 : 1 + Math.max(depth(n.left), depth(n.right));
  return root === null ? 0 : depth(root.left) + depth(root.right);
}

TypeScript Binary Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 8
Correct:
 function diameter<T>(root: TreeNode<T> | null): number {
  let best = 0;
  const depth = (n: TreeNode<T> | null): number => {
    if (n === null) return 0;
    const l = depth(n.left);
    const r = depth(n.right);
    best = Math.max(best, l + r);
    return 1 + Math.max(l, r);
  };
  depth(root);
  return best;
}
The lowest common ancestor is the node whose two subtrees each contain one target
ts-binarytree-lca   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-bt-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-binarytree-equality. Follow-up: ts-binarytree-diameter. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Return whichever side found something.
If both the left and the right search return a node, the current node is the split point and the answer. Returning left ??
right at every level passes a target upward and skips the split, which returns one of the targets instead of their
ancestor.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function lcaBad<T>(root: TreeNode<T> | null, p: T, q: T): TreeNode<T> | null {
  if (root === null || root.val === p || root.val === q) return root;
  const l = lcaBad(root.left, p, q);
  const r = lcaBad(root.right, p, q);
  return l ?? r;
}
Correct:
 function lca<T>(root: TreeNode<T> | null, p: T, q: T): TreeNode<T> | null {
  if (root === null || root.val === p || root.val === q) return root;
  const l = lca(root.left, p, q);
  const r = lca(root.right, p, q);
  if (l !== null && r !== null) return root;
  return l ?? r;
}

Prompt. When would you replace a recursive tree traversal with an explicit stack?

2. Overview and mental model: Type Alias
A type alias gives a name to any type: an object shape, a union, a tuple, a function type, or a computed type built
from other types. It exists only in the compiler and costs nothing at run time.
Aliases are where type-level programming happens: unions of literals, mapped types that rewrite properties,
conditional types that choose a type, and template literal types that build strings.
Most surprises come from widening (let and mutable properties), distribution of conditional types over unions, and
intersections of incompatible members.
Toolbox
 type Id = string | number;
type Point = { x: number; y: number };
type Pair<T> = [T, T];
type Json = string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | { [k: string]: Json };
type Getters<T> = { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K] };
const cfg = { port: 80 } satisfies Record<string, number | string>;

Intersecting two types with conflicting property types makes that property never; use Omit
and add
ts-typealias-intersection   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: ts-typealias-edge
Prerequisites: ts-typealias-recursive. Follow-up: ts-typealias-template-literal. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A & B with id: number and id: string lets id be either.
An intersection requires every member to hold, so id: number & string is never and no value fits (error TS2322 on any
assignment). To override a property, remove it first with Omit<A, "id"> and intersect with the new type.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2322):
 type ABad = { id: number } & { id: string };
const aBad: ABad = { id: 1 };
Correct:
 type A = { id: number; name: string };
type B = Omit<A, "id"> & { id: string };
function mk(): B {
  return { name: "n", id: "x" };
}

members
ts-typealias-satisfies   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-typealias-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-typealias-conditional. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Annotating with Record<string, string | number> keeps cfg.port typed as number.
An annotation replaces the inferred type, so cfg.port becomes string | number and calling toFixed is error TS2339.
The satisfies operator validates the shape but keeps the precise inferred type, so cfg.port stays number.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2339):
 const cfgB: Record<string, string | number> = { port: 80 };
const bad = cfgB.port.toFixed(1);
Correct:
 const cfg = { port: 80, host: "x" } satisfies Record<string, string | number>;
const fixed = cfg.port.toFixed(1);
A recursive alias must recurse through an object or array; a direct self-reference is error
TS2456
ts-typealias-recursive   lens: creation   level: L3   family: ts-typealias-creation
Prerequisites: ts-typealias-literal-widening. Follow-up: ts-typealias-intersection. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. type Json = Json | string is a valid recursive type.
An alias that refers to itself directly in a union has no structure and is error TS2456. Recursion is allowed inside object
properties, array elements and tuples, which is how a JSON value type is written.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2456):
 type LoopB = LoopB | string;
Correct:
 type Json = string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | { [k: string]: Json };
function depth(j: Json): number {
  if (Array.isArray(j)) return 1 + Math.max(0, ...j.map(depth));
  if (typeof j === "object" && j !== null) {
    return 1 + Math.max(0, ...Object.values(j).map(depth));
  }
  return 0;
}

A mapped type can remove readonly with -readonly; without it the property cannot be
assigned (TS2540)
ts-typealias-mapped   lens: transformation   level: L3   family: ts-typealias-transform
Prerequisites: ts-typealias-template-literal. Follow-up: ts-typealias-conditional. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Readonly<T> can be undone by assigning to a copy typed as T.
Mapped types rewrite every property: { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] } removes readonly, and -? removes optionality.
Assigning through a Readonly view is error TS2540. Define Mutable<T> and use it where mutation is intended.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2540):
 type FrozenB = Readonly<{ n: number }>;
function bumpB(f: FrozenB): void {
  f.n = 1;
}
Correct:
 type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
function bump(f: Mutable<Readonly<{ n: number }>>): number {
  f.n += 1;
  return f.n;
}
Template literal types build string unions; a value outside the pattern is error TS2322
ts-typealias-template-literal   lens: transformation   level: L3   family: ts-typealias-transform
Prerequisites: ts-typealias-intersection. Follow-up: ts-typealias-mapped. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A string type like `on${string}` accepts any string.
A template literal type constrains the text: `on${Capitalize<string>}` accepts "onClick" but rejects "click" (TS2322).
Combined with a union, it generates every name: `get${Capitalize<K>}`. The check happens at compile time only.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2322):
 type HandlerB = `on${Capitalize<string>}`;
const hBad: HandlerB = "click";
Correct:
 type Handler = `on${Capitalize<string>}`;
function onName(event: string): Handler {
  return `on${event[0]?.toUpperCase() ?? ""}${event.slice(1)}` as Handler;
}

Conditional types distribute over unions; wrap both sides in a tuple to stop distribution
ts-typealias-conditional   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-typealias-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-typealias-mapped. Follow-up: ts-typealias-satisfies. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. ToArray<string | number> is (string | number)[].
A conditional type on a naked type parameter applies to each union member, so ToArray<string | number> is string[] |
number[], and a mixed array is error TS2322. Wrapping the check in [T] extends [unknown] disables distribution and
gives (string | number)[].
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2322):
 type ToArrayB<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never;
const mixedBad: ToArrayB<string | number> = ["a", 1];
Correct:
 type ToArray<T> = [T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never;
const mixed: ToArray<string | number> = ["a", 1];

the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

2. Overview and mental model: Hash Table
A hash table maps keys to values in O(1) average time. A hash function turns a key into an integer, the integer
modulo the capacity picks a bucket, and each bucket stores the entries that collided there (separate chaining).
Correctness depends on four details: the hash must be a non-negative integer, colliding keys must coexist, an
existing key must be updated rather than duplicated, and resizing must rehash because the index depends on the
capacity.
TypeScript gives you typed keys and values, but nothing checks the hash arithmetic. JavaScript already ships Map
and Set; hand-written tables are for learning and for special cases.
Toolbox
 type Table<K, V> = { buckets: [K, V][][]; count: number };
const t = makeTable<string | number, number>(8);
put(t, "a", 1);
get(t, "a");              // 1
del(t, "a");              // true
resize(t, 16);            // rehash every key

Page 3
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
A string hash must be reduced to an unsigned 32-bit value, or the bucket index can be
negative
ts-hashtable-hash   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ts-hashtable-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-hashtable-collisions. Complexity: O(len).
 Common misconception. h = (h * 31 + code) | 0 gives a valid bucket index after % size.
The bitwise OR with 0 produces a signed 32-bit integer, which is negative for about half of long strings, and a
negative number modulo the capacity is negative or zero. Use >>> 0 to keep the hash as an unsigned 32-bit value
before taking the remainder. Multiplying by a small prime such as 31 spreads similar strings across buckets.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function hashBad(s: string): number {
  let h = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) h = (h * 31 + s.charCodeAt(i)) | 0;
  return h;
}
Correct:
 function hashString(s: string): number {
  let h = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) h = (h * 31 + s.charCodeAt(i)) >>> 0;
  return h;
}
put on an existing key must replace its value, not append a duplicate
ts-hashtable-update   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ts-hashtable-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-hashtable-collisions. Follow-up: ts-hashtable-resize. Complexity: O(1) average.
 Common misconception. Appending to the chain is enough because get finds the newest entry.
A second put for the same key adds another entry to the chain, so the count grows, the first entry is found first by get
and the stale value is returned. Search the chain for the key and update it in place; only append when it is missing.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 type Table<K, V> = { buckets: [K, V][][]; count: number };
function putDup<V>(t: Table<string, V>, k: string, v: V): void {
  t.buckets[hashString(k) % t.buckets.length]!.push([k, v]);
  t.count++;
}

TypeScript Hash Table: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Correct:
 function hashString(s: string): number {
  let h = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) h = (h * 31 + s.charCodeAt(i)) >>> 0;
  return h;
}
function indexOf(key: string | number, cap: number): number {
  return hashString(String(key)) % cap;
}
function sameKey(a: unknown, b: unknown): boolean {
  return a === b || (a !== a && b !== b);
}
type Table<K, V> = { buckets: [K, V][][]; count: number };
function makeTable<K, V>(cap: number): Table<K, V> {
  return { buckets: Array.from({ length: cap }, () => [] as [K, V][]), count: 0 };
}
function put<V>(t: Table<string | number, V>, k: string | number, v: V): void {
  const chain = t.buckets[indexOf(k, t.buckets.length)] as [string | number, V][];
  const hit = chain.find(([key]) => sameKey(key, k));
  if (hit) hit[1] = v;
  else {
    chain.push([k, v]);
    t.count++;
  }
}
function get<V>(t: Table<string | number, V>, k: string | number): V | undefined {
  const chain = t.buckets[indexOf(k, t.buckets.length)] as [string | number, V][];
  return chain.find(([key]) => sameKey(key, k))?.[1];
}
Separate chaining keeps a list per bucket; storing one entry per bucket loses colliding keys
ts-hashtable-collisions   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ts-hashtable-insert
Prerequisites: ts-hashtable-hash. Follow-up: ts-hashtable-update. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Writing buckets[index] = [key, value] stores every key.
Two keys can hash to the same index. A bucket that holds a single entry overwrites the first key when the second
arrives. Chaining keeps a list per bucket and appends to it, so colliding keys coexist and lookups scan the short
chain. The expected chain length is the load factor.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 type Table<K, V> = { buckets: [K, V][][]; count: number };
function putBad<V>(buckets: ([string, V] | undefined)[], k: string, v: V): void {
  buckets[hashString(k) % buckets.length] = [k, v];
}
Correct:
 type Table<K, V> = { buckets: [K, V][][]; count: number };
function chainPut<V>(t: Table<string, V>, k: string, v: V): void {
  t.buckets[hashString(k) % t.buckets.length]!.push([k, v]);
  t.count++;
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Delete removes one entry from its chain; clearing the chain removes the colliding keys too
ts-hashtable-delete   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ts-hashtable-delete
Prerequisites: ts-hashtable-resize. Follow-up: ts-hashtable-key-equality. Complexity: O(1) average.
 Common misconception. Emptying the bucket removes the key.
The bucket may contain other keys that collided with it. Clearing the whole chain deletes them silently. Find the entry
index with findIndex and splice that one entry, then decrement the count.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function delBad<V>(t: Table<string | number, V>, k: string | number): void {
  const chain = t.buckets[indexOf(k, t.buckets.length)] as [string | number, V][];
  if (chain.some(([key]) => sameKey(key, k))) {
    t.count -= chain.length;
    chain.length = 0;
  }
}
Correct:
 function del<V>(t: Table<string | number, V>, k: string | number): boolean {
  const chain = t.buckets[indexOf(k, t.buckets.length)] as [string | number, V][];
  const i = chain.findIndex(([key]) => sameKey(key, k));
  if (i < 0) return false;
  chain.splice(i, 1);
  t.count--;
  return true;
}
Resizing must rehash every key: the bucket index depends on the capacity
ts-hashtable-resize   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ts-hashtable-insert
Prerequisites: ts-hashtable-update. Follow-up: ts-hashtable-delete. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Copying the old buckets into a larger array keeps lookups working.
The index is hash % capacity, so a different capacity maps keys to different buckets. Copying old buckets as they are
leaves keys where lookup will not look. Create the new bucket array and insert every entry again. Doubling the
capacity when the load factor passes about 0.75 keeps chains short and makes insertion amortised O(1).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function resizeBad<V>(t: Table<string | number, V>, cap: number): void {
  const old = t.buckets;
  t.buckets = Array.from({ length: cap }, (_, i) => old[i] ?? []);
}
Correct:
 function resize<V>(t: Table<string | number, V>, cap: number): void {
  const old = t.buckets;
  t.buckets = Array.from({ length: cap }, () => [] as [string | number, V][]);
  for (const chain of old) {
    for (const entry of chain) t.buckets[indexOf(entry[0], cap)]!.push(entry);
  }
}

TypeScript Hash Table: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Compare keys with strict equality (and a NaN rule); loose == makes 1 and "1" the same key
ts-hashtable-key-equality   lens: equality   level: L2   family: ts-hashtable-equality
Prerequisites: ts-hashtable-delete. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1) average.
 Common misconception. Keys can be compared with == because both are hashed to the same string.
Loose equality converts types, so the number 1 and the string "1" are equal and one overwrites the other. Strict
equality keeps them separate. NaN is never equal to itself, so a table that must find NaN needs a SameValueZero
rule: a === b or both are NaN.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function getLoose<V>(t: Table<string | number, V>, k: string | number): V | undefined {
  const chain = t.buckets[indexOf(k, t.buckets.length)] as [string | number, V][];
  return chain.find(([key]) => key == k)?.[1];
}
Correct:
 function getStrict<V>(t: Table<string | number, V>, k: string | number): V | undefined {
  const chain = t.buckets[indexOf(k, t.buckets.length)] as [string | number, V][];
  return chain.find(([key]) => key === k || (key !== key && k !== k))?.[1];
}

Prompt. With const t = makeTable<string, number>(1) (every key collides), after put "a", put "b", del(t, "a"), what

ts-hashtable-resize-ex1   format: choose-the-structure   level: L2   grading: rubric   modes: practice, interview
Prompt. Explain load factor and why a hash table resizes by doubling and rehashing.
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). The load factor is count divided by capacity: it is the expected chain
length. When it grows past about 0.75 chains get long and operations slow down. Resizing allocates a larger bucket
array, typically double, and reinserts every key, because the index is hash modulo capacity and changes with the
capacity. Doubling makes the cost of rehashing amortised O(1) per insertion.

2. Overview and mental model: Set
A Set stores unique values and remembers insertion order. Membership checks, adds and deletes are O(1) on
average, which makes a Set the standard tool for de-duplication and "seen" tracking.
Uniqueness uses SameValueZero: primitives compare by value, NaN equals NaN, and objects compare by
reference. TypeScript types the members but cannot tell that two equal-looking objects are different entries.
The newer methods union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference, isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf and
isDisjointFrom return new Sets and are available in Node 22 and TypeScript 5.9 with lib esnext.
Toolbox
 const s = new Set<number>([3, 1, 3]);
s.add(2); s.has(1); s.delete(3);
const n = s.size;                 // not length
const both = s.intersection(new Set([1, 2]));
const arr = [...s].sort((a, b) => a - b);

TypeScript Set: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
A Set has size, not length, and no index access; spread to an array when you need either
ts-set-size-not-length   lens: access   level: L0   family: ts-set-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-set-dedupe-objects. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A Set can be measured with s.length and read with s[0].
Set exposes size and has/add/delete. Reading s.length is error TS2339 in TypeScript and undefined in plain
JavaScript. There is no index access either. Use s.size for the count and [...s] or an iterator for positional access.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2339):
 function sizeBad(s: Set<number>): number {
  return s.length;
}
Correct:
 function sizeOf(s: ReadonlySet<number>): number {
  return s.size;
}
function firstOf(s: ReadonlySet<number>): number | undefined {
  return s.values().next().value;
}
Set removes duplicates by SameValueZero, so equal-looking objects all stay; dedupe objects
by a primitive key
ts-set-dedupe-objects   lens: equality   level: L1   family: ts-set-equality
Prerequisites: ts-set-size-not-length. Follow-up: ts-set-order. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. new Set(points) removes points that have the same x and y.
A Set compares objects by reference. Two literals with the same fields are different members, so the duplicates
remain. Build a string or number key (for example `${x},${y}`) and track seen keys, or store only keys.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function dedupeBad(ps: { x: number; y: number }[]): { x: number; y: number }[] {
  return [...new Set(ps)];
}
Correct:
 function dedupe(ps: { x: number; y: number }[]): { x: number; y: number }[] {
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  return ps.filter((p) => {
    const key = `${p.x},${p.y}`;
    if (seen.has(key)) return false;
    seen.add(key);
    return true;
  });
}

TypeScript Set: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
A Set iterates in insertion order and is not sorted; sort the spread array when you need order
ts-set-order   lens: ordering   level: L1   family: ts-set-order
Prerequisites: ts-set-dedupe-objects. Follow-up: ts-set-algebra. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. [...new Set(xs)] returns the values in ascending order.
A Set remembers first insertion order only. Adding an existing value changes nothing. To get sorted output, spread to
an array and sort with a numeric comparator, because the default sort compares strings.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function sortedBad(xs: readonly number[]): number[] {
  return [...new Set(xs)];
}
Correct:
 function sorted(xs: readonly number[]): number[] {
  return [...new Set(xs)].sort((a, b) => a - b);
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
isSubsetOf tests membership of every element; comparing sizes is not a subset test
ts-set-subset   lens: equality   level: L2   family: ts-set-subset
Prerequisites: ts-set-algebra. Follow-up: ts-set-unique-by. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. a is a subset of b whenever a.size <= b.size.
A smaller set need not be contained in the larger one. Use a.isSubsetOf(b), isSupersetOf or isDisjointFrom. Two sets
are equal when their sizes match and one is a subset of the other.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function isSubsetBad(a: ReadonlySet<number>, b: ReadonlySet<number>): boolean {
  return a.size <= b.size;
}
Correct:
 function isSubset(a: ReadonlySet<number>, b: ReadonlySet<number>): boolean {
  return a.isSubsetOf(b);
}

TypeScript Set: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
union, intersection and difference return new Sets; hand-written loops often mutate an input
ts-set-algebra   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ts-set-methods
Prerequisites: ts-set-order. Follow-up: ts-set-subset. Complexity: O(min(n, m)).
 Common misconception. Removing items from a while iterating is a safe way to compute the intersection with b.
Deleting during iteration is legal, but it changes the input set, which surprises callers. The ES2025 methods
a.union(b), a.intersection(b), a.difference(b) and a.symmetricDifference(b) return new Sets and leave both inputs
alone. Check the runtime supports them (Node 22 does).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function commonBad(a: Set<number>, b: ReadonlySet<number>): Set<number> {
  for (const x of a) if (!b.has(x)) a.delete(x);
  return a;
}
Correct:
 function common(a: ReadonlySet<number>, b: ReadonlySet<number>): Set<number> {
  return a.intersection(b);
}
To keep the first item for each key, track seen keys in a Set; a Map built from pairs keeps the
last
ts-set-unique-by   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-set-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-set-subset. Follow-up: ts-set-readonly. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. new Map(items.map(i => [key(i), i])).values() keeps the first item per key.
When a Map is built from pairs, later pairs overwrite earlier ones, so it keeps the last item for each key. A filter with a
Set of seen keys keeps the first and preserves the original order.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function uniqueByBad<T>(xs: readonly T[], key: (x: T) => string): T[] {
  return [...new Map(xs.map((x) => [key(x), x] as const)).values()];
}
Correct:
 function uniqueBy<T>(xs: readonly T[], key: (x: T) => string): T[] {
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  return xs.filter((x) => {
    const k = key(x);
    if (seen.has(k)) return false;
    seen.add(k);
    return true;
  });
}

Page 7
Return ReadonlySet<T> to stop callers adding values; the type is erased, so copy when you
need real protection
ts-set-readonly   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ts-set-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-set-unique-by. Follow-up: ts-set-literal-narrowing. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A function that returns its internal Set can be trusted not to have it modified by callers.
A returned Set<T> lets callers call add and delete on your private state. The type ReadonlySet<T> removes those
methods at compile time (TS2339 on add). The restriction is not enforced at runtime, so return new Set(internal)
when callers are untrusted.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2339):
 function addBad(s: ReadonlySet<number>): void {
  s.add(1);
}
Correct:
 class Tags {
  private items = new Set<string>();
  add(t: string): void { this.items.add(t); }
  view(): ReadonlySet<string> { return this.items; }
  copy(): Set<string> { return new Set(this.items); }
}
Set<"a" | "b">.has(x) rejects a plain string; widen the Set to ReadonlySet<string> to use has
as a type guard
ts-set-literal-narrowing   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L3   family: ts-set-typing
Prerequisites: ts-set-readonly. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. ALLOWED.has(input) narrows input to the literal union.
Set.has is typed to accept only T, so a string argument is error TS2345 when T is a literal union, and has does not
narrow its argument anyway. Declare the Set as ReadonlySet<string>, then write an explicit type guard that returns
input is Role.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2345):
 const ROLES = new Set(["admin", "user"] as const);
type Role = "admin" | "user";
function isRoleBad(x: string): x is Role {
  return ROLES.has(x);
}
Correct:
 const ROLE_SET: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set(["admin", "user"]);
type Role = "admin" | "user";
function isRole(x: string): x is Role {
  return ROLE_SET.has(x);
}

Prompt. You must check whether any of 1,000,000 ids has already been seen, many times. Compare an array with
includes and a Set.
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Use a Set. has is O(1) on average, so each check is constant time; array
includes is O(n), so repeated checks cost O(n squared). A Set also drops duplicates, keeps insertion order and has a
size property. Use an array only when you need index access or duplicates.

2. Overview and mental model: Tuple
A tuple is an array type with a fixed length and a type for each position, such as [number, string]. It exists only in the
type checker: at run time a tuple is an ordinary array.
The compiler checks positions and the length of literals, but it does not stop push, pop or splice on a mutable tuple.
Declare readonly tuples when the shape must not change.
Use tuples for short, ordered, heterogeneous values (pairs, coordinates, function arguments, return values). Use an
object when fields need names.
Toolbox
 const p: [number, string] = [1, "a"];
const [n, s] = p;                       // n: number, s: string
const r = [1, "a"] as const;           // readonly [1, "a"]
type Range = [start: number, end?: number];
type Cat<A extends unknown[], B extends unknown[]> = [...A, ...B];
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
2 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

TypeScript Tuple: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
A tuple has a fixed length: reading an index past the end is error TS2493
ts-tuple-fixed-length   lens: access   level: L0   family: ts-tuple-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-tuple-push-hole. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A tuple behaves like an array, so t[2] on a two-element tuple is undefined and allowed.
The tuple type [number, string] knows it has exactly two elements. Reading t[2] is error TS2493 ("Tuple type of length
2 has no element at index 2"), unlike a number[] where any index is accepted. That is the main benefit of tuples:
wrong positions are caught at compile time. At run time a tuple is an ordinary array.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2493):
 function thirdBad(t: [number, string]): unknown {
  return t[2];
}
Correct:
 function second(t: [number, string]): string {
  return t[1];
}
TypeScript allows push on a tuple, so the runtime length can differ from the type; return a
new tuple instead
ts-tuple-push-hole   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ts-tuple-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-fixed-length. Follow-up: ts-tuple-inference. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A [number, number] tuple cannot grow, because its length is part of the type.
Methods such as push, pop and splice are still available on a mutable tuple and the compiler does not track them.
After t.push(3) the value has three elements while its type says two. Treat tuples as immutable: declare them
readonly, or build a new tuple with spread and an explicit return type.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function addBad(t: [number, number]): [number, number] {
  t.push(9);
  return t;
}
Correct:
 function add(t: readonly [number, number]): [number, number, number] {
  return [...t, 9];
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
An array literal is inferred as an array, not a tuple; annotate it or use as const
ts-tuple-inference   lens: creation   level: L1   family: ts-tuple-creation
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-push-hole. Follow-up: ts-tuple-optional-rest. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. const p = [1, "a"] has the tuple type [number, string].
TypeScript infers (string | number)[] for [1, "a"]. Assigning that variable to a [number, string] parameter is error
TS2322. Write the annotation (const p: [number, string] = [1, "a"]) or use as const, which gives readonly [1, "a"].
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2322):
 const pairBad = [1, "a"];
const tBad: [number, string] = pairBad;
Correct:
 const pair: [number, string] = [1, "a"];
const frozen = [1, "a"] as const;
function label(p: readonly [number, string]): string {
  return `${p[0]}:${p[1]}`;
}
Destructuring an array gives string, not string | undefined; check the length or use a tuple
ts-tuple-destructure   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-tuple-access
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-optional-rest. Follow-up: ts-tuple-labels. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. const [a, b] = xs always gives two strings when xs is a string[].
For an array type the compiler assumes every element exists, so b has type string even when the array has one
element, and the result is "undefined" at run time. A tuple type or a length check proves the shape. The compiler
option noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds undefined to array reads.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function joinBad(xs: string[]): string {
  const [a, b] = xs;
  return a + b;
}
Correct:
 function join(xs: string[]): string | null {
  if (xs.length < 2) return null;
  const [a, b] = xs as [string, string];
  return a + b;
}

Tuples are arrays, so a Set or Map keyed by a tuple compares references; key by a string
ts-tuple-identity   lens: equality   level: L1   family: ts-tuple-equality
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-labels. Follow-up: ts-tuple-variadic. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. new Set([[1, 2]]).has([1, 2]) is true.
Two tuple literals are different objects, so Set.has and Map.get never find an equal-looking key. For grids and
coordinate pairs, build a string key such as `${x},${y}` or a numeric key, and convert back when needed.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function visitedBad(seen: Set<[number, number]>, x: number, y: number): boolean {
  return seen.has([x, y]);
}
Correct:

  return seen.has(`${x},${y}`);
}
Optional and rest elements make a tuple flexible, but an optional element can be undefined
ts-tuple-optional-rest   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ts-tuple-creation
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-inference. Follow-up: ts-tuple-destructure. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. In [string, number?] the second element is always a number.
The ? marks an element that may be missing, so its type is number | undefined, and arithmetic on it is error TS2532.
A rest element ([number, ...string[]]) allows any number of trailing items. Handle the optional case with ?? or a check.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2532):
 function bumpBad(t: [string, number?]): number {
  return t[1] + 1;
}
Correct:
 function bump(t: [string, number?]): number {
  return (t[1] ?? 0) + 1;
}
function head(t: [number, ...string[]]): number {
  return t[0];
}

ts-tuple-labels   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-tuple-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-destructure. Follow-up: ts-tuple-identity. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. With [start: number, end: number], r.start reads the first element.
Labels exist only for editors and error messages. The tuple is still indexed by position, and r.start is error TS2339.
Destructure ([start, end]) or index with 0 and 1. If the data needs real names, use an object type.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2339):

  return r.end - r.start;
}
Correct:

  const [start, end] = r;
  return end - start;

ts-tuple-variadic   lens: transformation   level: L3   family: ts-tuple-transform
Prerequisites: ts-tuple-identity. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Spreading two tuples into an array literal keeps their element types.
Without an explicit return type, [...a, ...b] has type (A[number] | B[number])[], and assigning it to [number, string] is
error TS2322. A generic function with A extends unknown[] and B extends unknown[] can return [...A, ...B], which
keeps positions.

}

Correct:

  a: [...A],
  b: [...B],
): [...A, ...B] {
  return [...a, ...b];
}
const joined: [number, string] = concat([1], ["a"]);

Prompt. A function returns a start and an end position. Compare returning a tuple, an object and a two-element

more than two values or the order is not obvious.

1. How to use this document
This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

cannot leak a solution into a hint.
2. Overview and mental model: WeakSet
A WeakSet is a set of objects that does not keep them alive. Membership is by identity, and members vanish when
nothing else references them.
Only add, has and delete exist. There is no size, no iteration, no clear. That is deliberate: collection timing is not
observable.
It is best at marking: objects already processed, nodes already visited, objects issued by a factory. Use a Set
whenever you need to count or list.
Toolbox
 const done = new WeakSet<object>();
const job = {};
done.add(job);
done.has(job);        // true
done.has({});         // false
// done.size          // error TS2339

TypeScript WeakSet: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
A WeakSet holds objects only; adding a number is error TS2345
ts-weakset-object-members   lens: access   level: L0   family: ts-weakset-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-weakset-no-size. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A WeakSet is a Set that cleans itself, so it can hold any value.
WeakSet<T> requires T extends WeakKey: objects, functions or non-registered symbols. A primitive member is a
compile error (TS2345) and throws TypeError at runtime. Use a Set for strings and numbers.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2345):
 function markBad(ws: WeakSet<object>): void {
  ws.add(1);
}
Correct:
 function mark(ws: WeakSet<object>, o: object): void {
  ws.add(o);
}
A WeakSet has only add, has and delete; there is no size, no iteration and no clear
ts-weakset-no-size   lens: iteration   level: L1   family: ts-weakset-iteration
Prerequisites: ts-weakset-object-members. Follow-up: ts-weakset-identity. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A WeakSet can report how many objects it holds.
Because members may be collected at any time, the API hides them. Reading size is error TS2339 and undefined at
runtime. If you need a count or a listing, use a Set and remove members yourself.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2339):
 function sizeBad(ws: WeakSet<object>): number {
  return ws.size;
}
Correct:
 function sizeOfSet(s: ReadonlySet<object>): number {
  return s.size;
}

TypeScript WeakSet: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Membership is by identity: a clone of a member is not a member
ts-weakset-identity   lens: equality   level: L1   family: ts-weakset-equality
Prerequisites: ts-weakset-no-size. Follow-up: ts-weakset-run-once. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. ws.has({ ...o }) is true when o was added.
The WeakSet tests reference identity, like a Set of objects. A spread copy or structuredClone result is a different
object, so has returns false. Keep the original reference or compare by an id in a Set.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function seenBad(ws: WeakSet<object>, o: { id: number }): boolean {
  return ws.has({ ...o });
}
Correct:
 function seen(ws: WeakSet<object>, o: { id: number }): boolean {
  return ws.has(o);
}
