Count a component only for a start vertex that has not been visited yet
ts-undirectedgraph-components   lens: iteration   level: L2   family: ts-ug-iteration
Prerequisites: ts-undirectedgraph-edge-count. Follow-up: ts-undirectedgraph-cycle. Complexity: O(V + E).
 Common misconception. Every vertex is the start of a new component.
The outer loop visits all vertices as possible start points. A vertex already reached by an earlier traversal belongs to a
component that was already counted. Skip visited starts before incrementing the counter, otherwise the result is the
number of vertices.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function componentsBad(g: UGraph): number {
  const seen = new Array<boolean>(g.n).fill(false);
  let count = 0;
  for (let s = 0; s < g.n; s++) {
    count++;
    if (seen[s]) continue;
    const stack = [s];
    seen[s] = true;
    while (stack.length > 0) {
      const u = stack.pop() as number;
      for (const v of g.adj[u] as Set<number>) {
        if (!seen[v]) { seen[v] = true; stack.push(v); }
      }
    }
  }
  return count;
}
Correct:
 function components(g: UGraph): number {
  const seen = new Array<boolean>(g.n).fill(false);
  let count = 0;
  for (let s = 0; s < g.n; s++) {
    if (seen[s]) continue;
    count++;
    const stack = [s];
    seen[s] = true;
    while (stack.length > 0) {
      const u = stack.pop() as number;
      for (const v of g.adj[u] as Set<number>) {
        if (!seen[v]) { seen[v] = true; stack.push(v); }
      }
    }
  }
  return count;
}

Page 6
A path rebuilt from parent links runs target to source and must be reversed
ts-undirectedgraph-path   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-ug-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-undirectedgraph-bipartite. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(V + E).
 Common misconception. Following parent links from the target gives the path in order.
Parent pointers lead from the target back to the source, so walking them produces the path backwards. Reverse the
list before returning it. Return an empty list when the target was never reached.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function pathBad(g: UGraph, s: number, t: number): number[] {
  const prev = new Array<number>(g.n).fill(-2);
  prev[s] = -1;
  const queue = [s];
  for (let i = 0; i < queue.length; i++) {
    for (const v of g.adj[queue[i] as number] as Set<number>) {
      if (prev[v] === -2) { prev[v] = queue[i] as number; queue.push(v); }
    }
  }
  if (prev[t] === -2) return [];
  const path: number[] = [];
  for (let x = t; x !== -1; x = prev[x] as number) path.push(x);
  return path;
}
Correct:
 function shortestPath(g: UGraph, s: number, t: number): number[] {
  const prev = new Array<number>(g.n).fill(-2);
  prev[s] = -1;
  const queue = [s];
  for (let i = 0; i < queue.length; i++) {
    for (const v of g.adj[queue[i] as number] as Set<number>) {
      if (prev[v] === -2) { prev[v] = queue[i] as number; queue.push(v); }
    }
  }
  if (prev[t] === -2) return [];
  const path: number[] = [];
  for (let x = t; x !== -1; x = prev[x] as number) path.push(x);
  return path.reverse();
}
Bipartite checks must start a colouring from every uncoloured vertex
ts-undirectedgraph-bipartite   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-ug-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-undirectedgraph-cycle. Follow-up: ts-undirectedgraph-path. Complexity: O(V + E).
 Common misconception. Colour the graph from vertex 0 and check for conflicts.
A graph with several components is bipartite only if each component is. A search from vertex 0 colours only the first
component, so an odd cycle in another one goes unnoticed. Loop over all vertices and start a new colouring for each
one that is still uncoloured.

TypeScript Undirected Graph: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function isBipartiteBad(g: UGraph): boolean {
  const color = new Array<number>(g.n).fill(-1);
  color[0] = 0;

 function isBipartite(g: UGraph): boolean {
  const color = new Array<number>(g.n).fill(-1);
  for (let s = 0; s < g.n; s++) {
    if (color[s] !== -1) continue;
    color[s] = 0;
    const queue = [s];

Prerequisites: ts-undirectedgraph-components. Follow-up: ts-undirectedgraph-bipartite. Complexity: O(V + E).

In an undirected graph the edge to the parent is also a visited neighbour. Without ignoring the parent, every edge
looks like a cycle. Pass the parent into the recursion and skip it; any other visited neighbour closes a cycle.

Correct:
 function hasCycle(g: UGraph): boolean {
  const seen = new Array<boolean>(g.n).fill(false);
  const dfs = (u: number, parent: number): boolean => {
    seen[u] = true;
    for (const v of g.adj[u] as Set<number>) {
      if (v === parent) continue;
      if (seen[v] || dfs(v, u)) return true;
    }
    return false;
  };
  for (let s = 0; s < g.n; s++) if (!seen[s] && dfs(s, -1)) return true;
  return false;
}

1. How to use this document
This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

2. Overview and mental model: Binary Search Tree
A binary search tree keeps keys ordered: every key in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every key in the
right subtree is larger. Search, insert and delete follow one path from the root.
Operations cost O(h), where h is the height. Random inserts give h near log n, but sorted inserts make a chain with h
= n - 1. Balanced variants (AVL, red-black) keep h at O(log n).
Use a BST when you need sorted order together with updates: floor, ceiling, range and kth queries. Use a Map when
order is not needed.
Toolbox
 let r: BNode<number> | null = null;
for (const k of [5, 3, 8, 1]) r = insert(r, k, numCmp);
inorder(r);           // [1, 3, 5, 8]
floor(r, 4, numCmp);  // 3
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
4 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

Page 3
A recursive insert must assign the returned subtree back to the child link
ts-bst-insert-return   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ts-bst-insertion
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-bst-comparator. Complexity: O(h).
 Common misconception. Recursing into n.left is enough; the callee attaches the new node.
When the child is null, the recursive call creates a node and returns it, but it cannot change the parent link by itself.
The caller must write the result back with n.left = insert(n.left, ...). Ignoring the return value drops every key that would
become a new leaf.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function insertBad<K>(n: BNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): BNode<K> {
  if (n === null) return new BNode(key);
  if (cmp(key, n.key) < 0) insertBad(n.left, key, cmp);
  else insertBad(n.right, key, cmp);
  return n;
}
Correct:
 type Cmp<K> = (a: K, b: K) => number;
const numCmp: Cmp<number> = (a, b) => (a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0);
class BNode<K> {
  constructor(
    public key: K,
    public left: BNode<K> | null = null,
    public right: BNode<K> | null = null,
  ) {}
}
function insert<K>(n: BNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): BNode<K> {
  if (n === null) return new BNode(key);
  const c = cmp(key, n.key);
  if (c < 0) n.left = insert(n.left, key, cmp);
  else if (c > 0) n.right = insert(n.right, key, cmp);
  return n;
}
function inorder<K>(n: BNode<K> | null): K[] {
  return n === null ? [] : [...inorder(n.left), n.key, ...inorder(n.right)];
}
A comparator returns a number; returning a boolean is a type error and breaks the ordering
ts-bst-comparator   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: ts-bst-ordering
Prerequisites: ts-bst-insert-return. Follow-up: ts-bst-duplicates. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A comparator can return a > b.
A comparator must return a negative number, zero or a positive number. A boolean converts to 0 or 1 and can never
signal "less than", so the tree cannot order keys. TypeScript reports TS2322 when a boolean is returned where a
number is expected. Return -1, 0 or 1 explicitly.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2322):
 const cmpBad: Cmp<number> = (a, b) => a > b;
Correct:
 function byKey<K, T>(key: (t: T) => K): Cmp<T> {
  return (a, b) => (key(a) < key(b) ? -1 : key(a) > key(b) ? 1 : 0);
}

TypeScript Binary Search Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
A set-like tree ignores an equal key; inserting duplicates inflates the size
ts-bst-duplicates   lens: edge-cases   level: L2   family: ts-bst-edge-cases
Prerequisites: ts-bst-comparator. Follow-up: ts-bst-delete-two-children. Complexity: O(h).
 Common misconception. Equal keys can go to the left subtree.
Decide the duplicate policy up front. A set keeps one copy: when the comparator returns 0 the insert does nothing.
Sending equal keys left stores each copy, so the count grows with every repeated insert and a single remove leaves
the key present. If counts matter, store a count in the node.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function insertDupBad<K>(n: BNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): BNode<K> {
  if (n === null) return new BNode(key);
  if (cmp(key, n.key) <= 0) n.left = insertDupBad(n.left, key, cmp);
  else n.right = insertDupBad(n.right, key, cmp);
  return n;
}
Correct:
 function has<K>(n: BNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): boolean {
  let cur = n;
  while (cur !== null) {
    const c = cmp(key, cur.key);
    if (c === 0) return true;
    cur = c < 0 ? cur.left : cur.right;
  }
  return false;
}
Deleting a node with two children copies the in-order successor and removes it from the right
subtree
ts-bst-delete-two-children   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: ts-bst-deletion
Prerequisites: ts-bst-duplicates. Follow-up: ts-bst-validate. Complexity: O(h).
 Common misconception. A node with two children can be replaced by its left child.
Replacing the node with one child discards the other subtree. Copy the smallest key of the right subtree (the
successor) into the node, then remove that key from the right subtree. A node with at most one child is replaced by
that child.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function removeBad<K>(n: BNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): BNode<K> | null {
  if (n === null) return null;
  const c = cmp(key, n.key);
  if (c < 0) n.left = removeBad(n.left, key, cmp);
  else if (c > 0) n.right = removeBad(n.right, key, cmp);
  else return n.left ?? n.right;
  return n;
}

Page 5
Correct:
 function remove<K>(n: BNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): BNode<K> | null {
  if (n === null) return null;
  const c = cmp(key, n.key);
  if (c < 0) n.left = remove(n.left, key, cmp);
  else if (c > 0) n.right = remove(n.right, key, cmp);
  else {
    if (n.left === null) return n.right;
    if (n.right === null) return n.left;
    let succ = n.right;
    while (succ.left !== null) succ = succ.left;
    n.key = succ.key;
    n.right = remove(n.right, succ.key, cmp);
  }
  return n;
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Inserting sorted keys one by one builds a chain; build from the sorted middle instead
ts-bst-skewed   lens: complexity   level: L2   family: ts-bst-complexity
Prerequisites: ts-bst-floor. Follow-up: ts-bst-generator. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A BST is balanced no matter what order keys are inserted in.
Inserting keys in ascending order makes every new key a right child, so the tree becomes a linked list with height n -
1 and every operation is O(n). To build a balanced tree from sorted data, take the middle as the root and recurse on
each half. Self-balancing trees fix this on every insert.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function fromSortedBad(keys: number[]): BNode<number> | null {
  let root: BNode<number> | null = null;
  for (const k of keys) root = insert(root, k, numCmp);
  return root;
}
Correct:
 function fromSorted(keys: number[], lo = 0, hi = keys.length - 1): BNode<number> | null {
  if (lo > hi) return null;
  const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
  return new BNode(
    keys[mid] as number, fromSorted(keys, lo, mid - 1), fromSorted(keys, mid + 1, hi),
  );
}

TypeScript Binary Search Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
A recursive generator must use yield* to forward the values of its child generators
ts-bst-generator   lens: iteration   level: L3   family: ts-bst-iteration
Prerequisites: ts-bst-skewed. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Calling the child generator inside the generator yields its values.
Calling a generator function only creates an iterator object and runs nothing. Without yield* the values of the left and
right subtrees are never produced, so the generator yields only the root. Use yield* to delegate to the child
generators.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function* keysBad<K>(n: BNode<K> | null): Generator<K> {
  if (n === null) return;
  keysBad(n.left);
  yield n.key;
  keysBad(n.right);
}
Correct:
 function* keys<K>(n: BNode<K> | null): Generator<K> {
  if (n === null) return;
  yield* keys(n.left);
  yield n.key;
  yield* keys(n.right);
}
Floor keeps the best candidate seen so far; the last node visited may be larger than the query
ts-bst-floor   lens: ordering   level: L3   family: ts-bst-ordering
Prerequisites: ts-bst-validate. Follow-up: ts-bst-skewed. Complexity: O(h).
 Common misconception. The floor of a key is the last node visited on the search path.
The floor is the largest key that is at most the query. Moving right means the current node is a candidate, moving left
means it is too large. The path may end on a node that is too large, so remember the best candidate in a variable and
return it.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function floorBad<K>(n: BNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): K | null {
  let cur = n;
  let last: K | null = null;
  while (cur !== null) {
    last = cur.key;
    cur = cmp(key, cur.key) < 0 ? cur.left : cur.right;
  }
  return last;
}
Correct:
 function floor<K>(n: BNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): K | null {
  let cur = n;
  let best: K | null = null;
  while (cur !== null) {
    const c = cmp(key, cur.key);
    if (c === 0) return cur.key;
    if (c < 0) cur = cur.left;
    else { best = cur.key; cur = cur.right; }
  }
  return best;
}

Validate with lower and upper bounds that every node inherits, not only the parent
comparison
ts-bst-validate   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-bst-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-bst-delete-two-children. Follow-up: ts-bst-floor. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A tree is a BST if every node is greater than its left child and smaller than its right child.
Comparing a node with its direct children misses violations deeper down: a key in the left subtree must be smaller
than every ancestor on the path where the subtree hangs to the left. Pass the allowed open interval down the
recursion and tighten it at each step.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function isBstLocal(n: BNode<number> | null): boolean {
  if (n === null) return true;
  if (n.left !== null && n.left.key >= n.key) return false;
  if (n.right !== null && n.right.key <= n.key) return false;
  return isBstLocal(n.left) && isBstLocal(n.right);
}
Correct:
 function isBst(
  n: BNode<number> | null, lo: number | null = null, hi: number | null = null,
): boolean {
  if (n === null) return true;
  if (lo !== null && n.key <= lo) return false;
  if (hi !== null && n.key >= hi) return false;
  return isBst(n.left, lo, n.key) && isBst(n.right, n.key, hi);
}

2. Overview and mental model: Linked List
A singly linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a reference to the next node (null at the end). Access
by position is O(n), prepending is O(1), and deleting needs the predecessor.
In TypeScript the next reference is typed ListNode | null, so strict null checks force you to handle the end of the list.
Optional chaining and explicit loops over a cursor are the two safe styles.
Most list bugs are pointer bugs: losing the rest of the list, skipping a node after deletion, reversing before saving next,
or comparing pointers before moving them. Each chunk shows one of these and the fix.
Toolbox
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
const list: ListNode<number> = { value: 1, next: { value: 2, next: null } };
for (let n: ListNode<number> | null = list; n; n = n.next) { /* visit n.value */ }
list.next?.value;                     // number | undefined
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
3 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

TypeScript Linked List: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 3
Build a list by walking the array backwards, or prepending in forward order reverses it
ts-linkedlist-build   lens: creation   level: L0   family: ts-linkedlist-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-linkedlist-null-access. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Prepending each element while looping forward keeps the original order.
A singly linked list grows at the head in O(1), so each prepend puts the new value before all earlier ones. Looping
forward therefore produces the reverse order. Walk the input from the end, or keep a tail pointer when appending. A
ListNode<T> holds a value and a next reference that is null at the end.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function fromArrayBad<T>(xs: readonly T[]): ListNode<T> | null {
  let head: ListNode<T> | null = null;
  for (const value of xs) head = { value, next: head };
  return head;
}
Correct:
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function fromArray<T>(xs: readonly T[]): ListNode<T> | null {
  let head: ListNode<T> | null = null;
  for (let i = xs.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) head = { value: xs[i] as T, next: head };
  return head;
}
function toArray<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null): T[] {
  const out: T[] = [];
  for (let n = head; n; n = n.next) out.push(n.value);
  return out;
}
Under strict null checks, next is ListNode | null, so head.next.value is error TS18047
ts-linkedlist-null-access   lens: access   level: L0   family: ts-linkedlist-access
Prerequisites: ts-linkedlist-build. Follow-up: ts-linkedlist-prepend. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. head.next.value is safe because the list has at least two nodes.
The type of next includes null because the last node has none. Reading a property of it is error TS18047 ("possibly
null"). Use optional chaining (head?.next?.value) and handle the undefined result, or check the pointer before
dereferencing. At run time a missing node would throw TypeError.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS18047):
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function secondBad<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null): T {
  return head.next.value;
}
Correct:
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function second<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null): T | undefined {
  return head?.next?.value;
}

TypeScript Linked List: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Prepending must point the new node at the old head; pointing at null drops the rest of the list
ts-linkedlist-prepend   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ts-linkedlist-insert
Prerequisites: ts-linkedlist-null-access. Follow-up: ts-linkedlist-remove. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A new head node can be created with next set to null and the old list reattached later.
If the new node does not reference the old head, every old node becomes unreachable and the list silently has one
element. The correct insertion links first (new.next = head) and then moves the head, in O(1).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function prependBad<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null, value: T): ListNode<T> {
  return { value, next: null };
}
Correct:
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function prepend<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null, value: T): ListNode<T> {
  return { value, next: head };
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Reverse in place by saving next before redirecting the pointer
ts-linkedlist-reverse   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-linkedlist-reversal
Prerequisites: ts-linkedlist-remove. Follow-up: ts-linkedlist-middle. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Setting cur.next = prev and then moving to cur.next walks the original list.
After cur.next = prev, cur.next no longer points forward, so advancing through it walks backwards and the loop ends
after one step. Save next first, redirect, then advance with the saved reference. The three pointers prev, cur and next
make the reversal O(n) time and O(1) space.

TypeScript Linked List: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function reverseBad<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null): ListNode<T> | null {
  let prev: ListNode<T> | null = null;
  let cur = head;
  while (cur) {
    cur.next = prev;
    prev = cur;
    cur = cur.next;
  }
  return prev;
}
Correct:
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function reverse<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null): ListNode<T> | null {
  let prev: ListNode<T> | null = null;
  let cur = head;
  while (cur) {
    const next: ListNode<T> | null = cur.next;
    cur.next = prev;
    prev = cur;
    cur = next;
  }
  return prev;
}
Delete with a dummy head: it handles removing the first node and does not skip the node
after a deletion
ts-linkedlist-remove   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ts-linkedlist-delete
Prerequisites: ts-linkedlist-prepend. Follow-up: ts-linkedlist-reverse. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Looking one node ahead (cur.next) is enough to delete any value.
Looking ahead from the head never examines the head itself, so a matching first node stays. Advancing cur after a
deletion also skips the next node, so consecutive matches survive. A dummy node before the head removes the
special case, and cur advances only when nothing was deleted.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function removeBad<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null, v: T): ListNode<T> | null {
  let cur = head;
  while (cur?.next) {
    if (cur.next.value === v) cur.next = cur.next.next;
    cur = cur.next;
  }
  return head;
}
Correct:
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function remove<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null, v: T): ListNode<T> | null {
  const dummy: ListNode<T> = { value: v, next: head };
  let cur = dummy;
  while (cur.next) {
    if (cur.next.value === v) cur.next = cur.next.next;
    else cur = cur.next;
  }
  return dummy.next;
}

TypeScript Linked List: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Slow and fast pointers find the middle; the loop condition decides which middle an even list
returns
ts-linkedlist-middle   lens: patterns   level: L2   family: ts-linkedlist-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-linkedlist-reverse. Follow-up: ts-linkedlist-cycle. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Stopping when fast.next is null returns the second middle of an even list.
The slow pointer moves one step while fast moves two. For [1, 2, 3, 4] the loop condition fast && fast.next ends with
slow on 3 (second middle). The condition fast.next && fast.next.next ends on 2 (first middle). Decide which middle the
problem wants before writing the condition.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function middleBad<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null): T | undefined {
  let slow = head;
  let fast = head;
  while (fast?.next?.next) {
    slow = slow!.next;
    fast = fast.next.next;
  }
  return slow?.value;
}
Correct:
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function middle<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null): T | undefined {
  let slow = head;
  let fast = head;
  while (fast?.next) {
    slow = slow!.next;
    fast = fast.next.next;
  }
  return slow?.value;
}
Floyd cycle detection must move the pointers before comparing them
ts-linkedlist-cycle   lens: edge-cases   level: L3   family: ts-linkedlist-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-linkedlist-middle. Follow-up: ts-linkedlist-merge. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Comparing slow and fast at the top of the loop detects a cycle.
Both pointers start at the head, so comparing them before moving always succeeds for any list with at least two
nodes. Move first (slow one step, fast two) and then compare. A list with no cycle ends when fast or fast.next
becomes null, in O(n) time and O(1) space.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function hasCycleBad<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null): boolean {
  let slow = head;
  let fast = head;
  while (fast?.next) {
    if (slow === fast) return true;
    slow = slow!.next;
    fast = fast.next.next;
  }
  return false;
}

TypeScript Linked List: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 8
Correct:
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
function hasCycle<T>(head: ListNode<T> | null): boolean {
  let slow = head;
  let fast = head;
  while (fast?.next) {
    slow = slow!.next;
    fast = fast.next.next;
    if (slow === fast) return true;
  }
  return false;
}
Merging two sorted lists needs a dummy head and must attach the remaining nodes at the
end
ts-linkedlist-merge   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-linkedlist-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-linkedlist-cycle. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n + m).
 Common misconception. The merge loop is finished when one list runs out.
When one list is exhausted, the other still holds its largest values. Forgetting to attach the remainder truncates the
result. Use a dummy head to avoid special-casing the first node and finish with tail.next = a ?? b.

Correct:
 type ListNode<T> = { value: T; next: ListNode<T> | null };
type NumList = ListNode<number> | null;
function merge(a: NumList, b: NumList): NumList {
  const dummy: ListNode<number> = { value: 0, next: null };
  let tail = dummy;
  while (a && b) {
    if (a.value <= b.value) { tail.next = a; a = a.next; } else { tail.next = b; b = b.next; }
    tail = tail.next;
  }
  tail.next = a ?? b;
  return dummy.next;
}

2. Overview and mental model: Red-Black Tree
A red-black tree is a binary search tree whose nodes are coloured red or black so that the root is black, no red node
has a red child, and every path from a node to a leaf has the same number of black nodes.
The left-leaning variant also forbids red right links, which reduces the insert repair to three checks: rotate left, rotate
right and flip colours. Each repair is a constant-time local change on the way back from the recursion.
Search, insert and delete are O(log n) with height at most 2 log2(n + 1). No built-in sorted tree exists in JavaScript or
Mnemonist, so it is written here.
Toolbox

for (let k = 1; k <= 10; k++) t = put(t, k, numCmp);
isValidRb(t);         // true
height(t);            // 5, within 2 log2(11)

The recursive insert may leave a red root, for example after a flip at the top or for the first key. A red root is not

A colour flip toggles the parent and both children, which splits a temporary 4-node
ts-redblacktree-flip   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-rb-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-redblacktree-rotation-color. Follow-up: ts-redblacktree-fixup. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A flip toggles the two children only.
A node with two red children represents a temporary 4-node. Flipping turns both children black and the parent red,
which sends the extra red link up one level without changing any black height. Toggling only the children changes the
black height of the paths below and breaks the invariant.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function flipBad<K>(h: RbNode<K>): void {
  const l = h.left as RbNode<K>;
  const r = h.right as RbNode<K>;
  l.color = !l.color;
  r.color = !r.color;
}

TypeScript Red-Black Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 5
Correct:
 function flip<K>(h: RbNode<K>): void {
  const l = h.left as RbNode<K>;
  const r = h.right as RbNode<K>;
  h.color = !h.color;
  l.color = !l.color;
  r.color = !r.color;
}
A rotation hands the old root colour to the new root and colours the demoted node red
ts-redblacktree-rotation-color   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-rb-mutation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-redblacktree-flip. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A rotation only rearranges the links.
The subtree keeps the same colour at its top after a rotation, or black heights above it change. The new root takes
the colour of the old root, and the demoted old root becomes red. Rotating links without copying the colour can leave
a red root of the subtree under a red parent.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function rotateLeftBad<K>(h: RbNode<K>): RbNode<K> {
  const x = h.right as RbNode<K>;
  h.right = x.left;
  x.left = h;
  h.color = RED;
  return x;
}
Correct:
 const RED = true;
const BLACK = false;
class RbNode<K> {
  constructor(
    public key: K,
    public color: boolean = RED,
    public left: RbNode<K> | null = null,
    public right: RbNode<K> | null = null,
  ) {}
}
function isRed<K>(n: RbNode<K> | null): boolean {
  return n !== null && n.color === RED;
}
function rotateLeft<K>(h: RbNode<K>): RbNode<K> {
  const x = h.right as RbNode<K>;
  h.right = x.left;
  x.left = h;
  x.color = h.color;
  h.color = RED;
  return x;
}
function rotateRight<K>(h: RbNode<K>): RbNode<K> {
  const x = h.left as RbNode<K>;
  h.left = x.right;
  x.right = h;
  x.color = h.color;
  h.color = RED;
  return x;
}

TypeScript Red-Black Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
Every insert fixes the path with three checks in order: lean left, balance, split
ts-redblacktree-fixup   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L3   family: ts-rb-insertion
Prerequisites: ts-redblacktree-flip. Follow-up: ts-redblacktree-root-black. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Only the red-red case needs fixing after an insert.
A new red node can create a right-leaning red link, two reds in a row on the left, or two red children. A left-leaning tree
repairs them in order: rotate left when only the right child is red, rotate right when two left links are red, and flip when
both children are red. Omitting the first check leaves red right links.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function fixUpBad<K>(h: RbNode<K>): RbNode<K> {
  if (isRed(h.left) && isRed((h.left as RbNode<K>).left)) h = rotateRight(h);
  if (isRed(h.left) && isRed(h.right)) flip(h);
  return h;
}
function insertBad<K>(h: RbNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): RbNode<K> {
  if (h === null) return new RbNode(key);
  const c = cmp(key, h.key);
  if (c < 0) h.left = insertBad(h.left, key, cmp);
  else if (c > 0) h.right = insertBad(h.right, key, cmp);
  return fixUpBad(h);
}
Correct:
 type Cmp<K> = (a: K, b: K) => number;
const numCmp: Cmp<number> = (a, b) => (a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0);
function fixUp<K>(h: RbNode<K>): RbNode<K> {
  if (isRed(h.right) && !isRed(h.left)) h = rotateLeft(h);
  if (isRed(h.left) && isRed((h.left as RbNode<K>).left)) h = rotateRight(h);
  if (isRed(h.left) && isRed(h.right)) flip(h);
  return h;
}
function insert<K>(h: RbNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): RbNode<K> {
  if (h === null) return new RbNode(key);
  const c = cmp(key, h.key);
  if (c < 0) h.left = insert(h.left, key, cmp);
  else if (c > 0) h.right = insert(h.right, key, cmp);
  return fixUp(h);
}
function inorder<K>(n: RbNode<K> | null): K[] {
  return n === null ? [] : [...inorder(n.left), n.key, ...inorder(n.right)];
}

TypeScript Red-Black Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Colour rules cap the height at 2 log2(n + 1); an unbalanced insert gives a chain
ts-redblacktree-height   lens: complexity   level: L3   family: ts-rb-complexity
Prerequisites: ts-redblacktree-checker. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Colouring nodes red and black is enough to keep the tree shallow.
The colours only help if the fix-up runs. Because every path has the same number of black nodes and no path has
two reds in a row, the longest path is at most twice the shortest, so the height is at most 2 log2(n + 1). Plain insertion
of sorted keys with no fix-up builds a chain of height n.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function insertPlain<K>(h: RbNode<K> | null, key: K, cmp: Cmp<K>): RbNode<K> {
  if (h === null) return new RbNode(key, BLACK);
  const c = cmp(key, h.key);
  if (c < 0) h.left = insertPlain(h.left, key, cmp);
  else if (c > 0) h.right = insertPlain(h.right, key, cmp);
  return h;
}
Correct:
 function height<K>(n: RbNode<K> | null): number {
  return n === null ? 0 : 1 + Math.max(height(n.left), height(n.right));
}
function maxAllowed(n: number): number {
  return 2 * Math.log2(n + 1);
}
A validator must check equal black heights, not only the absence of red-red links
ts-redblacktree-checker   lens: testing   level: L3   family: ts-rb-testing
Prerequisites: ts-redblacktree-root-black. Follow-up: ts-redblacktree-height. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. No red node has a red child, so the tree is valid.
Red-black trees need three things: a black root, no red node with a red child, and the same number of black nodes on
every path from a node to a leaf. Checking only the second rule accepts a chain of black nodes. Return the black
height from each subtree, or -1 when the subtree breaks a rule.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function isValidBad<K>(n: RbNode<K> | null): boolean {
  if (n === null) return true;
  if (isRed(n) && (isRed(n.left) || isRed(n.right))) return false;
  return isValidBad(n.left) && isValidBad(n.right);
}
Correct:
 function blackHeight<K>(n: RbNode<K> | null): number {
  if (n === null) return 1;
  if (isRed(n.right)) return -1;
  if (isRed(n) && isRed(n.left)) return -1;
  const l = blackHeight(n.left);
  const r = blackHeight(n.right);
  if (l < 0 || r < 0 || l !== r) return -1;
  return l + (isRed(n) ? 0 : 1);
}
function isValidRb<K>(root: RbNode<K> | null): boolean {
  return !isRed(root) && blackHeight(root) > 0;
}

This document is both a study guide for a learner and source material for the DSA Mentor RAG collection. It follows
the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

2. Overview and mental model: TypedArray
A typed array is a fixed-length array of one numeric type, stored in an ArrayBuffer. There are eleven concrete
classes: Int8Array, Uint8Array, Uint8ClampedArray, Int16Array, Uint16Array, Int32Array, Uint32Array, Float32Array,
Float64Array, BigInt64Array and BigUint64Array. They share one API, but the element type changes the range and
the rounding.
The element type is the main design decision. Integer types wrap on overflow, Uint8ClampedArray clamps,
Float32Array loses precision, and the two BigInt arrays accept only bigint.
Typed arrays look like arrays but are not Arrays: the length is fixed, there is no push, JSON writes them as objects,
and sort is numeric.
Toolbox
 const u = new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3]);
const f = Float64Array.from([0.1, 0.2]);
const big = new BigInt64Array(2);
big[0] = 5n;                 // bigint only
const w = u.subarray(1);     // shares memory
const c = u.slice(1);        // copy

3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
4 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.
subarray returns a view that shares memory; slice returns an independent copy
ts-typedarray-subarray-slice   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ts-typedarray-views
Prerequisites: ts-typedarray-fixed-length. Follow-up: ts-typedarray-sort. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. u.subarray(0, 2) returns a copy of the first two elements.
subarray creates a new typed array over the same buffer, so writes through either array are visible in both. slice
copies the elements. Return slice from functions that hand data to callers, and use subarray when you intentionally
want a window without copying.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function headBad(u: Uint8Array, n: number): Uint8Array {
  return u.subarray(0, n);
}
Correct:
 function head(u: Uint8Array, n: number): Uint8Array {
  return u.slice(0, n);
}
A typed array has a fixed length and no push, pop or splice; allocate a new array and set
ts-typedarray-fixed-length   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L1   family: ts-typedarray-insertion
Prerequisites: ts-typedarray-overflow. Follow-up: ts-typedarray-subarray-slice. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A typed array grows with push like a normal array.
The length of a typed array is fixed at creation. push is error TS2339 and a TypeError in JavaScript. To append,
allocate a longer array, copy with set(), and write the new element. For many appends collect values in a normal
array first, or use a growable ArrayBuffer.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2339):
 function appendBad(u: Uint8Array, x: number): Uint8Array {
  u.push(x);
  return u;
}
Correct:
 function append(u: Uint8Array, x: number): Uint8Array {
  const r = new Uint8Array(u.length + 1);
  r.set(u);
  r[u.length] = x;
  return r;
}

TypeScript TypedArray: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 4
Integer typed arrays wrap on overflow and truncate decimals; Uint8ClampedArray clamps to
0-255 and rounds
ts-typedarray-overflow   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: ts-typedarray-values
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-typedarray-fixed-length. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Storing 300 in a Uint8Array stores 255, the nearest valid value.
Uint8Array keeps the value modulo 256: 300 becomes 44 and -5 becomes 251. Fractions are truncated.
Uint8ClampedArray clamps to 0..255 and rounds half to even, so it is the right type for colours and pixel data. Int8,
Int16, Int32 and their unsigned versions wrap in the same way.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function clampBad(x: number): number {
  return new Uint8Array([x])[0] ?? 0;
}
Correct:
 function clamp(x: number): number {
  return new Uint8ClampedArray([x])[0] ?? 0;
}
BigInt64Array holds only bigint values; assigning a number is error TS2322
ts-typedarray-bigint   lens: access   level: L2   family: ts-typedarray-typing
Prerequisites: ts-typedarray-float32. Follow-up: ts-typedarray-equality. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A BigInt64Array element can be set with a normal number.
BigInt64Array and BigUint64Array store 64-bit integers as bigint. Assigning 1 is error TS2322 (and TypeError at run
time); write 1n. Values wrap modulo 2^64 for BigUint64Array. They cannot be mixed with number arithmetic.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2322):
 function setBad(a: BigInt64Array): void {
  a[0] = 1;
}
Correct:
 function setOne(a: BigInt64Array): void {
  a[0] = 1n;
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
TypedArray.sort compares numerically by default, while Array.sort compares strings
ts-typedarray-sort   lens: ordering   level: L1   family: ts-typedarray-order
Prerequisites: ts-typedarray-subarray-slice. Follow-up: ts-typedarray-map-wrap. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. Array.sort() and TypedArray.sort() order numbers the same way.
Array.prototype.sort without a comparator converts elements to strings, so [10, 9, 1] becomes [1, 10, 9].
TypedArray.prototype.sort compares numerically, giving [1, 9, 10]. A typed array is also a quick way to sort numbers
without writing a comparator. toSorted returns a sorted copy.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function sortBad(xs: readonly number[]): number[] {
  return [...xs].sort();
}
Correct:
 function sortNums(xs: readonly number[]): number[] {
  return [...Float64Array.from(xs).sort()];
}

TypeScript TypedArray: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Typed arrays are compared by content with a loop; === and == compare identity
ts-typedarray-equality   lens: equality   level: L2   family: ts-typedarray-equality
Prerequisites: ts-typedarray-bigint. Follow-up: ts-typedarray-json. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. a === b is true for typed arrays holding the same values.
A typed array is an object, so === compares identity. Compare lengths, then elements. Array.prototype.every can be
called on typed arrays directly. NaN never equals itself, so use Object.is when floats may be NaN.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function sameBad(a: Uint8Array, b: Uint8Array): boolean {
  return a === b;
}
Correct:
 function same(a: Uint8Array, b: Uint8Array): boolean {
  return a.length === b.length && a.every((v, i) => v === b[i]);
}
JSON.stringify turns a typed array into an object with index keys; convert with Array.from
ts-typedarray-json   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ts-typedarray-transform
Prerequisites: ts-typedarray-equality. Follow-up: ts-typedarray-immutable-ops. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. JSON.stringify(new Uint8Array([1, 2])) gives "[1,2]".
A typed array is not an Array, so JSON writes an object: {"0":1,"1":2}. Receivers expecting an array then fail. Convert
with Array.from(u) before stringifying, and rebuild with new Uint8Array(JSON.parse(s)). Array.isArray(typedArray) is
false.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function toJsonBad(u: Uint8Array): string {
  return JSON.stringify(u);
}
Correct:
 function toJson(u: Uint8Array): string {
  return JSON.stringify(Array.from(u));
}
function fromJson(s: string): Uint8Array {
  return new Uint8Array(JSON.parse(s) as number[]);
}

Page 8
map on a typed array returns the same typed array type, so results wrap; use Array.from to
widen
ts-typedarray-map-wrap   lens: transformation   level: L2   family: ts-typedarray-transform
Prerequisites: ts-typedarray-sort. Follow-up: ts-typedarray-float32. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. u.map(x => x * 2) can exceed 255 safely.
The result of map is a new array of the same type, and each value is converted back into that type. For a Uint8Array
200 * 2 is stored as 144. Convert first with Array.from(u, fn) or Uint16Array.from(u, fn) when the results need more
range.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function doubleBad(u: Uint8Array): Uint8Array {
  return u.map((x) => x * 2);
}
Correct:
 function double(u: Uint8Array): number[] {
  return Array.from(u, (x) => x * 2);
}
Float32Array keeps about 7 digits; integers above 16,777,216 lose exactness, so use
Float64Array for exact values
ts-typedarray-float32   lens: fit-and-alternatives   level: L2   family: ts-typedarray-fit
Prerequisites: ts-typedarray-map-wrap. Follow-up: ts-typedarray-bigint. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Float32Array is just a smaller Float64Array with the same results.
Float32 has a 24-bit significand: 16,777,217 is stored as 16,777,216. Use it for graphics and memory-bound data. For
sums, ids and money-like values use Float64Array or Int32Array, and remember that JavaScript numbers are
Float64.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function storeBad(n: number): number {
  return new Float32Array([n])[0] ?? 0;
}
Correct:
 function store(n: number): number {
  return new Float64Array([n])[0] ?? 0;
}

Page 9
reverse and sort mutate in place; toReversed, toSorted and with return copies
ts-typedarray-immutable-ops   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-typedarray-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-typedarray-json. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. u.reverse() returns a reversed copy and keeps u as it was.
reverse, sort, fill and set change the array and return it. The ES2023 methods toReversed, toSorted and with(index,
value) leave the original alone. Prefer them in functions that must not change their input.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function reversedBad(u: Uint8Array): Uint8Array {
  return u.reverse();
}
Correct:
 function reversed(u: Uint8Array): Uint8Array {
  return u.toReversed();
}

2. Overview and mental model: Queue
A queue is first in, first out. Array.shift gives that behaviour but is O(n), so efficient queues use a head index (with
occasional compaction), a linked list or a circular buffer.
dequeue and peek return T | undefined, because the queue may be empty. The compiler forces the caller to handle it.
Queues drive breadth-first search, scheduling, buffering and rate limiting.
Toolbox
 class Queue<T> {
  private items: T[] = [];
  private head = 0;
  enqueue(x: T): void { this.items.push(x); }
  dequeue(): T | undefined { return this.items[this.head++]; }   // simplified
}
const q = new Queue<number>(); q.enqueue(1); q.dequeue();         // 1
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)

explanation.

Page 3
A queue with a head index is O(1) per dequeue, but size must subtract the head offset
ts-queue-core   lens: creation   level: L0   family: ts-queue-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-queue-compaction. Complexity: O(1) amortised.
 Common misconception. The size of an index-based queue is items.length.
Array.shift is O(n) because every element moves. A head index avoids that: dequeue reads items[head] and
advances. The live length is then items.length - head, not items.length. Counting consumed slots makes isEmpty
false forever. Mnemonist (npm) has a Queue class with the same operations.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class QueueBad<T> {
  private items: T[] = [];
  private head = 0;
  enqueue(x: T): void { this.items.push(x); }
  dequeue(): T | undefined { return this.items[this.head++]; }
  get size(): number { return this.items.length; }
  storage(): number { return this.items.length; }
}
Correct:
 class Queue<T> {
  private items: T[] = [];
  private head = 0;
  enqueue(x: T): void { this.items.push(x); }
  dequeue(): T | undefined {
    if (this.head >= this.items.length) return undefined;
    const x = this.items[this.head++] as T;
    if (this.head * 2 >= this.items.length) {
      this.items = this.items.slice(this.head);
      this.head = 0;
    }
    return x;
  }
  peek(): T | undefined { return this.items[this.head]; }
  get size(): number { return this.items.length - this.head; }
  storage(): number { return this.items.length; }
}
dequeue returns T | undefined; assigning it to T is error TS2322
ts-queue-empty   lens: access   level: L1   family: ts-queue-access
Prerequisites: ts-queue-compaction. Follow-up: ts-queue-bfs. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A queue of numbers always returns a number from dequeue.
The queue can be empty, so the return type includes undefined and the compiler rejects assigning it to number
(TS2322). Check size first, or handle undefined. The same holds for peek.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2322):
 function frontBad(q: Queue<number>): number {
  const x: number = q.dequeue();
  return x;
}
Correct:
 function front(q: Queue<number>): number | null {
  return q.size === 0 ? null : (q.dequeue() as number);
}

Without compaction an index-based queue never frees consumed slots
ts-queue-compaction   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-queue-memory
Prerequisites: ts-queue-core. Follow-up: ts-queue-empty. Complexity: O(1) amortised.
 Common misconception. Advancing the head index frees memory for consumed items.
Consumed slots stay in the array, so a long-running queue grows without bound even when it holds one element.
Compact the array when the head passes half the length (slice from head and reset to 0); the cost is amortised O(1)
per operation.

Level-order traversal needs the queue size at the start of each level
ts-queue-bfs   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-queue-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-queue-empty. Follow-up: ts-queue-ring. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Processing nodes until the queue is empty gives the nodes level by level.
The loop visits nodes in level order, but without a boundary every value lands in one flat list. Capture const n =
queue.length at the start of each level and process exactly n nodes, collecting them in a per-level array.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 type TNode = { val: number; left: TNode | null; right: TNode | null };
function levelsBad(root: TNode | null): number[][] {
  const out: number[][] = [];
  const q: TNode[] = root ? [root] : [];
  while (q.length) {
    const n = q.shift() as TNode;
    out.push([n.val]);
    if (n.left) q.push(n.left);
    if (n.right) q.push(n.right);
  }
  return out;
}
Correct:
 type TNode = { val: number; left: TNode | null; right: TNode | null };
function levels(root: TNode | null): number[][] {
  const out: number[][] = [];
  const q: TNode[] = root ? [root] : [];
  while (q.length) {
    const row: number[] = [];
    for (let n = q.length; n > 0; n--) {
      const node = q.shift() as TNode;
      row.push(node.val);
      if (node.left) q.push(node.left);
      if (node.right) q.push(node.right);
    }
    out.push(row);
  }
  return out;
}
A ring buffer needs a count (or a spare slot) to tell a full buffer from an empty one
ts-queue-ring   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-queue-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-queue-bfs. Follow-up: ts-queue-two-stacks. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. head === tail means the ring buffer is empty.
In a circular array, head and tail are equal both when it is empty and when it is full after tail wraps. Without a separate
count the two cases are indistinguishable. Keep an explicit count; enqueue fails (or overwrites) when count equals
capacity.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class RingBad {
  private data: number[];
  private head = 0;
  private tail = 0;
  constructor(private cap: number) { this.data = new Array<number>(cap); }
  push(x: number): void { this.data[this.tail] = x; this.tail = (this.tail + 1) % this.cap; }
  isEmpty(): boolean { return this.head === this.tail; }
}

TypeScript Queue: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 7
Correct:
 class Ring {
  private data: number[];
  private head = 0;
  private count = 0;
  constructor(private cap: number) { this.data = new Array<number>(cap); }
  push(x: number): boolean {
    if (this.count === this.cap) return false;
    this.data[(this.head + this.count++) % this.cap] = x;
    return true;
  }
  shift(): number | undefined {
    if (this.count === 0) return undefined;
    const x = this.data[this.head];
    this.head = (this.head + 1) % this.cap;
    this.count--;
    return x;
  }
  isEmpty(): boolean { return this.count === 0; }
}
A queue from two stacks moves items only when the output stack is empty
ts-queue-two-stacks   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-queue-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-queue-ring. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1) amortised.
 Common misconception. Moving all items to the output stack on every dequeue keeps FIFO order.
Items are pushed on an input stack and popped from an output stack. Transferring reverses their order once. If you
transfer on every dequeue, items already in the output stack end up beneath newer ones, so the order breaks.
Transfer only when the output stack is empty; each element moves at most once, giving amortised O(1).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class TwoStackBad<T> {
  private inp: T[] = [];
  private out: T[] = [];
  enqueue(x: T): void { this.inp.push(x); }
  dequeue(): T | undefined {
    while (this.inp.length) this.out.push(this.inp.pop() as T);
    return this.out.pop();
  }
}
Correct:
 class TwoStackQueue<T> {
  private inp: T[] = [];
  private out: T[] = [];
  enqueue(x: T): void { this.inp.push(x); }
  dequeue(): T | undefined {
    if (!this.out.length) while (this.inp.length) this.out.push(this.inp.pop() as T);
    return this.out.pop();
  }
}

2. Overview and mental model: SharedArrayBuffer
A SharedArrayBuffer is a block of memory that several threads (workers) can read and write at once. Typed arrays
over it see each other's writes immediately. That makes data races possible, so every shared update must go through
Atomics or a lock.
Atomics offers add, sub, and, or, xor, exchange, compareExchange, load, store, wait and notify. They work on integer
typed arrays only. Atomics.wait blocks the thread, so browsers forbid it on the main thread; Node permits it.
In browsers a page needs cross-origin isolation to use SharedArrayBuffer. Races are nondeterministic, so tests
assert exact results for the safe version and only bounds for the racy one.
Toolbox
 const sab = new SharedArrayBuffer(8);
const i = new Int32Array(sab);
Atomics.add(i, 0, 1);                  // returns the old value
Atomics.compareExchange(i, 1, 0, 1);   // claim slot 1
Atomics.wait(i, 0, 5, 100);            // "not-equal" | "timed-out" | "ok"
// pass sab to a Worker through workerData

Use Atomics.add for a counter shared between threads; i[0]++ is a separate read and write
that can lose updates
ts-sharedarraybuffer-atomics-counter   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-sab-mutation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-sharedarraybuffer-integer-views. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. i[0]++ on a shared Int32Array is safe because it is one statement.
A plain increment reads the value, adds one and writes it back. Two threads can read the same value and both write
it plus one, so an update is lost. Atomics.add performs the whole operation indivisibly and returns the previous value.
The plain version is wrong only sometimes, which is what makes it dangerous.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function incrementBad(i: Int32Array, n: number): void {
  for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) i[0]++;
}
Correct:
 function increment(i: Int32Array, n: number): void {
  for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) Atomics.add(i, 0, 1);
}
Cloning an ArrayBuffer copies it but cloning a SharedArrayBuffer shares the same memory
ts-sharedarraybuffer-clone   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-sab-ownership
Prerequisites: ts-sharedarraybuffer-grow. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. structuredClone copies a SharedArrayBuffer like any other buffer.
structuredClone and postMessage copy an ArrayBuffer, so the two sides stop seeing each other's writes. For a
SharedArrayBuffer they create a new object that points at the same memory, so both sides see every write. That is
the point of the type, and the reason for atomics.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function cloneSharedBad(buf: ArrayBuffer): ArrayBuffer {
  return structuredClone(buf);
}
Correct:
 function cloneShared(sab: SharedArrayBuffer): SharedArrayBuffer {
  return structuredClone(sab);
}

TypeScript SharedArrayBuffer: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 6
A growable SharedArrayBuffer can only grow, never shrink; grow below the current size
throws RangeError
ts-sharedarraybuffer-grow   lens: insertion-and-deletion   level: L2   family: ts-sab-resize
Prerequisites: ts-sharedarraybuffer-wait-result. Follow-up: ts-sharedarraybuffer-clone. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A growable SharedArrayBuffer can be resized to any size up to its maximum.
grow(n) requires the buffer to be created with maxByteLength, and n must be at least the current byteLength and at
most the maximum. Shrinking throws RangeError. Existing views with no fixed length follow the new size.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function shrinkBad(sab: SharedArrayBuffer): void {
  sab.grow(4);
}
Correct:
 function growShared(sab: SharedArrayBuffer, n: number): boolean {
  if (!sab.growable || n < sab.byteLength || n > sab.maxByteLength) return false;
  sab.grow(n);
  return true;
}
Claim a slot with compareExchange; checking a value and then writing it lets two threads
both win
ts-sharedarraybuffer-claim   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-sab-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-sharedarraybuffer-integer-views. Follow-up: ts-sharedarraybuffer-wait-result. Complexity:
O(1).
 Common misconception. if (i[k] === 0) { i[k] = 1 } is a safe way to claim a slot.
Another thread can write between the check and the write, so both threads think they claimed the slot.
Atomics.compareExchange(i, k, 0, 1) compares and writes as one step and returns the old value; the caller owns the
slot only when the old value was 0.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function claimBad(i: Int32Array, k: number): boolean {
  if (i[k] === 0) {
    i[k] = 1;
    return true;
  }
  return false;
}
Correct:
 function claim(i: Int32Array, k: number): boolean {
  return Atomics.compareExchange(i, k, 0, 1) === 0;
}

Atomics.wait returns "ok", "not-equal" or "timed-out"; only "ok" means another thread woke
you
ts-sharedarraybuffer-wait-result   lens: testing   level: L3   family: ts-sab-testing
Prerequisites: ts-sharedarraybuffer-claim. Follow-up: ts-sharedarraybuffer-grow. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. If Atomics.wait returns normally, another thread called notify.
Atomics.wait blocks until notified, until the timeout, or immediately when the value is not the expected one. It returns
"ok", "timed-out" or "not-equal". Treating anything other than "not-equal" as success reports a timeout as a
notification. Browsers forbid wait on the main thread; Node allows it.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function notifiedBad(i: Int32Array, ms: number): boolean {
  return Atomics.wait(i, 0, 0, ms) !== "not-equal";
}
Correct:
 function notified(i: Int32Array, ms: number): boolean {
  return Atomics.wait(i, 0, 0, ms) === "ok";
}

2. Overview and mental model: Fenwick Tree
A Fenwick tree stores partial sums in a single array so that point updates and prefix sums both take O(log n) time.
Node x (1-based) holds the sum of the lowbit(x) elements ending at x, where lowbit(x) = x & -x. A query walks down
by removing the lowest bit; an update walks up by adding it.
Use it for dynamic prefix sums, frequency counting, inversion counts and any invertible operation such as sum or xor.
It cannot answer min or max queries.
Toolbox
 const f = new Fenwick(8);
f.add(2, 5);          // point update at 0-based index 2
f.prefix(4);          // 5, sum of indexes 0..4
rangeSum(f, 2, 3);    // 5

x & -x isolates the lowest set bit, which is the size of the range a node covers
ts-fenwicktree-lowbit   lens: mental-model   level: L1   family: ts-fen-mental-model
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-fenwicktree-update. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. The lowest set bit of x can be found with x % 2 or x & 1.
A Fenwick node at 1-based index x stores the sum of the lowbit(x) elements ending at x. lowbit(x) is the value of the
lowest set bit, computed as x & -x using two's complement. x % 2 and x & 1 only report whether the lowest bit is set,
so they return 0 or 1, never 4 or 8.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function lowbitBad(x: number): number {
  return x & 1;
}
Correct:
 function lowbit(x: number): number {
  return x & -x;
}
The tree is 1-based internally, so a 0-based index must be shifted by one before walking
ts-fenwicktree-index-base   lens: access   level: L2   family: ts-fen-access
Prerequisites: ts-fenwicktree-update. Follow-up: ts-fenwicktree-range. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Start a query at x = i for a 0-based index i.
Index 0 has no lowest set bit, so a 1-based tree cannot store it. Public methods take a 0-based index and shift it with
x = i + 1. Starting a query at i leaves out element i, and an update starting at i = 0 would loop forever because x & -x is
0.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function prefixBad(tree: number[], i: number): number {
  let sum = 0;
  for (let x = i; x > 0; x -= x & -x) sum += tree[x] as number;
  return sum;
}
Correct:
 function prefixSum(tree: number[], i: number): number {
  let sum = 0;
  for (let x = i + 1; x > 0; x -= x & -x) sum += tree[x] as number;
  return sum;
}

Page 4
A range sum subtracts the prefix before l, so it uses l - 1
ts-fenwicktree-range   lens: access   level: L2   family: ts-fen-access
Prerequisites: ts-fenwicktree-index-base. Follow-up: ts-fenwicktree-set. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. sum(l, r) = prefix(r) - prefix(l).
prefix(l) includes element l, so subtracting it removes the first element of the range. The correct difference is prefix(r) -
prefix(l - 1). For l = 0 the argument is -1, which makes the walk start at 0 and return 0, so no special case is needed.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function rangeBad(f: Fenwick, l: number, r: number): number {
  return f.prefix(r) - f.prefix(l);
}
Correct:
 function rangeSum(f: Fenwick, l: number, r: number): number {
  return f.prefix(r) - f.prefix(l - 1);
}
An update walks up by adding the lowbit, touching every node whose range covers the index
ts-fenwicktree-update   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-fen-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-fenwicktree-lowbit. Follow-up: ts-fenwicktree-index-base. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. An update can walk down with x -= x & -x, like a query.
A query walks down, removing the lowest bit each step, to collect disjoint ranges. An update must reach every node
whose range contains the index, which means walking up with x += x & -x. Walking down updates only the nodes
below the index and later prefix sums miss the change.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function addBad(tree: number[], i: number, d: number): void {
  for (let x = i + 1; x > 0; x -= x & -x) tree[x] = (tree[x] as number) + d;
}
Correct:
 class Fenwick {
  tree: number[];
  constructor(readonly n: number) { this.tree = new Array<number>(n + 1).fill(0); }
  add(i: number, delta: number): void {
    for (let x = i + 1; x <= this.n; x += x & -x) this.tree[x]! += delta;
  }
  prefix(i: number): number {
    let sum = 0;
    for (let x = i + 1; x > 0; x -= x & -x) sum += this.tree[x] as number;
    return sum;
  }
}

4.4 Algorithm chunks
Build in linear time by pushing each node into its parent; copying the array is not a tree
ts-fenwicktree-build   lens: creation   level: L3   family: ts-fen-creation
Prerequisites: ts-fenwicktree-set. Follow-up: ts-fenwicktree-range-update. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. A Fenwick tree can be created by copying the input array.
Each tree node holds a partial sum, so the raw array is not a valid tree. Calling add for every element costs O(n log
n). A linear build puts the values at indexes 1..n, then adds each node into its parent at i + lowbit(i) once.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function fromArrayBad(a: number[]): number[] {
  return [...a];
}
Correct:
 function fromArray(a: number[]): number[] {
  const n = a.length;
  const tree = [0, ...a];
  for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    const parent = i + (i & -i);
    if (parent <= n) tree[parent] = (tree[parent] as number) + (tree[i] as number);
  }
  return tree;
}

Setting a value means adding the difference from the stored value, not the new value
ts-fenwicktree-set   lens: mutation   level: L3   family: ts-fen-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-fenwicktree-range. Follow-up: ts-fenwicktree-build. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. set(i, v) can call add(i, v).
A Fenwick tree stores sums, so add always accumulates. To replace a value, keep a plain array of the current values
and add v minus the old value. Calling add with the new value doubles the element on a repeated set.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class SetBad extends Fenwick {
  set(i: number, v: number): void {
    this.add(i, v);
  }
}
Correct:
 class FenwickSet extends Fenwick {
  vals: number[];
  constructor(n: number) {
    super(n);
    this.vals = new Array<number>(n).fill(0);
  }
  set(i: number, v: number): void {
    this.add(i, v - (this.vals[i] as number));
    this.vals[i] = v;
  }
}
Compress values to ranks with a numeric sort before counting inversions
ts-fenwicktree-inversions   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-fen-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-fenwicktree-range-update. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(n log n).
 Common misconception. Sorting the distinct values with sort() gives their ranks.
Counting inversions uses a Fenwick tree indexed by rank. The default sort compares strings, so 10 comes before 9
and the ranks are wrong. Sort with (x, y) => x - y, map each value to its rank, and for each element count the earlier
elements with a larger rank as i minus prefix(rank).
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function inversionsBad(a: number[]): number {
  const sorted = [...new Set(a)].sort();
  const rank = new Map<number, number>(sorted.map((v, i) => [v, i]));
  const f = new Fenwick(sorted.length);
  let inv = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    const r = rank.get(a[i] as number) as number;
    inv += i - f.prefix(r);
    f.add(r, 1);
  }
  return inv;
}

TypeScript Fenwick Tree: Training Data for the DSA Mentor RAG Chatbot
Page 8
Correct:
 function inversions(a: number[]): number {
  const sorted = [...new Set(a)].sort((x, y) => x - y);
  const rank = new Map<number, number>(sorted.map((v, i) => [v, i]));
  const f = new Fenwick(sorted.length);
  let inv = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    const r = rank.get(a[i] as number) as number;
    inv += i - f.prefix(r);
    f.add(r, 1);
  }
  return inv;
}
Range add with point query stores differences, so the range end must cancel the start
ts-fenwicktree-range-update   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-fen-patterns
Prerequisites: ts-fenwicktree-build. Follow-up: ts-fenwicktree-inversions. Complexity: O(log n).
 Common misconception. Adding d at l alone adds d to the range [l, r].
Store a difference array in the tree. A point query is the prefix sum of differences. Adding d at l raises every later
position, so a matching -d at r + 1 is needed to end the range. Without it the change leaks to the end of the array.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 class RangeAddBad {
  f: Fenwick;
  constructor(n: number) { this.f = new Fenwick(n); }
  rangeAdd(l: number, r: number, d: number): void {
    this.f.add(l, d);
  }
  get(i: number): number { return this.f.prefix(i); }
}
Correct:
 class RangeAdd {
  f: Fenwick;
  constructor(n: number) { this.f = new Fenwick(n); }
  rangeAdd(l: number, r: number, d: number): void {
    this.f.add(l, d);
    this.f.add(r + 1, -d);
  }
  get(i: number): number { return this.f.prefix(i); }
}

Prompt. When would you choose a Fenwick tree over a segment tree for range queries?
Answer key (mentor only, never embedded). Choose a Fenwick tree when the operation is invertible, such as sum or
xor, and the work is point updates with prefix or range queries. It uses n+1 numbers, a few lines of code and small
constants. Choose a segment tree when the operation has no inverse (min, max, gcd), or when lazy range updates and
range queries are both needed.

the same record schema as the other JavaScript and Java curriculum documents (a TypeScript version of each
topic), so its chunks can be ingested next to them with the same scripts.

2. Overview and mental model: Object
In TypeScript an object type describes a shape, and any object with at least those properties fits. Objects are used as
records (fixed, known keys) and as dictionaries (dynamic string keys). The two uses need different types: an interface
or type alias for records, Record or a Map for dictionaries.
The type system is structural and erased at compile time. It checks the shape of values you write, but it does not stop
extra properties travelling through variables, does not enforce readonly at runtime, and types dictionary lookups as
always present. Each chunk marks where the compiler helps and where only a runtime check does.
Runtime facts that surprise: objects inherit keys from Object.prototype, integer-like keys sort first, spread copies one
level, and Object.keys returns plain strings.
Toolbox
 type User = { id: number; name: string; email?: string };
const u: User = { id: 1, name: "Ada" };
const dict: Record<string, number> = { a: 1 };   // dynamic keys
const v = dict["missing"];                       // typed number, actually undefined
const copy = { ...u, name: "Grace" };             // shallow copy with an override

A Record<string, number> types every key as number, but a missing key gives undefined at
runtime
ts-object-index-signature   lens: access   level: L0   family: ts-object-access
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-object-prototype-keys. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. counts[key] is always a number when counts is Record<string, number>.
An index signature promises a value for every possible string key, which is never true. Reading a missing key returns
undefined, and arithmetic on it gives NaN. The compiler only complains if noUncheckedIndexedAccess is enabled.
Use ?? to give a default, or type the lookup result as number | undefined.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function countOfBad(counts: Record<string, number>, key: string): number {
  return counts[key]!;
}
Correct:
 function countOf(counts: Record<string, number>, key: string): number {
  return counts[key] ?? 0;
}
A type does not forbid extra properties: only fresh object literals are checked, so extra fields
can leak through variables
ts-object-excess-property   lens: equality   level: L1   family: ts-object-structural
Prerequisites: ts-object-keys-typing. Follow-up: ts-object-spread-merge. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A parameter typed { x: number } guarantees that the object has only x.
TypeScript is structural: any object with at least the declared properties fits. Excess property errors (TS2353) apply
only to object literals written directly at the call. The same object passed through a variable carries extra fields along,
and JSON.stringify or spread then exposes them. Copy the fields you want explicitly before sending data out.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function toJsonBad(p: { x: number }): string {
  return JSON.stringify(p);
}
Correct:
 function toJson(p: { x: number }): string {
  return JSON.stringify({ x: p.x });
}

Page 4
A plain object inherits keys such as toString and constructor; use Object.hasOwn, a
null-prototype object, or a Map
ts-object-prototype-keys   lens: edge-cases   level: L1   family: ts-object-prototype
Prerequisites: ts-object-index-signature. Follow-up: ts-object-keys-typing. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. An empty object literal has no keys, so counts[word] is undefined for a new word.
Object literals inherit from Object.prototype, so counts["constructor"] and counts["toString"] are functions, not
undefined. A word counter then computes "function Object() ..." plus 1. Check own properties with
Object.hasOwn(obj, key), create the object with Object.create(null), or use a Map, which has no inherited keys.

  const counts = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const w of words) counts.set(w, (counts.get(w) ?? 0) + 1);
  return counts;

Object.assign mutates its first argument; spread builds a new object, and the last spread
wins
ts-object-spread-merge   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ts-object-merge
Prerequisites: ts-object-excess-property. Follow-up: ts-object-optional-vs-undefined. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Object.assign(defaults, overrides) returns a merged copy and leaves defaults alone.
Object.assign copies properties onto its first argument and returns that same object, so a shared defaults object is
changed for every later caller. { ...defaults, ...overrides } creates a new object; for duplicate keys the later source
wins. Both copy only one level: nested objects stay shared.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function mergeBad<T extends object>(defaults: T, overrides: Partial<T>): T {
  return Object.assign(defaults, overrides);
}
Correct:
 function merge<T extends object>(defaults: T, overrides: Partial<T>): T {
  return { ...defaults, ...overrides };
}
Object.keys returns string[], not (keyof T)[]; indexing with those keys fails to compile unless
you narrow deliberately
ts-object-keys-typing   lens: iteration   level: L1   family: ts-object-keys
Prerequisites: ts-object-prototype-keys. Follow-up: ts-object-excess-property. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. for (const k of Object.keys(o)) o[k] type-checks, because k is a key of o.
An object of type T can have more properties than T declares, so TypeScript types Object.keys(o) as string[] and
rejects o[k] with error TS7053. When you know the object is exact, cast once in a helper: (Object.keys(o) as (keyof
T)[]). Object.entries(o) avoids indexing altogether.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS7053):
 function sumBad(o: { a: number; b: number }): number {
  let total = 0;
  for (const k of Object.keys(o)) total += o[k];
  return total;
}
Correct:
 function typedKeys<T extends object>(o: T): (keyof T)[] {
  return Object.keys(o) as (keyof T)[];
}
function sum(o: { a: number; b: number }): number {
  let total = 0;
  for (const k of typedKeys(o)) total += o[k];
  return total;
}

readonly is erased at runtime; Object.freeze is the runtime guard and is shallow
ts-object-readonly-freeze   lens: mutation   level: L2   family: ts-object-readonly
Prerequisites: ts-object-optional-vs-undefined. Follow-up: ts-object-key-order. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. A property marked readonly cannot be changed at runtime.
readonly and Readonly<T> exist only in the type checker. A cast, an alias with a looser type, or plain JavaScript can
still change the value. Object.freeze makes the object immutable at runtime (strict-mode writes throw TypeError), but
only for its own properties: nested objects stay writable. Freeze nested levels too, or use a copy-on-write style.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function bumpBad(o: Readonly<{ n: number }>): void {
  (o as { n: number }).n += 1;
}
Correct:
 function lock<T extends object>(o: T): Readonly<T> {
  return Object.freeze(o);
}
"a" in o tells whether the key exists; o.a !== undefined tells whether it holds a value; they
differ for { a: undefined }
ts-object-optional-vs-undefined   lens: equality   level: L2   family: ts-object-presence
Prerequisites: ts-object-spread-merge. Follow-up: ts-object-readonly-freeze. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Checking "key" in obj is the same as checking obj.key !== undefined.
A property can exist and hold undefined, for example after spreading an object with an optional field that was
explicitly set. in reports true, while the value check reports false. Choose by intent: use in (or Object.hasOwn) for
presence, and a value check for usable data. With optional properties, TypeScript allows both a missing key and an
explicit undefined unless exactOptionalPropertyTypes is on.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function hasValueBad(o: { a?: number }): boolean {
  return "a" in o;
}
Correct:
 function hasValue(o: { a?: number }): boolean {
  return o.a !== undefined;
}
function hasKey(o: object, k: string): boolean {
  return Object.hasOwn(o, k);
}

Integer-like keys come first in ascending order, then string keys in insertion order
ts-object-key-order   lens: ordering   level: L2   family: ts-object-order
Prerequisites: ts-object-readonly-freeze. Follow-up: ts-object-in-narrowing. Complexity: O(n).
 Common misconception. Object.keys returns keys in the order they were added.
For ordinary objects the engine orders integer-like keys (such as "1" or "42") numerically before all other keys,
whatever the insertion order; other string keys follow in insertion order, then symbols. Code that relies on insertion
order for numeric ids breaks. A Map always iterates in insertion order.
Incorrect (runs, but fails as described):
 function firstKeyBad(ids: number[]): string | undefined {
  const o: Record<number, boolean> = {};
  for (const id of ids) o[id] = true;
  return Object.keys(o)[0];
}
Correct:
 function firstKey(ids: readonly number[]): number | undefined {
  const m = new Map<number, boolean>();
  for (const id of ids) m.set(id, true);
  return m.keys().next().value;
}
Use the in operator or a discriminant property to narrow a union of object types
ts-object-in-narrowing   lens: patterns   level: L3   family: ts-object-narrowing
Prerequisites: ts-object-key-order. Follow-up: none. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Reading a property that exists on only one member of a union is fine if you know which one it
is.
Accessing s.radius on Circle | Square is error TS2339, because Square has no radius. The in operator narrows in the
true branch ("radius" in s). A discriminant property such as kind: "circle" is better, since it also works for members that
share property names.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2339):
 type Circle = { radius: number };
type Square = { side: number };
function areaBad(s: Circle | Square): number {
  return Math.PI * s.radius ** 2;
}
Correct:
 type Circle = { radius: number };
type Square = { side: number };
function area(s: Circle | Square): number {
  return "radius" in s ? Math.PI * s.radius ** 2 : s.side ** 2;
}

2. Overview and mental model: Interface
An interface names the shape of an object. It is purely a compile-time construct: it produces no JavaScript, so it
cannot be tested with instanceof or inspected at run time.
Interfaces can extend each other, merge when declared twice, describe callable objects, and be generic. A class can
implement an interface to promise its shape.
Checking is structural: any value with the right members fits. Excess-property checks apply to fresh object literals
only, and readonly is not enforced at run time.
Toolbox
 interface User { readonly id: number; name: string; email?: string }
interface Admin extends User { level: number }
interface Stack<T> { push(x: T): void; pop(): T | undefined }
interface Counter { (): number; reset(): void }
class ArrayStack<T> implements Stack<T> { /* ... */ }
3. Core concepts (tested chunks)
4 concept chunks, ordered by level. Read the misconception first and try to predict why it fails before reading the
explanation.

Page 3
A readonly property cannot be assigned (TS2540), but the check is compile-time only
ts-interface-readonly   lens: mutation   level: L1   family: ts-interface-mutation
Prerequisites: ts-interface-extends-conflict. Follow-up: ts-interface-index-signature. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. readonly in an interface prevents changes at run time.
Assigning to a readonly property is error TS2540. The modifier is erased, so a cast or plain JavaScript can still write
to it, and a mutable alias of the same object can change it. Use Object.freeze when the guarantee must hold at run
time.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2540):
 function renameBad(u: { readonly name: string }): void {
  u.name = "x";
}
Correct:
 interface User { readonly name: string }
function renamed(u: User, name: string): User {
  return { ...u, name };
}
Interfaces with the same name merge; a type alias declared twice is error TS2300
ts-interface-merging   lens: creation   level: L2   family: ts-interface-creation
Prerequisites: none. Follow-up: ts-interface-extends-conflict. Complexity: O(1).
 Common misconception. Declaring the same name twice always replaces the earlier declaration.
Two interface declarations of the same name in one scope are merged into one type with all members, which is how
libraries are augmented. Two type aliases with the same name are error TS2300 (duplicate identifier). Accidental
merging can also hide a typo, so keep declarations together.
Incorrect (rejected by the compiler, TS2300):
 type PointB = { x: number };
type PointB = { y: number };
Correct:
 interface Point { x: number }
interface Point { y: number }
function norm(p: Point): number {
  return Math.hypot(p.x, p.y);
}
